questions.solution: The indicated pattern is n consecutive values beginning at (n²−1)/n and increasing by 1. Their sum is n·(n²−1)/n+n(n−1)/2=(3n²−n−2)/2=(n−1)(3n+2)/2.
questions.hint: Find the first element and common difference of Sₙ.

questions.stem: Find log₂e−log₄e+log₈e−log₁₆e+⋯.
questions.solution: Since log₂ⁿe=1/(nln2), the sum is (1/ln2)Σₙ≥₁(−1)ⁿ⁺¹/n=(ln2)/(ln2)=1.
questions.hint: Factor out 1/ln2 and use the alternating harmonic series.

questions.stem: −1/α and −1/β are the roots of 3x²−18x+2=0. The equation whose roots are α,β is
questions.solution: Substitute x=−1/t into the original equation and multiply by t²: 3+18t+2t²=0. Thus α and β satisfy 2t²+18t+3=0.
questions.hint: Transform the quadratic under x=−1/t.

questions.stem: For which (a,b) is ax+3y+z=5, 2x−y+2az=3, x+4y+az=b inconsistent?
questions.solution: The coefficient determinant is 9(1−a²), so only a=±1 can be inconsistent. For a=1, row 3=(9row1−row2)/7, demanding b=6. For a=−1, row3=(9row1+7row2)/5, demanding b=66/5. Failure of these respective requirements gives D.
questions.hint: Check consistency only where the determinant vanishes.
questions.notes: The source joins the two parameter cases with “and”; this lists two alternative cases rather than requiring a to equal both 1 and −1.

questions.stem: For a given positive integer a, the maximum of aⁿ/n! over n=0,1,2,… is
questions.solution: For tₙ=aⁿ/n!, tₙ₊₁/tₙ=a/(n+1). Terms increase while n+1<a, are equal when n+1=a, and then decrease. The maximum occurs at n=a−1 and n=a, with the common value in C.
questions.hint: Compare consecutive terms.

questions.stem: Let y=log_{g(x)}f(x), where f(x)=eˣ, g(x)=x², x>1. Find dy/dx.
questions.solution: Change of base gives y=x/(2lnx). The quotient rule yields y′=[2lnx−2]/[4(lnx)²]=(lnx−1)/(2(lnx)²).
questions.hint: Change the logarithm base before differentiating.

questions.stem: The scanned piecewise formula gives f(x)=3x³+12x−1 on the first interval ending at 2, and f(x)=37−x on the second interval beginning at 2. Which assertion is true?
options: f is continuous and differentiable on [−1,3]
f is continuous on [−1,3] but f′(2) does not exist
questions.answer: With the printed cubic, the two branches have unequal limits at 2; the interval endpoints need source review
questions.solution: The magnified source shows an exponent resembling 3 and endpoint signs resembling ≤ on both intervals. The cubic’s left limit at 2 is 47, while the second branch’s right limit is 35; thus any unambiguous branch assignment would be discontinuous (A). If both include 2, the formula assigns two different values and does not define a function. Preserve the ambiguity for editorial checking.
questions.hint: Check the exponent and the branch assignments at 2 before testing continuity.
questions.notes: Needs source review for the superscript and overlapping endpoint inequalities. A guessed square would falsely force continuity.

options: Is singular of rank less than 3
questions.answer: Nonsingular with determinant +12, hence none of these
questions.solution: Expand along the third column, whose only nonzero entry is the first-row 1. The remaining determinant is det([[2,1,−1],[4,1,1],[8,1,−1]])=−4+12+4=12. Thus C has the wrong sign.
questions.hint: Expand down the sparse third column.

questions.stem: The roots of x³−9x²+23x−15=0 are in A.P. Their common difference is
questions.answer: 2 when the roots are ordered increasingly
questions.solution: The cubic factors as (x−1)(x−3)(x−5). Thus the increasing roots are 1,3,5 with common difference 2.
questions.hint: The middle root of three arithmetic-progression roots equals their average.

questions.stem: If a₁,a₂,… are in G.P., find Δ=det([[log aₙ,log aₙ₊₁,log aₙ₊₂],[log aₙ₊₃,log aₙ₊₄,log aₙ₊₅],[log aₙ₊₆,log aₙ₊₇,log aₙ₊₈]]).
questions.answer: Δ=0, but A, B and C all have this value
questions.solution: For positive G.P. terms, log aₖ=A+(k−1)d. The three rows differ by constant multiples of (1,1,1), so their determinant is zero. Also aₙaₙ₊₈=aₙ₊₄² and a₁a₃=a₂², making both alternatives A and B zero as well.
questions.hint: Logarithms convert a geometric progression to an arithmetic progression.
questions.notes: The alternatives A,B,C overlap exactly; all are zero. Positive terms are implicit in the real logarithms.

questions.stem: Let f(x)=x for 0<x<1; f(x)=2−x for 1≤x≤2; and f(x)=x−x²/2 for x>2. Then f is
options: Continuous at 2 but not differentiable at 1
Not continuous at 2 and not differentiable at 1
questions.answer: Continuous at 2 but not differentiable at 1
questions.solution: At 2 the defined value and both limiting values are zero. At 1 the branches meet at 1, but their slopes are +1 and −1, so the derivative does not exist.
questions.hint: Compare the one-sided slopes at 1 and values at 2.

questions.stem: Find limₓ→₀[1/x−log(1+x)/x²].
questions.solution: The expression is [x−ln(1+x)]/x². Using ln(1+x)=x−x²/2+O(x³) gives limit 1/2.
questions.hint: Use the second-order logarithm expansion.

questions.stem: For |a|<1, |b|<1, the series a(a+b)+a²(a²+b²)+a³(a³+b³)+⋯
questions.solution: The nth summand is a²ⁿ+(ab)ⁿ. Both are convergent geometric series because |a²|<1 and |ab|<1. Sum them separately.
questions.hint: Separate the two geometric series.

questions.stem: If a+1/a=2cosα, then aⁿ+1/aⁿ equals
questions.solution: The equation a²−2cosα·a+1=0 has roots e^(±iα). Taking integer nth powers and adding reciprocals gives e^(inα)+e^(−inα)=2cos(nα).
questions.hint: Use the quadratic equation for a or the cosine recurrence.

questions.stem: For positive a,b,c, the least value of (a+b+c)(1/a+1/b+1/c) is
questions.solution: Cauchy–Schwarz gives (a+b+c)(1/a+1/b+1/c)≥(1+1+1)²=9. Equality occurs at a=b=c.
questions.hint: Apply Cauchy–Schwarz.

questions.stem: Define f(x)=|x|−[x]−1 for −1<x<0; |x|−[x] for 0≤x<1; and 1 otherwise. Here [x] is the greatest integer ≤x. Then
options: f is discontinuous at only one real point
f is discontinuous at more than one real point
f is continuous but nondifferentiable at only one real point
questions.answer: None of these: continuous, with three nondifferentiable points
questions.solution: For −1<x<0, floor(x)=−1 and f=−x; for 0≤x<1, f=x. Outside that interval f=1. Thus f=min{|x|,1}, continuous everywhere, with slope changes at −1,0,1. It is not differentiable at three points, rather than just one.
questions.hint: Reduce the floor expressions on each interval.
questions.notes: The integer-part symbol is interpreted as conventional greatest integer ≤x, as printed in this source.

questions.stem: If a primal linear program has feasible solutions but no optimal solution, then its dual
options: Has feasible solutions but no optimal solution
questions.solution: A feasible finite-dimensional linear program without an optimum is unbounded in the optimizing direction. A feasible dual would supply a finite bound by weak duality, which is impossible.
questions.hint: Use weak duality to rule out dual feasibility.

questions.stem: Maximize 3x₁+2x₂ subject to x₁+2x₂≤16, x₁+x₂≤12, x₁,x₂≥0. The optimal value is
questions.solution: For nonnegative x₂, 3x₁+2x₂≤3(x₁+x₂)≤36. The feasible point (12,0) attains 36, so this bound is optimal.
questions.hint: Bound the objective by three times the second constraint.

questions.stem: Evaluate ∫₋₁¹(x+x²+x³)e^(−x²/2)dx.
questions.answer: None of the printed values matches the integral
questions.solution: The odd x and x³ terms integrate to zero, leaving ∫₋₁¹x²e^(−x²/2)dx>0. Integration by parts gives −2/√e+∫₋₁¹e^(−x²/2)dx≈0.498187. This is neither 2/√e≈1.213061 nor 2√e≈3.297443, and cannot be negative.
questions.hint: Use parity before evaluating the remaining even integral.
questions.notes: The printed integrand reads x+x²+x³, so the provided alternatives appear inconsistent; no official key supplied.

questions.stem: The series Σₙ₌₁^∞(−1)ⁿ⁺¹/n
questions.solution: Alternating decreasing terms 1/n tend to zero, so the alternating-series test gives convergence. Absolute values give the divergent harmonic series. Integrating the geometric expansion of 1/(1+x) on [0,1] gives the sum ln2.
questions.hint: Apply the alternating-series test and identify the logarithm series.

questions.stem: Solve (1+x)y dx+(1−y)x dy=0.
questions.solution: Divide by xy to get (1+1/x)dx+(1/y−1)dy=0. Integration gives x+ln|x|+ln|y|−y=C. The axis solution y=0 must be considered separately because division excluded it.
questions.hint: Divide by xy and separate the variables.
questions.notes: The logarithmic family describes solution curves away from the coordinate axes; y=0 is an additional solution.

questions.stem: Prove or disprove: (a) If a good’s price-offer curve is parallel to its quantity axis over a range, its demand curve is straight over that range. (b) Marginal product must fall with employment whenever marginal product exceeds average product.
questions.solution:
Test the price-offer assertion using the budget identity. Suppose the price-offer curve is horizontal in (x,y) space while p_x varies, so the chosen other-good quantity remains y_0. With unchanged income and p_y, the budget gives 
p_xx=M-p_yy_0 ⇒ x=(M-p_yy_0)/(p_x).
 This is a rectangular-hyperbola demand over the range, not a straight line except for a degenerate zero-spending case. The first assertion is false.

Differentiate average product correctly. If output is F(L), then AP=F(L)/L and MP=F'(L). Differentiating average product gives 
(dAP)/(dL)=(MP-AP)/(L).
 Thus MP>AP establishes that average product is increasing; it says nothing by itself about whether marginal product is increasing or decreasing.

Provide a decisive counterexample. For F(L)=L^2 at positive labour, MP=2L>AP=L, yet dMP/dL=2>0. Marginal product rises rather than falls. This disproves the second assertion without relying on a particular sketch of an S-shaped production function.
questions.hint: Derive demand from the budget and distinguish the slopes of marginal and average product.

solutionSteps.title: Test the price-offer assertion using the budget identity
solutionSteps.body: Suppose the price-offer curve is horizontal in $(x,y)$ space while $p_x$ varies, so the chosen other-good quantity remains $y_0$. With unchanged income and $p_y$, the budget gives $$p_xx=M-p_yy_0\quad\Rightarrow\quad x=\frac{M-p_yy_0}{p_x}.$$ This is a rectangular-hyperbola demand over the range, not a straight line except for a degenerate zero-spending case. The first assertion is false.

solutionSteps.title: Differentiate average product correctly
solutionSteps.body: If output is $F(L)$, then $AP=F(L)/L$ and $MP=F'(L)$. Differentiating average product gives $$\frac{dAP}{dL}=\frac{MP-AP}{L}.$$ Thus $MP>AP$ establishes that average product is increasing; it says nothing by itself about whether marginal product is increasing or decreasing.

solutionSteps.title: Provide a decisive counterexample
solutionSteps.body: For $F(L)=L^2$ at positive labour, $MP=2L>AP=L$, yet $dMP/dL=2>0$. Marginal product rises rather than falls. This disproves the second assertion without relying on a particular sketch of an S-shaped production function.

questions.stem: Utility over applesa and bananasb isW=a²+b². Prices are2 and1, income20. (i) Find the full-budget bundleX whereMRS equals the price ratio. Compare it with the all-apple bundleY and all-banana bundleZ. (ii) Find the optimum.
questions.answer: X=(8,4),W80;Y=(10,0),W100;Z=(0,20),W400. The optimum isZ, not the tangency.
questions.solution:
Find the full-budget tangency. The utility derivatives are W_a=2a and W_b=2b, so the marginal rate of substitution is a/b. Matching the price ratio 2 gives a=2b. With 2a+b=20, the tangency is X=(8,4) and utility W(X)=80. These conditions identify a stationary bundle, not automatically a maximum.

Compare the endpoint bundles. All-apple spending gives Y=(10,0) with utility 100. All-banana spending gives Z=(0,20) with utility 400. Both outperform the tangency. The boundary is part of the comparison because the question explicitly asks for these all-one-good bundles despite earlier positive-quantity notation.

Establish the global optimum. Substitute b=20-2a into utility: 
W(a)=a^2+(20-2a)^2=5a^2-80a+400, 0≤ a≤10.
 This is convex, so its stationary point at a=8 is a minimum and its maximum occurs at an endpoint. Comparing 100 with 400 selects (a,b)=(0,20). The exercise shows why a tangency is insufficient for nonconvex preferences.
questions.hint: A tangency need not maximize utility when preferences are not convex.
questions.notes: Boundary bundles explicitly requested by the source are included, notwithstanding the earlier positive-quantity notation.

solutionSteps.title: Find the full-budget tangency
solutionSteps.body: The utility derivatives are $W_a=2a$ and $W_b=2b$, so the marginal rate of substitution is $a/b$. Matching the price ratio 2 gives $a=2b$. With $2a+b=20$, the tangency is $X=(8,4)$ and utility $W(X)=80$. These conditions identify a stationary bundle, not automatically a maximum.

solutionSteps.title: Compare the endpoint bundles
solutionSteps.body: All-apple spending gives $Y=(10,0)$ with utility 100. All-banana spending gives $Z=(0,20)$ with utility 400. Both outperform the tangency. The boundary is part of the comparison because the question explicitly asks for these all-one-good bundles despite earlier positive-quantity notation.

solutionSteps.title: Establish the global optimum
solutionSteps.body: Substitute $b=20-2a$ into utility: $$W(a)=a^2+(20-2a)^2=5a^2-80a+400,\qquad0\le a\le10.$$ This is convex, so its stationary point at $a=8$ is a minimum and its maximum occurs at an endpoint. Comparing 100 with 400 selects $(a,b)=(0,20)$. The exercise shows why a tangency is insufficient for nonconvex preferences.

questions.stem: Two people share total stocks1kg rice and1kg dal, with identical utilityU=min(x,y). (a) Describe the indifference map. (b) Are these allocations efficient: (i) A(.3,.4), B remainder; (ii) A(.6,.6), B remainder? (c) Give a Pareto improvement for any inefficient allocation.
questions.answer: L-shaped indifference curves. (i) Inefficient: change toA(.35,.35),B(.65,.65), strictly improving both. (ii) Efficient.
questions.solution:
Draw and interpret the indifference curves. For U=min{x,y}, utility u has kink (u,u) and horizontal and vertical rays from it. Only matched quantities of rice and dal raise utility; extra units of one alone are redundant. The allocation subparts call the second good wheat, but the setup identifies it as dal; it is the same second good for this calculation.

Improve the first allocation. Initially A=(0.3,0.4) and B=(0.7,0.6), giving utilities 0.3 and 0.6. A has surplus dal and B surplus rice. Exchange 0.05 of A's dal for 0.05 of B's rice. The new bundles are A=(0.35,0.35) and B=(0.65,0.65), raising both utilities by 0.05. Hence the first allocation is inefficient.

Prove efficiency of the second allocation. At A=(0.6,0.6) and B=(0.4,0.4), utilities sum to 1. For every feasible allocation, 
min{x_A,y_A}+min{x_B,y_B}≤1,
 because total quantities of each good are only one. A Pareto improvement would have to raise this utility sum above one, which is impossible. Thus the second allocation is efficient, regardless of whether its distribution is judged fair.
questions.hint: Look for unmatched excess goods and bound the sum of Leontief utilities.
questions.notes: The allocation subparts say“wheat” although the setup says“dal”; the second good is consistently treated as the setup’s dal, with that source typo disclosed.

solutionSteps.title: Draw and interpret the indifference curves
solutionSteps.body: For $U=\min\{x,y\}$, utility $u$ has kink $(u,u)$ and horizontal and vertical rays from it. Only matched quantities of rice and dal raise utility; extra units of one alone are redundant. The allocation subparts call the second good wheat, but the setup identifies it as dal; it is the same second good for this calculation.

solutionSteps.title: Improve the first allocation
solutionSteps.body: Initially $A=(0.3,0.4)$ and $B=(0.7,0.6)$, giving utilities 0.3 and 0.6. A has surplus dal and B surplus rice. Exchange 0.05 of A's dal for 0.05 of B's rice. The new bundles are $A=(0.35,0.35)$ and $B=(0.65,0.65)$, raising both utilities by 0.05. Hence the first allocation is inefficient.

solutionSteps.title: Prove efficiency of the second allocation
solutionSteps.body: At $A=(0.6,0.6)$ and $B=(0.4,0.4)$, utilities sum to 1. For every feasible allocation, $$\min\{x_A,y_A\}+\min\{x_B,y_B\}\le1,$$ because total quantities of each good are only one. A Pareto improvement would have to raise this utility sum above one, which is impossible. Thus the second allocation is efficient, regardless of whether its distribution is judged fair.

questions.stem: A consumer hasu=xy, budget2x+3y=36 and quantity restrictionx≤10, with nonnegative consumption. Find the utility-maximizing bundle.
questions.answer: x9,y6. The cap does not bind.
questions.solution:
Find the unconstrained desired consumption. For product utility xy at positive prices, equal expenditure shares give 2x=18 and 3y=18. The candidate is therefore (x,y)=(9,6), which satisfies the added cap x≤10. The ration constraint is present but not binding.

Verify the maximum directly over the capped range. On the budget, y=(36-2x)/3, so 
u(x)=12x-(2)/(3)x^2, 0≤ x≤10.
 The derivative vanishes at x=9 and the second derivative is -4/3<0. Hence this is the unique maximum, with utility 54. Imposing x=10 merely because a cap is mentioned would unnecessarily reduce utility.
questions.hint: Find the unconstrained demand before checking the ration cap.
questions.notes: Visual source confirms budget2x+3y36; broken extraction can lose the leading2.

solutionSteps.title: Find the unconstrained desired consumption
solutionSteps.body: For product utility $xy$ at positive prices, equal expenditure shares give $2x=18$ and $3y=18$. The candidate is therefore $(x,y)=(9,6)$, which satisfies the added cap $x\le10$. The ration constraint is present but not binding.

solutionSteps.title: Verify the maximum directly over the capped range
solutionSteps.body: On the budget, $y=(36-2x)/3$, so $$u(x)=12x-\frac23x^2,\qquad0\le x\le10.$$ The derivative vanishes at $x=9$ and the second derivative is $-4/3<0$. Hence this is the unique maximum, with utility 54. Imposing $x=10$ merely because a cap is mentioned would unnecessarily reduce utility.

questions.stem: Industry inverse demand isP=a−Q and aggregate marginal costMC=Q,a>0. Compute monopoly deadweight loss relative to perfect competition with the same marginal-cost curve.
questions.solution:
Find the competitive and monopoly quantities. Competition equates willingness to pay to marginal cost: a-Q=Q, giving Q_C=a/2. A monopolist instead equates marginal revenue a-2Q to marginal cost Q, giving Q_M=a/3. Using P=MC for the monopoly would miss its withholding incentive.

Integrate the missing gains from trade. Between Q_M and Q_C, marginal willingness to pay exceeds marginal cost by a-2Q. Thus 
DWL =∫_(a/3)^(a/2)(a-2Q) dQ; =(1)/(2)((a)/(2)-(a)/(3))((a)/(3))=(a^2)/(36).
 Monopoly profit transfers are not part of this efficiency loss; only the forgone surplus on unproduced units is lost.
questions.hint: Compare marginal willingness to pay with marginal cost over the missing output range.

solutionSteps.title: Find the competitive and monopoly quantities
solutionSteps.body: Competition equates willingness to pay to marginal cost: $a-Q=Q$, giving $Q_C=a/2$. A monopolist instead equates marginal revenue $a-2Q$ to marginal cost $Q$, giving $Q_M=a/3$. Using $P=MC$ for the monopoly would miss its withholding incentive.

solutionSteps.title: Integrate the missing gains from trade
solutionSteps.body: Between $Q_M$ and $Q_C$, marginal willingness to pay exceeds marginal cost by $a-2Q$. Thus $$\begin{aligned}DWL&=\int_{a/3}^{a/2}(a-2Q)\,dQ\\&=\frac12\left(\frac a2-\frac a3\right)\left(\frac a3\right)=\frac{a^2}{36}.\end{aligned}$$ Monopoly profit transfers are not part of this efficiency loss; only the forgone surplus on unproduced units is lost.

questions.stem: A simple Keynesian model has investmentI=I₀+bY and savingS=sY, with1>s>b>0. How much does total equilibrium saving change for a small change in the marginal propensity to saves?
questions.answer: dS=−bI₀/(s−b)² ds. A higher saving propensity lowers equilibrium total saving.
questions.solution:
Solve the investment-saving equilibrium. Equilibrium requires sY=I_0+bY. Since s>b, 
Y=(I_0)/(s-b), S=sY=(sI_0)/(s-b).
 Saving must be evaluated after income adjusts, not at the old income.

Differentiate the equilibrium level of saving. Holding I_0 and b fixed, 
(dS)/(ds)=I_0((s-b)-s)/((s-b)^2)=-(bI_0)/((s-b)^2).
 Therefore a small change ds gives dS=-bI_0 ds/(s-b)^2. For positive autonomous investment, greater thrift reduces total equilibrium saving.

Explain the induced-investment channel. A higher saving propensity lowers consumption and output. Because investment increases with output, that income contraction also reduces investment. In the new equilibrium saving follows investment downward. If b=0, the usual fixed-investment paradox of thrift instead leaves total saving unchanged at I_0.
questions.hint: Differentiate equilibrium saving after solving for income.

solutionSteps.title: Solve the investment-saving equilibrium
solutionSteps.body: Equilibrium requires $sY=I_0+bY$. Since $s>b$, $$Y=\frac{I_0}{s-b},\qquad S=sY=\frac{sI_0}{s-b}.$$ Saving must be evaluated after income adjusts, not at the old income.

solutionSteps.title: Differentiate the equilibrium level of saving
solutionSteps.body: Holding $I_0$ and $b$ fixed, $$\frac{dS}{ds}=I_0\frac{(s-b)-s}{(s-b)^2}=-\frac{bI_0}{(s-b)^2}.$$ Therefore a small change $ds$ gives $dS=-bI_0\,ds/(s-b)^2$. For positive autonomous investment, greater thrift reduces total equilibrium saving.

solutionSteps.title: Explain the induced-investment channel
solutionSteps.body: A higher saving propensity lowers consumption and output. Because investment increases with output, that income contraction also reduces investment. In the new equilibrium saving follows investment downward. If $b=0$, the usual fixed-investment paradox of thrift instead leaves total saving unchanged at $I_0$.

questions.stem: There are100 competitive firms withq=√x. Derive industry supply if(a) input supply is horizontal at input price10,(b) total input supply is vertical at100 units.
questions.answer: (a) Q=5P, upward sloping. (b) Q100, vertical, with input priceP/2 for positive output priceP.
questions.solution:
Derive supply conditional on the input price. With q=√(x), producing q requires x=q^2. At input price w, a competitive firm maximizes Pq-wq^2. The first-order condition P=2wq gives q=P/(2w), with a negative profit second derivative. Aggregate output from 100 identical firms is Q=50P/w.

Hold the input price fixed in case (a). At the horizontal input supply price w=10, industry supply becomes Q=5P. In a price-vertical, quantity-horizontal diagram this is upward sloping, with inverse supply P=Q/5. Each firm can expand input use at the unchanged input price, but its own diminishing product generates increasing marginal cost.

Clear the constrained input market in case (b). If total input is 100, symmetry and strict concavity allocate one unit to each firm. Each then produces one output unit, so total output is 100. The optimality condition implies w=P/2 at this allocation. The input price, rather than aggregate output, adjusts to output price. Hence the industry's supply is vertical at Q=100 for positive output prices.
questions.hint: First derive input-price-conditional firm supply, then clear the input market.

solutionSteps.title: Derive supply conditional on the input price
solutionSteps.body: With $q=\sqrt x$, producing $q$ requires $x=q^2$. At input price $w$, a competitive firm maximizes $Pq-wq^2$. The first-order condition $P=2wq$ gives $q=P/(2w)$, with a negative profit second derivative. Aggregate output from 100 identical firms is $Q=50P/w$.

solutionSteps.title: Hold the input price fixed in case (a)
solutionSteps.body: At the horizontal input supply price $w=10$, industry supply becomes $Q=5P$. In a price-vertical, quantity-horizontal diagram this is upward sloping, with inverse supply $P=Q/5$. Each firm can expand input use at the unchanged input price, but its own diminishing product generates increasing marginal cost.

solutionSteps.title: Clear the constrained input market in case (b)
solutionSteps.body: If total input is 100, symmetry and strict concavity allocate one unit to each firm. Each then produces one output unit, so total output is 100. The optimality condition implies $w=P/2$ at this allocation. The input price, rather than aggregate output, adjusts to output price. Hence the industry's supply is vertical at $Q=100$ for positive output prices.

questions.stem: In a simple Keynesian model, private investment increases with aggregate income. Relative to1/MPS, what is the autonomous-spending multiplier?
questions.answer: B:Greater than1/MPS under the stable-equilibrium condition.
questions.solution:
Include induced investment in the equilibrium slope. With saving S=sY and investment I=I_0+vY, equilibrium gives (s-v)Y=I_0. For a stable model with 0<v<s, the autonomous-spending multiplier is 
(1)/(s-v)>(1)/(s).
 Choose B. Positive investment feedback magnifies the spending rounds; stability is needed for the standard positive multiplier comparison.
questions.hint: Induced investment adds a second positive expenditure feedback.
questions.notes: Assumes the marginal propensity to save exceeds the induced-investment coefficient.

solutionSteps.title: Include induced investment in the equilibrium slope
solutionSteps.body: With saving $S=sY$ and investment $I=I_0+vY$, equilibrium gives $(s-v)Y=I_0$. For a stable model with $0<v<s$, the autonomous-spending multiplier is $$\frac1{s-v}>\frac1s.$$ Choose B. Positive investment feedback magnifies the spending rounds; stability is needed for the standard positive multiplier comparison.

questions.stem: A farmer owns100 units of rice, consumes some and sells the rest for vegetables. If rice price rises with vegetable price fixed, how does his budget line change?
questions.answer: A:Rotates outward about the unchanged rice-axis intercept.
questions.solution:
Write the endowment budget. If consumed rice is r and vegetables are v, the budget is p_rr+p_vv=100p_r, or 
v=(p_r)/(p_v)(100-r).
 A rise in rice price leaves the rice intercept 100 unchanged while increasing the vegetable intercept 100p_r/p_v. The line rotates outward about the rice endowment point: A.
questions.hint: Account for the higher value of the rice endowment as well as its price.

solutionSteps.title: Write the endowment budget
solutionSteps.body: If consumed rice is $r$ and vegetables are $v$, the budget is $p_rr+p_vv=100p_r$, or $$v=\frac{p_r}{p_v}(100-r).$$ A rise in rice price leaves the rice intercept 100 unchanged while increasing the vegetable intercept $100p_r/p_v$. The line rotates outward about the rice endowment point: A.

questions.stem: A monopolist hasC=1.1+2Q and inverse demandP=4−Q. What is equilibrium output?
questions.answer: B:1 if the fixed cost1.1 is unavoidable atQ0. A:0 if shutting down avoids that fixed cost.
questions.solution:
Find the best positive-output choice. The profit expression for positive production is 
π(Q)=(4-Q)Q-(1.1+2Q)=2Q-Q^2-1.1.
 It is maximized at Q=1, where profit is -0.1. A loss at the positive-output optimum does not by itself establish shutdown; the shutdown payoff must also be specified.

Compare the two fixed-cost conventions. If the stated fixed cost is unavoidable even at zero output, shutdown gives -1.1, so producing one unit is better and B applies. If producing zero avoids the 1.1 cost, shutdown gives zero and A applies. The source does not state avoidability, so it supports these conditional answers rather than a unique unqualified key. The review flag is retained.
questions.hint: Compare the optimal positive-output profit with the correctly defined shutdown payoff.
questions.notes: Fixed-cost avoidability at zero output is unspecified, producing different answers.

solutionSteps.title: Find the best positive-output choice
solutionSteps.body: The profit expression for positive production is $$\pi(Q)=(4-Q)Q-(1.1+2Q)=2Q-Q^2-1.1.$$ It is maximized at $Q=1$, where profit is $-0.1$. A loss at the positive-output optimum does not by itself establish shutdown; the shutdown payoff must also be specified.

solutionSteps.body: If the stated fixed cost is unavoidable even at zero output, shutdown gives $-1.1$, so producing one unit is better and B applies. If producing zero avoids the 1.1 cost, shutdown gives zero and A applies. The source does not state avoidability, so it supports these conditional answers rather than a unique unqualified key. The review flag is retained.

questions.stem: In a simple Keynesian economyC=20+.9Y andI=G=20. Find equilibriumGDP.
questions.solution: Add all autonomous expenditure components. Goods balance is Y=C+I+G=20+0.9Y+20+20. Thus 0.1Y=60 and Y=600, option B. The autonomous consumption intercept counts in addition to investment and government spending; omitting it would give the wrong equilibrium.
questions.hint: Add all three autonomous spending terms.

solutionSteps.title: Add all autonomous expenditure components
solutionSteps.body: Goods balance is $Y=C+I+G=20+0.9Y+20+20$. Thus $0.1Y=60$ and $Y=600$, option B. The autonomous consumption intercept counts in addition to investment and government spending; omitting it would give the wrong equilibrium.

questions.stem: There are100 barbers, each capable of100 haircuts daily. Initial demand2000−100p and equilibrium price10. Demand becomes3000−100p. With free entry/exit and other things unchanged, what happens to long-run price?
questions.answer: C:Price stays10 in the usual constant-cost competitive-industry model.
questions.solution: Use free entry and unchanged long-run unit costs. Under the intended constant-cost competitive-industry interpretation, free entry makes price equal the minimum sustainable average cost. If technology and input prices remain unchanged, that price stays 10. Demand at 10 rises from 1000 to 2000 haircuts, accommodated through industry adjustment rather than a permanent price increase. Choose C. The listed capacities alone do not identify costs, so this conclusion uses the standard “other things unchanged” cost assumption.
questions.hint: Long-run free-entry price is governed by costs rather than demand alone.
questions.notes: Uses the standard constant-cost-industry interpretation; the stated barber capacities alone are not a complete supply model.

solutionSteps.title: Use free entry and unchanged long-run unit costs
solutionSteps.body: Under the intended constant-cost competitive-industry interpretation, free entry makes price equal the minimum sustainable average cost. If technology and input prices remain unchanged, that price stays 10. Demand at 10 rises from 1000 to 2000 haircuts, accommodated through industry adjustment rather than a permanent price increase. Choose C. The listed capacities alone do not identify costs, so this conclusion uses the standard “other things unchanged” cost assumption.

questions.stem: A competitive firm in short-run equilibrium uses variable inputA and fixed inputB. Which holds: (A)P=MC; (B)P=price(A)/MP_A; (C)P>AVC; (D)all?
questions.answer: IntendedD for an active interior firm strictly above shutdown. At the shutdown boundaryP=AVC, the strict inequalityC fails.
questions.solution:
Identify the interior marginal conditions. For an active differentiable competitive firm, P=MC. With one variable input A at price w_A, an additional output unit requires 1/MP_A input units, giving MC=w_A/MP_A. Thus A and B express the same interior optimality condition.

Check the strict shutdown inequality. Operating requires P≥ AVC at the chosen output, not always P>AVC. Equality is possible at shutdown indifference, so C and consequently “all of the above” need the additional strictly-above-shutdown assumption. A zero-output equilibrium need not satisfy the interior equalities either. D is the intended active-interior answer, but the record remains flagged because the source does not state those qualifications.
questions.hint: Check the weak shutdown inequality before treating it as strict.
questions.notes: Missing active-interior and strict-above-shutdown qualifications affect the universal MCQ answer.

solutionSteps.title: Identify the interior marginal conditions
solutionSteps.body: For an active differentiable competitive firm, $P=MC$. With one variable input A at price $w_A$, an additional output unit requires $1/MP_A$ input units, giving $MC=w_A/MP_A$. Thus A and B express the same interior optimality condition.

solutionSteps.body: Operating requires $P\ge AVC$ at the chosen output, not always $P>AVC$. Equality is possible at shutdown indifference, so C and consequently “all of the above” need the additional strictly-above-shutdown assumption. A zero-output equilibrium need not satisfy the interior equalities either. D is the intended active-interior answer, but the record remains flagged because the source does not state those qualifications.

questions.stem: In a below-full-employment economy, rich households save a higher fraction than poor households and investment is autonomous. Redistribute income from rich to poor. What happens to aggregate saving and income in the new simple-Keynesian equilibrium?
questions.answer: D:None of the listed combinations. Income rises but equilibrium aggregate saving remains equal to fixed investment.
questions.solution: Distinguish desired saving at old income from equilibrium saving. Redistributing income toward poorer, lower-saving households raises consumption at the original income. In a below-full-employment Keynesian model, this increases equilibrium output. However final goods equilibrium still requires S=I, and autonomous investment is unchanged. Income therefore rises while total equilibrium saving remains fixed. None of A–C states that combination, so choose D.
questions.hint: Distinguish the initial saving-schedule shift from the final equilibrium saving level.

solutionSteps.title: Distinguish desired saving at old income from equilibrium saving
solutionSteps.body: Redistributing income toward poorer, lower-saving households raises consumption at the original income. In a below-full-employment Keynesian model, this increases equilibrium output. However final goods equilibrium still requires $S=I$, and autonomous investment is unchanged. Income therefore rises while total equilibrium saving remains fixed. None of A–C states that combination, so choose D.

questions.stem: In the historical question’s standard money-multiplier framework, a reduction in commercial banks’ cash reserve ratio would normally…
questions.solution: Apply the textbook reserve-multiplier direction. For a given reserve base, reducing the required cash reserve ratio allows banks to support more deposits and lending. In the simplest model the multiplier is 1/rr, increasing as rr falls. Thus the normal other-things-equal direction is an increase in money supply: B. Actual lending also depends on other constraints, but the historical question asks for the standard model's normal direction, not a claim about current RBI actions.
questions.hint: Compare deposits supportable by a fixed reserve base.
questions.notes: The word“recently” belongs to the historical sample stem; this is not a claim about current RBI policy.

In the simplest model the multiplier is $1/rr$, increasing as $rr$ falls. Thus the normal other-things-equal direction is an increase in money supply: B. questions.stem: If (mx²+3x+4)/(x²+2x+2)<5 for every real x, then m satisfies
questions.answer: Exact condition m<71/24; choices B and D both follow
questions.solution: The denominator (x+1)²+1 is positive. The condition is (m−5)x²−7x−6<0 for all x. It requires m−5<0 and discriminant 49+24(m−5)<0, equivalently m<71/24. This implies both B and the weaker disjunction D, so the alternatives are not mutually exclusive.
questions.hint: Reduce to a quadratic that must stay strictly negative.
questions.notes: The likely intended necessary condition is B, but D is also a necessary consequence. No unique literal answer.

questions.stem: How many solutions satisfy x+y=2, y+z=2, 2x+3y+z=6?
options: More than one but finitely many
questions.solution: Twice the first equation plus the second is precisely the third. Letting y=t gives x=z=2−t for arbitrary real t.
questions.hint: Check whether one equation is dependent on the others.
questions.notes: The third right-hand side is 6, checked in a magnified crop.

questions.stem: Let f(x)=det([[cos x,x,1],[2sin x,x²,2x],[tan x,x,1]]). Find limₓ→₀f(x)/x².
questions.solution: Subtract the third row from the first. Expanding along the resulting row gives f(x)=(cosx−tanx)(x²−2x²)=x²(tanx−cosx). The quotient tends to −1.
questions.hint: Subtract the two rows that share their last entries.

questions.stem: What value must be assigned to f(x)=[1−cos(7(x−π))]/(x−π) at x=π to make f continuous?
questions.solution: Put h=x−π. Since 1−cos7h=O(h²), the quotient is O(h) and tends to zero.
questions.hint: Use 1−cosu≈u²/2 near zero.

questions.solution: For t=|x|≥0, t²+4t−4=0 gives t=−2+√8; the other quadratic root is negative and inadmissible. Hence x=±(√8−2).

questions.stem: The roots of x³−9x²+23x−15=0 are in A.P. Their common difference is
questions.answer: 2 when the roots are ordered increasingly
questions.solution: The cubic factors as (x−1)(x−3)(x−5). Thus the increasing roots are 1,3,5 with common difference 2.
questions.hint: The middle root of three arithmetic-progression roots equals their average.

questions.stem: If a₁,a₂,… are in G.P., find Δ=det([[log aₙ,log aₙ₊₁,log aₙ₊₂],[log aₙ₊₃,log aₙ₊₄,log aₙ₊₅],[log aₙ₊₆,log aₙ₊₇,log aₙ₊₈]]).
questions.answer: Δ=0, but A, B and C all have this value
questions.solution: For positive G.P. terms, log aₖ=A+(k−1)d. The three rows differ by constant multiples of (1,1,1), so their determinant is zero. Also aₙaₙ₊₈=aₙ₊₄² and a₁a₃=a₂², making both alternatives A and B zero as well.
questions.hint: Logarithms convert a geometric progression to an arithmetic progression.

questions.stem: Let f(x)=x for 0<x<1; f(x)=2−x for 1<x≤2; and f(x)=x−x²/2 for x>2. Then f is
options: Continuous at 2 but not differentiable at 1
Not continuous at 2 and not differentiable at 1
questions.answer: The source leaves f(1) undefined; intended continuous extension has a kink there
questions.solution: At 2 the middle value is zero and the right limit is 2−2=0, so f is continuous there. Neither of the first two branches includes 1, so differentiability at 1 is formally not defined. If one fills f(1)=1, the left and right slopes are 1 and −1, giving the intended first choice.
questions.hint: Check whether each joining point belongs to the displayed domain.
questions.notes: Both source inequalities at x=1 are strict. Missing f(1) is retained rather than silently supplied.

questions.stem: Find limₓ→₀[1/x−log(1+x)/x²].
questions.solution: The expression is [x−ln(1+x)]/x². Using ln(1+x)=x−x²/2+O(x³) gives limit 1/2.
questions.hint: Use the second-order logarithm expansion.

questions.stem: For |a|<1, |b|<1, the series a(a+b)+a²(a²+b²)+a³(a³+b³)+⋯
questions.solution: The nth summand is a²ⁿ+(ab)ⁿ. Both are convergent geometric series because |a²|<1 and |ab|<1. Sum them separately.
questions.hint: Separate the two geometric series.

questions.solution: The equation a²−2cosα·a+1=0 has roots e^(±iα). Taking integer nth powers and adding reciprocals gives e^(inα)+e^(−inα)=2cos(nα).

questions.stem: For positive a,b,c, the least value of (a+b+c)(1/a+1/b+1/c) is
questions.solution: Cauchy–Schwarz gives (a+b+c)(1/a+1/b+1/c)≥(1+1+1)²=9. Equality occurs at a=b=c.

questions.stem: Define f(x)=|x|−[x]−1 for −1<x<0; |x|−[x] for 0≤x<1; and 1 otherwise. The source defines [x] as the greatest integer strictly less than x. Then
options: f is discontinuous at only one real point
f is discontinuous at more than one real point
f is continuous but nondifferentiable at only one real point
questions.answer: Literal strict-integer definition gives one discontinuity; conventional floor gives a different answer
questions.solution: With the printed strict definition, [0]=−1. For −1<x<0, f=−x; for 0<x<1, f=x; and f(0)=1. Thus only 0 is discontinuous, giving A. With the conventional greatest-integer function floor(x), f(0)=0 and f=min{|x|,1}, continuous with three nondifferentiable points −1,0,1, giving D. The intended convention needs clarification.
questions.hint: Evaluate the integer-part symbol at the integer 0.
questions.notes: Source uses “greatest integer <x”, conflicting with conventional floor notation. Conditional answers are given without silently correcting the definition.

questions.stem: If a primal linear program has feasible solutions but no optimal solution, then its dual
options: Has feasible solutions but no optimal solution
questions.solution: A feasible finite-dimensional linear program without an optimum is unbounded in the optimizing direction. A feasible dual would supply a finite bound by weak duality, which is impossible.
questions.hint: Use weak duality to rule out dual feasibility.

questions.stem: Maximize 2x₁+3x₂ subject to 2x₁+x₂>2, x₁+x₂≤3, x₁−x₂≤−1 and x₁,x₂>0. Which is true?
questions.answer: No attained optimum under the printed strict positivity constraints
questions.solution: The objective is 3(x₁+x₂)−x₁≤9−x₁<9 since x₁>0. For arbitrarily small ε>0, (ε,3−ε) is feasible and has value 9−ε→9. Thus the supremum is 9 but it is not attained.
questions.hint: Distinguish strict positivity from nonnegativity.
questions.notes: Magnification confirms > in the first and nonnegativity lines, while the other two use ≤. If the intended final constraint were ≥0, choice A would instead be optimal.

questions.stem: Evaluate ∫₋₁¹(x+x²+x³)e^(−x²/2)dx.
questions.answer: None of the printed values matches the integral
questions.solution: The odd x and x³ terms integrate to zero, leaving ∫₋₁¹x²e^(−x²/2)dx>0. Integration by parts gives −2/√e+∫₋₁¹e^(−x²/2)dx≈0.498187. This is neither 2/√e≈1.213061 nor 2√e≈3.297443, and cannot be negative.
questions.hint: Use parity before evaluating the remaining even integral.

questions.stem: The series Σₙ₌₁^∞(−1)ⁿ⁺¹/n
questions.solution: Alternating decreasing terms 1/n tend to zero, so the alternating-series test gives convergence. Absolute values give the divergent harmonic series. Integrating the geometric expansion of 1/(1+x) on [0,1] gives the sum ln2.
questions.hint: Apply the alternating-series test and identify the logarithm series.

questions.stem: Murthy’s utility isf(√q₁+√q₂),f′>0, for idli and vara; only integer pieces are sold. Initial prices1,2. (a) He bought6 of each. Was this optimal within the same spending? Find the optimum. (b) Next day each item costs1.50. Can he attain the previous day’s optimal utility without spending more?
questions.answer: (a) No; optimum is12 idli and3 vara, costing18. (b) Impossible within18. The best new affordable bundles are(6,6), below the previous optimum’s utility.
questions.solution:
Remove the increasing outer transformation. Because f'>0, maximizing f(√(q_1)+√(q_2)) is equivalent to maximizing its inner index. The initial order costs 6+2(6)=18, so the comparison budget is q_1+2q_2≤18, with integer quantities.

Find and verify the first-day optimum. The continuous interior condition is 
(1/(2√(q_1)))/(1/(2√(q_2)))=(1)/(2) ⇒ q_1=4q_2.
 Together with the binding budget this gives (q_1,q_2)=(12,3). The inner utility is strictly concave, so it is the continuous maximum. Since it is already an integer bundle, it is also the integer maximum. Its index is 3√(3), exceeding the initial order's 2√(6).

Check the second-day spending limit. At the new price 1.50 per piece, a budget of 18 permits at most 12 pieces in total. For any given total number of pieces, concavity of the square root makes the index greatest when the pieces are divided as equally as possible. Thus the best affordable order is (6,6), giving index 2√(6)<3√(3).

Explain the infeasibility rather than inventing a bundle. No second-day order can provide the previous day's optimal satisfaction while spending at most 18. At least 14 integer pieces are needed even to weakly exceed the old index: the best 13-piece split gives √(6)+√(7)<3√(3), whereas 14 balanced pieces exceed it and cost 21. Exact equality is achieved by (12,3) or (3,12) at cost 22.50. The failure is a genuine feasibility result from the stated prices and indivisibility.
questions.hint: Use monotone transformation, then respect the indivisible-piece budget.
questions.notes: Visual inspection confirms the revised priceRs1.50, rather than1.60. The infeasibility in part(b) follows from the stated data.

solutionSteps.title: Remove the increasing outer transformation
solutionSteps.body: Because $f'>0$, maximizing $f(\sqrt{q_1}+\sqrt{q_2})$ is equivalent to maximizing its inner index. The initial order costs $6+2(6)=18$, so the comparison budget is $q_1+2q_2\le18$, with integer quantities.

solutionSteps.title: Find and verify the first-day optimum
solutionSteps.body: The continuous interior condition is $$\frac{1/(2\sqrt{q_1})}{1/(2\sqrt{q_2})}=\frac12\quad\Rightarrow\quad q_1=4q_2.$$ Together with the binding budget this gives $(q_1,q_2)=(12,3)$. The inner utility is strictly concave, so it is the continuous maximum. Since it is already an integer bundle, it is also the integer maximum. Its index is $3\sqrt3$, exceeding the initial order's $2\sqrt6$.

solutionSteps.title: Check the second-day spending limit
solutionSteps.body: At the new price 1.50 per piece, a budget of 18 permits at most 12 pieces in total. For any given total number of pieces, concavity of the square root makes the index greatest when the pieces are divided as equally as possible. Thus the best affordable order is $(6,6)$, giving index $2\sqrt6<3\sqrt3$.

solutionSteps.title: Explain the infeasibility rather than inventing a bundle
solutionSteps.body: No second-day order can provide the previous day's optimal satisfaction while spending at most 18. At least 14 integer pieces are needed even to weakly exceed the old index: the best 13-piece split gives $\sqrt6+\sqrt7<3\sqrt3$, whereas 14 balanced pieces exceed it and cost 21. Exact equality is achieved by $(12,3)$ or $(3,12)$ at cost 22.50. The failure is a genuine feasibility result from the stated prices and indivisibility.

questions.stem: Four sisters share farm output equally among those working. Output with1,2,3,4 sisters is1500,2500,3300,4000. Each may instead earn1110 in the city. How many migrate when maximizing(a) individual income,(b) family income?
questions.answer: (a) Two migrate, two remain. (b) Three migrate, one remains.
questions.solution:
Compute average farm earnings for private decisions. Sharing output equally gives farm incomes per worker of 1500, 1250, 1100 and 1000 when one through four sisters work. The city option is 1110. With two on the farm each earns 1250 and does not want to leave; a third entrant would earn only 1100 and does not want to join. Therefore two stay and two migrate in the individual-choice equilibrium.

Compare total family incomes. For zero through four farm workers, total income including city earnings is 
n=0: 4440,; n=1: 1500+3(1110)=4830,; n=2: 2500+2(1110)=4720,; n=3: 3300+1110=4410,; n=4: 4000.
 The family optimum has only one sister farming and three migrating.

Explain the difference between the criteria. A private entrant compares her farm average product with the city wage. The family instead compares each worker's marginal addition to farm output with the city earnings forgone. The second farm worker adds only 2500-1500=1000, below 1110, even though each of two farm workers receives 1250. This sharing externality explains the excessive farm employment under separate choices.
questions.hint: Private entrants compare average product; the family compares marginal product.

solutionSteps.body: Sharing output equally gives farm incomes per worker of 1500, 1250, 1100 and 1000 when one through four sisters work. The city option is 1110. With two on the farm each earns 1250 and does not want to leave; a third entrant would earn only 1100 and does not want to join. Therefore two stay and two migrate in the individual-choice equilibrium.

solutionSteps.body: For zero through four farm workers, total income including city earnings is $$\begin{aligned}n=0:&\quad4440,\\n=1:&\quad1500+3(1110)=4830,\\n=2:&\quad2500+2(1110)=4720,\\n=3:&\quad3300+1110=4410,\\n=4:&\quad4000.\end{aligned}$$ The family optimum has only one sister farming and three migrating.

The second farm worker adds only $2500-1500=1000$, below 1110, even though each of two farm workers receives 1250. This sharing externality explains the excessive farm employment under separate choices.

questions.stem: There are100 competitive firms withq=√x. Derive industry supply if(a) input supply is horizontal at input price10,(b) total input supply is vertical at100 units.
questions.answer: (a) Q=5P, upward sloping. (b) Q100, vertical, with input priceP/2 for positive output priceP.
questions.solution:
Derive supply conditional on the input price. With q=√(x), producing q requires x=q^2. At input price w, a competitive firm maximizes Pq-wq^2. The first-order condition P=2wq gives q=P/(2w), with a negative profit second derivative. Aggregate output from 100 identical firms is Q=50P/w.

Hold the input price fixed in case (a). At the horizontal input supply price w=10, industry supply becomes Q=5P. In a price-vertical, quantity-horizontal diagram this is upward sloping, with inverse supply P=Q/5. Each firm can expand input use at the unchanged input price, but its own diminishing product generates increasing marginal cost.

Clear the constrained input market in case (b). If total input is 100, symmetry and strict concavity allocate one unit to each firm. Each then produces one output unit, so total output is 100. The optimality condition implies w=P/2 at this allocation. The input price, rather than aggregate output, adjusts to output price. Hence the industry's supply is vertical at Q=100 for positive output prices.
questions.hint: First derive input-price-conditional firm supply, then clear the input market.

solutionSteps.title: Derive supply conditional on the input price
solutionSteps.body: With $q=\sqrt x$, producing $q$ requires $x=q^2$. At input price $w$, a competitive firm maximizes $Pq-wq^2$. The first-order condition $P=2wq$ gives $q=P/(2w)$, with a negative profit second derivative. Aggregate output from 100 identical firms is $Q=50P/w$.

solutionSteps.title: Hold the input price fixed in case (a)
solutionSteps.body: At the horizontal input supply price $w=10$, industry supply becomes $Q=5P$. In a price-vertical, quantity-horizontal diagram this is upward sloping, with inverse supply $P=Q/5$. Each firm can expand input use at the unchanged input price, but its own diminishing product generates increasing marginal cost.

solutionSteps.title: Clear the constrained input market in case (b)
solutionSteps.body: If total input is 100, symmetry and strict concavity allocate one unit to each firm. Each then produces one output unit, so total output is 100. The optimality condition implies $w=P/2$ at this allocation. The input price, rather than aggregate output, adjusts to output price. Hence the industry's supply is vertical at $Q=100$ for positive output prices.

questions.stem: Industry inverse demand isP=a−Q and aggregate marginal costMC=Q,a>0. Compute monopoly deadweight loss relative to perfect competition with the same marginal-cost curve.
questions.solution:
Find the competitive and monopoly quantities. Competition equates willingness to pay to marginal cost: a-Q=Q, giving Q_C=a/2. A monopolist instead equates marginal revenue a-2Q to marginal cost Q, giving Q_M=a/3. Using P=MC for the monopoly would miss its withholding incentive.

Integrate the missing gains from trade. Between Q_M and Q_C, marginal willingness to pay exceeds marginal cost by a-2Q. Thus 
DWL =∫_(a/3)^(a/2)(a-2Q) dQ; =(1)/(2)((a)/(2)-(a)/(3))((a)/(3))=(a^2)/(36).
 Monopoly profit transfers are not part of this efficiency loss; only the forgone surplus on unproduced units is lost.
questions.hint: Compare marginal willingness to pay with marginal cost over the missing output range.

solutionSteps.title: Find the competitive and monopoly quantities
solutionSteps.body: Competition equates willingness to pay to marginal cost: $a-Q=Q$, giving $Q_C=a/2$. A monopolist instead equates marginal revenue $a-2Q$ to marginal cost $Q$, giving $Q_M=a/3$. Using $P=MC$ for the monopoly would miss its withholding incentive.

solutionSteps.title: Integrate the missing gains from trade
solutionSteps.body: Between $Q_M$ and $Q_C$, marginal willingness to pay exceeds marginal cost by $a-2Q$. Thus $$\begin{aligned}DWL&=\int_{a/3}^{a/2}(a-2Q)\,dQ\\&=\frac12\left(\frac a2-\frac a3\right)\left(\frac a3\right)=\frac{a^2}{36}.\end{aligned}$$ Monopoly profit transfers are not part of this efficiency loss; only the forgone surplus on unproduced units is lost.

questions.stem: A farmer owns1000 bushels, with a physical return110 next year for each100 set aside. UtilityW=C₀C₁. (a) Without a capital market find consumption. (b) He can borrow any amount at5% annually only to finance current consumption: find consumption in both years.
questions.answer: (a) C₀500,C₁550. (b) Set aside all1000, borrow11000/21≈523.810 for current consumption; C₀11000/21,C₁550.
questions.solution:
Solve the no-borrowing case. With physical investment S, current and future consumption are 1000-S and 1.1S. Maximizing 1.1S(1000-S) gives S=500, so (C_0,C_1)=(500,550).

Apply the restriction on what borrowed resources may finance. Let borrowing be B≥0. It may finance current consumption but cannot be added to physical investment, so 0≤ S≤1000. The budgets are 
C_0=1000-S+B, C_1=1.1S-1.05B.
 Combining them at the financing rate gives C_0+C_1/1.05=1000+(1.1/1.05-1)S. Because the coefficient on S is positive, resources for consumption are maximized by setting aside all 1000 owned bushels.

Choose consumption timing after the investment decision. With S=1000, current consumption equals borrowing and future consumption is 1100-1.05B. Maximize 
W(B)=B(1100-1.05B).
 The derivative 1100-2.1B vanishes at B=11000/21. This gives C_0=11000/21≈523.810 and C_1=550, both positive, so the solution is feasible.

Explain why unlimited borrowing does not imply unlimited output here. The loan-use restriction prevents investing borrowed corn in the 10% physical-return technology. Without that restriction, financing at 5% and reinvesting at 10% would produce unbounded arbitrage in this linear model. With it, the original stock caps physical investment and yields the finite consumption solution above. The printed continuation is on PDF page 7, before the question's start in scan order.
questions.hint: Use the borrowing-use restriction and optimize physical investment before consumption timing.
questions.notes: Part(b) continues on PDFpage7, before the question’s start in the supplied scan order.

solutionSteps.title: Solve the no-borrowing case
solutionSteps.body: With physical investment $S$, current and future consumption are $1000-S$ and $1.1S$. Maximizing $1.1S(1000-S)$ gives $S=500$, so $(C_0,C_1)=(500,550)$.

solutionSteps.title: Apply the restriction on what borrowed resources may finance
solutionSteps.body: Let borrowing be $B\ge0$. It may finance current consumption but cannot be added to physical investment, so $0\le S\le1000$. The budgets are $$C_0=1000-S+B,\qquad C_1=1.1S-1.05B.$$ Combining them at the financing rate gives $C_0+C_1/1.05=1000+(1.1/1.05-1)S$. Because the coefficient on $S$ is positive, resources for consumption are maximized by setting aside all 1000 owned bushels.

solutionSteps.title: Choose consumption timing after the investment decision
solutionSteps.body: With $S=1000$, current consumption equals borrowing and future consumption is $1100-1.05B$. Maximize $$W(B)=B(1100-1.05B).$$ The derivative $1100-2.1B$ vanishes at $B=11000/21$. This gives $C_0=11000/21\approx523.810$ and $C_1=550$, both positive, so the solution is feasible.

solutionSteps.title: Explain why unlimited borrowing does not imply unlimited output here
solutionSteps.body: The loan-use restriction prevents investing borrowed corn in the 10% physical-return technology. Without that restriction, financing at 5% and reinvesting at 10% would produce unbounded arbitrage in this linear model. With it, the original stock caps physical investment and yields the finite consumption solution above. The printed continuation is on PDF page 7, before the question's start in scan order.

questions.stem: A small country faces world pricep_w. One domestic producer has increasingMC, sells both at home and abroad, and is protected against imports by tariffT per unit. Show that raisingT cannot lower exports. When are exports constant?
questions.answer: With positive exports total output is fixed byMC=p_w. Higher tariff weakly raises domestic monopoly price, weakly lowers domestic sales and therefore weakly raises exports. Exports are constant once the import-price ceiling is nonbinding.
questions.solution:
Use exports to pin down total production. The producer can sell an additional unit abroad at the fixed world price p_w. With positive export sales and increasing marginal cost, its total output satisfies MC(Q^*)=p_w. Neither the world price nor the technology changes when the home tariff changes, so this total quantity is fixed while exports remain positive.

Treat home sales as an allocation with an opportunity cost. Selling a unit domestically forgoes the world-price export receipt. The producer therefore chooses domestic sales to maximize domestic revenue minus p_wq_h, subject to the import-parity price ceiling p_h≤ p_w+T. The unconstrained domestic choice has MR_h=p_w.

Relax the tariff ceiling and infer exports. With a regular downward home demand and single-peaked domestic objective, a higher tariff relaxes the ceiling and weakly raises the chosen home price toward its unconstrained monopoly level. Home quantity weakly falls. Since exports are E=Q^*-q_h, they weakly increase and cannot decrease.

Identify when exports remain unchanged. If the import-price ceiling is already above the unconstrained domestic monopoly price, further tariff increases do not change the home choice, so exports remain constant. Any other reason home quantity stays fixed also produces constant exports. The conclusion is conditional on positive exports being maintained and the standard price-ceiling interpretation of protection.
questions.hint: Exports pin down marginal cost and total production; the tariff changes only the home allocation.
questions.notes: Uses the standard import-parity-price-ceiling and regular domestic-demand interpretation, with positive exports maintained.

solutionSteps.title: Use exports to pin down total production
solutionSteps.body: The producer can sell an additional unit abroad at the fixed world price $p_w$. With positive export sales and increasing marginal cost, its total output satisfies $MC(Q^*)=p_w$. Neither the world price nor the technology changes when the home tariff changes, so this total quantity is fixed while exports remain positive.

solutionSteps.title: Treat home sales as an allocation with an opportunity cost
solutionSteps.body: Selling a unit domestically forgoes the world-price export receipt. The producer therefore chooses domestic sales to maximize domestic revenue minus $p_wq_h$, subject to the import-parity price ceiling $p_h\le p_w+T$. The unconstrained domestic choice has $MR_h=p_w$.

solutionSteps.title: Relax the tariff ceiling and infer exports
solutionSteps.body: With a regular downward home demand and single-peaked domestic objective, a higher tariff relaxes the ceiling and weakly raises the chosen home price toward its unconstrained monopoly level. Home quantity weakly falls. Since exports are $E=Q^*-q_h$, they weakly increase and cannot decrease.

solutionSteps.title: Identify when exports remain unchanged
solutionSteps.body: If the import-price ceiling is already above the unconstrained domestic monopoly price, further tariff increases do not change the home choice, so exports remain constant. Any other reason home quantity stays fixed also produces constant exports. The conclusion is conditional on positive exports being maintained and the standard price-ceiling interpretation of protection.

questions.stem: There are100 identical competitive firms withq=x and price-taking behaviour in the input market. Derive industry supply if(a) input price is10 at any quantity,(b) aggregate input supply is fixed100.
questions.answer: (a) Horizontal output supply atP10. (b) Vertical supply atQ100, with input price equal toP.
questions.solution:
Use the one-for-one production technology. Because q=x, input price w is also unit output cost. A price-taking firm's profit is (P-w)q. If P<w it supplies zero; if P=w any nonnegative quantity is optimal; if P>w and inputs are unlimited there is no finite optimum. A constant-returns supply correspondence is therefore important here.

Derive supply with elastic input availability. When the input is available at w=10 at any quantity, competitive output supply is horizontal at P=10. It is not an upward-sloping quadratic-cost supply curve: the firm has neither diminishing input productivity nor a rising input price in this case.

Derive supply with fixed aggregate input. If the industry has exactly 100 units of input and positive output prices induce their full use, its output is exactly 100. Input-market bidding makes w=P, leaving zero per-unit profit. How those units are divided among firms does not affect total output under the linear technology. Industry supply is thus vertical at Q=100.
questions.hint: With constant returns, output supply may be horizontal rather than a single-valued quantity function.

solutionSteps.title: Use the one-for-one production technology
solutionSteps.body: Because $q=x$, input price $w$ is also unit output cost. A price-taking firm's profit is $(P-w)q$. If $P<w$ it supplies zero; if $P=w$ any nonnegative quantity is optimal; if $P>w$ and inputs are unlimited there is no finite optimum. A constant-returns supply correspondence is therefore important here.

solutionSteps.title: Derive supply with elastic input availability
solutionSteps.body: When the input is available at $w=10$ at any quantity, competitive output supply is horizontal at $P=10$. It is not an upward-sloping quadratic-cost supply curve: the firm has neither diminishing input productivity nor a rising input price in this case.

solutionSteps.title: Derive supply with fixed aggregate input
solutionSteps.body: If the industry has exactly 100 units of input and positive output prices induce their full use, its output is exactly 100. Input-market bidding makes $w=P$, leaving zero per-unit profit. How those units are divided among firms does not affect total output under the linear technology. Industry supply is thus vertical at $Q=100$.

questions.stem: In a simple Keynesian model, private investment increases with aggregate income. Relative to1/MPS, what is the autonomous-spending multiplier?
questions.answer: B:Greater than1/MPS under the stable-equilibrium condition.
questions.solution:
Include induced investment in the equilibrium slope. With saving S=sY and investment I=I_0+vY, equilibrium gives (s-v)Y=I_0. For a stable model with 0<v<s, the autonomous-spending multiplier is 
(1)/(s-v)>(1)/(s).
 Choose B. Positive investment feedback magnifies the spending rounds; stability is needed for the standard positive multiplier comparison.
questions.hint: Induced investment adds a second positive expenditure feedback.
questions.notes: Assumes the marginal propensity to save exceeds the induced-investment coefficient.

solutionSteps.title: Include induced investment in the equilibrium slope
solutionSteps.body: With saving $S=sY$ and investment $I=I_0+vY$, equilibrium gives $(s-v)Y=I_0$. For a stable model with $0<v<s$, the autonomous-spending multiplier is $$\frac1{s-v}>\frac1s.$$ Choose B. Positive investment feedback magnifies the spending rounds; stability is needed for the standard positive multiplier comparison.

questions.stem: A farmer owns100 units of rice, consumes some and sells the rest for vegetables. If rice price rises with vegetable price fixed, how does his budget line change?
questions.answer: A:Rotates outward about the unchanged rice-axis intercept.
questions.solution:
Write the endowment budget. If consumed rice is r and vegetables are v, the budget is p_rr+p_vv=100p_r, or 
v=(p_r)/(p_v)(100-r).
 A rise in rice price leaves the rice intercept 100 unchanged while increasing the vegetable intercept 100p_r/p_v. The line rotates outward about the rice endowment point: A.
questions.hint: Account for the higher value of the rice endowment as well as its price.

solutionSteps.title: Write the endowment budget
solutionSteps.body: If consumed rice is $r$ and vegetables are $v$, the budget is $p_rr+p_vv=100p_r$, or $$v=\frac{p_r}{p_v}(100-r).$$ A rise in rice price leaves the rice intercept 100 unchanged while increasing the vegetable intercept $100p_r/p_v$. The line rotates outward about the rice endowment point: A.

questions.stem: A new firm sells50000 of output and carries7000 of unsold finished goods into next year. It buys30000 of intermediate goods, of which2000 remain unused. Find value added.
questions.solution:
Measure output produced and inputs actually used. Production value is sales plus the finished-goods inventory increase: 50000+7000=57000. Intermediate consumption is purchases minus unused input inventory: 30000-2000=28000. Value added is therefore 
57000-28000=29000,
 option D. Neither sales alone nor intermediate purchases alone is the correct flow for this calculation.
questions.hint: Measure production rather than sales, and input use rather than purchases.
questions.notes: Visual inspection confirms salesRs50000, notRs60000 from broken extraction.

solutionSteps.title: Measure output produced and inputs actually used
solutionSteps.body: Production value is sales plus the finished-goods inventory increase: $50000+7000=57000$. Intermediate consumption is purchases minus unused input inventory: $30000-2000=28000$. Value added is therefore $$57000-28000=29000,$$ option D. Neither sales alone nor intermediate purchases alone is the correct flow for this calculation.

questions.stem: An economy has100 labour units and1000 capital units. Each output unit needs.5 labour and4 capital. Every household’sAPC=MPC1/2. What autonomous expenditure sustains maximum feasible output?
questions.solution:
Find the binding productive capacity. Labour can support 100/0.5=200 output units, while capital can support 1000/4=250. Hence maximum feasible production is 200, limited by labour. With consumption Y/2, equilibrium at that output needs autonomous expenditure 
A=Y-C=200-100=100.
 Choose A. The spending multiplier alone does not determine the capacity ceiling.
questions.hint: Find the binding factor capacity before applying the multiplier.

solutionSteps.title: Find the binding productive capacity
solutionSteps.body: Labour can support $100/0.5=200$ output units, while capital can support $1000/4=250$. Hence maximum feasible production is 200, limited by labour. With consumption $Y/2$, equilibrium at that output needs autonomous expenditure $$A=Y-C=200-100=100.$$ Choose A. The spending multiplier alone does not determine the capacity ceiling.

questions.stem: A competitive firm pays output taxt and has costC(q,k)+K, withC_k<0,C_q>0,C_qq>0. If efficiency parameterk rises whilet is fixed, what is necessarily true?
questions.solution:
Use the envelope theorem, not an assumed output change. After-tax profit is (P-t)q-C(q,k)-K. Since C_k<0, higher k lowers cost even if the firm keeps its previous feasible output; optimizing again cannot undo that gain. At a regular optimum, 
(dπ^*)/(dk)=-C_k>0.
 Thus C is necessarily correct. The output derivative depends on the unspecified cross derivative C_(qk), so the total output tax tq need not move in a known direction.
questions.hint: Use the old feasible output as a comparison, or apply the envelope theorem.

solutionSteps.title: Use the envelope theorem, not an assumed output change
solutionSteps.body: After-tax profit is $(P-t)q-C(q,k)-K$. Since $C_k<0$, higher $k$ lowers cost even if the firm keeps its previous feasible output; optimizing again cannot undo that gain. At a regular optimum, $$\frac{d\pi^*}{dk}=-C_k>0.$$ Thus C is necessarily correct. The output derivative depends on the unspecified cross derivative $C_{qk}$, so the total output tax $tq$ need not move in a known direction.

questions.stem: In a sealed-bid second-price(Vickrey) auction the highest bidder wins and pays the second-highest bid. A painting is worth20000 to you. What should you bid?
questions.solution: Match the bid to the private valuation. Bid 20000, option C. Conditional on winning a second-price auction, the amount paid is the highest rival bid, not one's own bid. If that rival bid is below 20000, winning creates nonnegative surplus; if it is above 20000, winning creates a loss. A truthful bid wins in the first case and loses in the second, while shading or overbidding can only create a wrong decision. This is the usual weakly dominant private-value strategy.
questions.hint: Your own bid controls whether you win, not the price paid conditional on winning.

solutionSteps.title: Match the bid to the private valuation
solutionSteps.body: Bid 20000, option C. Conditional on winning a second-price auction, the amount paid is the highest rival bid, not one's own bid. If that rival bid is below 20000, winning creates nonnegative surplus; if it is above 20000, winning creates a loss. A truthful bid wins in the first case and loses in the second, while shading or overbidding can only create a wrong decision. This is the usual weakly dominant private-value strategy.

questions.stem: A person earnsY only in period1, savesS and consumes allS plus interest in period2. If the return rises from10% to12%, what happens to saving?
questions.answer: D:It may rise, fall or stay unchanged.
questions.solution: Separate the two interest-rate effects. A higher return makes future consumption cheaper relative to current consumption, inducing substitution toward saving. It also lets the person finance future consumption with less saving, creating an opposing income effect. Their relative strength is a preference property not supplied in the question. Log utility can make saving unchanged; CRRA examples with parameter below or above one make it rise or fall. Choose D: any of the three responses is possible.
questions.hint: Interest changes both intertemporal prices and the value of future purchasing power.

solutionSteps.title: Separate the two interest-rate effects
solutionSteps.body: A higher return makes future consumption cheaper relative to current consumption, inducing substitution toward saving. It also lets the person finance future consumption with less saving, creating an opposing income effect. Their relative strength is a preference property not supplied in the question. Log utility can make saving unchanged; CRRA examples with parameter below or above one make it rise or fall. Choose D: any of the three responses is possible.

questions.stem: Fill the blanks: In standard macroeconomic goods and money markets, ___ interest affects investment and consumption, while ___ interest affects real money demand.
questions.solution: Use the appropriate opportunity cost in each market. Investment and intertemporal consumption compare purchasing power across dates, so they depend on the real rate r≈ i-π^e. Holding non-interest-bearing money instead of interest-bearing nominal assets forgoes nominal interest i, making that the opportunity cost in real money demand. The blanks are therefore real, nominal: B. Calling money demand “real” does not make its interest argument the real rate.
questions.hint: Distinguish purchasing-power borrowing cost from the opportunity cost of cash.

solutionSteps.title: Use the appropriate opportunity cost in each market
solutionSteps.body: Investment and intertemporal consumption compare purchasing power across dates, so they depend on the real rate $r\simeq i-\pi^e$. Holding non-interest-bearing money instead of interest-bearing nominal assets forgoes nominal interest $i$, making that the opportunity cost in real money demand. The blanks are therefore real, nominal: B. Calling money demand “real” does not make its interest argument the real rate.

questions.stem: The real domain of f(x)=√x−√(3−x)+√(x²−4x) is
questions.solution: The first two radicals require 0≤x≤3. The third requires x≤0 or x≥4. The intersection is {0}.
questions.hint: Intersect the three radicand conditions.

questions.stem: The sum of the first n terms of 1/2+3/4+7/8+15/16+⋯ is
questions.solution: The kth term is 1−2^(−k). Summing gives n−Σₖ₌₁ⁿ2^(−k)=n−1+2^(−n).
questions.hint: Write each term as 1 minus a power of 1/2.

questions.stem: The matrix [[a,b,c],[b,c,a],[c,a,b]] is nonsingular only if
questions.answer: Both the second and third conditions are necessary
questions.solution: Its determinant is −(a+b+c)(a²+b²+c²−ab−bc−ca). Nonsingularity requires a+b+c≠0 and also not all a,b,c equal. Therefore both B and C are necessary conditions; A is stronger than necessary. The single-choice wording is ambiguous.
questions.hint: Factor the determinant and distinguish necessary from sufficient conditions.
questions.notes: Both B and C are necessary under the printed “only if”; there is no unique literal choice.

questions.stem: Find log tan1°+log tan2°+⋯+log tan89°.
questions.solution: Pair θ with 90°−θ. Since tanθ·tan(90°−θ)=1, their logarithms sum to zero. The unpaired term logtan45° also equals zero.
questions.hint: Pair complementary angles.

questions.stem: Let xₙ=cos(π/2ⁿ)+i sin(π/2ⁿ). The infinite product x₁x₂x₃⋯ equals
questions.solution: The product through N is exp(iπΣₙ₌₁ᴺ2^(−n))=exp(iπ(1−2^(−N))). Its limit is exp(iπ)=−1.
questions.hint: Add the arguments and sum a geometric series.

questions.stem: Let f(x)=f(−x) for every real x. If f′(0) exists, it equals
questions.solution: The difference quotient at −h is the negative of that at h because f(−h)=f(h). If both converge to the same derivative, it must equal its negative and therefore be zero.
questions.hint: Use evenness in the difference quotient.

questions.stem: In what ratio should a line be divided into two parts to maximize the rectangle having those side lengths?
questions.solution: If the total length is L, x(L−x) is maximized at x=L/2, giving two equal parts.
questions.hint: Maximize the product with a fixed sum.

questions.stem: Given ∫₀^∞x²/[(x²+a²)(x²+b²)(x²+c²)]dx=π/[2(a+b)(b+c)(c+a)], find ∫₀^∞1/[(x²+4)(x²+9)]dx.
questions.solution: Partial fractions give 1/[(x²+4)(x²+9)]=(1/5)[1/(x²+4)−1/(x²+9)]. Using ∫₀^∞dx/(x²+k²)=π/(2k), the result is (1/5)(π/4−π/6)=π/60.
questions.hint: Use partial fractions or take a→0 in the supplied identity.

questions.stem: The derivative of f(x)=|x|³ at x=0 is
questions.solution: The difference quotient is |h|³/h, whose absolute value is h²→0. Therefore the derivative exists and equals zero.
questions.hint: Use the derivative definition.

questions.stem: The coefficient of x²⁰ in (1−x²⁰)/(1−x)²−20x²⁰/(1−x) is
questions.solution: The coefficient from (1−x)⁻² is 21, from −x²⁰(1−x)⁻² is −1, and from −20x²⁰(1−x)⁻¹ is −20. Their sum is zero.
questions.hint: Use the coefficients of the geometric series and its derivative.

questions.stem: Find limₓ→₀tan³x/x².

questions.stem: As one moves downward along a demand curve, absolute price elasticity will fall if…
questions.answer: D is the familiar straight-line case, but B (downward and concave) also suffices under the usual interpretation. The item has more than one sufficient option.
questions.solution:
Differentiate elasticity rather than slope. For positive inverse demand P(Q) with P'<0, absolute elasticity is ε=-P/(QP'). Hence 
(ε')/(ε)=(P')/(P)-(1)/(Q)-(P'')/(P').
 A downward straight line makes this expression negative. But a downward concave inverse demand, P''≤0, also makes all three terms nonpositive, with the first two strictly negative.

Explain the multiple-sufficient-option problem. Thus both the concave option B and the straight-line option D ensure falling elasticity over the positive range under the usual smooth interpretation. Concavity of direct demand Q(P) also gives the same direction as price falls. Merely saying downward slope is insufficient. The item therefore lacks a unique sufficient-condition key; its review status is retained.
questions.hint: Differentiate elasticity, rather than confusing elasticity with slope.
questions.notes: B and D are both sufficient for positive downward-sloping demand under standard smooth definitions; no unique MCQ key.
options: Downward sloping and a straight line

solutionSteps.title: Differentiate elasticity rather than slope
solutionSteps.body: For positive inverse demand $P(Q)$ with $P'<0$, absolute elasticity is $\varepsilon=-P/(QP')$. Hence $$\frac{\varepsilon'}{\varepsilon}=\frac{P'}P-\frac1Q-\frac{P''}{P'}.$$ A downward straight line makes this expression negative. But a downward concave inverse demand, $P''\le0$, also makes all three terms nonpositive, with the first two strictly negative.

solutionSteps.body: Thus both the concave option B and the straight-line option D ensure falling elasticity over the positive range under the usual smooth interpretation. Concavity of direct demand $Q(P)$ also gives the same direction as price falls. Merely saying downward slope is insufficient. The item therefore lacks a unique sufficient-condition key; its review status is retained.

questions.stem: Monopoly demandP=20−Q, costC=15+10Q. A lump-sum tax15 is imposed. What tax revenue is collected?
questions.answer: Intended D:0 if the monopolist can avoid the levy and fixed costs by exiting. If the lump-sum tax is unavoidable, revenue is B:15.
questions.solution:
Calculate monopoly profit before the levy. With demand P=20-Q and marginal cost 10, MR=20-2Q=10 gives Q=5,P=15. Revenue is 75 and the stated total production cost is 15+10(5)=65, leaving pretax profit 10. A levy of 15 exceeds that profit.

Make the shutdown and tax-liability assumptions explicit. If exiting avoids the levy and the operating fixed commitment, the firm exits and tax revenue is zero, the intended D. If the levy is truly unavoidable regardless of operation, it does not alter the marginal output choice and government collects 15, B. Sunk versus avoidable production fixed costs can also change the participation comparison. Since the source does not specify these rules, an unconditional tax-revenue answer would conceal an economically important assumption.
