questions.stem: The open Keynesian model hasC=a+bY, autonomousG,I,X and importsM=.1Y. Which is necessarily false: MPC>1, MPC<1, .5<MPC<.7, or none of these?
questions.answer: Under the conventional extra assumption0<b<1, A is false. The printed equations alone only requireb<1.1 for positive equilibrium and do not rule out1<b<1.1.
questions.solution:
Derive the restriction implied by the displayed model. With imports 0.1Y, goods equilibrium is 
Y=a+bY+G+I+X-0.1Y ⇒ Y=(a+G+I+X)/(1.1-b).
 Positive equilibrium income with positive autonomous expenditure requires b<1.1, not necessarily b<1. For example b=1.05 gives a stable expenditure slope b-0.1=0.95 despite an MPC above one.

Distinguish the conventional extra assumption. If the usual psychological assumption 0<b<1 is imposed, A is necessarily false and is the intended textbook choice. The printed equations do not explicitly impose it. Under their literal algebra, none of the first three proposed MPC ranges is necessarily false. The record preserves this assumption-dependent distinction and remains marked for review.
questions.hint: Separate an assumed MPC restriction from a condition derived from the displayed equations.
questions.notes: The source does not explicitly impose0<b<1; conventional textbook and literal-equation readings differ.

solutionSteps.title: Derive the restriction implied by the displayed model
solutionSteps.body: With imports $0.1Y$, goods equilibrium is $$Y=a+bY+G+I+X-0.1Y\quad\Rightarrow\quad Y=\frac{a+G+I+X}{1.1-b}.$$ Positive equilibrium income with positive autonomous expenditure requires $b<1.1$, not necessarily $b<1$. For example $b=1.05$ gives a stable expenditure slope $b-0.1=0.95$ despite an MPC above one.

solutionSteps.title: Distinguish the conventional extra assumption
solutionSteps.body: If the usual psychological assumption $0<b<1$ is imposed, A is necessarily false and is the intended textbook choice. The printed equations do not explicitly impose it. Under their literal algebra, none of the first three proposed MPC ranges is necessarily false. The record preserves this assumption-dependent distinction and remains marked for review.

questions.stem: (a) Marginal cost isMC(Q)=a+bQ+cQ², witha,b,c>0. DeriveAVC and describeMC/AVC in one diagram. (b) Productionq=xy and both input prices1. If minimized cost is4, findq.
questions.answer: (a) AVC=a+(b/2)Q+(c/3)Q², increasing and belowMC forQ>0. (b) q4.
questions.solution:
Integrate marginal cost from zero output. Variable cost is the integral of marginal cost, taking variable cost at zero to be zero: 
VC(Q)=∫_0^Q(a+bz+cz^2) dz=aQ+(b)/(2)Q^2+(c)/(3)Q^3.
 A fixed cost, if any, is not part of this integral or of average variable cost.

Describe average and marginal variable cost. Dividing by positive output gives AVC=a+(b/2)Q+(c/3)Q^2. Both MC and AVC start at intercept a and increase convexly because all three coefficients are positive. Their difference 
MC-AVC=(b)/(2)Q+(2c)/(3)Q^2>0
 puts MC above AVC for every positive output. These are not U-shaped curves under the stated coefficient signs.

Invert minimized input cost in part (b). With q=xy and unit input prices, cost is x+y≥2√(xy)=2√(q), with equality at x=y. Thus minimized cost is 2√(q). Setting it to 4 gives q=4, attained at x=y=2. Equality is feasible, so the AM–GM bound really is the minimum.
questions.hint: Integrate marginal cost and applyAM–GM.

solutionSteps.title: Integrate marginal cost from zero output
solutionSteps.body: Variable cost is the integral of marginal cost, taking variable cost at zero to be zero: $$VC(Q)=\int_0^Q(a+bz+cz^2)\,dz=aQ+\frac b2Q^2+\frac c3Q^3.$$ A fixed cost, if any, is not part of this integral or of average variable cost.

solutionSteps.title: Describe average and marginal variable cost
solutionSteps.body: Dividing by positive output gives $AVC=a+(b/2)Q+(c/3)Q^2$. Both MC and AVC start at intercept $a$ and increase convexly because all three coefficients are positive. Their difference $$MC-AVC=\frac b2Q+\frac{2c}{3}Q^2>0$$ puts MC above AVC for every positive output. These are not U-shaped curves under the stated coefficient signs.

solutionSteps.title: Invert minimized input cost in part (b)
solutionSteps.body: With $q=xy$ and unit input prices, cost is $x+y\ge2\sqrt{xy}=2\sqrt q$, with equality at $x=y$. Thus minimized cost is $2\sqrt q$. Setting it to 4 gives $q=4$, attained at $x=y=2$. Equality is feasible, so the AM–GM bound really is the minimum.

questions.stem: A short-run monopolist operates two plants withTC₁=ax₁²+bx₁+c andTC₂=ax₂²+dx₂+e, all coefficients positive. Both plants produce at the optimum. Show that the higher-output plant has lower average variable cost.
questions.answer: At the common marginal costm, AVCᵢ=m−axᵢ, so higherxᵢ means lowerAVCᵢ.
questions.solution:
Use the common marginal-cost condition. Because both plants are active, profit maximization allocates total output so their marginal costs are equal: 
2ax_1+b=2ax_2+d=m.
 The common value m also equals marginal revenue from the combined output. Otherwise output could be shifted from the higher-marginal-cost plant to the lower-cost one to raise profit.

Express each average variable cost in that common value. The fixed costs c,e do not enter AVC. From the marginal-cost equalities, 
AVC_1 =ax_1+b=m-ax_1,; AVC_2 =ax_2+d=m-ax_2.
 Since a>0, the larger x_i has the smaller AVC. This result depends on the common quadratic coefficient, not just on the generic equality of marginal costs.
questions.hint: Express each linear cost coefficient using the common marginal cost.

solutionSteps.title: Use the common marginal-cost condition
solutionSteps.body: Because both plants are active, profit maximization allocates total output so their marginal costs are equal: $$2ax_1+b=2ax_2+d=m.$$ The common value $m$ also equals marginal revenue from the combined output. Otherwise output could be shifted from the higher-marginal-cost plant to the lower-cost one to raise profit.

solutionSteps.title: Express each average variable cost in that common value
solutionSteps.body: The fixed costs $c,e$ do not enter AVC. From the marginal-cost equalities, $$\begin{aligned}AVC_1&=ax_1+b=m-ax_1,\\AVC_2&=ax_2+d=m-ax_2.\end{aligned}$$ Since $a>0$, the larger $x_i$ has the smaller AVC. This result depends on the common quadratic coefficient, not just on the generic equality of marginal costs.

questions.stem: Project1 costs1000 now and pays100 per year forever from next year. Project2 costs2000 now and also pays100 per year forever from next year. Draw investment demand in rupees for all market interest rates.
questions.answer: For independent projects: investment3000 if0<r<5%;1000 if5%<r<10%;0 ifr>10%. At the cutoff rates the respective project has zeroNPV.
questions.solution:
Discount the perpetual returns. At a positive market rate r, a payment of 100 from next year forever has present value 100/r. The projects differ only in their initial outlays: 1000 and 2000. Project 1 therefore has positive NPV below 10%, while project 2 has positive NPV below 5%.

Construct the investment-demand steps. Assuming the two projects are independent and each can be undertaken once, 
I(r)=3000, 0<r<0.05,; 1000, 0.05<r<0.10,; 0, r>0.10.
 Investment is measured by the current outlay, so undertaking both means 3000 rather than the sum of their annual returns.

Handle the cutoff rates and project interpretation. At 5% the second project has zero NPV, giving investment either 1000 or 3000 depending on the tie decision. At 10% the first has zero NPV, giving either 0 or 1000. If projects were mutually exclusive, the more expensive identical-return project would be dominated and there would be no 3000 step. That is why independence is an explicit assumption. The ordinary finite perpetuity formula is not valid at nonpositive rates.
questions.hint: Compare the perpetuity present value with each setup cost.
questions.notes: The step-demand answer assumes independent one-time projects, not mutually exclusive alternatives.

solutionSteps.title: Discount the perpetual returns
solutionSteps.body: At a positive market rate $r$, a payment of 100 from next year forever has present value $100/r$. The projects differ only in their initial outlays: 1000 and 2000. Project 1 therefore has positive NPV below 10%, while project 2 has positive NPV below 5%.

solutionSteps.title: Construct the investment-demand steps
solutionSteps.body: Assuming the two projects are independent and each can be undertaken once, $$I(r)=\begin{cases}3000,&0<r<0.05,\\1000,&0.05<r<0.10,\\0,&r>0.10.\end{cases}$$ Investment is measured by the current outlay, so undertaking both means 3000 rather than the sum of their annual returns.

solutionSteps.title: Handle the cutoff rates and project interpretation
solutionSteps.body: At 5% the second project has zero NPV, giving investment either 1000 or 3000 depending on the tie decision. At 10% the first has zero NPV, giving either 0 or 1000. If projects were mutually exclusive, the more expensive identical-return project would be dominated and there would be no 3000 step. That is why independence is an explicit assumption. The ordinary finite perpetuity formula is not valid at nonpositive rates.

questions.stem: Poor people earn500/month and consume all. Middle-class people earn2000 and consume1500. Rich people earn10000 and consume80%. (a)20% of people are poor,50% middle class: find aggregate average propensity to save. (b) Equal numbers move poor→middle and middle→rich: what happens toAPS?
questions.answer: (a) APS17/82≈20.732%. (b) It increases slightly under the stated class incomes and saving rules.
questions.solution:
Aggregate income and saving separately. The poor save zero, middle-class people save 2000-1500=500 and rich people save 0.2(10000)=2000. With population shares (0.2,0.5,0.3), per-person aggregate totals are 
Y =0.2(500)+0.5(2000)+0.3(10000)=4100,; S =0.2(0)+0.5(500)+0.3(2000)=850.
 Therefore APS is 850/4100=17/82, about 20.732%. Averaging the three class saving ratios directly would use the wrong weights.

Track both equal population movements. Let fraction h move from poor to middle, and the same fraction from middle to rich. The middle share stays 0.5, while poor and rich shares become 0.2-h and 0.3+h. Income is then 4100+9500h and saving is 850+2000h.

Determine the direction of the ratio. Differentiate the new APS: 
(d)/(dh)(850+2000h)/(4100+9500h)=(2000(4100)-9500(850))/((4100+9500h)^2)=(125000)/((4100+9500h)^2)>0.
 APS rises slightly for feasible positive h. The result is not obtained by comparing only the middle-class saving rate with the rich rate; the two simultaneous transitions change aggregate income as well.
questions.hint: Aggregate total saving divided by total income; middle-class population is unchanged by equal opposing flows.

solutionSteps.title: Aggregate income and saving separately
solutionSteps.body: The poor save zero, middle-class people save $2000-1500=500$ and rich people save $0.2(10000)=2000$. With population shares $(0.2,0.5,0.3)$, per-person aggregate totals are $$\begin{aligned}Y&=0.2(500)+0.5(2000)+0.3(10000)=4100,\\S&=0.2(0)+0.5(500)+0.3(2000)=850.\end{aligned}$$ Therefore APS is $850/4100=17/82$, about 20.732%. Averaging the three class saving ratios directly would use the wrong weights.

solutionSteps.title: Track both equal population movements
solutionSteps.body: Let fraction $h$ move from poor to middle, and the same fraction from middle to rich. The middle share stays 0.5, while poor and rich shares become $0.2-h$ and $0.3+h$. Income is then $4100+9500h$ and saving is $850+2000h$.

solutionSteps.title: Determine the direction of the ratio
solutionSteps.body: Differentiate the new APS: $$\frac d{dh}\frac{850+2000h}{4100+9500h}=\frac{2000(4100)-9500(850)}{(4100+9500h)^2}=\frac{125000}{(4100+9500h)^2}>0.$$ APS rises slightly for feasible positive $h$. The result is not obtained by comparing only the middle-class saving rate with the rich rate; the two simultaneous transitions change aggregate income as well.

questions.stem: A shop offers either a fixed meal80g rice+50g dal for15, or freely chosen quantities at1 per10g rice and2 per10g dal. R chooses the fixed meal; S orders120g rice+15g dal, also costing15. (a) Describe indifference-curve diagrams. (b) With fixed-meal and rice prices unchanged but a higher dal price, must they change choices?
questions.answer: R’s fixed meal remains optimal. S’s response is not uniquely determined from rationality alone; with a fixed15 food budget the old quantity bundle becomes unaffordable and must change.
questions.solution:
Describe the two food opportunities. Using rice grams r and dal grams d, the à-la-carte expenditure is 0.1r+0.2d. S's order (120,15) costs 15. The fixed meal (80,50) also costs 15, but would cost 18 at the separate prices, so it appears as a distinct package point beyond the à-la-carte 15-budget line.

Explain the observed preferences graphically. R's highest attainable indifference curve passes through the package point, while S's passes through the chosen point on the separate-purchase line. Different preferences can support these different choices at the same expenditure. One cannot infer a unique indifference curve or a fixed consumption ratio merely from one observed order.

Apply revealed preference to R after the dal price rises. The unchanged package remains affordable at the same cost, whereas the à-la-carte opportunity set contracts when dal becomes dearer. Since R chose the package from the larger old set, it remains a maximizer in the smaller new set. No newly attractive alternative has been created.

State precisely what can be inferred for S. At a fixed 15 food budget, the old S bundle now costs more than 15 and is unavailable, so S must change the order or switch to the package. If other consumption can be reduced, S could retain the food quantities by spending more on them. Rationality alone does not identify S's new food quantities or guarantee a switch to the fixed meal. The source does not state that the entire available income is the 15 spent on this order.
questions.hint: Use revealed preference for the unchanged package and distinguish a fixed food budget from total income.
questions.notes: Source does not specify a fixed total food budget or preferences beyond rationality; the conditional answer avoids asserting a unique S response.

questions.stem: A consumer hasU(x₁,x₂)=x₁x₂, income650 and pricesp₁8,p₂2. Club membership lowers only good1’s price by50%. What is the maximum fee the consumer would just pay?
questions.solution:
Calculate the original indirect utility. For U=x_1x_2, maximizing utility at income M and positive prices gives half-income demands and indirect utility V=M^2/(4p_1p_2). Before joining the club, 
V_0=(650^2)/(4(8)(2))=(650^2)/(64).
 The scanned source says income 650, which matters for the fee calculation.

Include both the discount and the membership fee. After paying fee F, available spending is 650-F and the new good-1 price is 4. Therefore V_1=(650-F)^2/32. The fee cannot be evaluated by applying the price saving to the old bundle alone, because the consumer reoptimizes purchases.

Solve the participation condition. The largest acceptable fee equates the two indirect utilities: 
((650-F)^2)/(32) =(650^2)/(64),; 650-F =(650)/(√(2)),; F_(max) =650-325√(2)≈190.381.
 Take the positive remaining-income root. At the maximum the consumer is indifferent; any smaller fee yields a strict gain.
questions.hint: Equalize indirect utilities before and after paying the fee.
questions.notes: Visual inspection confirms the scanned income isRs650, notRs600 as the broken text extraction suggests.

solutionSteps.title: Calculate the original indirect utility
solutionSteps.body: For $U=x_1x_2$, maximizing utility at income $M$ and positive prices gives half-income demands and indirect utility $V=M^2/(4p_1p_2)$. Before joining the club, $$V_0=\frac{650^2}{4(8)(2)}=\frac{650^2}{64}.$$ The scanned source says income 650, which matters for the fee calculation.

solutionSteps.title: Include both the discount and the membership fee
solutionSteps.body: After paying fee $F$, available spending is $650-F$ and the new good-1 price is 4. Therefore $V_1=(650-F)^2/32$. The fee cannot be evaluated by applying the price saving to the old bundle alone, because the consumer reoptimizes purchases.

solutionSteps.body: The largest acceptable fee equates the two indirect utilities: $$\begin{aligned}\frac{(650-F)^2}{32}&=\frac{650^2}{64},\\650-F&=\frac{650}{\sqrt2},\\F_{max}&=650-325\sqrt2\approx190.381.\end{aligned}$$ Take the positive remaining-income root. At the maximum the consumer is indifferent; any smaller fee yields a strict gain.

questions.stem: A farmer owns1000 bushels now. Setting aside100 bushels yields110 next year. Utility isW=C₀C₁. With no capital market, how much should he consume in each year?
questions.solution:
Write the physical intertemporal budget. If s bushels are set aside now, current consumption is C_0=1000-s and future consumption is C_1=1.1s. With no capital market the farmer cannot transfer resources by borrowing; the only transfer mechanism is this physical return, with 0≤ s≤1000.

Maximize the product of consumption quantities. Substitute the budgets into utility: 
W(s)=1.1s(1000-s).
 Its derivative is 1.1(1000-2s) and its second derivative is -2.2. The unique maximum is therefore at s=500.

Report consumption and distinguish the annotation. The farmer consumes 500 bushels now and 1.1(500)=550 next year. The printed question contains only this no-capital-market part. A handwritten borrowing extension on the scan is not treated as an official subpart or as an instruction to supply extra assumptions.
questions.hint: Substitute the physical return into the intertemporal resource constraint.
questions.notes: Only printed subpart(a) is included. A handwritten borrowing-at5% extension appears below it but is not treated as an official question or instruction.

solutionSteps.title: Write the physical intertemporal budget
solutionSteps.body: If $s$ bushels are set aside now, current consumption is $C_0=1000-s$ and future consumption is $C_1=1.1s$. With no capital market the farmer cannot transfer resources by borrowing; the only transfer mechanism is this physical return, with $0\le s\le1000$.

solutionSteps.title: Maximize the product of consumption quantities
solutionSteps.body: Substitute the budgets into utility: $$W(s)=1.1s(1000-s).$$ Its derivative is $1.1(1000-2s)$ and its second derivative is $-2.2$. The unique maximum is therefore at $s=500$.

questions.solution: Solving y=1/x for x gives x=1/y. Equivalently f(f(x))=x on its positive domain.

questions.stem: Find limₙ→∞(2n³−3n)/(5n³+4n²−2).
questions.solution: Divide numerator and denominator by n³. The lower-degree terms vanish, leaving 2/5.
questions.hint: Compare the leading terms.

questions.stem: If x=log₁₂18 and y=log₂₄54, then xy+5(x−y) is
questions.solution: Let a=ln2 and b=ln3. Then x=(a+2b)/(2a+b), y=(a+3b)/(3a+b). Over the common denominator (2a+b)(3a+b), the numerator of xy+5(x−y) is (a+2b)(a+3b)+5(a²−b²)=6a²+5ab+b², exactly that denominator.
questions.hint: Express both logarithms using ln2 and ln3.

questions.stem: Maximize x₁+x₂ subject to x₁≥x₂−1, x₂≤2+x₁/2 and x₁,x₂≥0. The linear program
options: Has more than one optimal solution
questions.answer: No optimal solution: the objective is unbounded
questions.solution: For every t≥0, (x₁,x₂)=(t,0) satisfies all constraints and has objective value t. Thus feasible objective values have no upper bound.
questions.hint: Try setting x₂=0 and increasing x₁.

questions.stem: Given f(16)=16 and f′(16)=4, find limₓ→₁₆[√f(x)−4]/[√x−4].
questions.solution: Rationalize both differences to obtain [(f(x)−16)/(x−16)]·[(√x+4)/(√f(x)+4)]. Continuity from differentiability makes the second factor tend to 1 and the first to 4.
questions.hint: Rationalize the two square-root differences.

questions.stem: The integral ∫(2x³+1)/(x⁴+2x) dx equals
questions.solution: The derivative of the denominator is 4x³+2, twice the numerator. The substitution u=x⁴+2x yields half the integral of du/u.

questions.stem: Let (aₙ) be a real sequence not converging to zero. Then
options: For every ε>0 there exists N such that |aₙ|>ε
There exists ε>0 such that for every N, |aₙ|>ε for all n>N
There exists N such that |aₙ|>1/n for all n>N
questions.answer: No alternative correctly states the negation of convergence to zero
questions.solution: The correct statement is: some ε>0 has the property that for every N there exists n>N with |aₙ|≥ε. The source’s C instead says “for all n>N”. A sequence alternating 0 and 1 does not converge to zero, yet fails A,C,D. B is malformed because N does not occur in its concluding inequality and is false for bounded sequences under its natural readings.
questions.hint: Negate the quantifiers in the definition of convergence.
questions.notes: Source C explicitly says “for all n>N”; it is not silently replaced by “there exists n>N”. B has an unbound n in the source.

questions.answer: Source uses undefined T; if XT was intended as XY, then Z=X

questions.stem: A consumer consumes only two goods. If good1 has income elasticity1.2, what is the income elasticity of good2?
questions.answer: C:Less than1, assuming positive budget shares and an exhausted budget.
questions.solution:
Use income-elasticity adding-up. Let the positive budget shares be w_1,w_2, with w_1+w_2=1. Differentiating an exhausted budget at fixed prices gives w_1η_1+w_2η_2=1. Hence 
η_2=(1-1.2w_1)/(1-w_1)=1-(0.2w_1)/(1-w_1)<1.
 Choose C. The second good's elasticity can even be negative; it is not constrained to lie between one and 1.2.
questions.hint: Income elasticities have a budget-share weighted average of one.

solutionSteps.title: Use income-elasticity adding-up
solutionSteps.body: Let the positive budget shares be $w_1,w_2$, with $w_1+w_2=1$. Differentiating an exhausted budget at fixed prices gives $w_1\eta_1+w_2\eta_2=1$. Hence $$\eta_2=\frac{1-1.2w_1}{1-w_1}=1-\frac{0.2w_1}{1-w_1}<1.$$ Choose C. The second good's elasticity can even be negative; it is not constrained to lie between one and 1.2.

questions.stem: A Keynesian economy has consumptionC=15+Y^0.5 and autonomous investment plus government spending585. Find equilibriumY.
questions.solution:
Solve the square-root equilibrium with its domain. Goods equilibrium is Y=15+√(Y)+585=600+√(Y). Put s=√(Y)≥0: 
s^2-s-600=(s-25)(s+24)=0.
 The negative root s=-24 is not a valid square root. Therefore s=25 and Y=625, option C.
questions.hint: Set s=√Y and discard the negative root.

solutionSteps.title: Solve the square-root equilibrium with its domain
solutionSteps.body: Goods equilibrium is $Y=15+\sqrt Y+585=600+\sqrt Y$. Put $s=\sqrt Y\ge0$: $$s^2-s-600=(s-25)(s+24)=0.$$ The negative root $s=-24$ is not a valid square root. Therefore $s=25$ and $Y=625$, option C.

questions.stem: For a monopolist, marginal cost increases at every output. What happens to the profit-maximizing price?
questions.answer: Under the usual smooth, interior, strictly downward-sloping monopoly demand and regular second-order conditions: B, price rises. Without these assumptions only weak monotonicity is assured.
questions.solution:
Give the regular interior monopoly result. Under smooth downward inverse demand and a regular interior maximum, the upward marginal-cost shift lowers the quantity solving MR=MC. Strictly downward demand then raises price, giving the usual answer B. More generally, the increase in cost is an increasing function of quantity, so the chosen quantity cannot rise.

questions.stem: If government taxes10% of a monopolist’s profit, the monopolist will…
questions.solution: Compare the taxed and untaxed objectives. A proportional 10% pure-profit tax changes the objective from π(q) to 0.9π(q). Because 0.9 is positive, every ranking of quantities is unchanged. The monopolist therefore chooses the same profit-maximizing output: C. This is different from a tax on each output unit or on sales revenue, which changes marginal incentives.
questions.hint: Compare the before- and after-tax objective functions.

solutionSteps.title: Compare the taxed and untaxed objectives
solutionSteps.body: A proportional 10% pure-profit tax changes the objective from $\pi(q)$ to $0.9\pi(q)$. Because 0.9 is positive, every ranking of quantities is unchanged. The monopolist therefore chooses the same profit-maximizing output: C. This is different from a tax on each output unit or on sales revenue, which changes marginal incentives.

questions.stem: Competitive petrol demandQ_D=100−2P_c and supplyQ_S=3P_s. (i) Find untaxed equilibrium. (ii) With tax1 per litre, find consumer price, supplier price, quantity and excess burden.
questions.solution:
Clear the untaxed petrol market. Without tax, consumers and suppliers face the same price. Equating 100-2P=3P gives P_0=20 and Q_0=60. This is the comparison point for both tax incidence and welfare loss.

Introduce the price wedge. A one-rupee unit tax makes P_c=P_s+1. Substitute this into demand and equate it to supply: 
100-2(P_s+1) =3P_s,; P_s =19.6, P_c=20.6,; Q_1 =3(19.6)=58.8.
 Consumers bear 0.6 of the rupee through a price rise and suppliers bear 0.4 through a lower net receipt.

Measure the excess burden. The tax reduces trade by 60-58.8=1.2 litres. With linear demand and supply, the lost gains from those units form a triangle: 
DWL=(1)/(2)(1)(1.2)=0.6.
 Tax revenue is a transfer to government, so it is not itself the deadweight loss.
questions.hint: Use the tax wedge between the two prices.

solutionSteps.title: Clear the untaxed petrol market
solutionSteps.body: Without tax, consumers and suppliers face the same price. Equating $100-2P=3P$ gives $P_0=20$ and $Q_0=60$. This is the comparison point for both tax incidence and welfare loss.

solutionSteps.title: Introduce the price wedge
solutionSteps.body: A one-rupee unit tax makes $P_c=P_s+1$. Substitute this into demand and equate it to supply: $$\begin{aligned}100-2(P_s+1)&=3P_s,\\P_s&=19.6,\qquad P_c=20.6,\\Q_1&=3(19.6)=58.8.\end{aligned}$$ Consumers bear 0.6 of the rupee through a price rise and suppliers bear 0.4 through a lower net receipt.

solutionSteps.title: Measure the excess burden
solutionSteps.body: The tax reduces trade by $60-58.8=1.2$ litres. With linear demand and supply, the lost gains from those units form a triangle: $$DWL=\tfrac12(1)(1.2)=0.6.$$ Tax revenue is a transfer to government, so it is not itself the deadweight loss.

questions.stem: A consumer has U(x₁,x₂)=min(2x₁,x₂). (i) Describe an indifference curve. (ii) At prices5,10 and income100, find the optimal bundle. (iii) Price1 rises to8: decompose the change in good1 into income and substitution effects.
questions.answer: Initial bundle(4,8); final(25/7,50/7). Good1 total effect−3/7, substitution effect0 and income effect−3/7.
questions.solution:
Identify the kink ratio. For U=min{2x_1,x_2}, utility level u has kink (u/2,u). An efficient purchased bundle satisfies x_2=2x_1; buying additional units of only one good leaves utility unchanged.

Find the original and new Marshallian bundles. Initially the budget at the kink is (5+2×10)x_1=100, yielding (x_1,x_2)=(4,8). After the price rise, 
(8+20)x_1 =100,; x_1' =25/7, x_2'=50/7.

Compensate at the new prices. The old kink bundle now costs 8(4)+10(8)=112. At this compensated income the optimal bundle remains (4,8). Both Hicks and Slutsky compensation give the same result for this fixed-proportion case: no change in the quantity ratio can save expenditure while preserving utility.

Allocate the total change. The substitution effect for good 1 is zero. Its entire total change is the income effect: 
Δ x_1=(25)/(7)-4=-(3)/(7).
 A zero substitution effect does not mean the price increase has no consequence; it lowers the amount of the fixed-proportion bundle the original income can buy.
questions.hint: Perfect complements retain the same optimal quantity ratio after a price change.

solutionSteps.title: Identify the kink ratio
solutionSteps.body: For $U=\min\{2x_1,x_2\}$, utility level $u$ has kink $(u/2,u)$. An efficient purchased bundle satisfies $x_2=2x_1$; buying additional units of only one good leaves utility unchanged.

solutionSteps.title: Find the original and new Marshallian bundles
solutionSteps.body: Initially the budget at the kink is $(5+2\cdot10)x_1=100$, yielding $(x_1,x_2)=(4,8)$. After the price rise, $$\begin{aligned}(8+20)x_1&=100,\\x_1'&=25/7,\qquad x_2'=50/7.\end{aligned}$$

solutionSteps.title: Compensate at the new prices
solutionSteps.body: The old kink bundle now costs $8(4)+10(8)=112$. At this compensated income the optimal bundle remains $(4,8)$. Both Hicks and Slutsky compensation give the same result for this fixed-proportion case: no change in the quantity ratio can save expenditure while preserving utility.

solutionSteps.title: Allocate the total change
solutionSteps.body: The substitution effect for good 1 is zero. Its entire total change is the income effect: $$\Delta x_1=\frac{25}{7}-4=-\frac37.$$ A zero substitution effect does not mean the price increase has no consequence; it lowers the amount of the fixed-proportion bundle the original income can buy.

questions.stem: In a simple open Keynesian model, investment and exports are autonomous. What happens toGDP and aggregate imports when the propensity to import rises?
questions.answer: GDP falls; imports rise under the standard linear model.
questions.solution:
Write the open-economy equilibrium. Use C=C_0+cY, imports M=mY and autonomous investment and exports. Let A=C_0+Ī+X̄>0. Goods-market equilibrium gives 
Y=A+cY-mY ⇒ Y=(A)/(1-c+m).
 This uses the standard linear simple-Keynesian specification.

Find the output effect. Differentiate holding the autonomous components fixed: 
(dY)/(dm)=-(A)/((1-c+m)^2)<0.
 A greater fraction of each spending round now leaks into imports, reducing domestic income and the multiplier.

Differentiate actual imports as well. Actual imports are M=mA/(1-c+m), not just the parameter m. Their derivative is 
(dM)/(dm)=(A(1-c))/((1-c+m)^2)>0.
 Thus imports rise even though income falls. The direct propensity effect exceeds the indirect reduction generated by the lower income.
questions.hint: Differentiate actual imports mY, not just income.
questions.notes: Uses the standard proportional-import, affine-consumption simple-Keynesian formulation implicit in the question.

solutionSteps.title: Write the open-economy equilibrium
solutionSteps.body: Use $C=C_0+cY$, imports $M=mY$ and autonomous investment and exports. Let $A=C_0+\bar I+\bar X>0$. Goods-market equilibrium gives $$Y=A+cY-mY\quad\Rightarrow\quad Y=\frac A{1-c+m}.$$ This uses the standard linear simple-Keynesian specification.

solutionSteps.title: Find the output effect
solutionSteps.body: Differentiate holding the autonomous components fixed: $$\frac{dY}{dm}=-\frac A{(1-c+m)^2}<0.$$ A greater fraction of each spending round now leaks into imports, reducing domestic income and the multiplier.

solutionSteps.title: Differentiate actual imports as well
solutionSteps.body: Actual imports are $M=mA/(1-c+m)$, not just the parameter $m$. Their derivative is $$\frac{dM}{dm}=\frac{A(1-c)}{(1-c+m)^2}>0.$$ Thus imports rise even though income falls. The direct propensity effect exceeds the indirect reduction generated by the lower income.

questions.stem: IS–LM has C=a+bY, a>0,0<b<1, exogenous I₀,G₀ and money demand L=kY−gr, k,g>0. Nominal money is M₀, initial price P₀. (i) Set up equilibrium equations. (ii) How does a rise to P₁>P₀ affect Y and r?
questions.answer: Y*=(a+I₀+G₀)/(1−b), unchanged by the price rise. r*=[kY*−M₀/P]/g rises by(M₀/g)(1/P₀−1/P₁).
questions.solution:
Solve the goods market first. IS equilibrium is Y=a+bY+I_0+G_0. Because none of its spending components depends on interest, it fixes 
Y^*=(a+I_0+G_0)/(1-b).
 Thus IS is vertical in a graph with output horizontal and interest vertical.

Use money equilibrium to find interest. The LM equation is M_0/P=kY-gr, giving r=(kY-M_0/P)/g. Substituting the goods-market income identifies the equilibrium interest rate. The money equation adjusts interest to clear the market; it does not change the already fixed goods-market income in this specification.

Evaluate the price increase exactly. When the price level rises from P_0 to P_1>P_0, real balances fall and LM shifts upward/leftward. The vertical IS keeps output unchanged, while 
Δ r=(M_0)/(g)((1)/(P_0)-(1)/(P_1))>0.
 There is no investment crowding-out feedback here because investment is explicitly exogenous.
questions.hint: Notice that no goods-market component depends on interest.

solutionSteps.title: Solve the goods market first
solutionSteps.body: IS equilibrium is $Y=a+bY+I_0+G_0$. Because none of its spending components depends on interest, it fixes $$Y^*=\frac{a+I_0+G_0}{1-b}.$$ Thus IS is vertical in a graph with output horizontal and interest vertical.

solutionSteps.title: Use money equilibrium to find interest
solutionSteps.body: The LM equation is $M_0/P=kY-gr$, giving $r=(kY-M_0/P)/g$. Substituting the goods-market income identifies the equilibrium interest rate. The money equation adjusts interest to clear the market; it does not change the already fixed goods-market income in this specification.

solutionSteps.title: Evaluate the price increase exactly
solutionSteps.body: When the price level rises from $P_0$ to $P_1>P_0$, real balances fall and LM shifts upward/leftward. The vertical IS keeps output unchanged, while $$\Delta r=\frac{M_0}{g}\left(\frac1{P_0}-\frac1{P_1}\right)>0.$$ There is no investment crowding-out feedback here because investment is explicitly exogenous.

questions.stem: A competitive firm makesY=K^0.25L^0.25. Labour adjusts weekly and capital monthly; wage and capital rental are both10. The question explicitly supplies short-run cost10Y⁴/K̄ and long-run cost20Y². (i) At January’s start output price400: find long-run output and input hires. (ii) At week3 price rises to691.20; fixed capital remains: find short-run output and additional labour for the rest of January.
questions.answer: Using the supplied cost functions: initiallyY10,L100,K100. From week3, Y12 andL207.36, requiring107.36 additional workers per remaining week.
questions.solution:
Use the cost functions explicitly supplied. This version of the source provides long-run cost 20Y^2 and short-run cost 10Y^4/K̄. Follow those supplied functions rather than replacing them with a different weekly/monthly accounting convention. Fixed-capital costs omitted from the short-run expression do not affect its marginal output condition.

Choose the initial long-run quantity and inputs. At price 400, maximize 400Y-20Y^2. The first-order condition gives 400-40Y=0, so Y=10. Equal factor prices and the symmetric production function imply K=L. Since Y=K^(1/4)L^(1/4)=√(L) when they are equal, initial capital and labour are both 100.

Hold capital fixed after the third-week price rise. With K̄=100, short-run variable cost is 0.1Y^4, so marginal cost is 0.4Y^3. At the new price, 
0.4Y^3=691.20 ⇒ Y^3=1728 ⇒ Y=12.
 Capital cannot be rehired until the next month, so the long-run cost curve is inappropriate for this adjustment.

Calculate the additional workers. The production constraint gives L=Y^4/K̄=12^4/100=207.36. Compared with the original workforce 100, the increase is 107.36 workers for each remaining week with these conditions. Fractional values reflect the continuous-factor model. The source's time-unit conventions are not fully reconciled, but these computations consistently use its stated cost formulas.
questions.hint: Use the expressly supplied cost functions and hold capital fixed in the third week.

Fixed-capital costs omitted from the short-run expression do not affect its marginal output condition.

questions.stem: A patented drug monopolist facesP=100−X andC=25+X². (i) Find monopoly price and output. (ii) The patent expires, allowing unlimited entry of identical firms with the same cost. Find long-run competitive price, total output and number of firms.
questions.answer: MonopolyX25,P75,profit1225. Free-entry competition: each firmq5, price10, total output90 and18 firms.
questions.solution:
Solve the patented monopoly problem. Profit is 
π(X)=(100-X)X-(25+X^2)=100X-2X^2-25.
 Setting its derivative 100-4X equal to zero gives X_M=25 and P_M=75. The second derivative is negative. Revenue 1875 minus cost 650 gives monopoly profit 1225.

Apply the free-entry zero-profit condition. With identical firms entering, long-run price equals minimum average cost, not the old monopoly price. For one firm, 
AC(q)=(25)/(q)+q, MC(q)=2q.
 Average cost is minimized where -25/q^2+1=0, so each active firm produces 5 and the common competitive price is 10.

Clear industry demand and count firms. At price 10, total demand is 100-10=90. With each firm producing 5, the industry contains 90/5=18 firms. Each earns revenue 50 equal to total cost 25+25=50, confirming zero economic profit. The question continues on PDF page 2 in the supplied scan order.
questions.hint: For free entry use minimum average cost, not monopoly marginal revenue.
questions.notes: Question starts on PDFpage5 and continues on PDFpage2, printedbookletpage8.

solutionSteps.title: Solve the patented monopoly problem
solutionSteps.body: Profit is $$\pi(X)=(100-X)X-(25+X^2)=100X-2X^2-25.$$ Setting its derivative $100-4X$ equal to zero gives $X_M=25$ and $P_M=75$. The second derivative is negative. Revenue 1875 minus cost 650 gives monopoly profit 1225.

solutionSteps.title: Apply the free-entry zero-profit condition
solutionSteps.body: With identical firms entering, long-run price equals minimum average cost, not the old monopoly price. For one firm, $$AC(q)=\frac{25}q+q,\qquad MC(q)=2q.$$ Average cost is minimized where $-25/q^2+1=0$, so each active firm produces 5 and the common competitive price is 10.

solutionSteps.body: At price 10, total demand is $100-10=90$. With each firm producing 5, the industry contains $90/5=18$ firms. Each earns revenue 50 equal to total cost $25+25=50$, confirming zero economic profit. The question continues on PDF page 2 in the supplied scan order.

questions.stem: Two consumersA,B have identical utilityU=x₁x₂. Endowments areA(1,0),B(0,1). (i) Describe efficient allocations. (ii) Find competitive equilibrium. (iii) Duplicate each type, giving twoA and twoB with the same individual endowments and preferences: find equilibrium allocation.
questions.answer: Efficient allocations giveA(t,t),B(1−t,1−t),0≤t≤1. Equilibrium price ratio1 and each consumer receives(1/2,1/2), both before and after cloning.
questions.solution:
Derive the efficient allocations. Total endowments are (1,1). For interior allocations, equality of marginal rates of substitution gives 
(x_(A2))/(x_(A1))=(1-x_(A2))/(1-x_(A1)) ⇒ x_(A1)=x_(A2).
 Thus the contract curve is A=(t,t), B=(1-t,1-t), 0≤ t≤1. The endpoints are efficient too: helping the zero-utility person would reduce the other person's positive product utility.

Clear markets using half-income demands. Let prices be p_1,p_2>0. A's wealth is p_1 and B's wealth is p_2. Cobb–Douglas demands spend half of wealth on each good. Clearing good 1 requires 
(1)/(2)+(p_2)/(2p_1)=1,
 hence p_1=p_2. Both consumers receive (1/2,1/2).

Show why cloning does not alter individual consumption. With two copies of each type, aggregate stocks double to (2,2) and aggregate demands also double at the old prices. Each person's endowment value and demand at equal prices remain unchanged. Consequently the same price ratio clears the enlarged economy and all four people consume (1/2,1/2). This is replication, not an increase in any person's wealth.
questions.hint: Compute individual half-income demands and then clear markets; cloning scales supply and aggregate demand equally.

solutionSteps.title: Derive the efficient allocations
solutionSteps.body: Total endowments are $(1,1)$. For interior allocations, equality of marginal rates of substitution gives $$\frac{x_{A2}}{x_{A1}}=\frac{1-x_{A2}}{1-x_{A1}}\quad\Rightarrow\quad x_{A1}=x_{A2}.$$ Thus the contract curve is $A=(t,t)$, $B=(1-t,1-t)$, $0\le t\le1$. The endpoints are efficient too: helping the zero-utility person would reduce the other person's positive product utility.

solutionSteps.title: Clear markets using half-income demands
solutionSteps.body: Let prices be $p_1,p_2>0$. A's wealth is $p_1$ and B's wealth is $p_2$. Cobb–Douglas demands spend half of wealth on each good. Clearing good 1 requires $$\frac12+\frac{p_2}{2p_1}=1,$$ hence $p_1=p_2$. Both consumers receive $(1/2,1/2)$.

solutionSteps.title: Show why cloning does not alter individual consumption
solutionSteps.body: With two copies of each type, aggregate stocks double to $(2,2)$ and aggregate demands also double at the old prices. Each person's endowment value and demand at equal prices remain unchanged. Consequently the same price ratio clears the enlarged economy and all four people consume $(1/2,1/2)$. This is replication, not an increase in any person's wealth.

questions.solution: Integrate from 0 to t: X(t)−X(0)=∫₀ᵗ3s^(1/2)ds=2t^(3/2).

questions.stem: A and B are n×n matrices with det(AB)=0. Which statement must be true?
options: A and B are both nonsingular
At least one of A and B is singular
questions.answer: At least one factor is singular
questions.solution: The multiplicative determinant identity gives det(A)det(B)=0. Hence at least one determinant is zero, which is precisely singularity.
questions.hint: Use det(AB)=det(A)det(B).

questions.stem: The matrix [[a,b,c],[b,c,a],[c,a,b]] is nonsingular only if
questions.answer: Both the second and third conditions are necessary
questions.solution: Its determinant is −(a+b+c)(a²+b²+c²−ab−bc−ca). Nonsingularity requires a+b+c≠0 and also not all a,b,c equal. Therefore both B and C are necessary conditions; A is stronger than necessary. The single-choice wording is ambiguous.
questions.hint: Factor the determinant and distinguish necessary from sufficient conditions.
questions.notes: Source labels the last option (E), not (D). B and C are both correct under the printed “only if”.

questions.solution: Since x²+y²≤(x+y)²≤1 and x²≤1, 2x²+y²≤2. Equality occurs at (x,y)=(1,0).

questions.stem: In what ratio should a given line be divided so the rectangle with those two side lengths has maximum area?
questions.solution: If the total length is L, the area is x(L−x)=L²/4−(x−L/2)². Its maximum occurs when both parts equal L/2.
questions.hint: Complete the square in the area.

questions.stem: For 0<x<1, find the sum 1²+2²x+3²x²+4²x³+⋯.
questions.answer: The sum is (1+x)/(1−x)³; no printed alternative matches
questions.solution: Differentiating Σₙ≥₁nxⁿ=x/(1−x)² gives Σₙ≥₁n²xⁿ⁻¹=(1+x)/(1−x)³. The last alternative places −3 on x inside the parentheses, which makes it negative on 0<x<1 and cannot equal this positive sum.

questions.stem: Maximize x₁+x₂ subject to x₁+2x₂≤4, x₁+6x₂≤6, x₁−2x₂≤2, x₁,x₂≥0. An optimal solution is
questions.solution: Add 3/4 of the first inequality to 1/4 of the third: x₁+x₂≤3.5. The point (3,1/2) is feasible, including equality in the second constraint, and attains 3.5. Hence it is optimal.
questions.hint: Construct an upper bound by combining two constraints.

questions.stem: A consumer consumes only two goods. If good1 has income elasticity1.2, what is the income elasticity of good2?
questions.answer: C:Less than1, assuming positive budget shares and an exhausted budget.
questions.solution:
Use income-elasticity adding-up. Let the positive budget shares be w_1,w_2, with w_1+w_2=1. Differentiating an exhausted budget at fixed prices gives w_1η_1+w_2η_2=1. Hence 
η_2=(1-1.2w_1)/(1-w_1)=1-(0.2w_1)/(1-w_1)<1.
 Choose C. The second good's elasticity can even be negative; it is not constrained to lie between one and 1.2.
questions.hint: Income elasticities have a budget-share weighted average of one.

solutionSteps.title: Use income-elasticity adding-up
solutionSteps.body: Let the positive budget shares be $w_1,w_2$, with $w_1+w_2=1$. Differentiating an exhausted budget at fixed prices gives $w_1\eta_1+w_2\eta_2=1$. Hence $$\eta_2=\frac{1-1.2w_1}{1-w_1}=1-\frac{0.2w_1}{1-w_1}<1.$$ Choose C. The second good's elasticity can even be negative; it is not constrained to lie between one and 1.2.

questions.stem: If government taxes10% of a monopolist’s profit, the monopolist will…
questions.solution: Compare the taxed and untaxed objectives. A proportional 10% pure-profit tax changes the objective from π(q) to 0.9π(q). Because 0.9 is positive, every ranking of quantities is unchanged. The monopolist therefore chooses the same profit-maximizing output: C. This is different from a tax on each output unit or on sales revenue, which changes marginal incentives.
questions.hint: Compare the before- and after-tax objective functions.

questions.stem: Which transaction is excluded from GDP: paid domestic cooking/cleaning; purchase of a new personal car; a leisure flight; or purchase of100 company shares?
questions.solution: Distinguish new production from a financial claim. Paid domestic services, a newly produced personal car and a leisure flight purchase current goods or services. A purchase of company shares instead changes the ownership of financial claims. Thus choose D: the value of the shares is excluded from GDP. A separately charged financial-intermediation or brokerage service could count, but it is not the share-purchase amount itself.
questions.hint: Distinguish financial ownership from new production.

questions.stem: GroupA receives income shareα and groupB the rest. A has a higher propensity to consume and a lower income-related propensity to demand money. In IS–LM, what happens when income shifts fromA toB?
questions.answer: D:Output decreases, while interest may rise or fall.
questions.solution: Shift both markets rather than just consumption. Redistribution from A to B lowers consumption at each income because B's consumption propensity is smaller: IS shifts left. It also raises money demand at each income and interest rate because B's income-related money propensity is larger: LM shifts upward/left. Both changes reduce output. The IS shift lowers interest while the LM shift raises it, so the combined interest response is ambiguous. Choose D.
questions.hint: Track the separate shifts ofIS andLM.
options: Y may rise or fall,r falls
Y decreases,r may rise or fall

solutionSteps.body: Redistribution from A to B lowers consumption at each income because B's consumption propensity is smaller: IS shifts left. It also raises money demand at each income and interest rate because B's income-related money propensity is larger: LM shifts upward/left. Both changes reduce output. The IS shift lowers interest while the LM shift raises it, so the combined interest response is ambiguous. Choose D.

questions.stem: (a) A consumer always uses two spoons sugar per cup tea. Sugar costs p₁ per spoon, tea p₂ per cup, and income isy. Find demands. (b) Show which two utilities yield identical demands: (i)√(x₁x₂), (ii)x₁²x₂, (iii)log x₁+log x₂.
questions.answer: (a) Tea=y/(2p₁+p₂), sugar=2y/(2p₁+p₂). (b) Utilities(i) and(iii) have demandsxᵢ=y/(2pᵢ). Utility(ii) spends2/3 of income on good1 and1/3 on good2.
questions.solution:
Apply the tea-sugar fixed proportions. Let tea consumption be t cups. Sugar is then 2t spoons. Each complete consumption bundle costs 2p_1+p_2, so 
t=(y)/(2p_1+p_2), sugar=(2y)/(2p_1+p_2).
 Buying an unmatched extra quantity of either component does not improve utility.

Identify the identical preferences. On positive quantities, 
log x_1+log x_2=log(x_1x_2)=2log√(x_1x_2).
 This is a strictly increasing transformation of utility (i), so (i) and (iii) rank every positive bundle the same way. At positive income and prices their common demands are x_1=y/(2p_1) and x_2=y/(2p_2).

Show why the remaining utility differs. For utility (ii), x_1^2x_2, take logarithms to maximize 2log x_1+log x_2. Its first-order conditions give expenditure shares 2/3 and 1/3: 
x_1=(2y)/(3p_1), x_2=(y)/(3p_2).
 These generally differ from the half-income demands, establishing that exactly the first and third functions share the same demands.
questions.hint: Use the fixed ratio and then compare utility functions through monotone transformations.

solutionSteps.title: Apply the tea-sugar fixed proportions
solutionSteps.body: Let tea consumption be $t$ cups. Sugar is then $2t$ spoons. Each complete consumption bundle costs $2p_1+p_2$, so $$t=\frac{y}{2p_1+p_2},\qquad\text{sugar}=\frac{2y}{2p_1+p_2}.$$ Buying an unmatched extra quantity of either component does not improve utility.

solutionSteps.title: Identify the identical preferences
solutionSteps.body: On positive quantities, $$\log x_1+\log x_2=\log(x_1x_2)=2\log\sqrt{x_1x_2}.$$ This is a strictly increasing transformation of utility (i), so (i) and (iii) rank every positive bundle the same way. At positive income and prices their common demands are $x_1=y/(2p_1)$ and $x_2=y/(2p_2)$.

solutionSteps.title: Show why the remaining utility differs
solutionSteps.body: For utility (ii), $x_1^2x_2$, take logarithms to maximize $2\log x_1+\log x_2$. Its first-order conditions give expenditure shares $2/3$ and $1/3$: $$x_1=\frac{2y}{3p_1},\qquad x_2=\frac{y}{3p_2}.$$ These generally differ from the half-income demands, establishing that exactly the first and third functions share the same demands.

questions.stem: (a) A short-run profit-maximizing firm uses variable inputx₁ and fixed inputx₂. If the price ofx₂ falls, what happens tox₁ and profit? (b) A monopolist’s marginal cost rises5% and its price rises5%. Give a condition making this profit maximizing.
questions.answer: (a) Variable input choice is unchanged and profit increases by the fall in the fixed-input bill. (b) Constant-elasticity demand with absolute elasticityε>1 and constant marginal cost gives this proportional markup rule.
questions.solution:
Separate the variable decision from fixed-input expenditure. With the fixed factor held at x̄_2, write profit as pf(x_1,x̄_2)-w_1x_1-w_2x̄_2. Lowering w_2 changes only the final constant term. It does not alter the first-order condition pf_1=w_1 or the ranking of different feasible x_1 choices. Variable-input demand and output are therefore unchanged.

Measure the profit gain. At the unchanged input choice, the fall in the fixed-factor payment raises profit by -x̄_2Δ w_2>0. This is a short-run result. If the quantity of the second factor could change, it would no longer be a fixed-cost-only comparison.

Give a sufficient condition for proportional cost pass-through. Suppose monopoly demand is isoelastic, q=Ap^(-ε) with ε>1, and marginal cost is constant at c. Profit maximization implies 
p(1-(1)/(ε))=c ⇒ p=(ε)/(ε-1)c.
 The markup factor stays fixed, so a 5% increase in marginal cost causes a 5% increase in the optimal price. This is a sufficient condition, not a claim that every demand curve has full proportional pass-through.
questions.hint: Fixed-input costs do not affect a short-run marginal choice; constant elasticity gives a constant markup.

solutionSteps.title: Separate the variable decision from fixed-input expenditure
solutionSteps.body: With the fixed factor held at $\bar x_2$, write profit as $pf(x_1,\bar x_2)-w_1x_1-w_2\bar x_2$. Lowering $w_2$ changes only the final constant term. It does not alter the first-order condition $pf_1=w_1$ or the ranking of different feasible $x_1$ choices. Variable-input demand and output are therefore unchanged.

solutionSteps.title: Measure the profit gain
solutionSteps.body: At the unchanged input choice, the fall in the fixed-factor payment raises profit by $-\bar x_2\Delta w_2>0$. This is a short-run result. If the quantity of the second factor could change, it would no longer be a fixed-cost-only comparison.

solutionSteps.title: Give a sufficient condition for proportional cost pass-through
solutionSteps.body: Suppose monopoly demand is isoelastic, $q=Ap^{-\varepsilon}$ with $\varepsilon>1$, and marginal cost is constant at $c$. Profit maximization implies $$p\left(1-\frac1\varepsilon\right)=c\quad\Rightarrow\quad p=\frac{\varepsilon}{\varepsilon-1}c.$$ The markup factor stays fixed, so a 5% increase in marginal cost causes a 5% increase in the optimal price. This is a sufficient condition, not a claim that every demand curve has full proportional pass-through.

questions.stem: A competitive two-product firm hasC(q₁,q₂)=2q₁²+q₁q₂+2q₂². Output prices are12 and18. Find profit-maximizing quantities.
questions.solution:
Write the joint-profit first-order conditions. Profit is 12q_1+18q_2-2q_1^2-q_1q_2-2q_2^2. Each output affects the marginal cost of the other through the interaction term. Thus 
12-4q_1-q_2 =0,; 18-q_1-4q_2 =0.
 Solving the two equations gives q_1=2, q_2=4.

Verify that the stationary point is the maximum. The profit Hessian is [-4 -1; -1 -4], with eigenvalues -5 and -3. It is negative definite, so profit is strictly concave and the positive stationary point is the unique global maximum. Revenue is 96 and production cost 48, leaving profit 48.
questions.hint: Equate each output price to its marginal joint cost and check concavity.

solutionSteps.title: Write the joint-profit first-order conditions
solutionSteps.body: Profit is $12q_1+18q_2-2q_1^2-q_1q_2-2q_2^2$. Each output affects the marginal cost of the other through the interaction term. Thus $$\begin{aligned}12-4q_1-q_2&=0,\\18-q_1-4q_2&=0.\end{aligned}$$ Solving the two equations gives $q_1=2$, $q_2=4$.

solutionSteps.title: Verify that the stationary point is the maximum
solutionSteps.body: The profit Hessian is $\begin{pmatrix}-4&-1\\-1&-4\end{pmatrix}$, with eigenvalues $-5$ and $-3$. It is negative definite, so profit is strictly concave and the positive stationary point is the unique global maximum. Revenue is 96 and production cost 48, leaving profit 48.

questions.stem: Each other street-garbage dumper imposes costa, so the external harm to a person is an, where n is the number of other dumpers and a>0. Dumping oneself yields benefitG and private costC/n, C>0. (a) Explain no dumping ifn0. (b) Find the threshold number of other dumpers making dumping optimal.
questions.answer: ForG>0, dump iff n≥C/G; the least positive integer threshold is ceiling(C/G). It depends onC andG, not a. At n0 the printed costC/n requires a limiting convention.
questions.solution:
Compare only the payoff changed by one's own action. The harm an from the other dumpers is suffered whether or not this person dumps. It therefore cancels when comparing the two actions. The incremental private benefit from dumping is G-C/n for n>0. The social external damage matters for welfare but not for this private comparison.

Derive the threshold. For positive gain G, dumping is privately optimal exactly when 
G-(C)/(n)≥0 ⇔ n≥(C)/(G).
 For integer numbers of other people, the smallest threshold is ⌈ C/G⌉. Equality means indifference. Larger C raises the threshold, larger G lowers it, and a does not enter it.

Handle the zero-dumper case honestly. The printed expression C/n is undefined at n=0. The intended conclusion that nobody starts dumping requires defining solitary dumping as prohibitively costly, or using the limiting value C/n→+∞ as n↓0. Under that convention not dumping is optimal at zero others. This missing boundary definition is why the record retains its review flag.
questions.hint: Compare the incremental private payoffs; others’ pollution is common to both options.
questions.notes: The printed costC/n is undefined atn0. Intended infinite-cost limiting interpretation is stated explicitly.

solutionSteps.title: Compare only the payoff changed by one's own action
solutionSteps.body: The harm $an$ from the other dumpers is suffered whether or not this person dumps. It therefore cancels when comparing the two actions. The incremental private benefit from dumping is $G-C/n$ for $n>0$. The social external damage matters for welfare but not for this private comparison.

solutionSteps.title: Derive the threshold
solutionSteps.body: For positive gain $G$, dumping is privately optimal exactly when $$G-\frac Cn\ge0\quad\Leftrightarrow\quad n\ge\frac CG.$$ For integer numbers of other people, the smallest threshold is $\lceil C/G\rceil$. Equality means indifference. Larger $C$ raises the threshold, larger $G$ lowers it, and $a$ does not enter it.

solutionSteps.title: Handle the zero-dumper case honestly
solutionSteps.body: The printed expression $C/n$ is undefined at $n=0$. The intended conclusion that nobody starts dumping requires defining solitary dumping as prohibitively costly, or using the limiting value $C/n\to+\infty$ as $n\downarrow0$. Under that convention not dumping is optimal at zero others. This missing boundary definition is why the record retains its review flag.

questions.stem: Consumption depends only on income, investment only on interest, and G is exogenous. A unit rise in G shifts IS vertically upward by.5 at every income. Find dI/dr.
questions.solution:
Interpret a vertical IS shift at fixed income. Start from Y=C(Y)+I(r)+G. When finding how far IS shifts vertically, hold Y fixed; consumption is then fixed too. Differentiation gives 0=I'(r) dr+dG. This is not a movement along the original IS curve.

Recover the investment derivative. Therefore dr/dG=-1/I'(r). A one-unit government-spending increase raises the IS interest coordinate by 0.5, so 
0.5=-(1)/(I'(r)) ⇒ I'(r)=-2.
 The sign is economically consistent: a higher interest rate must reduce investment enough to offset the extra government spending while output is held fixed.
questions.hint: Hold income fixed when interpreting the vertical shift.

solutionSteps.title: Interpret a vertical IS shift at fixed income
solutionSteps.body: Start from $Y=C(Y)+I(r)+G$. When finding how far IS shifts vertically, hold $Y$ fixed; consumption is then fixed too. Differentiation gives $0=I'(r)\,dr+dG$. This is not a movement along the original IS curve.

solutionSteps.title: Recover the investment derivative
solutionSteps.body: Therefore $dr/dG=-1/I'(r)$. A one-unit government-spending increase raises the IS interest coordinate by 0.5, so $$0.5=-\frac1{I'(r)}\quad\Rightarrow\quad I'(r)=-2.$$ The sign is economically consistent: a higher interest rate must reduce investment enough to offset the extra government spending while output is held fixed.

questions.stem: In a closed Keynesian economy, outputY=f(N), withf′>0>f″. ConsumptionC=aY,0<a<1; autonomous investment isĪ, aggregate expenditureE=C+Ī, and equilibriumY=E. Find the employment multiplierdN/dĪ.
questions.solution:
Obtain the output multiplier. Goods equilibrium is Y=aY+Ī, so (1-a)Y=Ī. Differentiating with respect to autonomous investment gives dY/dĪ=1/(1-a). This is an output response, not yet an employment response.

Convert additional output into required employment. Technology gives Y=f(N) with f'(N)>0. Hence dY=f'(N)dN. Combining the two relationships yields 
(dN)/(dĪ)=(1)/((1-a)f'(N))>0.
 The derivative is evaluated at the starting equilibrium employment.

Interpret diminishing productivity. Because f''(N)<0, the marginal product falls as employment expands. A given additional amount of output then requires more additional labour at higher employment. Thus the employment multiplier need not be constant even when the income multiplier is constant.
questions.hint: Combine the income multiplier with the inverse marginal product of labour.

solutionSteps.title: Obtain the output multiplier
solutionSteps.body: Goods equilibrium is $Y=aY+\bar I$, so $(1-a)Y=\bar I$. Differentiating with respect to autonomous investment gives $dY/d\bar I=1/(1-a)$. This is an output response, not yet an employment response.

solutionSteps.title: Convert additional output into required employment
solutionSteps.body: Technology gives $Y=f(N)$ with $f'(N)>0$. Hence $dY=f'(N)dN$. Combining the two relationships yields $$\frac{dN}{d\bar I}=\frac{1}{(1-a)f'(N)}>0.$$ The derivative is evaluated at the starting equilibrium employment.

solutionSteps.title: Interpret diminishing productivity
solutionSteps.body: Because $f''(N)<0$, the marginal product falls as employment expands. A given additional amount of output then requires more additional labour at higher employment. Thus the employment multiplier need not be constant even when the income multiplier is constant.

questions.solution: The radicand is 4−4(x−1/2)². On its real domain it runs from 0 to 4, so its square root runs from 0 to 2 inclusive.

questions.stem: For 0<x<1, find the sum 1²+2²x+3²x²+4²x³+⋯.
questions.solution: Differentiate x/(1−x)²=Σₙ≥₁nxⁿ termwise on |x|<1. The derivative is (1+x)/(1−x)³=Σₙ≥₁n²xⁿ⁻¹.
questions.hint: Differentiate the series for Σnxⁿ.

questions.stem: Let F(y)=∫₀¹x²y dx and G(y)=y+|y|. Then
questions.solution: F(y)=y/3. For y>0, G(y)=2y and y/3<2y. At zero both vanish, so the option that includes zero with a strict inequality is false.

questions.answer: It is the two-sided inverse; A, B and C are all true
