questions.stem: Var(X)=4 and Var(Y)=9. Let V=Var(X−Y) when X,Y are independent and R=Var(X−Y) when Cov(X,Y)=2. Then
questions.solution: Var(X−Y)=Var(X)+Var(Y)−2Cov(X,Y). Independence gives V=13; covariance 2 gives R=13−4=9.
questions.hint: Use the variance formula for a difference.

questions.stem: Veena always consumes y=3x and pₓ=3pᵧ. She owns18 units x and78 units y, tradable at market prices, with no other income. How much x does she buy from the market?
questions.answer: C:4 units of net x purchases.
questions.solution:
Value the endowment and enforce the consumption ratio. Use the banana-like second good's price as numeraire. Wealth is 3(18)+78=132. With y=3x, spending is 3x+y=6x, so final consumption is x=22,y=66.

Answer the net-purchase question. Veena already owns 18 units of x, so market purchases are 22-18=4, option C. She sells 12 units of y to finance them. Final consumption 22 is not the requested quantity bought from the market.
questions.hint: Value the endowment and distinguish final demand from net trade.
options: Cannot determine without the absolute price of x

solutionSteps.title: Value the endowment and enforce the consumption ratio
solutionSteps.body: Use the banana-like second good's price as numeraire. Wealth is $3(18)+78=132$. With $y=3x$, spending is $3x+y=6x$, so final consumption is $x=22,y=66$.

solutionSteps.title: Answer the net-purchase question
solutionSteps.body: Veena already owns 18 units of $x$, so market purchases are $22-18=4$, option C. She sells 12 units of $y$ to finance them. Final consumption 22 is not the requested quantity bought from the market.

questions.stem: Utility is U(C,M/P), depending on consumption C and real balances M/P. Budget is PC+M=M̄, where M̄ is initial nominal wealth. What is the substitution effect of higher P on C?
questions.solution:
Express the two utility arguments in real units. Divide PC+M=M̄ by P to obtain 
C+(M)/(P)=(M̄)/(P).
 Consumption and real balances always have relative price one. A higher P changes real wealth but does not change their relative price, so its pure substitution effect on consumption is zero. Choose A; any remaining demand change is an income effect.
questions.hint: Divide the nominal budget by P.

solutionSteps.title: Express the two utility arguments in real units
solutionSteps.body: Divide $PC+M=\bar M$ by $P$ to obtain $$C+\frac MP=\frac{\bar M}P.$$ Consumption and real balances always have relative price one. A higher $P$ changes real wealth but does not change their relative price, so its pure substitution effect on consumption is zero. Choose A; any remaining demand change is an income effect.

questions.stem: A monopolist has no fixed cost, MC5 and demand D(p)=10/p if0<p≤10, zero ifp>10. Only integer outputs are possible. Find optimal output.
questions.solution: Use revenue and the integer-output restriction. For any positive feasible integer quantity q, the inverse demand is p=10/q and revenue is 10. Profit is therefore 10-5q, greatest at the smallest positive integer q=1. That yields profit 5, above shutdown profit zero. Choose B. Sending output toward zero is not feasible because fractional production is forbidden.
questions.hint: Revenue is constant across positive feasible integer outputs.

solutionSteps.title: Use revenue and the integer-output restriction
solutionSteps.body: For any positive feasible integer quantity $q$, the inverse demand is $p=10/q$ and revenue is 10. Profit is therefore $10-5q$, greatest at the smallest positive integer $q=1$. That yields profit 5, above shutdown profit zero. Choose B. Sending output toward zero is not feasible because fractional production is forbidden.

questions.stem: Domestic production of capital goods rises by100, of which80 are sold and20 unsold. Imports of capital goods simultaneously decline by30. Everything else is unchanged. By how much does GDP rise?
questions.solution:
Include output inventories and imported investment consistently. Domestic capital-goods output adds 100, including the 20 not sold. Total investment rises by 80+20-30=70 because imported capital-goods purchases fall by 30. In expenditure accounting, 
Δ GDP=Δ I-Δ M=70-(-30)=100.
 Choose D. Adding the import decline directly to domestic output would count the import adjustment twice.
questions.hint: Include inventories and remove imported investment consistently.
questions.notes: Handwritten ticks in the scan are not an official answer key and are not used.

solutionSteps.title: Include output inventories and imported investment consistently
solutionSteps.body: Domestic capital-goods output adds 100, including the 20 not sold. Total investment rises by $80+20-30=70$ because imported capital-goods purchases fall by 30. In expenditure accounting, $$\Delta GDP=\Delta I-\Delta M=70-(-30)=100.$$ Choose D. Adding the import decline directly to domestic output would count the import adjustment twice.

questions.stem: A consumer buys X,Y. Y costs pᵧ; X can be bought at a high price p_H or a lower price p_L available only after t hours of search. He normally works8 hours daily at wage w. (i) Describe the budget set and an equilibrium choosing the lower price. (ii) Can higher w make him choose the higher price?
questions.answer: Budget is the union of p_Hx+pᵧy≤8w and p_Lx+pᵧy≤(8−t)w, if search displaces work. Yes, higher wages can make shopping time too costly.
questions.solution:
Value the search time. The cheaper shop saves money on each unit but requires t hours that could otherwise be worked. If search displaces paid work from an eight-hour day, high-price shopping leaves income 8w, while searching leaves (8-t)w. This opportunity-cost interpretation must be stated rather than treating search as free.

Describe the two budgets and their envelope. The alternatives are 
p_Hx+p_yy≤8w, p_Lx+p_yy≤(8-t)w,
 where p_L<p_H. The lines cross at x^*=wt/(p_H-p_L). The high-price line is the exposed boundary for smaller quantities, and the low-price line for larger quantities. An optimum choosing the cheaper shop is a highest attainable indifference curve touching that exposed low-price branch.

Demonstrate a wage-induced switch with an example. A higher wage increases the search cost wt, so a switch to the high-price shop is possible. Take p_y=1,p_H=2,p_L=1,t=1 and U=log x+y. At affordable interior choices, the high-price optimum has x=1/2 and indirect utility 8w-1-log2; the low-price optimum has x=1 and utility 7w-1. Search is preferred iff w<log2. Thus a wage rise from 0.5 to 1 switches the choice. This is a possibility result; homothetic preferences, for example, can give no switch when both opportunities simply scale with the wage.
questions.hint: Price savings must compensate for foregone wages while searching.
questions.notes: The source does not explicitly say search reduces paid work; this opportunity-cost interpretation is stated.

solutionSteps.title: Value the search time
solutionSteps.body: The cheaper shop saves money on each unit but requires $t$ hours that could otherwise be worked. If search displaces paid work from an eight-hour day, high-price shopping leaves income $8w$, while searching leaves $(8-t)w$. This opportunity-cost interpretation must be stated rather than treating search as free.

solutionSteps.title: Describe the two budgets and their envelope
solutionSteps.body: The alternatives are $$p_Hx+p_yy\le8w,\qquad p_Lx+p_yy\le(8-t)w,$$ where $p_L<p_H$. The lines cross at $x^*=wt/(p_H-p_L)$. The high-price line is the exposed boundary for smaller quantities, and the low-price line for larger quantities. An optimum choosing the cheaper shop is a highest attainable indifference curve touching that exposed low-price branch.

solutionSteps.title: Demonstrate a wage-induced switch with an example
solutionSteps.body: A higher wage increases the search cost $wt$, so a switch to the high-price shop is possible. Take $p_y=1,p_H=2,p_L=1,t=1$ and $U=\log x+y$. At affordable interior choices, the high-price optimum has $x=1/2$ and indirect utility $8w-1-\log2$; the low-price optimum has $x=1$ and utility $7w-1$. Search is preferred iff $w<\log2$. Thus a wage rise from $0.5$ to 1 switches the choice. This is a possibility result; homothetic preferences, for example, can give no switch when both opportunities simply scale with the wage.

questions.stem: Telephone planA costs fixed500 plus2 per call; planB costs fixed1000 plus1 per call. Three consumers have identical incomes: one choosesA, oneB, one neither. (i) Describe budget contours and indifference curves for these choices. (ii) Could the non-subscriber have an ordinary Cobb–Douglas utility over calls and other consumption?
questions.answer: With other consumption as numeraire: A gives o=M−500−2q, B gives o=M−1000−q; no subscription gives(q,o)=(0,M). The third cannot have Cobb–Douglas utility with strictly positive exponents when a positive-call plan is affordable.
questions.solution:
Plot the two subscription opportunities. Let calls be q and other consumption, priced at one, be o. The two subscription frontiers are 
o_A=M-500-2q, o_B=M-1000-q.
 They cross at q=500. Plan A is cheaper for fewer calls and plan B for more calls. Also include the no-subscription point (q,o)=(0,M); it is not obtained by paying a fixed fee and then making zero calls.

Represent the three observed choices. Consumers may have different indifference maps despite equal incomes. Draw a highest attainable indifference curve touching the exposed A branch for the first person, one touching the exposed B branch for the second, and one through the no-subscription point for the third. The third person values keeping the fixed fee more than access to calls at either tariff.

Test ordinary Cobb–Douglas preferences. If the third consumer had U=q^α o^β with both exponents positive, no subscription would give utility zero. An affordable bundle with positive calls and positive other consumption would give positive utility. The common income supports the second consumer's B subscription, so it certainly supports such a positive bundle under A. Therefore the third person's non-subscription cannot be optimal under ordinary two-good Cobb–Douglas preferences. A utility with a nonessential calls good could represent it.
questions.hint: Include the discrete no-subscription option outside the two subscription lines.

solutionSteps.title: Plot the two subscription opportunities
solutionSteps.body: Let calls be $q$ and other consumption, priced at one, be $o$. The two subscription frontiers are $$o_A=M-500-2q,\qquad o_B=M-1000-q.$$ They cross at $q=500$. Plan A is cheaper for fewer calls and plan B for more calls. Also include the no-subscription point $(q,o)=(0,M)$; it is not obtained by paying a fixed fee and then making zero calls.

solutionSteps.title: Represent the three observed choices
solutionSteps.body: Consumers may have different indifference maps despite equal incomes. Draw a highest attainable indifference curve touching the exposed A branch for the first person, one touching the exposed B branch for the second, and one through the no-subscription point for the third. The third person values keeping the fixed fee more than access to calls at either tariff.

solutionSteps.title: Test ordinary Cobb–Douglas preferences
solutionSteps.body: If the third consumer had $U=q^\alpha o^\beta$ with both exponents positive, no subscription would give utility zero. An affordable bundle with positive calls and positive other consumption would give positive utility. The common income supports the second consumer's B subscription, so it certainly supports such a positive bundle under A. Therefore the third person's non-subscription cannot be optimal under ordinary two-good Cobb–Douglas preferences. A utility with a nonessential calls good could represent it.

questions.stem: A buyer has one50-rupee note. Rice and pulses are sold at prices p_r,p_p. The rice seller gives change only if at least3kg rice is bought; the pulses seller never gives change. (i) Describe the budget. (ii) Find the optimum for fixed-proportion consumption. (iii) Find the maximum fee an outside money changer could charge. (iv) How does a pulses-price rise affect purchases and the fee?
questions.answer: Under the standard rice-first/change interpretation, ordinary trade with both goods requires rice≥3. Let desired ratio be(r,p)=(az,bz). If the unconstrained rice demand is below3, z₀=(50−3p_r)/(bp_p), and maximal change fee is F_max=50−(ap_r+bp_p)z₀. In that binding region higher p_p reduces z₀ and raises F_max.
questions.solution:
State the cash interpretation and preferred ratio. The source does not specify cash denominations or exact-payment arrangements. Use the standard interpretation: buying at least 3 kg of rice produces usable change for a later pulse purchase. Let rice and pulse prices be p_r,p_p, and the preferred fixed proportions be (r,p)=(az,bz), with a,b>0. Assume 3p_r≤50.

Find whether the minimum rice purchase binds. Without the change problem the balanced demand is z^*=50/(ap_r+bp_p). If az^*≥3, it is already attainable and the money-changing service has no value. If az^*<3, the ordinary optimum is excluded. On the relevant cash frontier rice must be at least 3, so buy rice 3 and spend the remainder on pulses.

Measure the utility of the restricted purchase. In the binding case, pulses are (50-3p_r)/p_p. The effective number of fixed-proportion consumption bundles is 
z_0=(50-3p_r)/(bp_p)<(3)/(a).
 The rice above az_0 is excess relative to the preferred ratio. The budget frontier is the ordinary line p_rr+p_pp=50 truncated at r≥3 for purchases of both goods, together with possible one-good cash purchases.

Calculate the maximal acceptable fee. Paying fee F restores an ordinary budget of 50-F and permits balanced demand z_F=(50-F)/(ap_r+bp_p). The largest fee that leaves the consumer no worse off solves z_F=z_0: 
F_(max)=50-(ap_r+bp_p)z_0.
 At this fee the consumer is indifferent; a slightly smaller fee gives strict participation. If the original minimum does not bind, F_(max)=0.

Explain the pulse-price comparative static. In the binding region, higher p_p lowers z_0. Moreover 
(dF_(max))/(dp_p)=(ap_r(50-3p_r))/(bp_p^2)>0
 when the remaining cash is positive. Without a changer, rice stays at 3 and pulses fall. With a fully extracting changer, both balanced quantities az_0,bz_0 fall. These are conditional symbolic conclusions, not a unique numerical purchase from an incomplete cash mechanism.
questions.hint: Compare utility under the minimum-rice restriction with utility under an ordinary budget reduced by a fee.
questions.notes: Cash/change mechanics are incomplete, and prices and desired ratio are unspecified. The standard continuous-goods, rice-first interpretation is explicit; source repeats subpart label(iii).

solutionSteps.title: State the cash interpretation and preferred ratio
solutionSteps.body: The source does not specify cash denominations or exact-payment arrangements. Use the standard interpretation: buying at least 3 kg of rice produces usable change for a later pulse purchase. Let rice and pulse prices be $p_r,p_p$, and the preferred fixed proportions be $(r,p)=(az,bz)$, with $a,b>0$. Assume $3p_r\le50$.

solutionSteps.title: Find whether the minimum rice purchase binds
solutionSteps.body: Without the change problem the balanced demand is $z^*=50/(ap_r+bp_p)$. If $az^*\ge3$, it is already attainable and the money-changing service has no value. If $az^*<3$, the ordinary optimum is excluded. On the relevant cash frontier rice must be at least 3, so buy rice 3 and spend the remainder on pulses.

solutionSteps.title: Measure the utility of the restricted purchase
solutionSteps.body: In the binding case, pulses are $(50-3p_r)/p_p$. The effective number of fixed-proportion consumption bundles is $$z_0=\frac{50-3p_r}{bp_p}<\frac3a.$$ The rice above $az_0$ is excess relative to the preferred ratio. The budget frontier is the ordinary line $p_rr+p_pp=50$ truncated at $r\ge3$ for purchases of both goods, together with possible one-good cash purchases.

solutionSteps.title: Calculate the maximal acceptable fee
solutionSteps.body: Paying fee $F$ restores an ordinary budget of $50-F$ and permits balanced demand $z_F=(50-F)/(ap_r+bp_p)$. The largest fee that leaves the consumer no worse off solves $z_F=z_0$: $$F_{max}=50-(ap_r+bp_p)z_0.$$ At this fee the consumer is indifferent; a slightly smaller fee gives strict participation. If the original minimum does not bind, $F_{max}=0$.

solutionSteps.title: Explain the pulse-price comparative static
solutionSteps.body: In the binding region, higher $p_p$ lowers $z_0$. Moreover $$\frac{dF_{max}}{dp_p}=\frac{ap_r(50-3p_r)}{bp_p^2}>0$$ when the remaining cash is positive. Without a changer, rice stays at 3 and pulses fall. With a fully extracting changer, both balanced quantities $az_0,bz_0$ fall. These are conditional symbolic conclusions, not a unique numerical purchase from an incomplete cash mechanism.

questions.stem: Each other street-garbage dumper imposes costa, so the external harm to a person is an, where n is the number of other dumpers and a>0. Dumping oneself yields benefitG and private costC/n, C>0. (a) Explain no dumping ifn0. (b) Find the threshold number of other dumpers making dumping optimal.
questions.answer: ForG>0, dump iff n≥C/G; the least positive integer threshold is ceiling(C/G). It depends onC andG, not a. At n0 the printed costC/n requires a limiting convention.
questions.solution:
Compare only the payoff changed by one's own action. The harm an from the other dumpers is suffered whether or not this person dumps. It therefore cancels when comparing the two actions. The incremental private benefit from dumping is G-C/n for n>0. The social external damage matters for welfare but not for this private comparison.

Derive the threshold. For positive gain G, dumping is privately optimal exactly when 
G-(C)/(n)≥0 ⇔ n≥(C)/(G).
 For integer numbers of other people, the smallest threshold is ⌈ C/G⌉. Equality means indifference. Larger C raises the threshold, larger G lowers it, and a does not enter it.

Handle the zero-dumper case honestly. The printed expression C/n is undefined at n=0. The intended conclusion that nobody starts dumping requires defining solitary dumping as prohibitively costly, or using the limiting value C/n→+∞ as n↓0. Under that convention not dumping is optimal at zero others. This missing boundary definition is why the record retains its review flag.
questions.hint: Compare the incremental private payoffs; others’ pollution is common to both options.
questions.notes: The printed costC/n is undefined atn0. Intended infinite-cost limiting interpretation is stated explicitly.

solutionSteps.title: Compare only the payoff changed by one's own action
solutionSteps.body: The harm $an$ from the other dumpers is suffered whether or not this person dumps. It therefore cancels when comparing the two actions. The incremental private benefit from dumping is $G-C/n$ for $n>0$. The social external damage matters for welfare but not for this private comparison.

solutionSteps.title: Derive the threshold
solutionSteps.body: For positive gain $G$, dumping is privately optimal exactly when $$G-\frac Cn\ge0\quad\Leftrightarrow\quad n\ge\frac CG.$$ For integer numbers of other people, the smallest threshold is $\lceil C/G\rceil$. Equality means indifference. Larger $C$ raises the threshold, larger $G$ lowers it, and $a$ does not enter it.

solutionSteps.title: Handle the zero-dumper case honestly
solutionSteps.body: The printed expression $C/n$ is undefined at $n=0$. The intended conclusion that nobody starts dumping requires defining solitary dumping as prohibitively costly, or using the limiting value $C/n\to+\infty$ as $n\downarrow0$. Under that convention not dumping is optimal at zero others. This missing boundary definition is why the record retains its review flag.

questions.stem: Consumption depends only on income, investment only on interest, and G is exogenous. A unit rise in G shifts IS vertically upward by.5 at every income. Find dI/dr.
questions.solution:
Interpret a vertical IS shift at fixed income. Start from Y=C(Y)+I(r)+G. When finding how far IS shifts vertically, hold Y fixed; consumption is then fixed too. Differentiation gives 0=I'(r) dr+dG. This is not a movement along the original IS curve.

Recover the investment derivative. Therefore dr/dG=-1/I'(r). A one-unit government-spending increase raises the IS interest coordinate by 0.5, so 
0.5=-(1)/(I'(r)) ⇒ I'(r)=-2.
 The sign is economically consistent: a higher interest rate must reduce investment enough to offset the extra government spending while output is held fixed.
questions.hint: Hold income fixed when interpreting the vertical shift.

solutionSteps.title: Interpret a vertical IS shift at fixed income
solutionSteps.body: Start from $Y=C(Y)+I(r)+G$. When finding how far IS shifts vertically, hold $Y$ fixed; consumption is then fixed too. Differentiation gives $0=I'(r)\,dr+dG$. This is not a movement along the original IS curve.

solutionSteps.title: Recover the investment derivative
solutionSteps.body: Therefore $dr/dG=-1/I'(r)$. A one-unit government-spending increase raises the IS interest coordinate by 0.5, so $$0.5=-\frac1{I'(r)}\quad\Rightarrow\quad I'(r)=-2.$$ The sign is economically consistent: a higher interest rate must reduce investment enough to offset the extra government spending while output is held fixed.

questions.stem: In a simple Keynesian economy without government, planned investment is7. AtY0, consumption is one-half of planned aggregate demand. AtY30, unplanned inventory accumulation is5. Find the autonomous-spending multiplier.
questions.answer: Multiplier30/19, assuming an affine consumption schedule.
questions.solution:
Recover autonomous consumption. Use the usual affine simple-Keynesian schedule C=a+bY, with planned investment 7. At zero output, planned demand is E_0=a+7. Consumption is half of that demand, so 
(a)/(a+7)=(1)/(2) ⇒ a=7, E_0=14.

Use the unplanned inventory information. Unplanned inventory accumulation means production exceeds intended expenditure. At Y=30, accumulation 5 implies E(30)=25. Hence 
14+30b=25 ⇒ b=(11)/(30).
 Confusing inventory accumulation with excess demand would reverse this subtraction.

Calculate the multiplier. The autonomous-spending multiplier is 
(1)/(1-b)=(1)/(1-11/30)=(30)/(19).
 The question's continuation is on PDF page 2, despite starting on page 6, so both pieces of source information are needed. Linearity is the standard simple-Keynesian interpretation used in obtaining a single slope from the observations.
questions.hint: Unplanned inventory accumulation meansY exceeds planned demand.
questions.notes: Question starts on PDFpage6 and continues on PDFpage2 because of the booklet’s unusual scan order. Linear consumption is the usual simple-Keynesian interpretation.

solutionSteps.title: Recover autonomous consumption
solutionSteps.body: Use the usual affine simple-Keynesian schedule $C=a+bY$, with planned investment 7. At zero output, planned demand is $E_0=a+7$. Consumption is half of that demand, so $$\frac{a}{a+7}=\frac12\quad\Rightarrow\quad a=7,\ E_0=14.$$

solutionSteps.title: Use the unplanned inventory information
solutionSteps.body: Unplanned inventory accumulation means production exceeds intended expenditure. At $Y=30$, accumulation 5 implies $E(30)=25$. Hence $$14+30b=25\quad\Rightarrow\quad b=\frac{11}{30}.$$ Confusing inventory accumulation with excess demand would reverse this subtraction.

solutionSteps.title: Calculate the multiplier
solutionSteps.body: The autonomous-spending multiplier is $$\frac1{1-b}=\frac1{1-11/30}=\frac{30}{19}.$$ The question's continuation is on PDF page 2, despite starting on page 6, so both pieces of source information are needed. Linearity is the standard simple-Keynesian interpretation used in obtaining a single slope from the observations.

questions.stem: A project costs200 now and pays100 per year from next year onward. Each year, conditional on survival, abandonment permanently occurs with probability1/4. At a10% annual discount rate, is investment profitable?
questions.answer: Yes. If abandonment occurs before each payment, PV=1500/7≈214.286 and NPV=100/7≈14.286.
questions.solution:
Model annual survival and payment timing. Treat the abandonment probability as a constant conditional hazard p=1/4. Then annual survival is q=3/4. If abandonment is tested before each payment, the probability of receiving the year-t payment is q^t, so expected revenue is 100q^t. The initial investment is paid now.

Sum the discounted expected stream. With discount rate 10%, 
PV =100Σ_(t=1)^∞((0.75)/(1.1))^t; =(100(0.75))/(1.1-0.75)=(1500)/(7).
 The geometric sum is finite because its ratio is below one. Net present value is 1500/7-200=100/7>0, so undertake the investment.

Check the alternative within-year timing. If the first payment is guaranteed and abandonment is tested only afterward, the stream starts with survival weight one instead. Then PV=100/(1.1-0.75)=2000/7 and NPV is 600/7, also positive. The source does not settle that timing, but the investment recommendation is robust to both standard conventions.
questions.hint: Discount the survival-weighted geometric stream.
questions.notes: Interprets abandonment probability as a constant conditional annual hazard; both common within-year payment timings give a positive NPV.

solutionSteps.title: Model annual survival and payment timing
solutionSteps.body: Treat the abandonment probability as a constant conditional hazard $p=1/4$. Then annual survival is $q=3/4$. If abandonment is tested before each payment, the probability of receiving the year-$t$ payment is $q^t$, so expected revenue is $100q^t$. The initial investment is paid now.

solutionSteps.title: Sum the discounted expected stream
solutionSteps.body: With discount rate 10%, $$\begin{aligned}PV&=100\sum_{t=1}^{\infty}\left(\frac{0.75}{1.1}\right)^t\\&=\frac{100(0.75)}{1.1-0.75}=\frac{1500}{7}.\end{aligned}$$ The geometric sum is finite because its ratio is below one. Net present value is $1500/7-200=100/7>0$, so undertake the investment.

solutionSteps.title: Check the alternative within-year timing
solutionSteps.body: If the first payment is guaranteed and abandonment is tested only afterward, the stream starts with survival weight one instead. Then $PV=100/(1.1-0.75)=2000/7$ and NPV is $600/7$, also positive. The source does not settle that timing, but the investment recommendation is robust to both standard conventions.

questions.stem: A firm producesy=x₁x₂ with positive input pricesr₁,r₂. If minimized production cost is4, findy.
questions.solution:
Formulate cost minimization. For a target output y, minimize r_1x_1+r_2x_2 subject to x_1x_2≥ y, where both input prices are positive. At the minimum the production constraint binds: buying unnecessary inputs would raise cost without being required for the target.

Derive minimized cost. AM–GM gives 
r_1x_1+r_2x_2≥2√(r_1r_2x_1x_2)=2√(r_1r_2y).
 Equality is attainable when the two input expenditures are equal, r_1x_1=r_2x_2. Thus the lower bound is the cost function, not just an inequality.

Invert the given cost level. Set minimized cost equal to 4: 2√(r_1r_2y)=4. Squaring gives r_1r_2y=4, hence y=4/(r_1r_2). At this optimum each input expenditure is 2, which provides a direct check on the total cost.
questions.hint: Use AM–GM or equalize the two input expenditures.

solutionSteps.title: Formulate cost minimization
solutionSteps.body: For a target output $y$, minimize $r_1x_1+r_2x_2$ subject to $x_1x_2\ge y$, where both input prices are positive. At the minimum the production constraint binds: buying unnecessary inputs would raise cost without being required for the target.

solutionSteps.title: Derive minimized cost
solutionSteps.body: AM–GM gives $$r_1x_1+r_2x_2\ge2\sqrt{r_1r_2x_1x_2}=2\sqrt{r_1r_2y}.$$ Equality is attainable when the two input expenditures are equal, $r_1x_1=r_2x_2$. Thus the lower bound is the cost function, not just an inequality.

solutionSteps.title: Invert the given cost level
solutionSteps.body: Set minimized cost equal to 4: $2\sqrt{r_1r_2y}=4$. Squaring gives $r_1r_2y=4$, hence $y=4/(r_1r_2)$. At this optimum each input expenditure is 2, which provides a direct check on the total cost.

questions.stem: X∼B(n,p). The maximum value of Var(X) is
questions.solution: Var(X)=np(1−p)=n[1/4−(p−1/2)²]≤n/4, attained at p=1/2.
questions.hint: Complete the square in p.

questions.stem: P(x) is a quadratic polynomial such that P(1)=−P(2). If one root is −1, the other root is
questions.solution: Write P(x)=k(x+1)(x−r) with k≠0. Then 2(1−r)=−3(2−r), so 8=5r and r=8/5.
questions.hint: Factor using the known root.

questions.stem: Let f(x)=(x−a)³+(x−b)³+(x−c)³, where a<b<c. The number of real roots of f(x)=0 is
questions.solution: The derivative is 3[(x−a)²+(x−b)²+(x−c)²]>0, since distinct a,b,c cannot all equal x. Thus f is strictly increasing. Its limits at ±∞ have opposite signs, so exactly one real zero exists.
questions.hint: Show the derivative is strictly positive.

questions.stem: Three students A,B,C independently solve a statistics problem with probabilities 1/3,1/4,1/5. The probability that the problem is solved is
questions.solution: The probability none solves it is (2/3)(3/4)(4/5)=2/5. Its complement is 3/5.
questions.hint: Use the complement event.

questions.stem: Let ρ₁ and ρ₂ be the correlations of x,y satisfying respectively (i) y=2+3x and (ii) 2y=5+8x. Then
questions.solution: Both are exact affine relationships with positive slopes, 3 and 4. For nonconstant x both correlations are +1.
questions.hint: Correlation does not depend on a positive slope’s magnitude.
questions.notes: Nonzero variance is implicit in the stated correlation coefficients.

questions.stem: The slope in the regression of y on x is Cov(x,y)/V(x). The slope in the regression of x on y is
questions.solution: Swap the response and explanatory variable in the least-squares slope formula. The explanatory variable is now y, so its variance belongs in the denominator.
questions.hint: The denominator is the explanatory variable’s variance.

questions.stem: For f(x)=eˣ, which statement is true?
options: The first strict inequality holds for some distinct pair, and the reverse holds for some distinct pair
Equality holds for at least one distinct pair
questions.answer: The strict midpoint convexity inequality in the second choice
questions.solution: Since f″(x)=eˣ>0 everywhere, f is strictly convex. Its value at the midpoint of distinct points lies strictly below their average function value.
questions.hint: Use strict convexity of the exponential.

questions.solution: The second is geometric with sum 1. Differentiating Σrⁿ=1/(1−r) gives Σₙ≥₁nrⁿ=r/(1−r)², so the first converges to 2 at r=1/2.
questions.hint: Use geometric-series identities.

questions.stem: The function x|x| is
options: Continuous but not differentiable at x=0
Continuous everywhere but not differentiable anywhere
questions.solution: Its derivative at zero is limₕ→₀h|h|/h=limₕ→₀|h|=0.
questions.hint: Use the difference quotient at zero.

questions.stem: The sequence (−1)ⁿ⁺¹ has
questions.solution: Its odd-index subsequence is constantly 1 and its even-index subsequence constantly −1. Distinct subsequential limits rule out convergence of the full sequence.
questions.hint: Compare the odd and even subsequences.

options: Converges to a number between 0 and 1
Converges to a number greater than 2
questions.answer: It converges to exactly 1; none of these
questions.solution: The nth term is 1/[n(n+1)]=1/n−1/(n+1). The partial sum through n is 1−1/(n+1)→1, which is neither strictly between 0 and 1 nor greater than 2.
questions.hint: Telescope the partial fractions.
questions.notes: Interprets “between 0 and 1” strictly; the sum is the endpoint 1.

questions.stem: For x>0, let fₜ(x)=(xᵗ−1)/(xᵗ+1). The limit as t→∞
options: Exists and is discontinuous at exactly one point
Exists and is discontinuous at exactly two points
questions.answer: Exists, with one discontinuity at x=1
questions.solution: For 0<x<1 the limit is −1; at x=1 it is 0; for x>1 it is 1. This function is continuous on each side of 1 and discontinuous at 1 alone.
questions.hint: Split into x<1, x=1, and x>1.

questions.stem: If u=sin⁻¹((x²+y²)/(x+y)), then x∂u/∂x+y∂u/∂x is equal to
questions.answer: The printed derivative repeats ∂u/∂x; intended Euler expression would give tan u
questions.solution: Put v=(x²+y²)/(x+y), homogeneous of degree 1. Euler’s theorem gives xvₓ+yvᵧ=v, and hence xuₓ+yuᵧ=tan u. But the source prints (x+y)uₓ, which equals (x²+2xy−y²)/[(x+y)cos u] and is not generally tan u. The question’s likely typo needs editorial resolution before grading.
questions.hint: Check the denominator on each partial derivative before applying Euler’s theorem.
questions.notes: Both displayed derivatives are with respect to x in the PDF. Preserve the printed formula rather than silently changing the second denominator to y.

questions.stem: The derivative of tan⁻¹(cos x/(1+sin x)) with respect to x is
questions.answer: −1/2 wherever the source expression is defined
questions.solution: For q=cosx/(1+sinx), q′=−1/(1+sinx) and 1+q²=2/(1+sinx). Thus (arctanq)′=q′/(1+q²)=−1/2.
questions.hint: Differentiate arctangent using the quotient rule.

questions.stem: The infinite series 1+3/4+7/16+15/64+31/256+⋯ has sum
questions.solution: The nth term for n≥0 is (2ⁿ⁺¹−1)/4ⁿ. Summing gives 2Σ(1/2)ⁿ−Σ(1/4)ⁿ=4−4/3=8/3.
questions.hint: Express each numerator as a power of 2 minus 1.

questions.stem: Five boys and four girls are seated in a row with no two girls together. The number of arrangements is
questions.solution: Arrange the five boys in 5! ways. They create six gaps, including the two ends. Assign four distinct girls to four distinct gaps in ⁶P₄ ways.
questions.hint: Place the boys first and use the gaps.

questions.stem: A point has distances from (−a,0) and (a,0) in the ratio 2:3. Its locus is
questions.solution: Squaring the ratio gives 9[(x+a)²+y²]=4[(x−a)²+y²]. Expanding and collecting yields the second equation.
questions.hint: Square the distance-ratio equation.

questions.stem: If Σₓ₌₁¹⁰⁰x! is divided by 36, the remainder is
questions.solution: For x≥6, x! is divisible by 36. The remaining sum is 1!+2!+3!+4!+5!=153, whose remainder on division by 36 is 9.
questions.hint: Only the first few factorials matter modulo 36.
questions.notes: The source’s old factorial symbol is normalized to !; it is not a floor function.

questions.stem: If a,b,c,d are in G.P., then (a³+b³)⁻¹,(b³+c³)⁻¹,(c³+d³)⁻¹ are in
questions.answer: G.P., when the displayed reciprocals exist
questions.solution: Write b=ar,c=ar²,d=ar³. The denominators are a³(1+r³), a³r³(1+r³), a³r⁶(1+r³). Their reciprocals have common ratio r⁻³.
questions.hint: Represent the geometric progression using its ratio.
questions.notes: The statement presupposes nonzero denominators; for example ratio −1 would make the displayed quantities undefined.

questions.stem: The solution set of ||x|−1|<1−x is
questions.solution: If x≥1 the right side is nonpositive, impossible. If 0≤x<1 both sides equal 1−x. For x<0, putting t=−x>0 gives |t−1|<t+1, always true.
questions.hint: Split into negative x and the two nonnegative ranges.

questions.stem: The distance of the curve y=x² from the line 2x−y=4 is minimum at
questions.solution: The distance is |2x−x²−4|/√5=[(x−1)²+3]/√5, minimized at x=1. The curve then has y=1.
questions.hint: Use the point-to-line distance formula and complete the square.

questions.stem: The dual of: maximize x₁+x₂ subject to −3x₁+2x₂≤−1, x₁−x₂≤2, x₁,x₂≥0, has
options: A feasible solution but no optimal solution
questions.solution: The primal is feasible at (1,0). Adding t(1,1), t≥0, preserves feasibility and increases its objective without bound. A feasible dual would give a finite upper bound by weak duality, so the dual is infeasible.
questions.hint: Find a feasible direction that increases the primal objective without bound.

questions.stem: The number of real roots of x²−3|x|+2=0 is
questions.solution: Put t=|x|≥0. Then (t−1)(t−2)=0, so x=±1,±2 gives four roots.
questions.hint: Solve the quadratic in |x|.

questions.stem: Four letters are placed into four addressed envelopes so every letter is in a wrong envelope. The number of ways is
questions.hint: Count derangements by inclusion–exclusion.

questions.stem: If a²x²+2bx+c=0 has one root greater than 1 and the other less than 1, then
questions.solution: There are two roots straddling 1, and the leading coefficient a² is positive. Hence the polynomial at 1 is negative: a²+2b+c<0. Therefore 2b+c<−a²<0.
questions.hint: Evaluate the upward-opening quadratic at 1.

questions.stem: Let aₙ=1/n and bₙ=1/(n+1). Find Σₙ₌₁⁹⁹(aₙ−bₙ)²/(aₙbₙ).
questions.solution: The summand simplifies to 1/[n(n+1)]=1/n−1/(n+1). Telescoping through n=99 gives 1−1/100=99/100.
questions.hint: Simplify a single summand before summing.

questions.stem: If A=[[1,−1],[2,−2]], then A¹⁰⁰+A⁵ is
questions.solution: Direct multiplication gives A²=−A. Hence Aᵏ=(−1)ᵏ⁻¹A for k≥1, so A¹⁰⁰+A⁵=−A+A=0.
questions.hint: Calculate A² first.

questions.stem: Find limₓ→₀(sin x/x)^(1/x²).
questions.solution: Since sinx/x=1−x²/6+O(x⁴), the logarithm of the expression is x⁻²ln(1−x²/6+O(x⁴))→−1/6. Exponentiating gives e^(−1/6).
questions.hint: Take logarithms and expand sin x at zero.

questions.stem: The system x+y+z=6, x+ay−z=1, 2x+2y+bz=12 has a unique solution if and only if
questions.answer: None of these: the correct condition is (a−1)(b−2)≠0
questions.solution: Subtract row 1 from row 2 and twice row 1 from row 3. The determinant becomes (a−1)(b−2). Unique solvability requires both a≠1 and b≠2. Equivalently ab≠2a+b−2, whereas the source’s third option prints +2.
questions.hint: Use row operations to compute the coefficient determinant.
questions.notes: Source choice (C) has +2, visually checked. It is not the determinant condition; do not silently replace its sign.

questions.stem: The number of times y=x³−3x+3 intersects the x-axis is
questions.solution: The derivative is 3(x²−1), with local maximum f(−1)=5 and local minimum f(1)=1, both positive. The strictly increasing branch on (−∞,−1) rises from −∞ to 5, crossing zero once; the remaining branches stay positive.
questions.hint: Evaluate the cubic at its two critical points.

questions.stem: U(x,y)=x+y and px+y=10. At p=1/2, what is the absolute own-price elasticity of demand for x?
questions.solution:
Derive demand on the cheaper-good branch. Since p=1/2<1, good x gives more utility per rupee than y under U=x+y. The optimum spends all 10 on x, so x=10/p in a neighbourhood of this price. Its signed elasticity is 
(dx)/(dp)(p)/(x)=(-(10)/(p^2))(p)/(10/p)=-1.
 The absolute elasticity is one: C.
questions.hint: Identify which perfect substitute is cheaper.

solutionSteps.title: Derive demand on the cheaper-good branch
solutionSteps.body: Since $p=1/2<1$, good $x$ gives more utility per rupee than $y$ under $U=x+y$. The optimum spends all 10 on $x$, so $x=10/p$ in a neighbourhood of this price. Its signed elasticity is $$\frac{dx}{dp}\frac px=\left(-\frac{10}{p^2}\right)\frac p{10/p}=-1.$$ The absolute elasticity is one: C.

questions.stem:
Good x costs p locally and q

C. Good y costs1 everywhere. For smooth downward-sloping convex indifference curves, if optimal x is x₀, which statement holds?
questions.answer: C is possible under the literal assumptions: (p−q)x₀=C may hold at a corner but cannot hold at an interior crossing.
questions.solution:
Find the crossing and explain the interior argument. The two budget lines are y=I-px and y=I-C-qx, crossing at x^*=C/(p-q). At an interior crossing, the upper envelope's slope becomes less negative, from -p to -q. Smooth increasing utility cannot have a local maximum there: the derivative along the right branch exceeds that along the left by (p-q)U_y>0. Thus the usual “never” answer is valid only for an interior optimum.

Check the corner omitted by that argument. Let p=2,q=1,C=1,I=2 and U=x+0.1log(1+y). These smooth downward-sloping strictly convex indifference curves support the corner (1,0) under both opportunities. It satisfies (p-q)x=C. Other preferences choose another bundle. Therefore equality can hold at a permitted boundary, making C possible under the literal assumptions. The missing interiority assumption is preserved as a review issue.
questions.hint: Inspect the crossing of the two budget lines, including its endpoints.
questions.notes: Corner counterexample prevents the usual interior-only answer from being universal; no automatic grading.
options: Equality may or may not hold depending on preferences

solutionSteps.title: Find the crossing and explain the interior argument
solutionSteps.body: The two budget lines are $y=I-px$ and $y=I-C-qx$, crossing at $x^*=C/(p-q)$. At an interior crossing, the upper envelope's slope becomes less negative, from $-p$ to $-q$. Smooth increasing utility cannot have a local maximum there: the derivative along the right branch exceeds that along the left by $(p-q)U_y>0$. Thus the usual “never” answer is valid only for an interior optimum.

solutionSteps.title: Check the corner omitted by that argument
solutionSteps.body: Let $p=2,q=1,C=1,I=2$ and $U=x+0.1\log(1+y)$. These smooth downward-sloping strictly convex indifference curves support the corner $(1,0)$ under both opportunities. It satisfies $(p-q)x=C$. Other preferences choose another bundle. Therefore equality can hold at a permitted boundary, making C possible under the literal assumptions. The missing interiority assumption is preserved as a review issue.

questions.stem: For Q=min(L/(2a),K/(4b)), with a,b>0 and factor prices w,r, what is the cost function?
questions.solution:
Translate the Leontief technology into required inputs. Producing Q requires L≥2aQ and K≥4bQ. Positive factor prices make both inequalities bind at the cost minimum. Therefore 
C(Q)=w(2aQ)+r(4bQ)=(2aw+4br)Q.
 None of the first three expressions matches this total, so choose D.
questions.hint: Use the fixed input requirements.

solutionSteps.title: Translate the Leontief technology into required inputs
solutionSteps.body: Producing $Q$ requires $L\ge2aQ$ and $K\ge4bQ$. Positive factor prices make both inequalities bind at the cost minimum. Therefore $$C(Q)=w(2aQ)+r(4bQ)=(2aw+4br)Q.$$ None of the first three expressions matches this total, so choose D.

questions.stem: An economy has positive net borrowing from abroad during a period. Under the standard net-borrowing/current-account identity, what follows?
questions.solution: Use the net foreign borrowing identity. Under the standard meaning of total net foreign borrowing, CA=S-I while net borrowing is I-S. Positive net borrowing therefore means CA<0: C. It does not identify the sign of the trade balance alone, factor income or reserve accumulation. A particular positive loan inflow, rather than aggregate net borrowing, would not by itself imply this conclusion.
questions.hint: Use the current-account identity.
questions.notes: “Net loan from abroad” is read as total net foreign borrowing, not just one loan flow.
options: Net factor income from abroad is negative

solutionSteps.title: Use the net foreign borrowing identity
solutionSteps.body: Under the standard meaning of total net foreign borrowing, $CA=S-I$ while net borrowing is $I-S$. Positive net borrowing therefore means $CA<0$: C. It does not identify the sign of the trade balance alone, factor income or reserve accumulation. A particular positive loan inflow, rather than aggregate net borrowing, would not by itself imply this conclusion.

questions.stem: In a simple Keynesian economy G=tY always balances total income-tax receipts. What happens to Y if government raises t?
questions.answer: A: Y increases under the usual proportional-consumption, exogenous-investment assumptions.
questions.solution:
Substitute the balanced-budget rule. In the usual simple model take C=c(1-t)Y, fixed positive investment I, and G=tY. Then 
Y=c(1-t)Y+I+tY ⇒ Y=(I)/((1-c)(1-t)).
 For 0<c<1 and 0≤ t<1, output increases with the tax rate: A. Government spends the full transferred rupee whereas households would have spent only fraction c.
questions.hint: Substitute G=tY into goods equilibrium.
questions.notes: Uses the standard simple-Keynesian proportional-consumption and fixed-investment setup implicit in the question.

solutionSteps.title: Substitute the balanced-budget rule
solutionSteps.body: In the usual simple model take $C=c(1-t)Y$, fixed positive investment $I$, and $G=tY$. Then $$Y=c(1-t)Y+I+tY\quad\Rightarrow\quad Y=\frac I{(1-c)(1-t)}.$$ For $0<c<1$ and $0\le t<1$, output increases with the tax rate: A. Government spends the full transferred rupee whereas households would have spent only fraction $c$.

questions.stem: Which statement is false? Under the conventional textbook treatment of public-debt interest, it is not a part of…
questions.answer: D: “personal income” is the false exclusion.
questions.solution: Separate personal receipts from current production income. In the conventional textbook transfer treatment intended here, public-debt interest enters the receiving household's personal income but is not government consumption or income generated by current production. Thus saying it is not part of personal income is false: D. Option A is read as “not included in both aggregates simultaneously”; a reading that excludes it from each aggregate separately would introduce a wording ambiguity.
questions.hint: Distinguish household receipts from income generated by current production.
questions.notes: Uses the source’s conventional public-interest-as-transfer classification; optionA has a scope ambiguity in ordinary language.
options: Both personal income and national income

solutionSteps.title: Separate personal receipts from current production income
solutionSteps.body: In the conventional textbook transfer treatment intended here, public-debt interest enters the receiving household's personal income but is not government consumption or income generated by current production. Thus saying it is not part of personal income is false: D. Option A is read as “not included in both aggregates simultaneously”; a reading that excludes it from each aggregate separately would introduce a wording ambiguity.

questions.stem: Explain true/false: (i) Fixed gallons of gasoline per barrel of crude imply a gasoline/crude price ratio independent of crude production. (ii) Without money illusion, all price elasticities of a commodity determine its income elasticity. (iii) If both people have homothetic preferences, an Edgeworth-box contract curve is the straight line between origins.
questions.answer: (i) False in general. (ii) True under differentiable degree-zero homogeneous demand. (iii) False.
questions.solution:
A fixed yield does not establish a fixed price ratio. The first statement is false in general. Suppose one barrel produces a gallons and requires processing cost c. Even with competitive pricing, p_g=(p_o+c)/a, so 
(p_g)/(p_o)=(1)/(a)+(c)/(ap_o).
 This ratio changes when the crude price changes. A physical conversion coefficient alone does not determine equilibrium relative prices.

Derive the elasticity restriction from no money illusion. No money illusion means demand is homogeneous of degree zero in all prices and income: x_i(λ p,λ M)=x_i(p,M). Differentiating at λ=1 and dividing by x_i gives 
Σ_jε_(ij)+η_i=0.
 Thus the second statement is true when the relevant derivatives exist: the income elasticity is minus the sum of all price elasticities.

Give a counterexample with two homothetic preferences. The third statement is false: homothetic does not mean identical. In a unit Edgeworth box take U_A=√(xy) and U_B=x^(1/4)y^(3/4). Equality of their marginal rates of substitution gives 
(y_A)/(x_A)=(1-y_A)/(3(1-x_A)) ⇒ y_A=(x_A)/(3-2x_A).
 This is a curved contract curve rather than the diagonal, although both utilities are homothetic.
questions.hint: Distinguish technology from pricing and apply homogeneity to demand.

solutionSteps.title: A fixed yield does not establish a fixed price ratio
solutionSteps.body: The first statement is false in general. Suppose one barrel produces $a$ gallons and requires processing cost $c$. Even with competitive pricing, $p_g=(p_o+c)/a$, so $$\frac{p_g}{p_o}=\frac1a+\frac{c}{ap_o}.$$ This ratio changes when the crude price changes. A physical conversion coefficient alone does not determine equilibrium relative prices.

solutionSteps.title: Derive the elasticity restriction from no money illusion
solutionSteps.body: No money illusion means demand is homogeneous of degree zero in all prices and income: $x_i(\lambda p,\lambda M)=x_i(p,M)$. Differentiating at $\lambda=1$ and dividing by $x_i$ gives $$\sum_j\varepsilon_{ij}+\eta_i=0.$$ Thus the second statement is true when the relevant derivatives exist: the income elasticity is minus the sum of all price elasticities.

solutionSteps.title: Give a counterexample with two homothetic preferences
solutionSteps.body: The third statement is false: homothetic does not mean identical. In a unit Edgeworth box take $U_A=\sqrt{xy}$ and $U_B=x^{1/4}y^{3/4}$. Equality of their marginal rates of substitution gives $$\frac{y_A}{x_A}=\frac{1-y_A}{3(1-x_A)}\quad\Rightarrow\quad y_A=\frac{x_A}{3-2x_A}.$$ This is a curved contract curve rather than the diagonal, although both utilities are homothetic.

questions.stem: Duopoly demand is P=10−q₁−q₂. For positive output, costs are C₁=1+2q₁ and C₂=1+4q₂; a firm producing nothing avoids its fixed cost. Find Cournot outputs and profits. What if firm2 fixed cost rises from1 to2?
questions.answer: Initially q₁=10/3,q₂=4/3, profits91/9 and7/9. After firm2 fixed cost becomes2, equilibrium is q₁=4,q₂=0, profits15 and0.
questions.solution:
Solve conditional on both firms producing. With positive outputs the profits are (8-q_1-q_2)q_1-1 and (6-q_1-q_2)q_2-1. Their interior best-response conditions are 
2q_1+q_2=8, q_1+2q_2=6.
 They yield q_1=10/3, q_2=4/3.

Check the avoidable fixed costs. At a conditional optimum, operating profit equals q_i^2. Subtracting the fixed cost gives 
π_1=100/9-1=91/9, π_2=16/9-1=7/9.
 Both are positive, so neither firm prefers the zero-output payoff of zero. The conditional interior solution is therefore an equilibrium.

Reconsider entry when firm 2’s fixed cost rises. With fixed cost 2, the old firm-2 output would earn 16/9-2=-2/9, so simply retaining the old first-order solution is incorrect. If firm 2 exits, firm 1’s monopoly best response is q_1=4. Against that quantity, firm 2’s best positive output is 1 and yields operating profit 1, less than its fixed cost 2.

Confirm the new equilibrium and profits. Firm 2 therefore optimally stays out and firm 1 optimally produces 4. The new equilibrium is (q_1,q_2)=(4,0) with profits (15,0). This change is driven by the avoidable participation cost, not by a change in firm 2’s positive-output marginal cost.
questions.hint: Check shutdown as well as the positive-output first-order conditions.

solutionSteps.title: Solve conditional on both firms producing
solutionSteps.body: With positive outputs the profits are $(8-q_1-q_2)q_1-1$ and $(6-q_1-q_2)q_2-1$. Their interior best-response conditions are $$2q_1+q_2=8,\qquad q_1+2q_2=6.$$ They yield $q_1=10/3$, $q_2=4/3$.

solutionSteps.body: At a conditional optimum, operating profit equals $q_i^2$. Subtracting the fixed cost gives $$\pi_1=100/9-1=91/9,\qquad\pi_2=16/9-1=7/9.$$ Both are positive, so neither firm prefers the zero-output payoff of zero. The conditional interior solution is therefore an equilibrium.

solutionSteps.title: Reconsider entry when firm 2’s fixed cost rises
solutionSteps.body: With fixed cost 2, the old firm-2 output would earn $16/9-2=-2/9$, so simply retaining the old first-order solution is incorrect. If firm 2 exits, firm 1’s monopoly best response is $q_1=4$. Against that quantity, firm 2’s best positive output is 1 and yields operating profit 1, less than its fixed cost 2.

solutionSteps.title: Confirm the new equilibrium and profits
solutionSteps.body: Firm 2 therefore optimally stays out and firm 1 optimally produces 4. The new equilibrium is $(q_1,q_2)=(4,0)$ with profits $(15,0)$. This change is driven by the avoidable participation cost, not by a change in firm 2’s positive-output marginal cost.

questions.stem: Group1 income is fixed800; its propensity to consume is.8 and propensity to import.4. Group2 consumes only domestic output with propensity.5. Investment is domestically produced and fixed600. (i) Find GDP. (ii) Group2 transfers100 to group1 and imports are capped250: find new GDP. (iii) Repeat with import cap400.
questions.answer: Initial Y1040. After transfer with cap250, Y1240 (rise200). With cap400, Y1020 (fall20 from initial).
questions.solution:
Construct the original expenditure balance. Original consumption is C_1=0.8(800)=640 and C_2=0.5(Y-800). Imports are 0.4(800)=320. With domestic investment 600, 
Y=640+0.5(Y-800)+600-320,
 giving Y=1040.

Apply the transfer and the binding import ceiling. The transfer makes disposable group incomes 900 and Y-900. Thus C_1=720, C_2=0.5(Y-900) and desired imports are 360. With a ceiling of 250, actual imports are 250. The new balance is 
Y=720+0.5(Y-900)+600-250,
 so Y=1240, 200 above the original income.

Repeat when the ceiling is relaxed. With a ceiling of 400, desired imports 360 are fully allowed. Replace 250 by 360 in the preceding equation to obtain Y=1020. This is 20 below the original 1040, and 220 below the binding-ceiling case. The transfer itself is not new production; it changes spending propensities, while the import rule changes how much spending falls on domestic goods.
questions.hint: Track each group’s disposable income and subtract actual, capped imports.

solutionSteps.title: Construct the original expenditure balance
solutionSteps.body: Original consumption is $C_1=0.8(800)=640$ and $C_2=0.5(Y-800)$. Imports are $0.4(800)=320$. With domestic investment 600, $$Y=640+0.5(Y-800)+600-320,$$ giving $Y=1040$.

solutionSteps.title: Apply the transfer and the binding import ceiling
solutionSteps.body: The transfer makes disposable group incomes 900 and $Y-900$. Thus $C_1=720$, $C_2=0.5(Y-900)$ and desired imports are 360. With a ceiling of 250, actual imports are 250. The new balance is $$Y=720+0.5(Y-900)+600-250,$$ so $Y=1240$, 200 above the original income.

solutionSteps.title: Repeat when the ceiling is relaxed
solutionSteps.body: With a ceiling of 400, desired imports 360 are fully allowed. Replace 250 by 360 in the preceding equation to obtain $Y=1020$. This is 20 below the original 1040, and 220 below the binding-ceiling case. The transfer itself is not new production; it changes spending propensities, while the import rule changes how much spending falls on domestic goods.

questions.stem: A consumer buys electricity E and other goods O priced1. Electricity requires fixed charge R and a quantity-dependent per-unit price p=E/2. Utility is E+O and income I>R. (i) Describe the budget boundary. (ii) For R0,I1 find the optimum. (iii) Find the largest extractable fixed charge.
questions.answer: Reading p as the price applied to all units: O=I−R−E²/2 when connected. At R0,I1: E1,O1/2. At I1 the maximal fixed charge is1/2, leaving the consumer indifferent to no connection.
questions.solution:
Write the actual electricity bill. Treat p(E)=E/2 as the unit price applied to all units. Total usage expenditure is p(E)E=E^2/2, so a connected consumer faces 
O=I-R-(E^2)/(2), 0<E≤√(2(I-R)).
 If the connection fee is avoidable, the no-connection option (E,O)=(0,I) is also available. The connected frontier is a parabola rather than a straight budget line.

Optimize usage at zero fee and income one. With R=0,I=1, utility along the frontier is 1+E-E^2/2. Its derivative 1-E vanishes at E=1, an affordable interior choice, and the second derivative is negative. Thus the optimum is (E,O)=(1,1/2).

Find the consumer’s willingness to pay for access. The gross utility surplus from electricity is max_E(E-E^2/2)=1/2. At income one, a fixed fee R=1/2 leaves E=1,O=0 and utility 1, equal to the no-connection utility. Hence R_(max)=1/2; charge slightly less for strict participation.

State affordability and tariff qualifications. For general income, the same fee is feasible if I≥1. If 0<I<1, the affordability constraint binds and the maximal fee is I-I^2/2, attained at E=I,O=0. A marginal-block tariff would require integrating the marginal price rather than multiplying by quantity; that is a different interpretation from the all-units price used here.
questions.hint: The total bill is quantity times the all-units price, plus the connection fee.
questions.notes: The price function is interpreted as an all-units price rather than a marginal tariff; the continuation of I1 is used for the main fixed-charge answer.

solutionSteps.title: Write the actual electricity bill
solutionSteps.body: Treat $p(E)=E/2$ as the unit price applied to all units. Total usage expenditure is $p(E)E=E^2/2$, so a connected consumer faces $$O=I-R-\frac{E^2}{2},\qquad0<E\le\sqrt{2(I-R)}.$$ If the connection fee is avoidable, the no-connection option $(E,O)=(0,I)$ is also available. The connected frontier is a parabola rather than a straight budget line.

solutionSteps.title: Optimize usage at zero fee and income one
solutionSteps.body: With $R=0,I=1$, utility along the frontier is $1+E-E^2/2$. Its derivative $1-E$ vanishes at $E=1$, an affordable interior choice, and the second derivative is negative. Thus the optimum is $(E,O)=(1,1/2)$.

solutionSteps.title: Find the consumer’s willingness to pay for access
solutionSteps.body: The gross utility surplus from electricity is $\max_E(E-E^2/2)=1/2$. At income one, a fixed fee $R=1/2$ leaves $E=1,O=0$ and utility 1, equal to the no-connection utility. Hence $R_{max}=1/2$; charge slightly less for strict participation.

solutionSteps.title: State affordability and tariff qualifications
solutionSteps.body: For general income, the same fee is feasible if $I\ge1$. If $0<I<1$, the affordability constraint binds and the maximal fee is $I-I^2/2$, attained at $E=I,O=0$. A marginal-block tariff would require integrating the marginal price rather than multiplying by quantity; that is a different interpretation from the all-units price used here.

questions.stem: Income is25, prices are3 for x and4 for y, and U=12x+16y−x²−y² on x,y≥0. What happens to the optimum if income rises to50 or more?
questions.answer: At income25, bundle(3,4). At income50 or more, bundle(6,8); any income above50 is left unspent.
questions.solution:
Locate the bliss point. Complete the squares: 
U(x,y)=100-(x-6)^2-(y-8)^2.
 The unconstrained maximum is therefore at (6,8), with utility 100. This point costs 3(6)+4(8)=50.

Find the optimum at income 25. The problem is equivalent to finding the feasible point closest to (6,8). The budget boundary is 3x+4y=25. Projecting onto it gives 
(x,y)=(6,8)-(50-25)/(3^2+4^2)(3,4)=(3,4).
 This point is nonnegative and therefore is the constrained optimum.

Explain the response to additional income. At income 50 the bliss point becomes affordable. At every income above 50 it is still the unique utility-maximizing bundle. The consumer leaves any excess income unspent instead of buying beyond satiation. Spending all income is not a general requirement when utility is not everywhere increasing.
questions.hint: Locate the bliss point by completing squares.

solutionSteps.title: Locate the bliss point
solutionSteps.body: Complete the squares: $$U(x,y)=100-(x-6)^2-(y-8)^2.$$ The unconstrained maximum is therefore at $(6,8)$, with utility 100. This point costs $3(6)+4(8)=50$.

solutionSteps.title: Find the optimum at income 25
solutionSteps.body: The problem is equivalent to finding the feasible point closest to $(6,8)$. The budget boundary is $3x+4y=25$. Projecting onto it gives $$ (x,y)=(6,8)-\frac{50-25}{3^2+4^2}(3,4)=(3,4).$$ This point is nonnegative and therefore is the constrained optimum.

solutionSteps.title: Explain the response to additional income
solutionSteps.body: At income 50 the bliss point becomes affordable. At every income above 50 it is still the unique utility-maximizing bundle. The consumer leaves any excess income unspent instead of buying beyond satiation. Spending all income is not a general requirement when utility is not everywhere increasing.

questions.stem: IS–LM has desired private saving s=s(Y−tθY),0<s′<1; investment i=i(r),i′<0; money demand l(Y,r) with l_Y>0,l_r<0. Labour share θ, real money M/P, G and tax rate t are exogenous. (i) Can equilibrium tax collections tθY fall when t rises? (ii) If tax instead applies to all GNP, reformulate saving and reconsider.
questions.answer: Under these assumptions equilibrium tax revenue strictly increases with t; no downward Laffer segment occurs. Replacing labour taxation by all-income taxation sets θ1 and leaves that conclusion intact.
questions.solution:
Include government saving in goods equilibrium. Private saving is s((1-θ t)Y), but government tax revenue is θ tY. With spending G, total saving equals investment: 
s((1-θ t)Y)+θ tY=i(r)+G.
 Omitting the tax term on this equation would give the wrong revenue response.

Differentiate along the unchanged money market. Let a=s', with 0<a<1, and k=-l_Y/l_r>0, so dr=k dY. Define 
D=a(1-θ t)+θ t-i'k>0.
 Differentiating the goods equation then gives 
(dY)/(dt)=-(θ Y(1-a))/(D)<0.
 A higher tax rate lowers equilibrium output in this model.

Differentiate collections rather than output alone. Tax revenue is R=θ tY. Its derivative is 
(dR)/(dt) =θ Y+θ t(dY)/(dt); =θ Y(a-i'k)/(D)>0.
 Output falls, but not enough to outweigh the direct effect of the higher rate. Hence this model has no downward-sloping Laffer segment under its stated behavioural assumptions.

Extend the base to all factor income. With an all-income tax, private saving becomes s((1-t)Y) and receipts become tY. Set θ=1 throughout the derivation. Then 
(d(tY))/(dt)=Y(a-i'k)/(a(1-t)+t-i'k)>0.
 Broadening the tax base therefore does not reverse the conclusion. The signs assume positive income and economically admissible rates.
questions.hint: Include government saving, differentiate both equilibrium conditions and then differentiate tax revenue.
questions.notes: Assumes positive income, 0<θ≤1 and economically admissible tax rates0≤t<1.

solutionSteps.title: Include government saving in goods equilibrium
solutionSteps.body: Private saving is $s((1-\theta t)Y)$, but government tax revenue is $\theta tY$. With spending $G$, total saving equals investment: $$s((1-\theta t)Y)+\theta tY=i(r)+G.$$ Omitting the tax term on this equation would give the wrong revenue response.

solutionSteps.title: Differentiate along the unchanged money market
solutionSteps.body: Let $a=s'$, with $0<a<1$, and $k=-l_Y/l_r>0$, so $dr=k\,dY$. Define $$D=a(1-\theta t)+\theta t-i'k>0.$$ Differentiating the goods equation then gives $$\frac{dY}{dt}=-\frac{\theta Y(1-a)}D<0.$$ A higher tax rate lowers equilibrium output in this model.

solutionSteps.title: Differentiate collections rather than output alone
solutionSteps.body: Tax revenue is $R=\theta tY$. Its derivative is $$\begin{aligned}\frac{dR}{dt}&=\theta Y+\theta t\frac{dY}{dt}\\&=\theta Y\frac{a-i'k}{D}>0.\end{aligned}$$ Output falls, but not enough to outweigh the direct effect of the higher rate. Hence this model has no downward-sloping Laffer segment under its stated behavioural assumptions.

solutionSteps.title: Extend the base to all factor income
solutionSteps.body: With an all-income tax, private saving becomes $s((1-t)Y)$ and receipts become $tY$. Set $\theta=1$ throughout the derivation. Then $$\frac{d(tY)}{dt}=Y\frac{a-i'k}{a(1-t)+t-i'k}>0.$$ Broadening the tax base therefore does not reverse the conclusion. The signs assume positive income and economically admissible rates.

questions.stem: X∼B(n,p). The maximum value of Var(X) is
questions.solution: Var(X)=np(1−p)=n[1/4−(p−1/2)²]≤n/4, attained at p=1/2.
questions.hint: Complete the square in p.

Continuous everywhere but not differentiable anywhere

questions.stem: The maximum and minimum values of f(x)=|x²+2x−3|+1.5logₑx on [1/2,4] are
questions.solution: On [1/2,1], f=3−2x−x²+1.5lnx, with derivative −2−2x+1.5/x≤0. On [1,4], f=x²+2x−3+1.5lnx is increasing. Thus the minimum is f(1)=0. Compare endpoint values: f(4)=21+3ln2 exceeds f(1/2)=7/4−1.5ln2.
questions.hint: Split at the positive zero of the expression inside the absolute value.

questions.stem: Let α and β be roots of x²−px+q=0 and xₙ=αⁿ+βⁿ. Then xₙ₊₁ is
questions.solution: Each root r satisfies r²=pr−q. Multiply by rⁿ⁻¹ and sum over α and β to obtain xₙ₊₁=pxₙ−qxₙ₋₁.
questions.hint: Use the quadratic equation satisfied by each root.

questions.stem: Let f:[−1,1]→ℝ be twice differentiable at 0, f(0)=f′(0)=0 and f″(0)=4. Find limₓ→₀[2f(x)−3f(2x)+f(4x)]/x².
questions.solution: Taylor expansion at zero gives f(t)=2t²+o(t²). The numerator is [4−24+32]x²+o(x²)=12x²+o(x²), yielding 12.
questions.hint: Use the second-order expansion at zero.

questions.stem: For e<x₁<x₂<∞, (logₑx₂)/(logₑx₁) is
options: Greater than x₂/x₁ but less than (x₂/x₁)²
questions.solution: The derivative of (lnx)/x is (1−lnx)/x²<0 for x>e. Thus (lnx₂)/x₂<(lnx₁)/x₁, which rearranges to the first choice.
questions.hint: Study the monotonicity of (lnx)/x.

questions.solution: Rationalizing each summand gives 1/(√k+√(k+1))=√(k+1)−√k. The sum telescopes to √100−√1=9. Since 9 is excluded from (0,9), the third choice is correct.
questions.hint: Rationalize each denominator.

questions.stem: A combination lock has 3 buttons, pressed in any sequence including multiple buttons simultaneously, with each number pressed exactly once. The number of possible combinations is
questions.solution: There are 3!=6 sequences of three individual presses, 3·2=6 ways to choose the pair pressed together and order that pair relative to the singleton, and 1 way to press all together. Total 6+6+1=13.
questions.hint: Count by the number of simultaneous groups.

questions.stem: Let R be the correlation between x and y, and R₁ the correlation between x and y+x. Then
questions.answer: None of these is universally true
questions.solution: For uncorrelated unit-variance x,y, R=0 while R₁=1/√2>0. For y=x with positive variance, R=R₁=1. Therefore neither universal strict increase nor universal equality holds; a decrease is also not a universal rule. Choose none.
questions.hint: Test both an uncorrelated pair and a perfectly correlated pair.
questions.notes: Correlations are interpreted only where both are defined; y=−x makes the second one undefined.

questions.stem: Evaluate ∫₋₁¹(x+|x|)dx.
questions.solution: For negative x the integrand is zero, and for positive x it is 2x. The integral is ∫₀¹2xdx=1.
questions.hint: Split the integral at zero.

questions.solution: The feasible vertices are (0,0),(20,0),(10,12),(0,18). Their objective values are 0,900,1110,990, respectively. The maximum 1110 occurs at (10,12).
