questions.stem: Let disjoint sets A and B contain m and n elements, respectively, and C=A∪B. The number of subsets S of C containing k elements with S∩A containing i elements is
questions.solution: Choose the i elements from A and the remaining k−i from B independently. The product rule gives the fourth choice.
questions.hint: Choose separately from the disjoint sets.

questions.stem: The number of disjoint intervals over which f(x)=|0.5x²−|x|| is decreasing is
questions.solution: For x≥0, f=x−x²/2 on [0,2] and f=x²/2−x on [2,∞). It decreases on (1,2). By evenness the negative-side decreasing intervals are (−∞,−2) and (−1,0). Thus there are three maximal decreasing intervals.
questions.hint: Split at the zeros and turning points of the absolute-value expression.

questions.stem: For real numbers x₁,…,xₙ, RMS={N⁻¹Σᵢ₌₁ⁿxᵢ²}^(1/2). If AM denotes their arithmetic mean, which statement is correct?
options: RMS<AM when the numbers are not all equal
RMS>AM when the numbers are not all equal
questions.answer: RMS>AM when the numbers are not all equal
questions.solution: Interpreting N as the number n of observations, RMS²−AM²=n⁻¹Σ(xᵢ−AM)². For unequal observations this is positive, so RMS>|AM|≥AM.
questions.hint: Relate the difference of squared means to variance.
questions.notes: Source uses uppercase N in the denominator but lowercase n for the number of observations; they are interpreted as the same sample size.

questions.stem: Let Δf(x)=f(x+1)−f(x), and for k>1 put Δᵏf=Δ(Δᵏ⁻¹f). Then Δᵏf(x) equals
questions.solution: If E is the shift operator Ef(x)=f(x+1), then Δ=E−I. The binomial expansion of (E−I)ᵏ gives precisely the third expression.
questions.hint: Use the binomial theorem for the shift operator.

questions.stem: Let Iₙ=∫₀^∞xⁿe^(−x)dx for a positive integer n. Then Iₙ equals
questions.solution: Integrate by parts with u=xⁿ and dv=e^(−x)dx. The boundary term −xⁿe^(−x) vanishes at both ends, leaving n∫₀^∞xⁿ⁻¹e^(−x)dx.
questions.hint: Integrate by parts.

questions.stem: If x³=1, then Δ=det([[a,b,c],[b,c,a],[c,a,b]]) equals
questions.solution: Replace the first column by C₁+xC₂+x²C₃. Its entries are s, x²s, xs, where s=a+bx+cx² and x³=1. By determinant multilinearity this operation leaves Δ unchanged, and factoring out s gives the fourth choice.
questions.hint: Combine the columns with coefficients 1,x,x².
questions.notes: The identity is valid for every complex cube root of unity. At x=1 all four displayed options coincide; the fourth is the generally valid identity.

questions.stem: Consider I=m²+n², where m and n are any two odd integers. Then
questions.solution: Every odd square is 1 modulo 4, hence I≡2 modulo 4. It is even, and m=n=3 gives I=18 divisible by 6.
questions.hint: Reduce odd squares modulo 4.

questions.stem: A box has 10 red and 5 black balls. A selected red ball is returned. If a black ball is selected, it and 2 additional black balls are put in the box. The probability that the second selected ball is red is
questions.solution: Conditioning on the first draw gives (10/15)(10/15)+(5/15)(10/17)=4/9+10/51=98/153.
questions.hint: Condition on the first ball’s colour.

questions.stem: Let f(x)=[log(1+x/p)−log(1−x/q)]/x for x≠0. If f is continuous at x=0, then f(0) equals
questions.solution: The numerator vanishes at zero and its derivative there is 1/p+1/q. Consequently its ratio to x tends to this value, which continuity forces to equal f(0).
questions.hint: Use the derivative of the numerator at zero.
questions.notes: Nonzero p and q are required for the source formula to be defined.

questions.stem: Four positive numbers x₁,x₂,y₁,y₂ satisfy y₁y₂>x₁x₂. Consider S=(x₁y₂+x₂y₁)−2x₁x₂. The number S is
questions.solution: AM–GM gives x₁y₂+x₂y₁≥2√(x₁x₂y₁y₂)>2x₁x₂ because y₁y₂>x₁x₂>0. Hence S>0.
questions.hint: Apply AM–GM to the two mixed products.

questions.stem: Given x≥y≥z and x+y+z=12, the maximum value of x+3y+5z is
questions.solution: The expression is 3(x+y+z)−2(x−z)=36−2(x−z)≤36. Equality occurs at x=y=z=4.
questions.hint: Compare the expression with three times the sum.

questions.stem: The number of positive integral pairs (x,y) solving 2xy−4x²+12x−5y=11 is
questions.solution: Rearrange to (2x−5)y=4x²−12x+11, or y=2x−1+6/(2x−5). The odd integer 2x−5 must divide 6, so it is ±1 or ±3. The resulting positive pairs are (3,11) and (4,9); x=1,2 give negative y.
questions.hint: Divide the quadratic by 2x−5 and use divisibility.

questions.stem: For any continuous f:[0,1]→[0,1], which statement is incorrect?
options: f always has at least one maximum in [0,1]
f always has at least one minimum in [0,1]
There exists x∈[0,1] such that f(x)=x
f(0)∈{0,1}, f(1)∈{0,1}, and f(0)+f(1)=1 must always hold
questions.answer: The endpoint assertion in the fourth option is incorrect
questions.solution: The extreme value theorem proves the first two. For g(x)=f(x)−x, g(0)≥0 and g(1)≤0, so the intermediate value theorem proves a fixed point. The constant function f(x)=1/2 disproves the fourth assertion.
questions.hint: Use compactness and the intermediate value theorem, then test a constant function.

questions.stem: (a) Two competitive sectors produce the same good with Fᵢ(Lᵢ)=15√Lᵢ. Labour moves freely, and total labour is100. Find allocation. (b) All variable-factor prices and the output price double: what happens to short-run output and profit? (c) Year1 wheat production750 includes exports150 and unsold stock600; year2 has no production, old wheat is sold domestically and shirts250 are imported. Fill GDP=C+I+X−M.
questions.answer: (a) L₁=L₂=50. (b) Output unchanged; profit doubles only if fixed cost also doubles or is zero. (c) Year1 (GDP,C,I,X,M)=(750,0,600,150,0); year2 (0,850,−600,0,250).
questions.solution:
Allocate the mobile labour. Both sectors sell the same output at the same price. Competitive firms hire until the value marginal product equals the common wage. Therefore 
(15)/(2√(L_1))=(15)/(2√(L_2)), L_1+L_2=100.
 Identical technologies imply L_1=L_2=50.

Separate the output decision from the fixed-cost bill. Let original profit be π=pq-VC(q)-F. Doubling output and all variable-input prices doubles the function pq-VC(q) at every output, leaving its maximizer unchanged. If fixed cost stays F, new profit is 
π'=2[pq-VC(q)]-F=2π+F.
 Profit doubles only when fixed cost also doubles, or is zero. A statement about variable prices alone does not establish that.

Record production and inventory investment. Year-1 wheat production is 750, including exports 150 and inventory investment 600. Thus (Y,C,I,X,M)=(750,0,600,150,0). In year 2, consumption is 600+250=850, inventories fall by 600 and imports are 250. Therefore Y_2=850-600-250=0, and the complete tuple is (0,850,-600,0,250). Counting the old wheat as new output would double count it.
questions.hint: Equalize marginal products and distinguish variable from fixed cost and inventory changes.
questions.notes: Subpart (c) concerns macroeconomic accounting.

solutionSteps.title: Allocate the mobile labour
solutionSteps.body: Both sectors sell the same output at the same price. Competitive firms hire until the value marginal product equals the common wage. Therefore $$\frac{15}{2\sqrt{L_1}}=\frac{15}{2\sqrt{L_2}},\qquad L_1+L_2=100.$$ Identical technologies imply $L_1=L_2=50$.

solutionSteps.title: Separate the output decision from the fixed-cost bill
solutionSteps.body: Let original profit be $\pi=pq-VC(q)-F$. Doubling output and all variable-input prices doubles the function $pq-VC(q)$ at every output, leaving its maximizer unchanged. If fixed cost stays $F$, new profit is $$\pi'=2[pq-VC(q)]-F=2\pi+F.$$ Profit doubles only when fixed cost also doubles, or is zero. A statement about variable prices alone does not establish that.

solutionSteps.title: Record production and inventory investment
solutionSteps.body: Year-1 wheat production is 750, including exports 150 and inventory investment 600. Thus $(Y,C,I,X,M)=(750,0,600,150,0)$. In year 2, consumption is $600+250=850$, inventories fall by 600 and imports are 250. Therefore $Y_2=850-600-250=0$, and the complete tuple is $(0,850,-600,0,250)$. Counting the old wheat as new output would double count it.

questions.stem: A price-taking farmer has production F(L)=10√L−2L, four units of free family labour and cannot hire outside labour. (a) Find output. (b) Does a10% income tax change it? (c) Would he adopt F̃(L)=11√L−L−15 instead?
questions.answer: (a) L=4, output12. (b) Unchanged. (c) No; the alternative’s maximum feasible output is3.
questions.solution:
Respect the available family labour. The farmer maximizes output revenue with no labour expense, but cannot use more than four units. For 0<L≤4, 
F'(L)=(5)/(√(L))-2≥(1)/(2)>0.
 Output therefore rises throughout the feasible range and is maximized at L=4, giving F(4)=20-8=12.

Apply a proportional income tax. A 10% tax scales positive revenue by 0.9. It does not change the ranking of feasible labour choices, so the farmer still uses four units and produces 12. An unconstrained optimum beyond four units is irrelevant because outside hiring is prohibited.

Compare technologies at their own feasible optima. For the alternative, F (alternative)'(L)=11/(2√(L))-1>0 over the same feasible range. Its best feasible output is therefore 
F (alternative)(4)=11(2)-4-15=3.
 Since 3 is below 12, the farmer rejects it. A larger leading coefficient alone is not enough to make the alternative better; its constant deduction matters.
questions.hint: Respect the family-labour constraint before comparing technologies.

solutionSteps.title: Respect the available family labour
solutionSteps.body: The farmer maximizes output revenue with no labour expense, but cannot use more than four units. For $0<L\le4$, $$F'(L)=\frac5{\sqrt L}-2\ge\frac12>0.$$ Output therefore rises throughout the feasible range and is maximized at $L=4$, giving $F(4)=20-8=12$.

solutionSteps.title: Apply a proportional income tax
solutionSteps.body: A 10% tax scales positive revenue by 0.9. It does not change the ranking of feasible labour choices, so the farmer still uses four units and produces 12. An unconstrained optimum beyond four units is irrelevant because outside hiring is prohibited.

solutionSteps.title: Compare technologies at their own feasible optima
solutionSteps.body: For the alternative, $\widetilde F'(L)=11/(2\sqrt L)-1>0$ over the same feasible range. Its best feasible output is therefore $$\widetilde F(4)=11(2)-4-15=3.$$ Since 3 is below 12, the farmer rejects it. A larger leading coefficient alone is not enough to make the alternative better; its constant deduction matters.

questions.stem: A zero-cost monopolist cannot discriminate. TypeI is one customer with demand Q_I=100−P for0≤P≤100. TypeII consists of n customers each demanding one unit only at prices at most5. Does the optimal price depend on n?
questions.answer: Price50 if n<405; price5 if n>405; either price if n=405, assuming customers buy at reservation price.
questions.solution:
Identify the two demand regimes. At a price above 5, only the first customer buys and revenue is R_H(P)=P(100-P). At a price at most 5, the additional n customers each buy one unit, so R_L(P)=P(100+n-P). Production costs are zero, making revenue the objective.

Optimize within each regime. The high-price regime is maximized at P=50, giving revenue 2500. On 0≤ P≤5, the derivative 100+n-2P is positive, so the best low price is 5. Its revenue is 5(95+n)=475+5n. No other price in either regime can beat these respective candidates.

Compare the candidates and state the threshold. Low-price sales are preferable exactly when 
475+5n>2500 ⇔ n>405.
 Thus charge 50 for n<405, charge 5 for n>405, and either price for n=405. This uses buying at reservation-value indifference; if type-II customers refuse at the tie, use a price just below 5 and the corresponding revenue limit.
questions.hint: Compare the best high-price regime with the best low-price regime.

solutionSteps.title: Identify the two demand regimes
solutionSteps.body: At a price above 5, only the first customer buys and revenue is $R_H(P)=P(100-P)$. At a price at most 5, the additional $n$ customers each buy one unit, so $R_L(P)=P(100+n-P)$. Production costs are zero, making revenue the objective.

solutionSteps.title: Optimize within each regime
solutionSteps.body: The high-price regime is maximized at $P=50$, giving revenue 2500. On $0\le P\le5$, the derivative $100+n-2P$ is positive, so the best low price is 5. Its revenue is $5(95+n)=475+5n$. No other price in either regime can beat these respective candidates.

solutionSteps.title: Compare the candidates and state the threshold
solutionSteps.body: Low-price sales are preferable exactly when $$475+5n>2500\quad\Leftrightarrow\quad n>405.$$ Thus charge 50 for $n<405$, charge 5 for $n>405$, and either price for $n=405$. This uses buying at reservation-value indifference; if type-II customers refuse at the tie, use a price just below 5 and the corresponding revenue limit.

questions.stem: A consumer has U(x,y)=xy, income100 and initial prices pₓ=5,pᵧ=10. Then pₓ rises to10, with other data fixed. Decompose price effects using Slutsky compensation.
questions.answer: x: total−5, substitution−2.5, income−2.5. y: total0, substitution+2.5, income−2.5.
questions.solution:
Calculate uncompensated demand before and after the price change. For U=xy, half of income is spent on each good: x=M/(2p_x) and y=M/(2p_y). Consequently the initial bundle is (10,5) and the final bundle is (5,5). The total change is (-5,0).

Construct Slutsky compensation. Slutsky compensation makes the original bundle just affordable at the new prices. Its cost is 
M^c=10(10)+10(5)=150.
 At income 150 and the new equal prices, optimal demand is (7.5,7.5). This is a reoptimized bundle, not necessarily the original bundle.

Separate the two movements. The substitution effect moves from old demand to compensated demand; the income effect removes the compensation at the new prices: 
SE =(7.5,7.5)-(10,5)=(-2.5,2.5),; IE =(5,5)-(7.5,7.5)=(-2.5,-2.5),; PE =SE+IE=(-5,0).
 The unchanged final quantity of y therefore conceals two nonzero, offsetting effects.
questions.hint: Raise income just enough to afford the original bundle at the new prices.

solutionSteps.title: Calculate uncompensated demand before and after the price change
solutionSteps.body: For $U=xy$, half of income is spent on each good: $x=M/(2p_x)$ and $y=M/(2p_y)$. Consequently the initial bundle is $(10,5)$ and the final bundle is $(5,5)$. The total change is $(-5,0)$.

solutionSteps.title: Construct Slutsky compensation
solutionSteps.body: Slutsky compensation makes the original bundle just affordable at the new prices. Its cost is $$M^c=10(10)+10(5)=150.$$ At income 150 and the new equal prices, optimal demand is $(7.5,7.5)$. This is a reoptimized bundle, not necessarily the original bundle.

solutionSteps.title: Separate the two movements
solutionSteps.body: The substitution effect moves from old demand to compensated demand; the income effect removes the compensation at the new prices: $$\begin{aligned}SE&=(7.5,7.5)-(10,5)=(-2.5,2.5),\\IE&=(5,5)-(7.5,7.5)=(-2.5,-2.5),\\PE&=SE+IE=(-5,0).\end{aligned}$$ The unchanged final quantity of $y$ therefore conceals two nonzero, offsetting effects.

questions.stem: In a closed IS–LM economy, consumption depends on disposable income z=Y−T. Lump-sum taxes are T. Investment and speculative money demand decrease with interest r; transactions money demand depends on z rather than Y. What happens to private investment, private saving, government saving, disposable income and income when T rises, holding G and real money supply fixed?
questions.answer: Disposable income falls, interest falls, investment rises, private saving falls, government saving rises. Total income Y has an ambiguous response.
questions.solution:
Rewrite the model in disposable income. Let z=Y-T. Goods-market equilibrium becomes z+T=C(z)+I(r)+G, and money equilibrium is L(z,r)=M/P. Using z is essential here: transactions money demand is specified as a function of disposable income, not total output.

Derive the joint equilibrium response. Write k=-L_z/L_r>0, so along the unchanged LM relation dr=k dz. Differentiating goods equilibrium gives 
[1-C'(z)-I'(r)k],dz =-dT,; D =1-C'-I'k>0,; (dz)/(dT) =-(1)/(D)<0.
 Interest also falls because dr=k dz.

Track investment and the two saving components. With I'<0, the fall in interest raises private investment. Private saving S_p=z-C(z) falls because dS_p=(1-C')dz<0. Government saving T-G increases by the tax rise, since spending is held fixed. Their sum adjusts to the higher investment level.

Explain why total output has no fixed sign. Total income includes taxes: Y=z+T. Therefore 
(dY)/(dT)=1-(1)/(D)=(-C'-I'k)/(D).
 It is positive if the investment stimulus -I'k exceeds C', negative if it is smaller, and zero if they tie. Disposable income falls unambiguously, but total income need not. Applying the usual total-income money-demand model would miss this distinction.
questions.hint: Rewrite the system in disposable income and derive the implied LM movement.

solutionSteps.title: Rewrite the model in disposable income
solutionSteps.body: Let $z=Y-T$. Goods-market equilibrium becomes $z+T=C(z)+I(r)+G$, and money equilibrium is $L(z,r)=M/P$. Using $z$ is essential here: transactions money demand is specified as a function of disposable income, not total output.

solutionSteps.title: Derive the joint equilibrium response
solutionSteps.body: Write $k=-L_z/L_r>0$, so along the unchanged LM relation $dr=k\,dz$. Differentiating goods equilibrium gives $$\begin{aligned}[1-C'(z)-I'(r)k],dz&=-dT,\\D&=1-C'-I'k>0,\\\frac{dz}{dT}&=-\frac1D<0.\end{aligned}$$ Interest also falls because $dr=k\,dz$.

solutionSteps.title: Track investment and the two saving components
solutionSteps.body: With $I'<0$, the fall in interest raises private investment. Private saving $S_p=z-C(z)$ falls because $dS_p=(1-C')dz<0$. Government saving $T-G$ increases by the tax rise, since spending is held fixed. Their sum adjusts to the higher investment level.

solutionSteps.title: Explain why total output has no fixed sign
solutionSteps.body: Total income includes taxes: $Y=z+T$. Therefore $$\frac{dY}{dT}=1-\frac1D=\frac{-C'-I'k}{D}.$$ It is positive if the investment stimulus $-I'k$ exceeds $C'$, negative if it is smaller, and zero if they tie. Disposable income falls unambiguously, but total income need not. Applying the usual total-income money-demand model would miss this distinction.

questions.stem: A person likes bus distance x and dislikes smoke s, with utility U(x,s). (a) Describe plausible indifference-curve shapes. (b) Smoke is s=αx, α>0; fare is p per km and available income M. Describe the budget set in(s,x) space. (c) Characterize optimal travel: must all income be spent?
questions.answer: Indifference curves slope upward. Feasible choices form the segment(s,x)=(αx,x),0≤x≤M/p. All, some or none of the income may be spent.
questions.solution:
Describe indifference between a good and a bad. Travel is desirable, so U_x>0; smoke is undesirable, so U_s<0. Along a smooth indifference curve, ds/dx=-U_x/U_s>0. More travel must therefore be accompanied by more tolerated smoke to keep utility fixed. Its curvature is not determined by these signs alone.

Combine the technological linkage with affordability. Smoke cannot be chosen separately from travel: s=α x. The fare restriction is px≤ M. Thus the feasible set is 
{(s,x):s=α x, 0≤ x≤ M/p}.
 In a diagram with s horizontal and x vertical, this is a line segment ending at (α M/p,M/p), not the entire region below a budget line.

Characterize the optimum along that segment. Define V(x)=U(x,α x). An interior optimum satisfies V'(x)=U_x+α U_s=0, with an appropriate maximum condition. The optimal choice can also be either endpoint. Since increasing travel produces a bad as well as a good, V may turn downward before M/p; the consumer need not spend all income on travel.
questions.hint: Combine the smoke linkage with the fare constraint.

solutionSteps.title: Describe indifference between a good and a bad
solutionSteps.body: Travel is desirable, so $U_x>0$; smoke is undesirable, so $U_s<0$. Along a smooth indifference curve, $ds/dx=-U_x/U_s>0$. More travel must therefore be accompanied by more tolerated smoke to keep utility fixed. Its curvature is not determined by these signs alone.

solutionSteps.title: Combine the technological linkage with affordability
solutionSteps.body: Smoke cannot be chosen separately from travel: $s=\alpha x$. The fare restriction is $px\le M$. Thus the feasible set is $$\{(s,x):s=\alpha x,\ 0\le x\le M/p\}.$$ In a diagram with $s$ horizontal and $x$ vertical, this is a line segment ending at $(\alpha M/p,M/p)$, not the entire region below a budget line.

solutionSteps.title: Characterize the optimum along that segment
solutionSteps.body: Define $V(x)=U(x,\alpha x)$. An interior optimum satisfies $V'(x)=U_x+\alpha U_s=0$, with an appropriate maximum condition. The optimal choice can also be either endpoint. Since increasing travel produces a bad as well as a good, $V$ may turn downward before $M/p$; the consumer need not spend all income on travel.

questions.stem: (a) A household maximizes u=c^(2/3)h^(1/3), h+l=24, c=wl, with wage w>0. Find labour supply and its wage dependence. (b) In a one-good Keynesian economy, I=36, household consumption c=wl, fixed real wage w=4 and output y=24√l. Find output, employment and involuntary unemployment.
questions.answer: (a) Labour supply16, independent of w. (b) Employment9, output72, involuntary unemployment7 labour units.
questions.solution:
Derive desired labour supply. Substitute h=24-l and c=wl into u=c^(2/3)h^(1/3). Equivalently maximize (2)/(3)log(wl)+(1)/(3)log(24-l). The interior condition is 
(2)/(l)-(1)/(24-l)=0,
 giving l=16 and leisure 8. The wage enters log utility only through a constant, so labour supply does not depend on w>0.

Combine demand with the production function. At wage 4, consumption is 4l. Goods-market equilibrium requires 
24√(l) =4l+36,; 6√(l) =l+9,; (√(l)-3)^2 =0.
 Thus employment is 9 and output is 24(3)=72. Consumption and investment are each 36.

Check the wage and measure unemployment. The marginal product is 12/√(l), which equals the given wage 4 at l=9. The household would supply 16 labour units at that wage but only 9 are employed. Involuntary unemployment is therefore 16-9=7 units; it is not the difference between employment and the entire 24-hour time endowment.
questions.hint: Find desired labour supply first, then combine expenditure and production.

solutionSteps.title: Derive desired labour supply
solutionSteps.body: Substitute $h=24-l$ and $c=wl$ into $u=c^{2/3}h^{1/3}$. Equivalently maximize $\tfrac23\log(wl)+\tfrac13\log(24-l)$. The interior condition is $$\frac2l-\frac1{24-l}=0,$$ giving $l=16$ and leisure 8. The wage enters log utility only through a constant, so labour supply does not depend on $w>0$.

solutionSteps.title: Combine demand with the production function
solutionSteps.body: At wage 4, consumption is $4l$. Goods-market equilibrium requires $$\begin{aligned}24\sqrt l&=4l+36,\\6\sqrt l&=l+9,\\(\sqrt l-3)^2&=0.\end{aligned}$$ Thus employment is 9 and output is $24(3)=72$. Consumption and investment are each 36.

solutionSteps.title: Check the wage and measure unemployment
solutionSteps.body: The marginal product is $12/\sqrt l$, which equals the given wage 4 at $l=9$. The household would supply 16 labour units at that wage but only 9 are employed. Involuntary unemployment is therefore $16-9=7$ units; it is not the difference between employment and the entire 24-hour time endowment.

questions.stem: Two-period utility is (C₁^(1−θ)−1)/(1−θ)+(1/(1+ρ))(C₂^(1−θ)−1)/(1−θ), with printed restrictions 0<θ<1, ρ>0. Youth income is w from inelastic unit labour supply, saving is s and old-age income is (1+r)s. (i) Interpret θ as marginal-utility elasticity. (ii) State the optimization. (iii) Find saving. (iv) Explain how saving responds to r for θ below or above 1. (v) Give intuition.
questions.answer: s=w/[1+(1+ρ)^(1/θ)(1+r)^((θ−1)/θ)]. It rises with r when θ<1, falls when θ>1, and is independent of r in the θ=1 log limit.
questions.solution:
Interpret the preference parameter and the budgets. For one-period CRRA utility, u'(C)=C^(-θ), so 
(dlog u'(C))/(dlog C)=-θ.
 Thus θ is the magnitude of the elasticity of marginal utility, not its signed value. Saving s gives budgets C_1=w-s and C_2=(1+r)s, with 0≤ s≤ w, w>0 and r>-1.

Derive the Euler condition. Substitute the two budgets into lifetime utility and differentiate with respect to saving. At an interior optimum, 
(w-s)^(-θ) =(1+r)/(1+ρ)big[(1+r)sbig]^(-θ); =((1+r)^(1-θ))/(1+ρ)s^(-θ).
 This equates the marginal loss from giving up current consumption to the discounted marginal gain from the additional future consumption.

Solve explicitly for saving. Rearranging the Euler condition yields 
((s)/(w-s))^θ =((1+r)^(1-θ))/(1+ρ),; s =(w)/(1+(1+ρ)^(1/θ)(1+r)^((θ-1)/θ)).
 With positive income the solution is strictly between zero and w, so both consumption quantities are positive.

Explain the interest response and the source restriction. The derivative of saving has the sign of 1-θ. Saving rises with interest for θ<1 because intertemporal substitution dominates; it falls for θ>1 because the income effect dominates. In the logarithmic limit θ=1, saving is w/(2+ρ) and does not depend on interest. The source first imposes 0<θ<1 but later requests the θ>1 comparison. The latter is an explicitly stated extension of the formula beyond the printed restriction.
questions.hint: Substitute the two consumption budgets and derive the Euler condition.
questions.notes: The printed restriction θ<1 conflicts with a later request to consider θ>1; the extension is stated explicitly. “Elasticity” means magnitude, since signed elasticity is −θ.

solutionSteps.title: Interpret the preference parameter and the budgets
solutionSteps.body: For one-period CRRA utility, $u'(C)=C^{-\theta}$, so $$\frac{d\log u'(C)}{d\log C}=-\theta.$$ Thus $\theta$ is the magnitude of the elasticity of marginal utility, not its signed value. Saving $s$ gives budgets $C_1=w-s$ and $C_2=(1+r)s$, with $0\le s\le w$, $w>0$ and $r>-1$.

solutionSteps.title: Derive the Euler condition
solutionSteps.body: Substitute the two budgets into lifetime utility and differentiate with respect to saving. At an interior optimum, $$\begin{aligned}(w-s)^{-\theta}&=\frac{1+r}{1+\rho}\big[(1+r)s\big]^{-\theta}\\&=\frac{(1+r)^{1-\theta}}{1+\rho}s^{-\theta}.\end{aligned}$$ This equates the marginal loss from giving up current consumption to the discounted marginal gain from the additional future consumption.

solutionSteps.title: Solve explicitly for saving
solutionSteps.body: Rearranging the Euler condition yields $$\begin{aligned}\left(\frac{s}{w-s}\right)^{\theta}&=\frac{(1+r)^{1-\theta}}{1+\rho},\\s&=\frac{w}{1+(1+\rho)^{1/\theta}(1+r)^{(\theta-1)/\theta}}.\end{aligned}$$ With positive income the solution is strictly between zero and $w$, so both consumption quantities are positive.

solutionSteps.title: Explain the interest response and the source restriction
solutionSteps.body: The derivative of saving has the sign of $1-\theta$. Saving rises with interest for $\theta<1$ because intertemporal substitution dominates; it falls for $\theta>1$ because the income effect dominates. In the logarithmic limit $\theta=1$, saving is $w/(2+\rho)$ and does not depend on interest. The source first imposes $0<\theta<1$ but later requests the $\theta>1$ comparison. The latter is an explicitly stated extension of the formula beyond the printed restriction.

questions.stem: A consumer has U(x₁,x₂)=min(2x₁,x₂). (i) Describe an indifference curve. (ii) At prices5,10 and income100, find the optimal bundle. (iii) Price1 rises to8: decompose the change in good1 into income and substitution effects.
questions.answer: Initial bundle(4,8); final(25/7,50/7). Good1 total effect−3/7, substitution effect0 and income effect−3/7.
questions.solution:
Identify the kink ratio. For U=min{2x_1,x_2}, utility level u has kink (u/2,u). An efficient purchased bundle satisfies x_2=2x_1; buying additional units of only one good leaves utility unchanged.

Find the original and new Marshallian bundles. Initially the budget at the kink is (5+2×10)x_1=100, yielding (x_1,x_2)=(4,8). After the price rise, 
(8+20)x_1 =100,; x_1' =25/7, x_2'=50/7.

Compensate at the new prices. The old kink bundle now costs 8(4)+10(8)=112. At this compensated income the optimal bundle remains (4,8). Both Hicks and Slutsky compensation give the same result for this fixed-proportion case: no change in the quantity ratio can save expenditure while preserving utility.

Allocate the total change. The substitution effect for good 1 is zero. Its entire total change is the income effect: 
Δ x_1=(25)/(7)-4=-(3)/(7).
 A zero substitution effect does not mean the price increase has no consequence; it lowers the amount of the fixed-proportion bundle the original income can buy.
questions.hint: Perfect complements retain the same optimal quantity ratio after a price change.

solutionSteps.title: Identify the kink ratio
solutionSteps.body: For $U=\min\{2x_1,x_2\}$, utility level $u$ has kink $(u/2,u)$. An efficient purchased bundle satisfies $x_2=2x_1$; buying additional units of only one good leaves utility unchanged.

solutionSteps.title: Find the original and new Marshallian bundles
solutionSteps.body: Initially the budget at the kink is $(5+2\cdot10)x_1=100$, yielding $(x_1,x_2)=(4,8)$. After the price rise, $$\begin{aligned}(8+20)x_1&=100,\\x_1'&=25/7,\qquad x_2'=50/7.\end{aligned}$$

solutionSteps.title: Compensate at the new prices
solutionSteps.body: The old kink bundle now costs $8(4)+10(8)=112$. At this compensated income the optimal bundle remains $(4,8)$. Both Hicks and Slutsky compensation give the same result for this fixed-proportion case: no change in the quantity ratio can save expenditure while preserving utility.

solutionSteps.title: Allocate the total change
solutionSteps.body: The substitution effect for good 1 is zero. Its entire total change is the income effect: $$\Delta x_1=\frac{25}{7}-4=-\frac37.$$ A zero substitution effect does not mean the price increase has no consequence; it lowers the amount of the fixed-proportion bundle the original income can buy.

questions.stem: A competitive firm produces Y=K^0.25L^0.25. Labour can be hired weekly and capital monthly; a month is four weeks. Wage is10 per worker-week and capital rental10 per unit-month. (i) Find short- and long-run costs. (ii) At the beginning of January, output price is400. Find optimal long-run output and factor hires.
questions.answer: If the production function measures weekly output y: weekly SR cost10y⁴/K̄+2.5K̄ and weekly LR cost10y². Optimal y=20 per week (80/month), L=200 workers and K=800. The output period must be specified.
questions.solution:
Choose a consistent time unit before calculating costs. The statement gives labour cost per week and capital rent per month but leaves the output period unspecified. On a weekly-output interpretation write output as y and convert capital rent to 10/4=2.5 per unit-week. With capital fixed at K̄, the production constraint gives L=y^4/K̄.

Derive weekly short-run and long-run costs. The weekly short-run accounting cost is 10y^4/K̄+2.5K̄. In the long run minimize 10L+2.5K subject to LK=y^4. The cost-minimizing ratio is K=4L, hence 
L=(y^2)/(2), K=2y^2, C_(LR,week)(y)=10y^2.
 Fixed-capital rent does not change the short-run marginal cost.

Maximize profit under that convention. With output price 400, monthly profit is four times weekly operating profit: 4(400y-10y^2). The first-order condition gives y=20. Therefore labour is 200 each week, capital hired for the month is 800 and monthly output is 80. Equivalently the cost for monthly total Q=4y is C_(month)(Q)=(5)/(2)Q^2, whose marginal cost 5Q equals 400 at Q=80.

State the alternative and preserve the source caveat. If the printed production function instead refers directly to monthly output Y with a workforce retained for four weeks, monthly factor prices are 40 and 10. Then minimized cost is 40Y^2 and the optimum is Y=5, L=12.5, K=50. These conventions cannot be mixed. Because the source never assigns a period to output, the record remains marked for review rather than asserting one interpretation as unconditional.
questions.hint: Convert capital and labour prices to the same time period before minimizing cost.
questions.notes: Source gives weekly wages and monthly rentals but no time unit for output in the production function; conditional consistent conventions are supplied.

solutionSteps.title: Choose a consistent time unit before calculating costs
solutionSteps.body: The statement gives labour cost per week and capital rent per month but leaves the output period unspecified. On a weekly-output interpretation write output as $y$ and convert capital rent to $10/4=2.5$ per unit-week. With capital fixed at $\bar K$, the production constraint gives $L=y^4/\bar K$.

solutionSteps.title: Derive weekly short-run and long-run costs
solutionSteps.body: The weekly short-run accounting cost is $10y^4/\bar K+2.5\bar K$. In the long run minimize $10L+2.5K$ subject to $LK=y^4$. The cost-minimizing ratio is $K=4L$, hence $$L=\frac{y^2}{2},\qquad K=2y^2,\qquad C_{LR,week}(y)=10y^2.$$ Fixed-capital rent does not change the short-run marginal cost.

solutionSteps.title: Maximize profit under that convention
solutionSteps.body: With output price 400, monthly profit is four times weekly operating profit: $4(400y-10y^2)$. The first-order condition gives $y=20$. Therefore labour is 200 each week, capital hired for the month is 800 and monthly output is 80. Equivalently the cost for monthly total $Q=4y$ is $C_{month}(Q)=\tfrac52Q^2$, whose marginal cost $5Q$ equals 400 at $Q=80$.

solutionSteps.title: State the alternative and preserve the source caveat
solutionSteps.body: If the printed production function instead refers directly to monthly output $Y$ with a workforce retained for four weeks, monthly factor prices are 40 and 10. Then minimized cost is $40Y^2$ and the optimum is $Y=5$, $L=12.5$, $K=50$. These conventions cannot be mixed. Because the source never assigns a period to output, the record remains marked for review rather than asserting one interpretation as unconditional.

questions.stem: In a neoclassical one-sector growth model, Y=√(KL), saving/investment is 30% of income, depreciation is 7% and labour growth is 3%. Find steady-state income per capita.
questions.answer: Income per capita y*=3 (capital per worker k*=9).
questions.solution:
Express technology per worker. Divide Y=√(KL) by labour L and write k=K/L. Output per worker is y=√(k). With no technological growth, a positive steady state keeps k constant.

Equate saving to break-even investment. The capital stock per worker loses resources through depreciation and through the need to equip additional workers. Hence 
s√(k) =(δ+n)k,; 0.3√(k) =(0.07+0.03)k.
 For k>0, divide by √(k) to obtain √(k)=3.

Read off the requested income level. Thus k^*=9 and y^*=√(9)=3. The question asks for income per capita, so the answer is 3 rather than the capital-labour ratio 9. This is the positive steady state; the mathematical zero-capital state is not the economically relevant interior equilibrium.
questions.hint: Set saving per worker equal to break-even investment.

solutionSteps.title: Express technology per worker
solutionSteps.body: Divide $Y=\sqrt{KL}$ by labour $L$ and write $k=K/L$. Output per worker is $y=\sqrt{k}$. With no technological growth, a positive steady state keeps $k$ constant.

solutionSteps.title: Equate saving to break-even investment
solutionSteps.body: The capital stock per worker loses resources through depreciation and through the need to equip additional workers. Hence $$\begin{aligned}s\sqrt{k}&=(\delta+n)k,\\0.3\sqrt{k}&=(0.07+0.03)k.\end{aligned}$$ For $k>0$, divide by $\sqrt{k}$ to obtain $\sqrt{k}=3$.

solutionSteps.title: Read off the requested income level
solutionSteps.body: Thus $k^*=9$ and $y^*=\sqrt{9}=3$. The question asks for income per capita, so the answer is 3 rather than the capital-labour ratio 9. This is the positive steady state; the mathematical zero-capital state is not the economically relevant interior equilibrium.

questions.stem: For positive real α and β, evaluate lim(x→0) [(1+x)^α−1]/[(1+x)^β−1].
questions.solution: Both numerator and denominator vanish. Their first-order expansions are αx+o(x) and βx+o(x), giving α/β.
questions.hint: Use the derivative of a power at 1.

questions.stem: Suppose the integer X is odd. Then X²−1 is
questions.solution: For odd X, X²−1=(X−1)(X+1) is divisible by 8. It is either zero (X=±1) or a positive composite number. Thus it is never prime and need not be positive.
questions.hint: Factor the difference of squares.

questions.stem: For which k is f(x)=k exp(kx) a probability density on [0,1]?
questions.solution: The total integral is exp(k)−1. Setting it to 1 gives exp(k)=2 and k=log 2, which also makes the density nonnegative.
questions.hint: Normalize the density by integration.

questions.stem: Positive integers p and q satisfy that p²−q² is prime. Then p−q is
options: An odd number greater than 1 but not prime
questions.solution: Since (p−q)(p+q) is positive prime and p+q>p−q>0, necessarily p−q=1. None of the first three statements describes 1.
questions.hint: Use the factorization of a difference of squares.

questions.stem: Any non-decreasing function on [a,b]
options: Is continuous on [a,b] but not differentiable
questions.solution: A step function is non-decreasing but discontinuous, so (A) and (B) need not hold. A constant function is non-decreasing but has no inverse.
questions.hint: Consider a step function and a constant function.

questions.stem: The determinant equation det[[x,3,4],[1,2,1],[1,8,1]]=0 is satisfied by
questions.solution: Replace the third row by the third minus the second, giving [0,6,0]. Expansion along this row gives −6(x−4)=0, hence x=4.
questions.hint: Subtract the second row from the third.

questions.stem: If f(x)=√(x+√(x+√(x+⋯))), find f′(x) where the positive radical converges and is differentiable.
questions.solution: The repeated tail equals f(x), so f(x)²=x+f(x). Differentiating gives (2f(x)−1)f′(x)=1.
questions.hint: Express the infinite tail using f itself.
questions.notes: The derivative is on the positive-input branch; the radical at the isolated endpoint x=0 needs a separate limiting convention.

questions.stem: If P=logₓ(xy) and Q=logᵧ(xy), then P+Q equals
questions.solution: Write a=log x and b=log y. Then P=(a+b)/a and Q=(a+b)/b, so P+Q=(a+b)²/(ab)=PQ.
questions.hint: Change both logarithms to the same base.
questions.notes: Assume the displayed logarithms exist: x,y>0 and x,y≠1.

questions.stem: Evaluate ∫(2x³+1)/(x⁴+2x) dx.
questions.solution: The derivative of the denominator is 4x³+2, twice the numerator. Substitution u=x⁴+2x yields (1/2)∫du/u.
questions.hint: Compare the numerator with the denominator’s derivative.

questions.stem: Find all x for which x²−3x+2>0.
questions.solution: Factor (x−1)(x−2). The product is positive outside the two roots, excluding both roots.
questions.hint: Use a sign chart.

questions.stem: On the real line let f₁(x)=x² and f₂(x)=4x³+7. Which statement is correct?
options: f₁ is one-to-one and onto but f₂ is not
f₂ is one-to-one and onto but f₁ is not
questions.answer: f₂ is one-to-one and onto but f₁ is not
questions.solution: The cubic is strictly increasing and has range ℝ. The square takes the same value at x and −x and never takes negative values.
questions.hint: Check injectivity and the full real range.

questions.stem: If f(x)=((a+x)/(b+x))^(a+b+2x), with a,b>0, find f′(0).
questions.solution: Logarithmic differentiation gives f′/f=2 log((a+x)/(b+x))+(a+b+2x)[1/(a+x)−1/(b+x)]. At zero the bracketed second contribution is (a+b)(b−a)/(ab)=(b²−a²)/(ab), and f(0)=(a/b)^(a+b).
questions.hint: Take logarithms before differentiating.

questions.stem: Maximize z=0.5x+1.5y subject to x+y≤6, 3x+y≤15, x+3y≤15, x,y≥0. The problem has
questions.solution: The objective is 0.5(x+3y), so it cannot exceed 7.5. Every point on the feasible segment from (0,5) to (1.5,4.5) attains 7.5; hence infinitely many optima exist.
questions.hint: Compare the objective with the third constraint.

questions.stem: For 0<θ<1, let f(x;θ)=θf(x;1)+(1−θ)f(x;0), where f(x;1) and f(x;0) are probability densities. Then
options: f(x;θ) is a density for all allowed θ
It is a density only for 0<θ<1/2
It is a density only for 1/2≤θ<1
questions.answer: f(x;θ) is a density for all allowed θ
questions.solution: A convex combination of nonnegative functions is nonnegative. Its integral is θ+(1−θ)=1 for every allowed θ.
questions.hint: Check nonnegativity and total integral.

questions.stem: For observations (x,y)=(5,0),(1,4),(4,2),(3,0),(2,−1), the correlation r satisfies
questions.solution: The means are x̄=3 and ȳ=1. The centered cross-product sum is −5; the centered square sums are 10 and 16. Thus r=−5/√160≈−0.395, between −0.5 and zero.
questions.hint: Compute centered cross products.

questions.stem: A function is homothetic if it is an increasing transformation of a degree-one homogeneous function. For xᵢ>0, 0<r<1 and aᵢ>0, let f₁=Σxᵢʳ and f₂=Σaᵢxᵢ+b. Then
questions.solution: The function g₁=(Σxᵢʳ)^(1/r) is homogeneous of degree one, and f₁=g₁ʳ is an increasing transformation. Also g₂=Σaᵢxᵢ is homogeneous of degree one, and f₂=g₂+b is an increasing transformation.
questions.hint: Apply the power 1/r to the first function.

questions.stem: If h(x)=1/(1−x), find h(h(h(x))).
questions.solution: The second iterate is (x−1)/x. Applying h again gives 1/[1−(x−1)/x]=x. The composition requires x≠0,1.
questions.hint: Calculate the second iterate first.

questions.stem: The function x|x|+(|x|/x)³ is
options: Continuous but not differentiable at x=0
questions.solution: For x>0 the function is x²+1, whose right limit is 1. For x<0 it is −x²−1, whose left limit is −1. No value assigned at zero can make it continuous.
questions.hint: Evaluate the two one-sided limits.
questions.notes: The printed formula is undefined at zero; it has no continuous extension there.

questions.stem: Evaluate ∫2/[(x−2)(x−1)x] dx.
questions.solution: Partial fractions give 1/x−2/(x−1)+1/(x−2). Integrating and combining logarithms gives log|x(x−2)/(x−1)²|+C.
questions.hint: Use partial fractions at the three simple poles.

questions.stem: Each restaurant reservation independently has a 20% chance of not showing up. There are 50 tables and 52 reservations. What is the probability of accommodating everyone?
questions.solution: If N is the number showing up, N~Binomial(52,0.8). Failure occurs only when 51 or 52 show. Its probability is 52(0.8)^51(0.2)+(0.8)^52=14(0.8)^52. Subtract from 1.
questions.hint: Only two possible attendance counts exceed capacity.
questions.notes: The source does not explicitly state independence; the standard binomial model is used.

questions.stem: With [x]=floor(x), evaluate I=∫₀^(3/2) {[x]+[x²]} dx.
questions.solution: On [0,1), both floors vanish. On [1,√2), their sum is 2; on [√2,3/2], their sum is 3. Thus I=2(√2−1)+3(3/2−√2)=5/2−√2.
questions.hint: Split at the integer thresholds of x and x².

questions.stem: Every integer of the form (n³−n)(n²−4), n=3,4,…, is
questions.solution: The expression is (n−2)(n−1)n(n+1)(n+2), the product of five consecutive integers. It equals 5! times an integer, hence is divisible by 120. At n=3 it equals 120, which is not divisible by 720.
questions.hint: Factor into five consecutive integers.

questions.stem: Mango varieties A and B cost p₁ and p₂ rupees per kg. Buyer 1 buys 5 kg A and 10 kg B; buyer 2 spends Rs 100 on A and Rs 150 on B. If their average expenditure per mango (irrespective of variety) is the same, which statement is most appropriate?
questions.answer: Intended: C, p₁=p₂ or p₂=3p₁/4; literal wording lacks unit-weight information.
questions.solution: If “per mango” means per kg, equality gives (5p₁+10p₂)/15=250/(100/p₁+150/p₂). Simplifying yields (p₁−p₂)(3p₁−4p₂)=0, so option C. Literally per mango requires the number or average weight of mangoes of each variety, which is not provided.
questions.hint: Write each buyer’s total spending divided by total quantity.
questions.notes: Source mixes prices per kg with an average per mango; intended answer requires equal average mango weights or replacing “per mango” with “per kg”.

questions.stem: For paired data, the squared correlation coefficient between x² and y is 1. Which statement follows about the (x,y) scatter diagram?
options: All points lie on a straight line
All points lie on y=a+bx² with a>0,b>0
All points lie on y=a+bx² for real a,b
questions.answer: All points lie on y=a+bx² for real a,b
questions.solution: Absolute correlation one means an exact affine relation between y and the transformed variable x²: y=a+bx², with nonzero b when correlation is defined. Neither intercept nor slope has a required positive sign.
questions.hint: Treat x² as a new variable.

questions.stem: How many permutations of 1,…,7 have both 1 and 2 before 3 and both 6 and 7 after 3?
questions.solution: Among the 5! relative orders of {1,2,3,6,7}, exactly 2!·2!=4 satisfy the restrictions. Each relative order occurs equally often in the 7! full permutations, so the count is 7!·4/5!=168.
questions.hint: First count the allowed relative orders of five constrained entries.

questions.stem: A continuous real function on [0,∞) satisfies f(x)=xf(x). What is f(2)?
questions.solution: For every x≠1, (1−x)f(x)=0 forces f(x)=0. Continuity then forces f(1)=0 too. Consequently f(2)=0=f(1).
questions.hint: Rearrange the functional equation, then use continuity at 1.

questions.stem: A variable X takes 0,1,…,n with probabilities proportional to C(n,0),C(n,1),…,C(n,n). Find mean μ and variance σ².
questions.solution: The binomial coefficients sum to 2ⁿ, so P(X=k)=C(n,k)(1/2)ⁿ. This is Binomial(n,1/2), with mean n/2 and variance n/4.
questions.hint: Identify the normalized binomial distribution.

questions.stem: Five points are placed anywhere inside a square of side 2. Which statement is incorrect?
options: No two points have distance greater than 2√2
Partition into four unit squares: some unit square has at least two points on or inside it
At least two points have distance less than √2
Statements A, B and C are all incorrect
questions.answer: Intended D for strict interior points; C and D are false if the boundary is included.
questions.solution: A follows from the square’s diameter and B from the pigeonhole principle. If “inside” means strict interior, C is true: two points in a common half-square cannot be opposite external corners, hence a pair has distance strictly below √2, making D the sole false statement. If boundary points are allowed, the four vertices and center have minimum distance √2, so C is false as well as D.
questions.hint: Partition the square into four equal squares and check strict versus weak inequalities.
questions.notes: Strict “less than” creates a boundary-convention ambiguity. Four vertices plus the center are a counterexample if boundary points are allowed.

questions.stem: A differentiable real function satisfies f(x)f′(x)<0 for all real x. Then
questions.solution: The condition ensures f never vanishes. Thus |f| is differentiable with derivative f f′/|f|<0. The sign of f itself may be positive or negative, so its direction of change alone is not determined.
questions.hint: Differentiate |f| using that f never equals zero.

questions.stem: For positive p,q,r,s, (p²+p+1)(q²+q+1)(r²+r+1)(s²+s+1)/(pqrs) is at least
questions.solution: Each factor after division by its variable is t+1+1/t≥3 by t+1/t≥2. Multiplying four such bounds gives 3⁴=81, attained at p=q=r=s=1.
questions.hint: Apply AM–GM to t and 1/t.

questions.stem: (a) A cake of size 1 is cut into two pieces by person 1; person 2 chooses a piece first and person 1 receives the remainder. What cut is optimal for person 1? (b) Kamal has a free classical-concert ticket and values the concert at Rs 30. A competing film-music event costs Rs 200 and is worth Rs X to him. Which event, or neither, should he choose?
questions.answer: (a) Equal halves. (b) Classical if X<230, film if X>230; indifferent at X=230.
questions.solution:
Choose the cut by anticipating the chooser. Write the two cake sizes as z and 1-z, where 0≤ z≤1. Person 2 chooses the larger piece. Consequently person 1 receives min{z,1-z}, rather than being able to select the preferred piece herself.

Maximize the guaranteed share. If z<1/2, increasing z improves the smaller piece. If z>1/2, decreasing z improves the smaller piece. Thus the unique best size division is z=1/2: each piece is one-half, and person 1 guarantees herself one-half.

Compare the entertainment options on a common basis. The free concert still provides a benefit: its net benefit is Rs 30. The film event provides benefit X but requires a payment of Rs 200. Staying home is the zero-benefit benchmark. Hence 
B_(concert) =30,; B_(film) =X-200,; B_(neither) =0.

State the decision and the tie. Choose the concert if X<230 and the film if X>230. At X=230 they give the same net benefit. Neither is optimal because the available concert has positive net benefit. This comparison assumes that the free ticket cannot be resold; the question supplies no resale opportunity.
questions.hint: Use the chooser’s best response, then compare net benefits.

solutionSteps.title: Choose the cut by anticipating the chooser
solutionSteps.body: Write the two cake sizes as $z$ and $1-z$, where $0\le z\le1$. Person 2 chooses the larger piece. Consequently person 1 receives $\min\{z,1-z\}$, rather than being able to select the preferred piece herself.

solutionSteps.title: Maximize the guaranteed share
solutionSteps.body: If $z<1/2$, increasing $z$ improves the smaller piece. If $z>1/2$, decreasing $z$ improves the smaller piece. Thus the unique best size division is $z=1/2$: each piece is one-half, and person 1 guarantees herself one-half.

solutionSteps.title: Compare the entertainment options on a common basis
solutionSteps.body: The free concert still provides a benefit: its net benefit is Rs 30. The film event provides benefit $X$ but requires a payment of Rs 200. Staying home is the zero-benefit benchmark. Hence $$\begin{aligned} B_{\mathrm{concert}}&=30,\\ B_{\mathrm{film}}&=X-200,\\ B_{\mathrm{neither}}&=0.\end{aligned}$$

solutionSteps.title: State the decision and the tie
solutionSteps.body: Choose the concert if $X<230$ and the film if $X>230$. At $X=230$ they give the same net benefit. Neither is optimal because the available concert has positive net benefit. This comparison assumes that the free ticket cannot be resold; the question supplies no resale opportunity.

questions.stem: Demand is P=300−Q and short-run competitive supply is P=−180+5Q. Find initial equilibrium and verify it is also on long-run supply P=60+2Q. Demand at every price then doubles. Find new demand and very-short-run, short-run and long-run equilibria. If a ceiling fixes price at the old equilibrium, find the shortage. Describe the diagram.
questions.answer: Initial (Q,P)=(80,220). New demand P=300−Q/2. Very short run (80,260), short run (960/11,2820/11), long run (96,252). Ceiling shortage 80.
questions.solution:
Find the initial competitive equilibrium. Equate the original demand price to the short-run supply price: 
300-Q =-180+5Q,; 6Q =480,; Q_0 =80, P_0=220.
 The long-run supply price at this same quantity is 60+2(80)=220, so the initial point is also a long-run equilibrium.

Translate a doubling of demand correctly. The original direct demand is Q=300-P. Doubling the quantity demanded at every price gives Q=600-2P, or P=300-Q/2. The intercept on the price axis stays 300; the slope changes. In the very short run quantity remains fixed at 80, so the new demand price is 300-80/2=260.

Allow supply to adjust over the two horizons. For short-run adjustment, keep the original short-run supply curve. For long-run adjustment, use long-run supply: 
300-(1)/(2)Q =-180+5Q ⇒ Q_(SR)=(960)/(11), P_(SR)=(2820)/(11),; 300-(1)/(2)Q =60+2Q ⇒ Q_(LR)=96, P_(LR)=252.
 Price falls from its immediate level as production expands, but remains above the old price.

Interpret the ceiling and describe the graph. At the old price ceiling P=220, new demand is 600-2(220)=160 while supply is 80. The shortage is therefore 160-80=80. In a graph with quantity horizontal and price vertical, show the old and flatter new demand curves, the two supply curves, the vertical immediate-supply line at 80 and the horizontal ceiling at 220. Mark the four equilibrium points calculated above.
questions.hint: Doubling demand means doubling Q at each P.

solutionSteps.title: Find the initial competitive equilibrium
solutionSteps.body: Equate the original demand price to the short-run supply price: $$\begin{aligned}300-Q&=-180+5Q,\\6Q&=480,\\Q_0&=80,\qquad P_0=220.\end{aligned}$$ The long-run supply price at this same quantity is $60+2(80)=220$, so the initial point is also a long-run equilibrium.

solutionSteps.title: Translate a doubling of demand correctly
solutionSteps.body: The original direct demand is $Q=300-P$. Doubling the quantity demanded at every price gives $Q=600-2P$, or $P=300-Q/2$. The intercept on the price axis stays 300; the slope changes. In the very short run quantity remains fixed at 80, so the new demand price is $300-80/2=260$.

solutionSteps.title: Allow supply to adjust over the two horizons
solutionSteps.body: For short-run adjustment, keep the original short-run supply curve. For long-run adjustment, use long-run supply: $$\begin{aligned}300-\tfrac12Q&=-180+5Q &&\Rightarrow Q_{SR}=\frac{960}{11},\ P_{SR}=\frac{2820}{11},\\300-\tfrac12Q&=60+2Q &&\Rightarrow Q_{LR}=96,\ P_{LR}=252.\end{aligned}$$ Price falls from its immediate level as production expands, but remains above the old price.

solutionSteps.title: Interpret the ceiling and describe the graph
solutionSteps.body: At the old price ceiling $P=220$, new demand is $600-2(220)=160$ while supply is 80. The shortage is therefore $160-80=80$. In a graph with quantity horizontal and price vertical, show the old and flatter new demand curves, the two supply curves, the vertical immediate-supply line at 80 and the horizontal ceiling at 220. Mark the four equilibrium points calculated above.

questions.stem: (a) Year 1 produces wheat worth Rs 750, exports Rs 150 and holds the rest unsold. Year 2 has no production, consumes the old wheat domestically and imports shirts worth Rs 250. Fill GDP=C+I+X−M for both years. (b) In a linear IS–LM model an increase in government expenditure crowds out 50 units of investment. I′(r)=−50, LM slope dr/dY=1/250, IS slope −1/125. Government adjusts real money balances minimally to prevent this crowding out. Find total change in Y from initial to final equilibrium.
questions.solution:
Count output when it is produced, not when it is sold. In year 1, output worth 750 is produced. Exports account for 150 and the remaining 600 becomes an inventory asset. Unsold current output counts as investment, so 
Y_1 =C_1+I_1+X_1-M_1; 750 =0+600+150-0.

Remove the old inventory from year-2 production. Year-2 consumption is 600+250=850: old wheat plus imported shirts. Selling the old wheat runs down inventories by 600, so investment is -600. Imports must also be subtracted. Thus Y_2=850-600+0-250=0, consistent with the statement that no current production occurs.

Recover the initial crowding-out movement. The fiscal expansion reduces investment by 50. Because dI/dr=-50, this means that interest initially rises by one unit. Along the unchanged LM curve, dr/dY=1/250, so this first movement raises output by 250.

Undo the interest increase with monetary accommodation. To prevent investment crowding out, interest must return to its original level. The economy remains on the shifted IS curve, whose slope is -1/125. Moving down that IS curve by one interest unit raises output by another 125. Therefore 
Δ Y_(fiscal) =250,; Δ Y_(accommodation) =125,; Δ Y_(total) =375.
 The additional money supply is just enough to restore the original interest rate.
questions.hint: Inventory changes count as investment; use the slopes to undo the interest increase.

solutionSteps.title: Count output when it is produced, not when it is sold
solutionSteps.body: In year 1, output worth 750 is produced. Exports account for 150 and the remaining 600 becomes an inventory asset. Unsold current output counts as investment, so $$\begin{aligned}Y_1&=C_1+I_1+X_1-M_1\\750&=0+600+150-0.\end{aligned}$$

solutionSteps.title: Remove the old inventory from year-2 production
solutionSteps.body: Year-2 consumption is $600+250=850$: old wheat plus imported shirts. Selling the old wheat runs down inventories by 600, so investment is $-600$. Imports must also be subtracted. Thus $Y_2=850-600+0-250=0$, consistent with the statement that no current production occurs.

solutionSteps.title: Recover the initial crowding-out movement
solutionSteps.body: The fiscal expansion reduces investment by 50. Because $dI/dr=-50$, this means that interest initially rises by one unit. Along the unchanged LM curve, $dr/dY=1/250$, so this first movement raises output by 250.

solutionSteps.title: Undo the interest increase with monetary accommodation
solutionSteps.body: To prevent investment crowding out, interest must return to its original level. The economy remains on the shifted IS curve, whose slope is $-1/125$. Moving down that IS curve by one interest unit raises output by another 125. Therefore $$\begin{aligned}\Delta Y_{\mathrm{fiscal}}&=250,\\\Delta Y_{\mathrm{accommodation}}&=125,\\\Delta Y_{\mathrm{total}}&=375.\end{aligned}$$ The additional money supply is just enough to restore the original interest rate.

questions.stem: (a) A consumer has income W and utility U(x₁,x₂,x₃)=x₁√(x₂x₃), with positive prices pᵢ. Set up the Lagrangian, derive interior first-order conditions and Marshallian demands. (b) F(K,L) has constant returns to scale, is symmetric in inputs, and F(1,1)=1. Each input costs Rs 2 and output sells at Rs 3. Without calculus, find optimal production.
questions.answer: (a) x₁=W/(2p₁), x₂=W/(4p₂), x₃=W/(4p₃). (b) Zero output if concavity is additionally assumed; the stated properties alone are insufficient.
questions.solution:
Set up the consumer problem. For positive income and prices, maximize U=x_1√(x_2x_3) subject to p_1x_1+p_2x_2+p_3x_3≤ W. Utility increases in each good, so the budget binds. Taking logarithms is an increasing transformation and simplifies the derivatives without changing the optimum.

Use the first-order conditions to identify expenditure shares. The log-utility Lagrangian is 
L=log x_1+(1)/(2)log x_2+(1)/(2)log x_3+λ(W-Σ_(i=1)^3p_ix_i).
 Its interior conditions imply 
p_1x_1 =(1)/(λ), p_2x_2 =(1)/(2λ), p_3x_3 =(1)/(2λ).
 Adding these expenditures gives λ=2/W. Thus x_1=W/(2p_1) and x_2=W/(4p_2), x_3=W/(4p_3). Concavity of log utility makes these conditions sufficient.

Derive the intended production answer conditionally. If the production function is also concave, symmetry gives 
F(K,L)≤ F((K+L)/(2),(K+L)/(2))=(K+L)/(2).
 The equality uses constant returns and F(1,1)=1. Profit is then at most 3(K+L)/2-2(K+L)=-(K+L)/2, so zero production is optimal.

Explain why the printed assumptions are insufficient. Concavity is not one of the stated properties. The counterexample F(K,L)=max{K,L} is symmetric, has constant returns and satisfies F(1,1)=1. Yet using only capital gives profit 3K-2K=K, which can be made arbitrarily large. Therefore part (b) does not have an unconditional zero-output conclusion; the missing concavity assumption must be disclosed.
questions.hint: Use expenditure shares in (a); check whether concavity is actually among the assumptions in (b).
questions.notes: Production subpart lacks concavity or convex-technology assumption needed for the intended zero-output result.

solutionSteps.title: Set up the consumer problem
solutionSteps.body: For positive income and prices, maximize $U=x_1\sqrt{x_2x_3}$ subject to $p_1x_1+p_2x_2+p_3x_3\le W$. Utility increases in each good, so the budget binds. Taking logarithms is an increasing transformation and simplifies the derivatives without changing the optimum.

solutionSteps.title: Use the first-order conditions to identify expenditure shares
solutionSteps.body: The log-utility Lagrangian is $$\mathcal L=\log x_1+\tfrac12\log x_2+\tfrac12\log x_3+\lambda\!\left(W-\sum_{i=1}^{3}p_ix_i\right).$$ Its interior conditions imply $$\begin{aligned}p_1x_1&=\frac1\lambda, &p_2x_2&=\frac1{2\lambda}, &p_3x_3&=\frac1{2\lambda}.\end{aligned}$$ Adding these expenditures gives $\lambda=2/W$. Thus $x_1=W/(2p_1)$ and $x_2=W/(4p_2)$, $x_3=W/(4p_3)$. Concavity of log utility makes these conditions sufficient.

solutionSteps.title: Derive the intended production answer conditionally
solutionSteps.body: If the production function is also concave, symmetry gives $$F(K,L)\le F\!\left(\frac{K+L}{2},\frac{K+L}{2}\right)=\frac{K+L}{2}.$$ The equality uses constant returns and $F(1,1)=1$. Profit is then at most $3(K+L)/2-2(K+L)=-(K+L)/2$, so zero production is optimal.

solutionSteps.title: Explain why the printed assumptions are insufficient
solutionSteps.body: Concavity is not one of the stated properties. The counterexample $F(K,L)=\max\{K,L\}$ is symmetric, has constant returns and satisfies $F(1,1)=1$. Yet using only capital gives profit $3K-2K=K$, which can be made arbitrarily large. Therefore part (b) does not have an unconditional zero-output conclusion; the missing concavity assumption must be disclosed.

questions.stem: (a) A monopolist sells a positive amount to government at Rs 100 per unit and also to private buyers at Rs 150. Find private demand elasticity. (b) Mrs Pathak always uses 50 g sugar per 20 g tea. Monthly budget Rs 55; sugar costs 2 paisa per 10 g and tea 50 paisa per 10 g. Find monthly quantities. (c) In IS–LM, a tax change moves (Y,r) from (3000,4%) to (3500,6%). Money-demand income derivative is 0.25; all relations are linear and money supply is unchanged. Find the change in real money demand from a one-percentage-point rate increase.
questions.answer: (a) Absolute elasticity 3. (b) Tea 1000 g, sugar 2500 g. (c) Money demand falls by 62.5 per percentage point.
questions.solution:
Equate marginal revenues across the monopolist’s outlets. Positive sales to government at the fixed price 100 mean that the marginal revenue from that outlet is 100. At an interior allocation, private-market marginal revenue must equal it. If ε>0 is the absolute private demand elasticity, 
150(1-(1)/(ε))=100 ⇒ ε=3.
 The signed price elasticity is -3.

Price one fixed-proportion tea bundle. One bundle contains 20 g of tea and 50 g of sugar. The prices per gram are Rs 0.05 and Rs 0.002, respectively. The cost is therefore 20(0.05)+50(0.002)=1.10. A budget of 55 buys 50 bundles: tea demand is 1,000 g and sugar demand is 2,500 g. Extra sugar or tea alone has no value under the fixed-ratio preference.

Use the unchanged money-market equilibrium. The tax change does not change real money supply, so the rise in money demand due to income must be offset by the interest change. Income rises by 500 and interest by two percentage points: 
0 =0.25(500)+L_r(2),; L_r =-62.5 per percentage point.
 If interest is written as a decimal, the same derivative is -6250 per unit of the decimal rate. Keeping the rate units explicit prevents a factor-of-100 error.
questions.hint: Equate marginal revenues; price a fixed-ratio bundle; use money-market equilibrium.
questions.notes: Subpart (c) is macroeconomics; rate units are explicitly distinguished.

solutionSteps.title: Equate marginal revenues across the monopolist’s outlets
solutionSteps.body: Positive sales to government at the fixed price 100 mean that the marginal revenue from that outlet is 100. At an interior allocation, private-market marginal revenue must equal it. If $\varepsilon>0$ is the absolute private demand elasticity, $$150\!\left(1-\frac1\varepsilon\right)=100\quad\Rightarrow\quad\varepsilon=3.$$ The signed price elasticity is $-3$.

solutionSteps.title: Price one fixed-proportion tea bundle
solutionSteps.body: One bundle contains 20 g of tea and 50 g of sugar. The prices per gram are Rs 0.05 and Rs 0.002, respectively. The cost is therefore $20(0.05)+50(0.002)=1.10$. A budget of 55 buys 50 bundles: tea demand is 1,000 g and sugar demand is 2,500 g. Extra sugar or tea alone has no value under the fixed-ratio preference.

solutionSteps.title: Use the unchanged money-market equilibrium
solutionSteps.body: The tax change does not change real money supply, so the rise in money demand due to income must be offset by the interest change. Income rises by 500 and interest by two percentage points: $$\begin{aligned}0&=0.25(500)+L_r(2),\\L_r&=-62.5\quad\text{per percentage point}.\end{aligned}$$ If interest is written as a decimal, the same derivative is $-6250$ per unit of the decimal rate. Keeping the rate units explicit prevents a factor-of-100 error.

questions.stem: (a) One unit of corn requires 0.1 corn, 0.3 machines and 5 labour-hours; one machine requires 0.4 corn, 0.6 machines and 20 labour-hours. (i) Final demand is 48 corn and zero machines: find gross outputs and labour. (ii) At wage Rs 2/hour, find prices equaling average production costs. (b) Consumers A and B each spend income W on x,y, with utilities U_A=x+y and U_B=x²+y². Compare their demands.
questions.answer: (a) Gross corn 80, machines 60, labour 1600 hours; corn price 200/3 and machine price 500/3. (b) Same demands at unequal prices; different demand correspondences when prices tie.
questions.solution:
Write the gross-output balances. Let C and M be gross corn and machine output. Production must cover intermediate requirements as well as final demand: 
C =0.1C+0.4M+48,; M =0.3C+0.6M.
 The second equation gives M=0.75C; substituting into the first gives C=80 and M=60. Required labour is 5(80)+20(60)=1600 hours.

Include intermediate inputs in cost prices. At wage 2, unit costs equal prices: 
p_C =0.1p_C+0.3p_M+10,; p_M =0.4p_C+0.6p_M+40.
 The second equation implies p_M=p_C+100. The first then gives 0.6p_C=40, so p_C=200/3 and p_M=500/3. Ignoring intermediate inputs would understate both prices.

Compare the two consumers away from tied prices. For U_A=x+y, all spending goes to the cheaper good. For U_B=x^2+y^2, utility is convex along a linear budget segment, so its maximum is at an endpoint. The endpoint utilities are (W/p_x)^2 and (W/p_y)^2, again selecting the cheaper good. Thus at unequal positive prices their demands coincide.

Handle the price tie separately. When p_x=p_y, consumer A is indifferent among every bundle on the budget line because x+y is constant. Consumer B instead maximizes x^2+y^2 at the two corners only; any nontrivial split gives lower utility. Their demand correspondences therefore differ at the tie, even though their demands agree at unequal prices.
questions.hint: Separate gross from final outputs, and compare utilities at budget endpoints.

solutionSteps.title: Write the gross-output balances
solutionSteps.body: Let $C$ and $M$ be gross corn and machine output. Production must cover intermediate requirements as well as final demand: $$\begin{aligned}C&=0.1C+0.4M+48,\\M&=0.3C+0.6M.\end{aligned}$$ The second equation gives $M=0.75C$; substituting into the first gives $C=80$ and $M=60$. Required labour is $5(80)+20(60)=1600$ hours.
