questions.stem: A college must fill one seat by testing applicants sequentially; accepting one precludes later applicants and rejections are irrevocable. It maximizes expected admitted score. (i) With two applicants and the second score uniform on [0,100], what is the first-applicant acceptance threshold? (ii) With three independent uniform scores on [0,100], find the first and, after rejection, second thresholds.
questions.solution:
Use backward induction: the value of rejecting an applicant is the expected score obtainable from the applicants still available. The last applicant must be accepted.

$$\begin{aligned}
V_1&=E[X]=50,\\
V_2&=E[\max\{X,50\}],\\
V_2&=\frac1{100}\left[\int_0^{50}50\,dx+\int_{50}^{100}x\,dx\right]=62.5.
\end{aligned}$$

With two applicants, compare the observed first score against $50$. With three, the first applicant competes against the option value $62.5$ of optimally selecting from the last two, not against a simple average of their scores. After rejecting the first, the remaining threshold returns to $50$.

With only the final applicant remaining, expected score is50, so accept the current applicant iff her observed score is at least50. In the three-applicant case the value of rejecting the first is the expected value obtainable from the final two. That value is E[max(X,50)] for X uniform[0,100]: (1/100)[∫₀⁵⁰50 dx+∫₅₀¹⁰⁰x dx]=(2500+3750)/100=62.5.

Thus accept the first at score≥62.5; if she is rejected, accept the second at score≥50 and otherwise take the third. At a threshold either decision has equal expected value.

Two applicants:50. Three applicants:first62.5, second50.

$$\begin{aligned}
V_1&=E[X]=50,\\
V_2&=E[\max\{X,50\}],\\
V_2&=\frac1{100}\left[\int_0^{50}50\,dx+\int_{50}^{100}x\,dx\right]=62.5.
\end{aligned}$$

With two applicants, compare the observed first score against $50$. With three, the first applicant competes against the option value $62.5$ of optimally selecting from the last two, not against a simple average of their scores. After rejecting the first, the remaining threshold returns to $50$.

solutionSteps.title: Complete the argument
solutionSteps.body:
With only the final applicant remaining, expected score is50, so accept the current applicant iff her observed score is at least50. In the three-applicant case the value of rejecting the first is the expected value obtainable from the final two. That value is E[max(X,50)] for X uniform[0,100]: (1/100)[∫₀⁵⁰50 dx+∫₅₀¹⁰⁰x dx]=(2500+3750)/100=62.5.

Thus accept the first at score≥62.5; if she is rejected, accept the second at score≥50 and otherwise take the third. At a threshold either decision has equal expected value.

solutionSteps.title: Conclusion
solutionSteps.body: Two applicants:50. Three applicants:first62.5, second50.

questions.solution: Since 1/[k(k+1)]=1/k−1/(k+1), the bracket telescopes to 1−1/100=99/100. Multiplication by 100 gives 99.
questions.hint: Use telescoping partial fractions.

questions.stem: The function f(x)=x(√x+√(x+9)) is
options: Continuous but not differentiable at x=0
Differentiable but the derivative is not continuous at x=0
questions.answer: (a) with one-sided differentiation on [0,∞); two-sided differentiation is not defined at this endpoint.
questions.solution: The real domain is [0,∞). The right difference quotient at 0 is √h+√(h+9)→3. For x>0, f′(x)=√x+√(x+9)+√x/2+x/[2√(x+9)], which tends to 3 as x→0⁺. Thus the function is C¹ from the right. The source does not specify a one-sided convention at the domain endpoint.
questions.hint: Determine the real domain before discussing differentiability at zero.
questions.notes: Endpoint differentiability convention is unspecified; the intended answer is likely (a).

questions.stem: A GP has first term 1 and positive integer common ratio r>1. An AP has first term 1 and its (r+2)th term equals the GP’s third term. Find its common difference.
questions.solution: The third GP term is r² and the indicated AP term is 1+(r+1)d. Hence d=(r²−1)/(r+1)=r−1.
questions.hint: Write the two terms using their general-term formulas.

questions.stem: The first three terms of (1+x)ⁿ are 1,−9,297/8 respectively. Find n.
questions.solution: The second term gives nx=−9. The third gives n(n−1)x²/2=297/8. Substitute x²=81/n² to obtain 81(n−1)/(2n)=297/8, hence 324(n−1)=297n and n=12.
questions.hint: Eliminate x using the second term.

questions.stem: Given logₚx=α and log_qx=β, find log_(p/q)x.
questions.solution: Change of base gives ln p=ln x/α and ln q=ln x/β. Therefore ln x/ln(p/q)=1/(1/α−1/β)=αβ/(β−α), on the domain where the logarithms exist.
questions.hint: Use a common logarithm base.

questions.stem: P={1,2,3,4,5}, Q={1,2}. How many subsets X of P satisfy X∩Q={2}?
questions.solution: Such a subset must contain 2 and exclude 1. Each of 3,4,5 can be included or excluded independently, giving 2³=8 possibilities.
questions.hint: Identify the forced and free membership choices.

questions.stem: An unbiased coin is tossed until a head appears. The expected number of tosses is
questions.solution: The waiting time is geometric with success probability 1/2. Its mean is 1/(1/2)=2. Equivalently E(T)=1+(1/2)E(T), so E(T)=2.
questions.hint: Condition on the first toss.

questions.stem: X has density f(x)=c/x² for x≥c and 0 for x<c. Find E(X).
questions.solution: The density premise requires c>0. Then E(X)=∫_c^∞x(c/x²)dx=c∫_c^∞dx/x, which diverges to infinity.
questions.hint: Check whether the first-moment integral converges.

questions.stem: How many real solutions does x²−5|x|+4=0 have?
questions.solution: Let u=|x|≥0. Then (u−1)(u−4)=0, giving |x|=1 or 4. Thus x∈{−4,−1,1,4}.
questions.hint: Solve a quadratic in |x|.

questions.stem: The range of f(x)=x²/(1+x²) is
questions.solution: For all real x, f(x)=1−1/(1+x²) is at least 0 and strictly below 1. It equals 0 at x=0 and approaches 1 as |x|→∞. Every value between 0 and 1 is attained.
questions.hint: Rewrite the function as one minus a positive fraction.

questions.stem: If a,b,c are in arithmetic progression, find the determinant of [[x+2,x+3,x+2a],[x+3,x+4,x+2b],[x+4,x+5,x+2c]].
questions.solution: Since a+c=2b, the row combination R₁−2R₂+R₃ equals the zero row. Thus the rows are linearly dependent and the determinant is zero. The third option equals zero under the AP assumption.
questions.hint: Apply R₁−2R₂+R₃.

questions.stem: If a<b<c<d, then (x−a)(x−b)+2(x−c)(x−d)=0 has
options: One root in (a,b) and the other in (c,d)
One root in [a,b] and the other in [c,d]
questions.answer: No listed statement is universally true.
questions.solution: Take a=0,b=1,c=2,d=3. The equation becomes x(x−1)+2(x−2)(x−3)=3x²−11x+12=0, whose discriminant is 121−144=−23<0. Thus it has no real roots, contradicting every listed location statement.
questions.hint: Test the universal claim with four simple increasing numbers.
questions.notes: Visually confirmed the plus sign and factor 2. No “none” option is supplied; do not force an answer.

questions.stem: Let f,g be differentiable on (0,1), with f(0)=2,f(1)=6,g(0)=0,g(1)=2. Then some θ∈(0,1) satisfies f′(θ) equal to
questions.answer: Intended answer (b), provided endpoint continuity is added.
questions.solution: If f,g are continuous on [0,1], Rolle’s theorem applied to f−2g gives f′(θ)=2g′(θ), because f−2g has the same endpoint value 2. As printed, differentiability is asserted only inside (0,1). For instance f(x)=x,g(x)=0 in the interior, with the specified endpoint values assigned separately, satisfies the printed assumptions but has f′=1,g′=0, defeating every option.
questions.hint: Check the endpoint continuity assumptions needed for Rolle’s theorem.
questions.notes: The missing endpoint continuity assumption prevents a universal conclusion.

questions.stem: The minimum value of logₓa+logₐx, for 1<a<x, is
questions.answer: No minimum is attained; the infimum is 2. Every allowed value is greater than 2.
questions.solution: Set t=logₐx>1. The expression is t+1/t. It exceeds 2 for every t>1 and approaches 2 as t↓1. Because x=a is excluded, equality cannot occur, so the expression has no minimum on the stated domain. The likely intended choice (b) describes each attained value, not an existing minimum.
questions.hint: Distinguish an unattained infimum from a minimum.
questions.notes: The strict inequality a<x makes the purported minimum nonexistent.

questions.stem: Evaluate ∫ from 4 to 9 of 1/[2x(1+√x)] dx.
questions.solution: Set u=√x, so dx=2u du. The integral becomes ∫₂³1/[u(1+u)]du=[ln u−ln(1+u)]₂³=ln(3/4)−ln(2/3)=ln(9/8)=2ln3−3ln2.
questions.hint: Substitute u=√x.

questions.stem: The inverse of f(x)=1/(1+x), x>0, is
questions.solution: Solve y=1/(1+x) for x: 1+x=1/y, so x=(1−y)/y. The range of the original function is (0,1), which is the inverse’s domain.
questions.hint: Solve the defining equation for the input.

questions.stem: Xᵢ have identical variance σ² and Cov(Xᵢ,Xⱼ)=ρ whenever i≠j. Put X̄ₙ=(1/n)∑Xᵢ and aₙ=Var(X̄ₙ). Find lim as n→∞ of aₙ.
questions.solution: Variance of the sum is nσ²+n(n−1)ρ. Dividing by n² gives aₙ=σ²/n+(n−1)ρ/n, which tends to ρ.
questions.hint: Include all covariance terms when computing the sample-mean variance.

questions.stem: X is standard normal and Φ is its cumulative distribution function. Find E[Φ(X)].
questions.solution: For a continuous random variable, its own CDF evaluated at that variable is uniform on (0,1). Thus Φ(X) is uniform and has mean 1/2. Alternatively symmetry gives Φ(X)+Φ(−X)=1 with identical expectations.
questions.hint: Use normal symmetry or the probability integral transform.

questions.stem: For finite integer r≥2, find lim as x→0 of ln(∑ from k=0 to r of xᵏ) / (∑ from k=1 to infinity of xᵏ/k!).
questions.solution: The denominator is eˣ−1. Near zero, the numerator is ln(1+x+O(x²))=x+O(x²), and the denominator is x+O(x²). Their ratio tends to 1.
questions.hint: Compare first-order terms of numerator and denominator.

questions.stem: Five boxes each contain balls labeled 1,…,6. Draw one from each; bᵢ is the label from box i. How many choices satisfy b₁<b₂<b₃<b₄<b₅?
questions.solution: Choose any five distinct labels from the six available. Their strictly increasing order then determines the choices in the five boxes uniquely. There are C(6,5)=6 possibilities.
questions.hint: Choose the set of labels; their order is forced.

questions.stem: Find ∑ from r=0 to m of C(n+r,r).
questions.solution: Use C(n+r,r)=C(n+r,n). Summing along a diagonal of Pascal’s triangle gives the hockey-stick identity ∑ᵣ₌₀ᵐC(n+r,n)=C(n+m+1,n+1).
questions.hint: Use Pascal’s identity to telescope.

questions.stem: In yᵢ=α+β(xᵢ−x̄)+εᵢ, errors are i.i.d. with mean 0 and variance 1. If α̂,β̂ are OLS estimates, their correlation is
questions.solution: For a nonconstant fixed design, α̂=ȳ and β̂=∑(xᵢ−x̄)yᵢ/∑(xᵢ−x̄)². Their covariance is proportional to ∑(xᵢ−x̄)=0. Both have positive variances, so their correlation is zero.
questions.hint: Centering makes the constant regressor orthogonal to the slope regressor.
questions.notes: As usual, a nonconstant fixed regressor design is required to identify the slope.

questions.stem: f is real-valued and continuous on [0,3], takes only rational values, and f(1)=1. Then f(2) equals
questions.solution: If a continuous real function took two distinct values, the intermediate value theorem would force it to take every value between them, including irrational values. Therefore f is constant, and f(1)=1 implies f(2)=1.
questions.hint: Apply the intermediate value theorem to a rational-valued function.

questions.stem: Let f(x₁,x₂)=∫ from 0 to √(x₁²+x₂²) of exp[−w²/(x₁²+x₂²)]dw, with f(0,0)=0. It is
questions.solution: For r=√(x₁²+x₂²)>0, substitute w=ru. Then f=r∫₀¹e^(−u²)du. Scaling (x₁,x₂) by a positive t scales r and f by t, proving degree-one homogeneity; the definition at the origin agrees.
questions.hint: Substitute w=u√(x₁²+x₂²).

questions.stem: If f(1)=0 and f′(x)>f(x) for all x>1, then f(x) is
questions.answer: Intended answer (a) requires continuity at x=1; the printed conditions alone do not force a sign.
questions.solution: If f is continuous at 1, then h(x)=e^(−x)f(x) has h′(x)=e^(−x)(f′−f)>0 and h(1)=0, so h(x)>0 for x>1. Without continuity at 1, define f(x)=−eˣ/x for x>1 and f(1)=0. Then f′−f=eˣ/x²>0 but f remains negative, disproving the intended conclusion under the literal assumptions.
questions.hint: Use an integrating factor, but verify continuity at the initial endpoint.
questions.notes: Endpoint continuity is missing; do not automatically grade the intended positive-sign answer.

questions.stem: Maximize ax+by over x,y≥0 subject to cx+dy≤100, where a,b,c,d>0 and d/b>(c+d)/(a+b). The unique solution is
questions.solution: The parameter condition simplifies to d(a+b)>b(c+d), hence ad>bc and a/c>b/d. Thus x yields strictly more objective per unit of budget than y, so all budget is allocated to x: cx=100,y=0.
questions.hint: Compare objective gain per unit of constraint cost.

questions.stem: For [x]=floor(x), the domain of f(x)=[√(|[|x|−2]|−3)]⁻¹ is
questions.solution: The reciprocal square root requires |floor(|x|−2)|−3>0. Since |x|≥0, floor(|x|−2)≥−2, so its absolute value exceeds 3 only when floor(|x|−2)≥4. This is equivalent to |x|−2≥4, or |x|≥6.
questions.hint: The radicand must be strictly positive, not merely nonnegative.

questions.stem: Define f(x)=−1 if x<−1/2, f(x)=−1/2 if −1/2≤x<0, f(0)=0, and f(x)=1 if x>0. Define g(x)=1+x−floor(x). Find f(g(x)).
questions.solution: The fractional part x−floor(x) always belongs to [0,1). Thus g(x)∈[1,2), so it is strictly positive and f(g(x))=1.
questions.hint: Find the range of g first.

questions.stem: Suppose a₁f(x)+a₂f(−x)=b₁−b₂x for all real x, with a₁≠a₂ and b₂≠0. Then f(b₁/b₂) equals
options: More information is required to find the exact value
questions.answer: (b) when a₁+a₂≠0; an omitted degeneracy prevents that answer from being universally valid.
questions.solution: If a₁²≠a₂², solve the equations at x and −x to obtain f(x)=b₁/(a₁+a₂)−b₂x/(a₁−a₂), hence f(b₁/b₂)=−2a₂b₁/(a₁²−a₂²). But a₁≠a₂ does not exclude a₁=−a₂. In that case consistency forces b₁=0, and the equation constrains only the odd part of f; f(0) can be arbitrary. Thus the intended formula needs the additional assumption a₁+a₂≠0.
questions.hint: Check the determinant when solving the paired equations.
questions.notes: The source omits a₁≠−a₂. The point being evaluated becomes 0 in the degenerate consistent case, and its function value is not determined.

questions.stem: For every x,y>0, f:(0,∞)→ℝ satisfies |f(x)−f(y)|≤|x−y|³. Then f is
questions.solution: For fixed x and small nonzero h, |(f(x+h)−f(x))/h|≤|h|²→0. Thus f′(x)=0 everywhere on the connected interval (0,∞), and the mean value theorem shows that f is constant.
questions.hint: Divide the inequality by |x−y| and take a limit.

questions.stem: (a) In a closed economy income tax is tY, government must balance its budget G=tY, consumption is proportional to disposable income and investment is exogenous. (i) Why is G endogenous? (ii) Compare its multiplier with fixed-G policy. (iii) How does higher t affect income? (b) C=100+1.3Y, I=500/r, money demand=150Y+100−1500r and money supply=2100. Is there an economically admissible IS–LM equilibrium?
questions.answer: (a) G depends on Y; investment multiplier 1/[(1−c)(1−t)], larger than 1/[1−c(1−t)] for fixed G when t>0; higher t raises Y. (b) No equilibrium with Y≥0,r>0.
questions.solution:
Under a balanced-budget rule, government spending is a function of income rather than a fixed autonomous term. Insert this rule before calculating a multiplier. In part (b), check the economic sign restrictions before solving two nonlinear equations.

$$\begin{aligned}
Y&=c(1-t)Y+I+tY,\\
(1-c)(1-t)Y&=I,\\
\frac{\partial Y}{\partial I}&=\frac1{(1-c)(1-t)},\\
\text{part (b): }-0.3Y&=100+500/r.
\end{aligned}$$

A higher tax rate transfers spending power from households, who spend only fraction $c$, to a government spending every receipt. This explains the positive output response in this particular policy rule. In part (b), the left side is nonpositive at $Y\ge0$, while the right is positive at $r>0$; the contradiction already rules out an admissible equilibrium.

Let C=c(1−t)Y, 0<c<1,0≤t<1. Goods balance gives Y=c(1−t)Y+I+tY, hence Y=I/[(1−c)(1−t)]. G is endogenous because income determines tax revenue and spending.

With G held exogenous, the autonomous-spending multiplier is 1/[1−c(1−t)]. Its denominator exceeds the balanced-budget denominator by t, so the latter multiplier is larger. Raising t shifts spending from households, who spend only fraction c, to government, who spends all receipts; dY/dt>0 for I>0.

In (b), IS requires −.3Y=100+500/r, impossible for nonnegative Y and positive r. LM is r=Y/10−4/3. Even allowing negative r does not produce a nonnegative-Y intersection: substitution into IS yields .03Y²+9.6Y+1100/3=0, whose terms are all nonnegative for Y≥0.

(a) G depends on Y; investment multiplier 1/[(1−c)(1−t)], larger than 1/[1−c(1−t)] for fixed G when t>0; higher t raises Y. (b) No equilibrium with Y≥0,r>0.
questions.hint: Substitute the budget rule into goods balance before comparing multipliers.

questions.stem: Two firms have cost C(q)=mq, inverse demands p₁=a−q₁−sq₂ and p₂=a−q₂−sq₁, where 0<s<1 and a>m>0. (a) Find Cournot quantities. (b) Derive direct demand functions. (c) Find Bertrand prices.
questions.answer: Cournot q₁=q₂=(a−m)/(2+s). Interior direct demands qᵢ=[a(1−s)−pᵢ+spⱼ]/(1−s²). Bertrand p₁=p₂=[a(1−s)+m]/(2−s).
questions.solution:
Quantity competition uses inverse demand directly. Price competition requires first solving the inverse-demand system for quantities, because each firm must know how its own price affects sales.

$$\begin{aligned}
2q_i+sq_j&=a-m\Longrightarrow q_i^C=\frac{a-m}{2+s},\\
q_i(p_i,p_j)&=\frac{a(1-s)-p_i+sp_j}{1-s^2},\\
\frac{\partial[(p_i-m)q_i]}{\partial p_i}&=
\frac{a(1-s)-2p_i+sp_j+m}{1-s^2},\\
p_i^B&=\frac{a(1-s)+m}{2-s}.
\end{aligned}$$

The symmetry of primitives lets us impose equal quantities or prices only after deriving individual first-order conditions. Own-decision profit curvature is negative in each problem, and the stated $a>m$, $0<s<1$ ensure the symmetric solutions are interior.

Cournot profit is (a−m−qᵢ−sqⱼ)qᵢ. Its first-order condition is 2qᵢ+sqⱼ=a−m, giving the symmetric quantities. Inverting the 2×2 inverse-demand system gives q₁=[a(1−s)−p₁+sp₂]/(1−s²) and its counterpart.

These formulas apply when both demands are positive; outside that region nonnegativity requires appropriate corner demand. In Bertrand competition maximize (pᵢ−m)qᵢ. The interior first-order condition is a(1−s)−2pᵢ+spⱼ+m=0.

Solving the two conditions gives p=[a(1−s)+m]/(2−s)>m and positive demand. Own-price profit curvature is −2/(1−s²)<0.

Cournot q₁=q₂=(a−m)/(2+s). Interior direct demands qᵢ=[a(1−s)−pᵢ+spⱼ]/(1−s²). Bertrand p₁=p₂=[a(1−s)+m]/(2−s).
questions.hint: Invert the inverse-demand matrix before solving the price game.

questions.stem: (a) A monopolist has TC=5+3(Q_A+Q_B), inverse demands P_A=15−Q_A and P_B=25−2Q_B, and can discriminate across separated markets. Find prices, quantities, profit and deadweight loss. (b) An airline optimally sells 1500 business tickets at Rs 200 and 6000 economy tickets at Rs 80. Both demand curves are linear and MC=Rs 50. Derive both demands and find uniform-price equilibrium if discrimination is disallowed.
questions.solution:
For separated markets, equate each marginal revenue to the common marginal cost. For the airline, use the observed discriminatory optimum to recover the slope of each linear demand before aggregating.

$$\begin{aligned}
MR_A=15-2Q_A&=3\Longrightarrow Q_A=6,\\
MR_B=25-4Q_B&=3\Longrightarrow Q_B=11/2,\\
b_j&=\frac{P_j-MC}{Q_j},\quad A_j=P_j+b_jQ_j,\\
Q^{\mathrm{uniform}}&=25500-210p,\\
\frac{d[(p-50)(25500-210p)]}{dp}&=36000-420p=0.
\end{aligned}$$

The fixed cost affects profit but not the market-specific quantity conditions. Deadweight loss compares each monopoly quantity with its own efficient quantity at $p=MC$. In the airline case, also compare the both-market solution with the best business-only solution, because a uniform price can exclude economy travellers.

(a) Set market marginal revenues equal to MC=3: 15−2Q_A=3 and 25−4Q_B=3. Profit is (9−3)6+(14−3)5.5−5=91.5. Efficient quantities at price 3 are 12 and 11.

The lost-surplus triangles are (1/2)(12−6)(9−3)=18 and (1/2)(11−5.5)(14−3)=30.25, totaling 48.25. (b) If P=A−bQ, then MR=P−bQ=50 at the observed optimum. Business b=(200−50)/1500=.1,A=350; economy b=(80−50)/6000=.005,A=110.

For a uniform price p≤110, total demand is Q=25500−210p. Maximizing (p−50)Q gives p=(25500+210·50)/420=600/7 and the stated market quantities. This earns profit 1875000/7≈267857, more than the best business-only regime (p=200,Q=1500,profit225000), so it is globally optimal.

(a) Q_A=6,P_A=9; Q_B=5.5,P_B=14; profit 91.5, deadweight loss 48.25. (b) P_b=350−0.1Q_b, P_e=110−0.005Q_e; uniform price 600/7≈85.714, Q_b=18500/7, Q_e=34000/7, total 7500.
questions.hint: Use MR=MC separately, then check both segments of the aggregate uniform-price demand.

solutionSteps.title: Set up the problem
solutionSteps.body: For separated markets, equate each marginal revenue to the common marginal cost. For the airline, use the observed discriminatory optimum to recover the slope of each linear demand before aggregating.

solutionSteps.title: Work through the equations
solutionSteps.body:
$$\begin{aligned}
MR_A=15-2Q_A&=3\Longrightarrow Q_A=6,\\
MR_B=25-4Q_B&=3\Longrightarrow Q_B=11/2,\\
b_j&=\frac{P_j-MC}{Q_j},\quad A_j=P_j+b_jQ_j,\\
Q^{\mathrm{uniform}}&=25500-210p,\\
\frac{d[(p-50)(25500-210p)]}{dp}&=36000-420p=0.
\end{aligned}$$

The fixed cost affects profit but not the market-specific quantity conditions. Deadweight loss compares each monopoly quantity with its own efficient quantity at $p=MC$. In the airline case, also compare the both-market solution with the best business-only solution, because a uniform price can exclude economy travellers.

solutionSteps.body:

The lost-surplus triangles are (1/2)(12−6)(9−3)=18 and (1/2)(11−5.5)(14−3)=30.25, totaling 48.25. (b) If P=A−bQ, then MR=P−bQ=50 at the observed optimum. Business b=(200−50)/1500=.1,A=350; economy b=(80−50)/6000=.005,A=110.

For a uniform price p≤110, total demand is Q=25500−210p. Maximizing (p−50)Q gives p=(25500+210·50)/420=600/7 and the stated market quantities. This earns profit 1875000/7≈267857, more than the best business-only regime (p=200,Q=1500,profit225000), so it is globally optimal.

questions.stem: A competitive economy has X₁=√(L₁K), X₂=√(L₂T), fixed positive K,T and total labour L₁+L₂=L, with labour mobile between sectors. Relative demand is D₁/D₂=γ(p₁/p₂)^−2. (a) Relate X₁/X₂ to p₁/p₂. (b) How does equilibrium relative price change when γ increases?
questions.answer: Relative supply X₁/X₂=(K/T)(p₁/p₂); equilibrium p₁/p₂=(γT/K)^(1/3), which rises with γ.
questions.solution:
Mobile labour earns the same wage in both sectors. Equalize the value marginal products, then use the resulting allocation ratio to obtain relative supply.

$$\begin{aligned}
\frac{p_1\sqrt K}{2\sqrt{L_1}}&=\frac{p_2\sqrt T}{2\sqrt{L_2}},\\
\frac{L_1}{L_2}&=\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)^2\frac KT,\\
\frac{X_1}{X_2}&=\frac KT\frac{p_1}{p_2}
=\gamma\left(\frac{p_1}{p_2}\right)^{-2},\\
\frac{p_1}{p_2}&=\left(\frac{\gamma T}{K}\right)^{1/3}.
\end{aligned}$$

The supply ratio rises with the relative price, whereas the demand ratio falls. Equating them produces a unique positive cube-root solution. Its elasticity with respect to the relative-demand parameter is $1/3$, so the price response is positive but less than proportional.

Equal wages imply p₁√K/(2√L₁)=p₂√T/(2√L₂). Thus L₁/L₂=(p₁/p₂)²K/T. Substituting into the output ratio gives X₁/X₂=√[(L₁/L₂)(K/T)]=(p₁/p₂)K/T.

Market clearing equates this to γ(p₁/p₂)^−2, so the relative price cubed is γT/K. Higher relative demand raises the relative price with elasticity 1/3.

Relative supply X₁/X₂=(K/T)(p₁/p₂); equilibrium p₁/p₂=(γT/K)^(1/3), which rises with γ.

questions.stem: An open IS–LM economy has flexible exchange rate e (domestic currency per foreign unit), no capital mobility, fixed domestic and foreign price levels P,P*, and balanced trade in equilibrium. The source prints TB=T̄+βP*/P−mY, T̄,β,m>0, while saying e adjusts to balance trade. (a) Derive the Y–r relation and compare it with closed-economy IS; describe LM. (b) What do higher G do to Y and e? (c) What does higher P* do to Y and e?
questions.answer: The printed TB equation omits e and cannot determine its adjustment. If the intended term is βeP*/P, balanced trade gives the ordinary closed-economy IS; higher G raises Y,r and depreciates e, while higher P* leaves Y,r unchanged and lowers e proportionally.
questions.solution:
Balanced trade must be imposed alongside goods and money clearing. First read the printed trade equation literally: because it contains no exchange rate, it cannot determine exchange-rate adjustment.

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{printed }TB=0&\Longrightarrow Y=\frac{\bar T+\beta P^*/P}{m},\\
\text{conditional correction: }0&=\bar T+\beta eP^*/P-mY,\\
e&=\frac{P(mY-\bar T)}{\beta P^*},\\
Y&=C(Y-T)+I(r)+G.
\end{aligned}$$

Only after expressly adding the omitted exchange-rate term can one derive the conventional comparative statics. With zero net exports, the goods-market equation has the closed-economy form. A fiscal expansion raises income and imports, requiring depreciation to restore trade balance; a foreign-price rise can instead be offset entirely through the exchange rate.

Literally the printed TB=0 fixes Y=(T̄+βP*/P)/m independently of e. Since e appears nowhere, its comparative statics cannot be obtained, and arbitrary IS/LM shifts may be incompatible with that fixed Y. Conditional on inserting the usual omitted e, TB=0 gives e=P(mY−T̄)/(βP*), requiring mY>T̄ for a positive rate.

Goods balance then becomes Y=C(Y−T)+I(r)+G, identical to closed-economy IS because net exports are zero. With ordinary increasing money demand in Y and decreasing demand in r, fixed real balances give an upward-sloping LM. A rise in G shifts this IS right: its intersection with LM has higher Y and r.

The trade-balance formula then requires higher e, a depreciation, to offset increased imports. Higher P* leaves IS and LM unchanged and hence leaves Y,r unchanged; e falls in inverse proportion to P*, keeping eP*/P constant.

The printed TB equation omits e and cannot determine its adjustment. If the intended term is βeP*/P, balanced trade gives the ordinary closed-economy IS; higher G raises Y,r and depreciates e, while higher P* leaves Y,r unchanged and lowers e proportionally.

questions.stem: (a) Technologies Y=min(K/3,L/2) and Y=min(K/2,L/3) each have marginal cost Rs 20 at the same competitive factor prices. Find the expansion path for Y=K^(2/3)L^(1/3). (b) A consumer buys X at its market price. Compare market purchase of Y with an alternative providing a fixed free ration of Y through government shops. Is the ration necessarily better for (i) strictly convex indifference curves, (ii) perfect substitutes, (iii) perfect complements?
questions.answer: (a) Factor prices both 4; expansion path K=2L. (b) Under a ration-only alternative with no supplementary Y purchases, none of the three preference types guarantees improvement; the ration quantity matters.
questions.solution:
Each fixed-proportions technology gives a unit-cost equation in the same factor prices. The ration comparison requires an explicit feasible set: a free allotment replacing the market is different from an allotment that can be supplemented by purchases.

$$\begin{aligned}
3r+2w&=20,\qquad2r+3w=20,\\
r=w&=4,\\
\frac{MP_K}{MP_L}&=\frac{2L}{K}=\frac rw=1,\\
K&=2L.
\end{aligned}$$

Once factor prices are recovered, the cost-minimizing expansion path follows from equalizing technical and market substitution rates. For rationing, test whether the original optimal bundle remains affordable. It need not if purchases of the rationed good are prohibited, so preference curvature alone cannot guarantee a welfare improvement.

(a) With capital rental r and wage w, 3r+2w=20 and 2r+3w=20 give r=w=4. For Cobb–Douglas cost minimization MP_K/MP_L=2L/K=r/w=1, hence K=2L. (b) Let the ration be Ȳ, income M and X price pₓ; the free-ration allocation can have X=M/pₓ,Y=Ȳ.

This may fail to match the original preferred bundle. For strictly convex preferences U=XY, M=pₓ=pᵧ=1, market optimum has utility 1/4, while free ration Ȳ=.1 yields utility .1. For substitutes U=X+Y, M=1,pₓ=2,pᵧ=1, market utility is 1 but the same ration gives .5+.1=.6.

For complements U=min(X,Y), M=pₓ=pᵧ=1, market utility .5 exceeds ration utility .1. Large enough rations can improve each case. If supplementary Y purchases are permitted, the old affordable set is preserved (or expanded) and the consumer is weakly better off under all three types.

(a) Factor prices both 4; expansion path K=2L. (b) Under a ration-only alternative with no supplementary Y purchases, none of the three preference types guarantees improvement; the ration quantity matters.

questions.stem: Explain whether each statement is true or false: (a) If higher own price increases demand, higher income reduces demand; by the same argument, if higher own price reduces demand, higher income increases demand. (b) A farmer earns all income by selling his crop at an exogenous price and consumes more crop when that price rises; therefore the crop is normal. (c) If higher non-wage income reduces labour supplied, higher wages must increase labour supplied. (d) ISI student stipends are part of GDP.
questions.answer: (a) First implication true under standard assumptions, converse false. (b) True under the usual fixed-harvest model. (c) False. (d) False for stipends treated as transfers.
questions.solution:
Use the Slutsky decomposition to distinguish a compensated substitution effect from an income effect. A producer-consumer also experiences an endowment-income effect when the price of the crop changes.

$$\begin{aligned}
x_p&=h_p-x x_M,\qquad h_p\le0,\\
x_p>0&\Longrightarrow x_M<0,\\
\left.\frac{dx}{dp}\right|_{M=pE}&=h_p+(E-x)x_M.
\end{aligned}$$

The first implication is one-way: an ordinary downward-sloping demand can belong to a normal or an inferior good. For a fixed-harvest seller, a positive total own-price response requires a positive income effect because net crop sales are nonnegative. Labour choice has the same competing substitution and income forces; a wage increase therefore has no predetermined total sign.

(a) Slutsky gives x_p=h_p−x x_M, with h_p≤0. A positive x_p requires x_M<0, but negative x_p is possible for either normal or inferior goods, so the converse is invalid. (b) With a fixed harvest E and other-good price fixed, wealth is pE.

Endowment Slutsky gives total dx/dp=h_p+(E−x)x_M. The farmer finances consumption from the harvest and has E−x≥0; therefore a positive total response requires x_M>0. If harvest itself responds to price, additional production assumptions are needed.

(c) Normal leisure creates a negative income effect on labour; a wage rise also has a substitution effect toward work, so their net sign is ambiguous and labour supply may bend backward. (d) A stipend paid without a current productive service is a transfer, not payment for newly produced output. Educational services may enter GDP separately, but the transfer amount itself does not.

(a) First implication true under standard assumptions, converse false. (b) True under the usual fixed-harvest model. (c) False. (d) False for stipends treated as transfers.
questions.hint: Apply Slutsky with fixed income versus endowment income; distinguish transfers from production.
questions.notes: (b) assumes a fixed crop endowment. (d) is the standard national-accounting classification of a stipend as a transfer, rather than remuneration for services.

questions.stem: In the Solow model Y=√(KL), saving rate is .2 and labour growth .05. (a) Find steady capital/labour ratio, output and saving growth and wage. (b) If saving rises to .4, find the new steady output growth. (c) Compare output growth during transition with growth in the new steady state.
questions.answer: With zero depreciation: old k*=16, wage 2, output and saving growth 5%; new k*=64, wage 4 and long-run output growth still 5%. Transition growth is above 5% and converges to it.
questions.solution:
Use capital per worker $k=K/L$. Because no depreciation rate is given, state the zero-depreciation convention before deriving numerical steady states.

$$\begin{aligned}
\dot k&=s\sqrt k-0.05k,\\
k^*&=(s/0.05)^2,\qquad w^*=\tfrac12\sqrt{k^*},\\
s=0.2:&\quad k^*=16,\quad w^*=2,\\
s=0.4:&\quad k^*=64,\quad g_Y^*=0.05,\\
g_Y&=0.05+\tfrac12g_k.
\end{aligned}$$

The saving increase raises the level of capital and output per worker, not their long-run growth rates. During convergence $g_k>0$, so aggregate output grows faster than labour; this excess growth declines to zero as capital per worker approaches its new steady level.

No depreciation is supplied, so take δ=0. Per-worker dynamics are k̇=s√k−.05k. The old positive steady state satisfies √k=.2/.05=4, giving k=16 and competitive wage ∂Y/∂L=.5√k=2.

With constant k, K,Y and S=sY all grow with L at 5%. Raising s to .4 gives k*=64 but does not alter long-run aggregate growth 5%. During adjustment from k=16, k rises, so g_Y=.05+(1/2)g_k>.05 until the limit.

Immediately after the change g_K=s/√k=.10, hence g_Y=(g_K+g_L)/2=.075. As k approaches 64, g_Y approaches .05 from above; in continuous time the new steady state is approached asymptotically. If depreciation δ were specified, k*=[s/(.05+δ)]² and wages adjust accordingly.

With zero depreciation: old k*=16, wage 2, output and saving growth 5%; new k*=64, wage 4 and long-run output growth still 5%. Transition growth is above 5% and converges to it.
questions.hint: The saving rate changes the level of steady output per worker, not its long-run growth rate.
questions.notes: Depreciation is not stated; zero depreciation is used explicitly.

questions.stem: (a) A consumer has U=√[(x₁−s₁)(x₂−s₂)], s₁,s₂>0 and xᵢ≥sᵢ. Derive demands and budget shares under standard budget p₁x₁+p₂x₂≤M; are they linear in prices? (b) A symmetric utility function U(x₁,x₂)=U(x₂,x₁) is maximized subject to p(x₁+x₂)≤M. If the maximizer exists and is unique, prove x₁*=x₂*.
questions.answer: (a) xᵢ=sᵢ+[M−p₁s₁−p₂s₂]/(2pᵢ); budget shares are 1/2+(pᵢsᵢ−pⱼsⱼ)/(2M), affine in prices at fixed M. Demands are generally nonlinear in prices. (b) Uniqueness plus symmetry forces equal quantities.
questions.solution:
Shift consumption variables by subsistence amounts and define discretionary income $E$. This turns the first part into an ordinary equal-share Cobb–Douglas allocation. For the second part, a symmetry argument is stronger than unnecessary calculus.

$$\begin{aligned}
E&=M-p_1s_1-p_2s_2,\qquad z_i=x_i-s_i,\\
p_iz_i&=E/2,\\
x_i^*&=s_i+\frac{E}{2p_i},\\
\frac{p_ix_i^*}{M}&=\frac12+\frac{p_is_i-p_js_j}{2M}.
\end{aligned}$$

Feasibility must be checked before using the interior formula: $E<0$ permits no subsistence-feasible bundle, and $E=0$ fixes the unique subsistence bundle. Multiplying quantity demand by price removes its reciprocal term, which explains why budget shares can be affine in prices even when quantities are not.

(a) Feasibility requires M≥p₁s₁+p₂s₂. For strictly positive discretionary income E=M−p₁s₁−p₂s₂, write zᵢ=xᵢ−sᵢ; maximize √(z₁z₂) with discretionary budget E, giving pᵢzᵢ=E/2. Thus x₁=M/(2p₁)+s₁/2−p₂s₂/(2p₁), with the analogous expression for x₂.

These are not jointly linear in prices because of reciprocals and price ratios. But p₁x₁/M=1/2+(p₁s₁−p₂s₂)/(2M) and the other share is analogous, so shares are affine in prices holding M fixed. At E=0 the only feasible bundle is subsistence.

(b) If (a,b) is optimal, (b,a) is feasible and gives equal utility by symmetry. If a≠b this supplies two distinct maximizers, contradicting uniqueness. Hence a=b without requiring differentiability or concavity.

(a) xᵢ=sᵢ+[M−p₁s₁−p₂s₂]/(2pᵢ); budget shares are 1/2+(pᵢsᵢ−pⱼsⱼ)/(2M), affine in prices at fixed M. Demands are generally nonlinear in prices. (b) Uniqueness plus symmetry forces equal quantities.

solutionSteps.body: (a) xᵢ=sᵢ+[M−p₁s₁−p₂s₂]/(2pᵢ); budget shares are 1/2+(pᵢsᵢ−pⱼsⱼ)/(2M), affine in prices at fixed M. Demands are generally nonlinear in prices. (b) Uniqueness plus symmetry forces equal quantities.

questions.stem: (a) Two people have U_A=x_A1^α+x_A2^α, 0<α<1, and U_B=x_B1+x_B2. Derive the contract curve and its properties. (b) A firm has MC=AC=4 and demand q=100−10p. (i) Maximize revenue subject to profit at least 80. (ii) What if the target is 100? (iii) What if marginal cost rises to 8?
questions.answer: (a) Interior contract curve x_A1=x_A2, completed by boundary segments when one aggregate stock binds. (b)(i) q=40,p=6. (ii) Target100 infeasible (maximum profit90). (iii) At MC8, maximum profit10, so targets80 and100 are infeasible.
questions.solution:
The linear-utility consumer cares only about the sum of her holdings. Fixing that sum fixes her utility, leaving the concave-utility consumer to choose the most balanced feasible bundle. In the revenue problem, distinguish the objective from the profit constraint.

$$\begin{aligned}
R(q)&=10q-q^2/10,\\
\pi_4(q)&=6q-q^2/10,\\
\pi_4(q)\ge80&\Longleftrightarrow20\le q\le40,\\
R\prime(q)&=10-q/5>0\quad(20\le q\le40),\\
\max_q\pi_4(q)&=90,\qquad\max_q\pi_8(q)=10.
\end{aligned}$$

The revenue maximum over the feasible profit interval is therefore its right endpoint, not the profit-maximizing quantity. Raising the profit target to $100$ makes the feasible set empty. Increasing marginal cost to eight makes even the original target unattainable; cost does not change the unconstrained revenue curve, but it changes feasibility.

(a) Let total stocks be Ω₁,Ω₂>0. For any fixed total S=x_A1+x_A2, B utility is Ω₁+Ω₂−S. Strict concavity of t^α makes A prefer the most equal feasible division of S.

Therefore efficient interior allocations have x_A1=x_A2. If Ω₁≤Ω₂, the complete curve is (t,t),0≤t≤Ω₁, plus (Ω₁,t),Ω₁≤t≤Ω₂; if Ω₂≤Ω₁, interchange labels. Any unequal nonboundary allocation permits a balancing transfer raising A utility without changing B utility.

No point on the stated curve permits a Pareto improvement because raising A utility requires raising A total consumption and reducing B utility. (b) Inverse demand is p=10−q/10; revenue R=10q−q²/10, maximized without the constraint at q=50. Profit at MC4 is π=6q−q²/10.

The target π≥80 restricts q to [20,40], where revenue is increasing; choose q=40,p=6. Maximum profit is 90 at q=30, so a target of 100 has no feasible output. At MC8, π=2q−q²/10 has maximum10 at q=10,p=9; thus even the old 80 target is impossible.

If the profit constraint is dropped entirely, revenue maximization stays q=50,p=5 independently of cost, but would then lose money at MC8.

(a) Interior contract curve x_A1=x_A2, completed by boundary segments when one aggregate stock binds. (b)(i) q=40,p=6. (ii) Target100 infeasible (maximum profit90). (iii) At MC8, maximum profit10, so targets80 and100 are infeasible.
questions.hint: For the contract curve, hold A’s total quantity fixed; for the firm, check profit feasibility before optimizing revenue.

options: A rational number but not a natural number
questions.solution: Squaring the positive sum gives 26+2√(169−9·23/3)=26+2√100=46. The sum is √46, which is irrational and greater than √36=6.
questions.hint: Square the entire sum of square roots.

questions.stem: The domain of f(x)=√(x+3)/(x²+5x+4) is
questions.solution: The square root requires x≥−3. The denominator factors as (x+1)(x+4), so x≠−1,−4. Since −4 is outside x≥−3 anyway, the domain is [−3,∞)\{−1}, absent from the options.
questions.hint: Intersect the square-root domain with the nonzero-denominator condition.
questions.notes: Source option (b) begins (−0,∞); it is preserved rather than silently repaired.

questions.stem: Find log₄2−log₈2+log₁₆2−⋯ .
questions.solution: Change of base gives 1/2−1/3+1/4−⋯ . Since ln2=1−1/2+1/3−1/4+⋯, the given sum is 1−ln2.
questions.hint: Compare with the alternating harmonic series.

questions.stem: The function max{1,x,x²}, for real x, has
questions.solution: The maximum of finitely many continuous real-valued functions is continuous. Here 1, x and x² are all continuous everywhere.
questions.hint: A finite maximum preserves continuity.

questions.stem: If x,y,z>0 are in harmonic progression, then (x−y)/(y−z) equals
questions.answer: x/z, wherever the displayed ratio is defined.
questions.solution: Harmonic progression gives y=2xz/(x+z). Then x−y=x(x−z)/(x+z) and y−z=z(x−z)/(x+z), whose ratio is x/z when x≠z.
questions.hint: Express the harmonic mean y using x and z.
questions.notes: The all-equal case makes the source ratio 0/0; the identity is interpreted on its natural domain.

questions.stem: For every real x, f(x)=x/(1+|x|) is
options: Everywhere differentiable but its derivative has one discontinuity
Everywhere differentiable but its derivative has two discontinuities
questions.solution: For x>0, f′(x)=1/(1+x)²; for x<0, f′(x)=1/(1−x)². At 0, the difference quotient is 1/(1+|h|)→1. Both one-sided derivative formulas also tend to 1, so f′ is continuous at 0 and elsewhere.
questions.hint: Compute the derivative on each side, then check 0 separately.

questions.stem: Let f:ℝ₊₊→ℝ₊₊ satisfy f(1)=3 and f′(1)=9. Find lim as x→0 of [f(1+x)/f(1)]^(1/x).
questions.solution: Take logarithms. The logarithm of the expression is [ln f(1+x)−ln f(1)]/x, which tends to f′(1)/f(1)=9/3=3. Exponentiating gives e³.
questions.hint: Take the logarithm of the limit.

questions.stem: Let f,g:[0,∞)→[0,∞) be decreasing and increasing respectively, and define h(x)=f(g(x)). If h(0)=0, then h(x)−h(1) is
questions.answer: As printed, h(x)−h(1)=0 for every x, so no option is valid.
questions.solution: Under non-strict monotonicity, h is nonincreasing. Its nonnegative codomain and h(0)=0 imply 0≤h(x)≤0 for every x≥0. Therefore h≡0 and h(x)−h(1)=0. None of the choices allows zero for all x. Under strict decreasing/increasing conventions, the stated nonnegative codomain and h(0)=0 are themselves incompatible.
questions.hint: Combine monotonicity with the nonnegative codomain.
questions.notes: The intended monotonicity answer may have been (a), but the codomain and h(0)=0 make the printed problem inconsistent with that choice.

questions.stem: A committee of three men and two women is to be chosen from six men and four women. In how many ways can this be done if Mr. X and Mrs. Y are not included together?
questions.solution: There are C(6,3)C(4,2)=120 unrestricted committees. Those containing both specified persons number C(5,2)C(3,1)=30. Subtracting gives 90.
questions.hint: Subtract committees containing both named people.

questions.stem: How many continuous functions f satisfy x f(y)+y f(x)=(x+y)f(x)f(y) for all real x,y?
questions.solution: Set y=x≠0 to get f(x)=f(x)², so f(x)∈{0,1}. Continuity forces f to be constant on the connected real line; the value at zero is fixed by continuity too. Both f≡0 and f≡1 satisfy the identity.
questions.hint: Set x=y and use continuity.

questions.stem: If positive x₁,…,xₙ are in arithmetic progression, find 1/(√x₁+√x₂)+1/(√x₂+√x₃)+⋯+1/(√xₙ₋₁+√xₙ).
questions.answer: (n−1)/(√x₁+√xₙ), hence none of the listed general formulas.
questions.solution: If the common difference is d≠0, rationalize each term as (√xᵢ₊₁−√xᵢ)/d. The sum telescopes to (√xₙ−√x₁)/d=(n−1)/(√x₁+√xₙ). For d=0 the sum is (n−1)/(2√x₁), the same formula.
questions.hint: Rationalize each denominator and telescope.
questions.notes: The third option is labeled (b) again in the source; options are indexed by position. For the natural sum n≥2 is understood.

questions.stem: For any real x,y,z, which is always true?
questions.solution: If x≥y, |x−y|=x−y and the formula yields x. If y≥x, it yields y. Adding z to a maximum can leave the maximum unchanged, so the strict inequalities are not universal.
questions.hint: Split into x≥y and y≥x.

questions.stem: If x₁,x₂,x₃,x₄>0 and their sum is 2, then P=(x₁+x₂)(x₃+x₄) is
questions.solution: Let u=x₁+x₂, so x₃+x₄=2−u and 0<u<2. Then P=u(2−u)=1−(u−1)²≤1 and is positive.
questions.hint: Group the terms into two positive numbers summing to 2.

questions.stem: Everyone in a room shakes hands with everyone else. There are 91 handshakes. How many persons are in the room?
questions.solution: With n people, C(n,2)=n(n−1)/2=91. Solving n²−n−182=0 gives the positive integer n=14.
questions.hint: Count unordered pairs of persons.

questions.stem: In how many ways can six pencils be distributed between two boys so each boy receives at least one pencil?
questions.answer: 62 if the pencils are distinguishable; 5 if identical.
questions.solution: If each physical pencil is treated as distinct, assign each independently to one of the two boys: 2⁶ possibilities. Exclude the two assignments giving all pencils to one boy, leaving 62. If pencils are identical, only the five splits (1,5),(2,4),(3,3),(4,2),(5,1) are different. The source does not specify distinguishability.
questions.hint: Clarify whether individual pencils are distinguishable.
questions.notes: The intended option is likely (c)=62, but distinguishability is not stated.

questions.stem: How many continuous functions satisfy x f(x)+2f(−x)=−1 for every real x?
questions.solution: Replacing x by −x gives 2f(x)−x f(−x)=−1. Solving these two equations yields f(x)=−(x+2)/(x²+4), which is continuous everywhere and satisfies the original equation. The solution is uniquely determined.
questions.hint: Write the equation at both x and −x.

questions.stem: The function f(x)=x+∫ from 0 to 1 of (xy²+x²y)f(y)dy has the form px+qx², where
questions.answer: p=180/119, q=80/119; none of the above.
questions.solution: The integral formula implies f(x)=px+qx². Equating coefficients gives p=1+p/4+q/5 and q=p/3+q/4. The latter yields q=4p/9. Substitution gives p(1−1/4−4/45)=1, so p=180/119 and q=80/119.
questions.hint: Substitute px+qx² into the integral equation.

questions.stem: If real x,y satisfy x²+y²=1, the maximum of |x|+|y| is
questions.solution: Cauchy–Schwarz gives (|x|+|y|)²≤(1²+1²)(x²+y²)=2. Equality holds when |x|=|y|=1/√2.
questions.hint: Apply Cauchy–Schwarz.

questions.stem: How many onto functions are there from A={p,q,r,s} to B={p,r}?
questions.solution: There are 2⁴=16 functions from a four-element set to a two-element set. Exactly two are constant and fail to be onto. Thus 16−2=14.
questions.hint: Remove the constant maps.

questions.stem: If the coefficients of the (2r+5)th and (r−6)th terms in (1+x)³⁹ are equal, then C(r,12) equals
questions.solution: The two coefficients are C(39,2r+4) and C(39,r−7). Equal binomial coefficients have equal indices or complementary indices. The equal-index case gives r=−11, outside valid term indices. Complementarity gives 2r+4+r−7=39, hence r=14. Therefore C(14,12)=C(14,2)=91.
questions.hint: Remember that the kth term uses binomial index k−1.

questions.stem: If X=[[C,2],[1,C]] and det(X⁷)=128, find C.
questions.solution: det(X⁷)=(det X)⁷=(C²−2)⁷=128=2⁷. Because the seventh power is one-to-one over the reals, C²−2=2, so C=±2.
questions.hint: Use det(X⁷)=(det X)⁷.

questions.stem: Let f(x)=Ax²+Bx+C with real A,B,C. If f(x) is an integer whenever x is an integer, then
options: 2A and A+B are integers, but C is not
A+B and C are integers, but 2A is not
questions.solution: C=f(0) is an integer and A+B=f(1)−f(0) is an integer. The second finite difference f(2)−2f(1)+f(0)=2A is also an integer. Conversely f(n)=A n(n−1)+(A+B)n+C is integral under these conditions.
questions.hint: Evaluate the polynomial and its finite differences at integers.

questions.stem: Four people board a lift on the ground floor of a seven-storey building. In how many ways can they leave at four different floors?
questions.solution: Counting the ground floor as one of the seven storeys leaves six upper floors. The four distinct people choose different exit floors in 6·5·4·3=360 ways.
questions.hint: Assign distinct exit floors to the four people.
questions.notes: Uses the standard intended convention: seven storeys include the ground floor. Seven upper floors would produce a different count.

questions.stem: How many positive triples (x,x₁,x₂) satisfy |log x₁+log x₂|+|log(x/x₁)|+|log(x/x₂)|=|log x₁+log x₂|?
questions.answer: Infinitely many; none of the above.
questions.solution: Cancel the identical absolute-value term from both sides. The remaining two nonnegative terms must both vanish, giving x/x₁=x/x₂=1. Hence all triples (t,t,t) with t>0 are solutions, and there are infinitely many.
questions.hint: Cancel the identical first term, then use nonnegativity.

questions.stem: In a sample invaded by smallpox, 70% of inhabitants are attacked and 85% have been vaccinated. What is the minimum attacked percentage among those vaccinated, to the nearest integer?
questions.solution: If A means attacked and V vaccinated, P(A∩V)≥P(A)+P(V)−1=0.55. Thus P(A|V)≥0.55/0.85=11/17≈0.6471, rounding to 65%. This bound is attainable.
questions.hint: Use the lower bound on an intersection probability.

questions.stem: Bivariate data have Var(X)=9. The product of the Y-on-X and X-on-Y regression coefficients is 0.36, and the Y-on-X coefficient is 0.8. Find Var(Y).
questions.solution: The coefficient product is r²=0.36. Since the Y-on-X coefficient is positive, r=0.6. Using βᵧₓ=rσᵧ/σₓ with σₓ=3 gives σᵧ=0.8·3/0.6=4, so Var(Y)=16.
questions.hint: Recover correlation from the product of regression slopes.

questions.stem: Two tyre brands are tested on independent samples of 50 customers each under similar conditions. Sample means are 13,200 and 13,650 km, and standard deviations 300 and 400 km. What is the 5% significance-level conclusion about wear quality?
options: The brands are not the same
The data are inadequate to perform a test
questions.answer: Reject equality of mean wear life.
questions.solution: The estimated standard error of the difference is √(300²/50+400²/50)=√5000≈70.71 km. The test statistic is (13650−13200)/70.71≈6.36, well above the two-sided 5% normal critical value 1.96 (and the relevant large-sample t critical value). Hence equality is rejected.
questions.hint: Standardize the difference of sample means.
questions.notes: Uses the intended independent-samples large-sample comparison.

questions.stem: A continuous random variable has density f(x)=(α/x₀)(x₀/x)^(α+1) for x>x₀ and α>1. Its distribution function on x>x₀ and mean respectively are
questions.solution: Integrating αx₀ᵅx^(−α−1) from x₀ to x gives 1−(x₀/x)ᵅ. Integrating x times this density over [x₀,∞) gives αx₀/(α−1), finite for α>1.
questions.hint: Integrate the Pareto density and its first moment.
questions.notes: The standard density requires x₀>0, implicit in this Pareto specification; F(x)=0 for x≤x₀.

questions.stem: X takes values 0,1,…,n with probabilities proportional to C(n,0),C(n,1),…,C(n,n). Its mean μ and variance σ² are
questions.solution: The binomial coefficients sum to 2ⁿ, so P(X=k)=C(n,k)/2ⁿ. This is Binomial(n,1/2), with mean n/2 and variance n(1/2)(1/2)=n/4.
questions.hint: Normalize the probabilities and identify the distribution.

questions.stem: Let Xᵢ be i.i.d. with P(Xᵢ=1)=p and P(Xᵢ=0)=1−p. Define y=1 if ∑ from i=1 to n of Xᵢ=100, and y=0 otherwise. Then E(y²) is
questions.solution: Because y is an indicator, y²=y, and E(y²)=P(∑Xᵢ=100). The sum is Binomial(n,p), giving the stated binomial probability. For n<100 the probability is zero.
questions.hint: An indicator squared equals itself.

questions.stem: A zero-cost monopolist sells X and Y to three consumers with reservation values (X,Y): consumer 1 (4,0), consumer 2 (3,3), consumer 3 (0,4). Each buys at most one unit of each good. Compare separate pricing, pure bundling, and mixed bundling and find the best strategy.
questions.answer: Mixed bundling is best: pₓ=pᵧ=4 and bundle price 6, giving revenue 14 under the usual buy-at-indifference convention. Separate sales and pure bundling each yield at most 12.
questions.solution:
Because production cost is zero, compare revenues. List each consumer's bundle value as the sum of her two reservation values; mixed bundling can extract different values through different purchase options.

$$\begin{aligned}
R_{\mathrm{separate}}^*&=2(2\cdot3)=12,\\
(v_1^{XY},v_2^{XY},v_3^{XY})&=(4,6,4),\\
R_{\mathrm{bundle}}^*&=\max\{3(4),1(6)\}=12,\\
R_{\mathrm{mixed}}&=4+6+4=14.
\end{aligned}$$

The mixed menu serves the two specialist consumers with individual goods and the middle consumer with the bundle. Its revenue equals the sum of all three consumers' maximum total payments, establishing a global upper bound rather than merely a comparison with two candidate strategies.

Separate pricing: each product sells to two consumers at price 3, giving 6 per product and total 12; price 4 gives only 4 per product. Pure bundling: bundle values are 4,6,4, so price 4 sells three bundles and yields 12, while price 6 yields only 6. Mixed bundling: set separate prices at 4 and bundle price at 6.

Consumers 1 and 3 buy their preferred single goods for 4 each; consumer 2 buys the bundle for 6. Revenue is 14, equal to the sum of all consumers’ total reservation values and therefore an upper bound, so this strategy is optimal. If indifferent consumers refuse to buy, choose prices just below these levels and revenue approaches 14.

Mixed bundling is best: pₓ=pᵧ=4 and bundle price 6, giving revenue 14 under the usual buy-at-indifference convention. Separate sales and pure bundling each yield at most 12.
questions.hint: The extreme consumers prefer different single goods; the middle consumer values the bundle more highly.
questions.notes: No production costs are supplied; payoffs are interpreted as revenue. Standard weak participation permits buying at reservation value.

questions.stem: Two consumers each have income M and utility U=xy, where x is restaurant consumption and y another good, with prices pₓ,pᵧ. Plan A: each pays her own restaurant bill. Plan B: each pays half the combined restaurant bill. Find equilibrium consumption under both plans and explain any difference.
questions.answer: Each person: plan A x=M/(2pₓ), y=M/(2pᵧ); plan B x=2M/(3pₓ), y=M/(3pᵧ).
questions.solution:
Under a shared bill, an individual chooses her meal while taking the other person's meal as fixed. The private marginal price is half the restaurant price, but the other diner's bill also reduces disposable income.

$$\begin{aligned}
p_yy_i&=M-\frac{p_x}{2}(x_i+x_j),\\
\frac{\partial(x_iy_i)}{\partial x_i}=0
&\Longrightarrow M-p_xx_i-\frac{p_x}{2}x_j=0,\\
x_i= x_j&\Longrightarrow x_i=\frac{2M}{3p_x},\quad y_i=\frac{M}{3p_y}.
\end{aligned}$$

Impose symmetry only after deriving the unilateral best response. The equilibrium spends two-thirds of each budget on restaurant consumption rather than one-half. Each diner ignores the cost imposed on the other, so sharing a bill can lower both people's utility despite appearing cooperative.

Under A, maximize xy subject to pₓx+pᵧy=M, giving equal expenditure shares and x=M/(2pₓ),y=M/(2pᵧ). Under B, If the other consumer chooses xⱼ, consumer i pays (pₓ/2)(xᵢ+xⱼ). Her remaining spending gives yᵢ=[M−(pₓ/2)(xᵢ+xⱼ)]/pᵧ.

Maximizing xᵢyᵢ while taking xⱼ as fixed yields M−pₓxᵢ−(pₓ/2)xⱼ=0. Hence the best response is xᵢ=M/pₓ−xⱼ/2 when positive. Symmetry xᵢ=xⱼ=x gives (3/2)pₓx=M, so x=2M/(3pₓ).

Each pays pₓx=2M/3 on the common bill and spends M/3 on the other good, giving y=M/(3pᵧ). The shared bill lowers the perceived marginal price of restaurant consumption to pₓ/2. Each person ignores the extra cost imposed on the other, so restaurant consumption rises and utility falls: plan-A utility is M²/(4pₓpᵧ), whereas plan-B utility is 2M²/(9pₓpᵧ).

Each person: plan A x=M/(2pₓ), y=M/(2pᵧ); plan B x=2M/(3pₓ), y=M/(3pᵧ).
questions.hint: Each consumer perceives only half the marginal restaurant cost and takes the other person’s order as fixed.

solutionSteps.body:
Under A, maximize xy subject to pₓx+pᵧy=M, giving equal expenditure shares and x=M/(2pₓ),y=M/(2pᵧ). Under B, If the other consumer chooses xⱼ, consumer i pays (pₓ/2)(xᵢ+xⱼ). Her remaining spending gives yᵢ=[M−(pₓ/2)(xᵢ+xⱼ)]/pᵧ.

Maximizing xᵢyᵢ while taking xⱼ as fixed yields M−pₓxᵢ−(pₓ/2)xⱼ=0. Hence the best response is xᵢ=M/pₓ−xⱼ/2 when positive. Symmetry xᵢ=xⱼ=x gives (3/2)pₓx=M, so x=2M/(3pₓ).

Each pays pₓx=2M/3 on the common bill and spends M/3 on the other good, giving y=M/(3pᵧ). The shared bill lowers the perceived marginal price of restaurant consumption to pₓ/2. Each person ignores the extra cost imposed on the other, so restaurant consumption rises and utility falls: plan-A utility is M²/(4pₓpᵧ), whereas plan-B utility is 2M²/(9pₓpᵧ).

solutionSteps.title: Conclusion
solutionSteps.body: Each person: plan A x=M/(2pₓ), y=M/(2pᵧ); plan B x=2M/(3pₓ), y=M/(3pᵧ).

questions.stem: A community has exhaustible resource stock X and maximizes Σ(t=0 to ∞) δᵗ log Cₜ subject to ΣCₜ≤X, with 0<δ<1. (a) Set up the optimization and interpret the first-order condition. (b) Find optimal Cₜ. (c) At the beginning of period T, an unanticipated additional stock X′ is discovered. Find consumption from T onward.
questions.answer: Initially Cₜ=(1−δ)δᵗX. After discovery, Cₜ=(1−δ)δ^(t−T)(δᵀX+X′), t≥T.
questions.solution:
There is one stock constraint across all dates rather than a separate budget each period. Its multiplier is the common shadow value of one extra unit of the resource.

$$\begin{aligned}
\mathcal L&=\sum_{t=0}^\infty\delta^t\log C_t
+\lambda\left(X-\sum_{t=0}^\infty C_t\right),\\
\frac{\delta^t}{C_t}&=\lambda,\qquad
X=\frac1\lambda\sum_{t=0}^\infty\delta^t,\\
C_t^*&=(1-\delta)\delta^tX.
\end{aligned}$$

The geometric allocation equalizes discounted marginal utilities and exactly exhausts the stock. At the surprise date, discard the old plan for future periods but keep past consumption fixed. Apply the same geometric rule to the remaining old stock plus the newly discovered stock, resetting the time index to the discovery date.

The Lagrangian is Σδᵗ log Cₜ+λ(X−ΣCₜ). Its first-order condition δᵗ/Cₜ=λ equates the discounted marginal utility of resource consumption across dates. The resource constraint binds, so Cₜ=(1−δ)δᵗX.

Before period T the old plan has used X(1−δᵀ), leaving δᵀX. The surprise discovery raises available stock at T to δᵀX+X′. Reoptimizing from that date gives Cₜ=(1−δ)δ^(t−T)(δᵀX+X′).

Consumption before T is unaffected because the discovery was unanticipated.

Initially Cₜ=(1−δ)δᵗX. After discovery, Cₜ=(1−δ)δ^(t−T)(δᵀX+X′), t≥T.

questions.stem: A consumer has income M and positive prices p₁,…,pₙ. (a) For U=max(x₁,…,xₙ), find Marshallian demand for good i and describe its graph. (b) For U=min(x₁,…,xₙ), find income and own-price elasticities for good i.
questions.answer: Max utility: spend all income on one cheapest good; tied cheapest goods generate alternative corners. Min utility: xᵢ=M/Σpⱼ, income elasticity 1 and own-price elasticity −pᵢ/Σpⱼ.
questions.solution:
Maximum and minimum utility select opposite geometries. A maximum rewards concentrating spending on one component; a minimum rewards matching every component so that no expenditure is wasted above the bottleneck.

$$\begin{aligned}
\max_i x_i&\le M/\min_jp_j,\\
U=\min_i x_i:&\quad x_i^*=\frac{M}{\sum_jp_j},\\
\eta_{iM}&=\frac{\partial x_i}{\partial M}\frac{M}{x_i}=1,\\
\eta_{ip_i}&=\frac{\partial x_i}{\partial p_i}\frac{p_i}{x_i}
=-\frac{p_i}{\sum_jp_j}.
\end{aligned}$$

For maximum utility, attain the bound by spending everything on one cheapest good. At a tie, alternative corner bundles maximize utility, but their mixtures generally do not. For minimum utility, differentiate the common quantity formula to obtain elasticities instead of confusing an absolute derivative with a proportional response.

For max utility, the largest attainable component is M/p_min. To attain it one must spend all income on one cheapest good. Hence xᵢ=M/pᵢ if i alone is cheapest, xᵢ=0 if it is not cheapest, and xᵢ∈{0,M/pᵢ} if it shares the lowest price with another good; mixtures of the tied corners do not maximize max utility.

Holding other prices fixed and writing p*=min(j≠i)pⱼ, its demand graph is M/pᵢ for pᵢ<p*, zero for pᵢ>p*, and the two endpoints at equality. For min utility, all goods are consumed in equal quantities x=M/Σpⱼ, because extra units of one good alone add no utility. Differentiation gives ∂log xᵢ/∂log M=1 and ∂log xᵢ/∂log pᵢ=−pᵢ/Σpⱼ.

Max utility: spend all income on one cheapest good; tied cheapest goods generate alternative corners. Min utility: xᵢ=M/Σpⱼ, income elasticity 1 and own-price elasticity −pᵢ/Σpⱼ.

questions.notes: Positive income and prices and n≥2 are assumed; n=1 reduces to ordinary one-good demand.

questions.stem: An economy has m individuals, n goods with aggregate endowments ωⱼ and identical product utilities Uᵢ=∏ⱼCⱼⁱ. (a) Define an allocation, a Pareto-inferior allocation and a Pareto-optimal allocation. (b) Give an example of each type of efficiency. (c) Is Cⱼⁱ=λⁱωⱼ for every good, where λⁱ≥0 and Σᵢλⁱ=1, Pareto optimal?
questions.answer: Proportional allocations are Pareto optimal. For positive endowments, a feasible allocation wasting all goods is Pareto inferior; allocating every good equally among individuals is Pareto optimal.
questions.solution:
Normalize each holding by the corresponding aggregate stock. This turns feasibility into a common unit upper bound for every good, making the proportional-allocation proof independent of units.

$$\begin{aligned}
z_j^i&=C_j^i/\omega_j,\qquad\sum_i z_j^i\le1,\\
\prod_jz_j^i&\ge(\lambda^i)^n,\\
\frac1n\sum_jz_j^i&\ge\left(\prod_jz_j^i\right)^{1/n}\ge\lambda^i,\\
\text{a strict Pareto gain}&\Longrightarrow
\frac1n\sum_j\sum_i z_j^i>\sum_i\lambda^i=1.
\end{aligned}$$

AM–GM converts each person's required product utility into a lower bound on her average resource share. A strict gain for anyone makes the aggregate inequality strict, contradicting the normalized feasibility bound. This proves efficiency directly, including consumers assigned zero shares, rather than relying only on tangency conditions.

(a) A feasible allocation assigns Cⱼⁱ≥0 to each person with ΣᵢCⱼⁱ≤ωⱼ for each good. It is Pareto inferior if some feasible allocation makes every person at least as well off and at least one person strictly better off. It is Pareto optimal if no such improvement exists.

(b) Suppose ωⱼ>0 and define normalized shares zⱼⁱ=Cⱼⁱ/ωⱼ. The proposed allocation gives each person utility (λⁱ)ⁿ∏ⱼωⱼ. Any Pareto improvement must satisfy ∏ⱼzⱼⁱ≥(λⁱ)ⁿ for all i, strictly for someone.

By AM–GM, (Σⱼzⱼⁱ)/n≥(∏ⱼzⱼⁱ)^(1/n)≥λⁱ, strictly for that person. Summing over i would then give (1/n)ΣⱼΣᵢzⱼⁱ>Σᵢλⁱ=1, violating feasibility Σᵢzⱼⁱ≤1. Therefore no Pareto improvement exists.

This proof also covers zero λⁱ. If an aggregate endowment is zero, all product utilities are zero and no feasible strict utility improvement is possible. For the requested examples, assigning zero of every good to everyone is Pareto inferior if every aggregate endowment is positive: distributing the stock equally raises every person’s product utility above zero.

Equal proportional shares λⁱ=1/m give a Pareto-optimal example by the preceding proof. If allocations are required to exhaust every stock, with at least two individuals and goods one can instead place all of good 1 with individual 1 and all of goods 2,…,n with individual 2, giving all utilities zero; equal sharing is then a strict improvement. Degenerate zero-endowment cases need no Pareto-inferior example because every feasible product utility is zero.

Proportional allocations are Pareto optimal. For positive endowments, a feasible allocation wasting all goods is Pareto inferior; allocating every good equally among individuals is Pareto optimal.

questions.stem: A monopolist faces domestic inverse demand p=5−(3/2)qₕ, can sell abroad at constant price 3, and has total cost C(q)=q², q=qₕ+q_f. (a) Find domestic and foreign sales without restrictions. (b) Repeat if foreign sales cannot exceed 1/6.
questions.solution:
Domestic and export sales share the same total-production cost. When exports are unconstrained, their price sets the marginal revenue to which domestic sales are compared. A binding export ceiling changes that condition.

$$\begin{aligned}
\pi&=(5-1.5q_h)q_h+3q_f-(q_h+q_f)^2,\\
\text{unrestricted: }2(q_h+q_f)&=3,\quad5-3q_h=3,\\
q_f=1/6:&\quad5-3q_h-2(q_h+1/6)=0,\\
q_h&=14/15,\qquad q_h+q_f=11/10.
\end{aligned}$$

First solve the unconstrained allocation and check it against the cap. Because its exports exceed $1/6$, the cap binds. Re-optimize domestic sales with exports fixed at that boundary, then verify the export marginal profit remains positive to confirm that relaxing the cap would help.

Profit is (5−1.5qₕ)qₕ+3q𝒻−(qₕ+q𝒻)². Without the export cap, foreign marginal revenue 3 would imply total quantity 3/2, while domestic MR=5−3qₕ=3 gives qₕ=2/3 and q𝒻=5/6, exceeding the cap. Thus the cap binds: q𝒻=1/6.

The domestic first-order condition is 5−3qₕ−2(qₕ+1/6)=0, giving qₕ=14/15. At this point total quantity is 11/10 and foreign marginal profit is 3−2·11/10=4/5>0, confirming the desire to export more if allowed. The profit Hessian is negative definite, so this constrained solution is the unique maximum.

(a) qₕ=2/3, q_f=5/6. (b) qₕ=14/15, q_f=1/6.

questions.stem: An economy produces F=√(L𝒻T) and M=√(LₘK), with mobile labour L𝒻+Lₘ=100, K=36, T=49 and both output prices 1. Landlords own land and capitalists own capital. (a) Find sectoral labour allocation. (b) If land is unowned and available free, find the new allocation. (c) Suggest an aggregate welfare measure. (d) Compare welfare under the two ownership arrangements. (e) Explain the difference.
questions.answer: (a) L𝒻=980/17 and Lₘ=720/17. (b) Under open-access self-employment on unowned land, L𝒻=2450/29 and Lₘ=450/29. With total output F+M as welfare, owned-land output is 10√85≈92.195; open-access output is 670/√58≈87.975, lower by about 4.220.
questions.solution:
Owned land rewards hired labour at its marginal product. Under open access, a self-employed entrant keeps average product instead, creating an externality on other food workers.

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{private land: }\frac7{2\sqrt{L_F}}&=\frac6{2\sqrt{L_M}}
\Longrightarrow\frac{L_F}{L_M}=\frac{49}{36},\\
\text{open access: }\frac7{\sqrt{L_F}}&=\frac3{\sqrt{L_M}}
\Longrightarrow\frac{L_F}{L_M}=\frac{49}{9},\\
L_F+L_M&=100.
\end{aligned}$$

Use each ratio together with the labour endowment to recover levels. At common unit output prices, total output is a transparent efficiency criterion, though it is not a complete distributional welfare function. Comparing the two totals shows the cost of excessive entry into food production.

(a) Competitive labour mobility equates marginal products: 7/(2√L𝒻)=6/(2√Lₘ). Hence L𝒻/Lₘ=49/36. Together with total labour 100, this gives L𝒻=4900/85=980/17 and Lₘ=3600/85=720/17.

(b) Under the common-property/open-access interpretation, a worker entering food production receives average food product F/L𝒻=7/√L𝒻 because no landlord collects rent. Manufacturing still pays marginal product 3/√Lₘ. Mobility therefore gives 7/√L𝒻=3/√Lₘ, so L𝒻/Lₘ=49/9 and L𝒻=4900/58=2450/29, Lₘ=900/58=450/29.

Open access attracts excessive labour into food relative to the private-land allocation. A natural efficiency measure at the given common unit output prices is total output F+M, ignoring distributional utility differences. Owned-land labour gives F+M=10√85≈92.195.

Under the open-access allocation, L_F=100·49/58 and L_M=100·9/58, so F=490/√58 and M=180/√58, total 670/√58≈87.975. Open access lowers aggregate output through the common-property congestion externality: food entrants compare average product with the manufacturing wage, attracting too many workers into food. A distribution-sensitive welfare ranking would require additional preferences or social weights.

questions.stem: A competitive economy produces Y=AF(L,K), with F homogeneous of degree one. Labour and capital are fully employed, and total labour earnings always equal total capital earnings. (a) L grows 4%, K 3%, Y 9%: find productivity growth. (b) Nominal wage grows 30%, nominal capital rental 10%, output price 5%: find productivity growth. (c) With productivity unchanged, wage grows 30% and rental 10%: find output-price growth.
questions.answer: Using conventional growth-rate accounting: (a) 5.5%, (b) 15%, (c) 20%. If the quoted percentages are exact finite-period increases: approximately 5.315%, 13.888%, 19.583%, respectively.
questions.solution:
Equal factor earnings and constant returns imply income shares of one-half. Use the primal identity when output and inputs are observed, and the dual unit-cost identity when factor and output prices are observed.

$$\begin{aligned}
g_Y&=g_A+\tfrac12g_L+\tfrac12g_K,\\
g_P&=\tfrac12g_W+\tfrac12g_R-g_A,\\
g_A^{(a)}&=9-(4+3)/2=5.5\%,\\
g_A^{(b)}&=(30+10)/2-5=15\%,\\
g_P^{(c)}&=(30+10)/2=20\%.
\end{aligned}$$

These are log-growth identities. For finite annual percentage changes, multiply growth factors and take geometric means rather than adding percentages exactly. Keeping the two conventions separate explains the alternative numerical values without changing the underlying economic accounting.

Competition and constant returns imply labour and capital income shares sum to one. Equal earnings make both shares 1/2. Therefore g_Y=g_A+(g_L+g_K)/2, yielding g_A=9−(4+3)/2=5.5%.

The dual cost-growth identity is g_P=(g_w+g_r)/2−g_A, so in (b) g_A=(30+10)/2−5=15%, and in (c) g_P=20%. These are instantaneous/log growth identities, often used as percentage approximations. Because the shares remain exactly one-half at every date, integrating gives exact finite-factor formulas: 1+g_A=1.09/√(1.04·1.03) for (a), 1+g_A=√(1.30·1.10)/1.05 for (b), and 1+g_P=√(1.30·1.10) for (c).

Their finite percentage changes are 5.315%,13.888%,19.583%.

Using conventional growth-rate accounting: (a) 5.5%, (b) 15%, (c) 20%. If the quoted percentages are exact finite-period increases: approximately 5.315%, 13.888%, 19.583%, respectively.

questions.notes: The source does not distinguish instantaneous growth rates from finite percentage changes; both conventions are supplied.

solutionSteps.title: Set up the problem
solutionSteps.body: Equal factor earnings and constant returns imply income shares of one-half. Use the primal identity when output and inputs are observed, and the dual unit-cost identity when factor and output prices are observed.

solutionSteps.title: Work through the equations
solutionSteps.body:
$$\begin{aligned}
g_Y&=g_A+\tfrac12g_L+\tfrac12g_K,\\
g_P&=\tfrac12g_W+\tfrac12g_R-g_A,\\
g_A^{(a)}&=9-(4+3)/2=5.5\%,\\
g_A^{(b)}&=(30+10)/2-5=15\%,\\
g_P^{(c)}&=(30+10)/2=20\%.
\end{aligned}$$

These are log-growth identities. For finite annual percentage changes, multiply growth factors and take geometric means rather than adding percentages exactly. Keeping the two conventions separate explains the alternative numerical values without changing the underlying economic accounting.

solutionSteps.title: Complete the argument
solutionSteps.body:
Competition and constant returns imply labour and capital income shares sum to one. Equal earnings make both shares 1/2. Therefore g_Y=g_A+(g_L+g_K)/2, yielding g_A=9−(4+3)/2=5.5%.

The dual cost-growth identity is g_P=(g_w+g_r)/2−g_A, so in (b) g_A=(30+10)/2−5=15%, and in (c) g_P=20%. These are instantaneous/log growth identities, often used as percentage approximations. Because the shares remain exactly one-half at every date, integrating gives exact finite-factor formulas: 1+g_A=1.09/√(1.04·1.03) for (a), 1+g_A=√(1.30·1.10)/1.05 for (b), and 1+g_P=√(1.30·1.10) for (c).

Their finite percentage changes are 5.315%,13.888%,19.583%.

solutionSteps.title: Conclusion
solutionSteps.body: Using conventional growth-rate accounting: (a) 5.5%, (b) 15%, (c) 20%. If the quoted percentages are exact finite-period increases: approximately 5.315%, 13.888%, 19.583%, respectively.

questions.stem: An economy has goods m and g. Capitalists earn R=R_m+R_g and consume only m, spending C=cR. Workers in m earn W, spend αW on g and (1−α)W on m and do not save. Wages in g are excluded on both income and expenditure sides because they are entirely spent on g. Investment I is autonomous and buys only m. Sector-m income distribution obeys R_m=θW. (a) Show how capitalists’ income is determined by their expenditure and find the investment multiplier. (b) Find W in terms of I,c,α,θ.
questions.solution:
Aggregate the two sectors only after cancelling wages that are spent and received entirely within the omitted sector. The remaining identity exposes why capitalists' spending determines their collective income.

$$\begin{aligned}
R+W&=cR+(1-\alpha)W+\alpha W+I,\\
R&=cR+I=\frac{I}{1-c},\\
R_g&=\alpha W,\qquad R_m=\theta W,\\
W&=\frac{I}{(1-c)(\theta+\alpha)}.
\end{aligned}$$

Workers' spending cancels with their earnings at the aggregate level, but its allocation across goods still matters for the division of profits between sectors. Combine that distributional relation with the aggregate multiplier to recover the wage bill.

Aggregate income net of the cancelling g-sector wages is R+W. Expenditure is cR+(1−α)W+αW+I=cR+W+I. Equating them cancels W and gives R=cR+I, hence R=I/(1−c).

Thus autonomous investment has a multiplier 1/(1−c) on capitalists’ income when 0≤c<1. In sector g, R_g=αW. Since R_m=θW, total R=(θ+α)W.

Combining yields W=I/[(1−c)(θ+α)], assuming θ+α>0. The sector-m balance θW+W=cR+(1−α)W+I gives the same result.

R=C+I=I/(1−c), so dR/dI=1/(1−c). W=I/[(1−c)(θ+α)].
questions.hint: Cancel workers’ total consumption against their income, then use R_g=αW.
questions.notes: Standard parameter restrictions 0≤c<1 and θ+α>0 are required.

questions.stem: An economy initially has Y₀=100 and C₀=I₀=S₀=50, with autonomous investment and Cₜ=0.5Yₜ₋₁. A zero-interest foreign loan of 100 in year 1 may be used only for investment and must be repaid at the start of the next year. It may be renewed annually on the same terms. Find (Y,C,I,S) in years 1,2 and final equilibrium: (a) loan taken only in year 1; (b) loan renewed each year.
questions.answer: Conditional net-expenditure interpretation: both cases year 1 (200,50,150,150). (a) Year 2 (50,100,−50,−50). (b) Year 2 (150,100,50,50). Both converge to (100,50,50,50). Gross-investment interpretations require repayment-financing assumptions.
questions.solution:
The loan is a financial inflow, while principal repayment is a financial outflow. A GDP calculation therefore needs an expenditure convention specifying how those flows change demand. State the conditional net-spending interpretation explicitly.

$$\begin{aligned}
J_t&=50+\text{new loan}_t-\text{repayment}_t,\\
C_t&=0.5Y_{t-1},\qquad Y_t=C_t+J_t,\\
Y_1&=50+150=200,\\
Y_2^{\mathrm{one\ loan}}&=100-50=50,\\
Y_2^{\mathrm{renewed}}&=100+50=150.
\end{aligned}$$

The consumption lag transmits the initial investment surge into the following year even if new borrowing stops. Under the stated net-spending convention, both later paths obey the same stable recurrence and return to the original output level. These tables must not relabel principal repayment as negative gross investment without explaining the financing mechanism.

A common intended expenditure model is Yₜ=Cₜ+Jₜ, where Jₜ=50+new loan−principal repayment. Then J₁=150, C₁=0.5·100=50, so Y₁=200 and S₁=150. In year 2, C₂=0.5·200=100 and J₂=50−100=−50, giving Y₂=50 and S₂=−50.

For t≥3, Jₜ=50 and Yₜ=0.5Yₜ₋₁+50, so Y converges to 100 and C,I,S converge to 50. However, repayment of principal is a financial transaction, not automatically negative gross investment or a subtraction from GDP. If I is meant as ordinary gross investment fixed autonomously at 50 after year 1, the problem must specify how repayment is financed and how it changes expenditure; the quoted year-2 values cannot be asserted from national accounting alone.

Hence the numerical table above is conditional on interpreting I as net autonomous spending including the repayment withdrawal. If the loan is renewed annually, the new loan exactly offsets the principal repayment from year 2 onward, so net autonomous spending is Jₜ=50. Then C₂=100,Y₂=150,S₂=50, and the subsequent recurrence Yₜ=.5Yₜ₋₁+50 converges to 100.

Under this convention both cases have final C=J=S=50. In the renewal case actual loan-financed gross investment can be 150 while a separate 100 withdrawal finances repayment; the column called I above is net expenditure J, not ordinary gross investment. Repayment itself does not identify that withdrawal mechanism, so neither conditional table should be used as an unqualified national-accounting identity.

Conditional net-expenditure interpretation: both cases year 1 (200,50,150,150). (a) Year 2 (50,100,−50,−50). (b) Year 2 (150,100,50,50). Both converge to (100,50,50,50). Gross-investment interpretations require repayment-financing assumptions.
questions.hint: Track the consumption lag separately from the loan injection and its subsequent withdrawal, and state how repayment enters expenditure.
questions.notes: The source does not specify repayment financing or distinguish gross investment from net autonomous expenditure. Conditional solution supplied; requires review before being treated as an unqualified answer.
