questions.notes: The standard fair, independent dice interpretation is used.

questions.stem: Let p>2 be prime. Tₚ consists of matrices A=[[0,a],[b,0]] with integer a,b∈{0,1,…,p−1}. A matrix is p-special if its determinant is not divisible by p. How many p-special matrices are in Tₚ?
questions.solution: The determinant is −ab. Since p is prime, p fails to divide ab precisely when both a and b are nonzero modulo p. Each has p−1 possible values, giving (p−1)² matrices.
questions.hint: Use primality to determine when p divides a product.

questions.stem: A good seven-letter word uses letters from {A,B,C}, allowing repeats and absent letters, but A cannot be followed by B, B cannot be followed by C, and C cannot be followed by A. How many good words are there?
questions.solution: The first letter has 3 choices. After any letter, exactly one of the three possible next letters is forbidden, leaving 2 choices for each of the remaining 6 positions. The number is 3·2⁶=192.
questions.hint: Count choices position by position.

questions.stem: Let n be a positive integer and 0<a<b<∞. The total number of real roots of (x−a)^(2n+1)+(x−b)^(2n+1)=0 is
questions.solution: The odd-power map t↦t^(2n+1) is strictly increasing and one-to-one. The equation says (x−a)^(2n+1)=(b−x)^(2n+1), so x−a=b−x and x=(a+b)/2. This is the unique real root.
questions.hint: Use the one-to-one property of an odd power.

questions.stem: Maximize x+y subject to 2x+y≤14, −x+2y≤8, 2x−y≤10, x,y≥0. The optimal objective value
questions.solution: Multiply the first inequality by 3/5 and the second by 1/5 and add to get x+y≤10. The point (x,y)=(4,6) attains this bound and satisfies 2x−y=2≤10 as well as nonnegativity. Thus the optimum is 10.
questions.hint: Combine constraints to obtain an upper bound on x+y.

questions.stem: X is supported on [0,1]. Mr. Fox believes its CDF is F, Mr. Goat believes its CDF is G. Assume F,G are differentiable, F≠G and F(x)≤G(x) for every x∈[0,1]. Which relation between their expected values is true?
questions.solution: For a variable supported on [0,1], its expectation is ∫₀¹[1−CDF(t)]dt. Since F≤G, one has 1−F≥1−G pointwise. Integration yields E_F[X]≥E_G[X]. In fact the differentiability and F≠G imply strict inequality somewhere over an interval.
questions.hint: Write expectation as the integral of a survival function.

questions.stem: Let f:[0,2]→[0,1] satisfy f(x)=x when x≤α and f(x)=1/2 when x∈(α,2], with α∈(0,2). X has probability density f. What is P(X>1)?
questions.solution: Normalization gives ∫₀²f(x)dx=α²/2+(2−α)/2=1, so α(α−1)=0. Since α>0, α=1. Therefore P(X>1)=∫₁²(1/2)dx=1/2.
questions.hint: Use the density’s total integral to find α.

questions.stem: Find ∑ from k=1 to 100 of ∫ from 0 to 1 of xᵏ/k dx.
questions.solution: The kth integral is 1/[k(k+1)]=1/k−1/(k+1). The finite sum telescopes to 1−1/101=100/101.
questions.hint: Integrate first, then use partial fractions.

questions.stem: Consider x₁−x₂≤3, x₂−x₃≤−2, x₃−x₄≤10, x₄−x₂≤α, x₄−x₃≤−4. A value of the real number α for which this system has a solution is
questions.answer: None of the above; feasibility requires α≥−8.
questions.solution: Adding x₂−x₃≤−2, x₃−x₄≤10 and x₄−x₂≤α gives 0≤8+α, so α≥−8 is necessary. It is also sufficient: choose x₂=0,x₃=2,x₄=−8,x₁=0. All constraints hold for any α≥−8. None of the listed numbers meets that condition.
questions.hint: Sum inequalities around the cycle x₂→x₃→x₄→x₂.

questions.stem: A fair coin is tossed infinitely many times. The probability that a head turns up for the first time after an even number of tosses is
questions.solution: Let T be the toss number of the first head. For T=2k, the first 2k−1 tosses are tails and toss 2k is a head, with probability 2^(−2k). Thus P(T even)=∑ₖ₌₁∞(1/4)ᵏ=(1/4)/(1−1/4)=1/3.
questions.hint: Sum over toss numbers 2,4,6,… .
questions.notes: Interprets “after an even number of tosses” in the customary intended sense that the first head occurs on an even-numbered toss.

questions.stem: An entrance exam has 10 true-false questions. A student answers randomly, correctly with probability 0.5 on each. Correct answers score 1 and incorrect answers score 0. What is the probability of obtaining the mean score?
questions.solution: With independent guesses, the score S has Binomial(10,1/2) distribution and mean 5. Thus P(S=5)=C(10,5)(1/2)¹⁰=252/1024=63/256.
questions.hint: Find the binomial mean, then its probability mass.

questions.stem: For every positive integer k, Sₖ is the sum of the infinite geometric progression with first term (k−1)/k! and common ratio 1/k. Find ∑ from k=1 to infinity of Sₖ.
questions.answer: e−1, which is not listed, if the k=1 progression is interpreted term by term.
questions.solution: For k≥2, Sₖ=[(k−1)/k!]/(1−1/k)=1/(k−1)!. At k=1, the first term is 0 and ratio 1, so every term is zero and S₁=0. Hence the total is ∑ⱼ₌₁∞1/j!=e−1. Cancelling k−1 in the geometric-sum formula at k=1 would illegally assign S₁=1 and yield the likely intended answer e. None of the printed choices matches the termwise series.
questions.hint: Handle k=1 separately before cancelling factors.
questions.notes: The source includes k=1 although its geometric ratio is 1. Its zero-term series sums to 0, but the usual geometric-sum formula has 0/0 there.

questions.stem: Let G(x)=∫ from 0 to x of teᵗ dt for all nonnegative real x. Find lim as x→0 of G′(x)/x.
questions.solution: By the fundamental theorem of calculus, G′(x)=xeˣ for x>0. Therefore G′(x)/x=eˣ→1 as x→0⁺.
questions.hint: Differentiate the integral before taking the limit.

questions.stem: Let α∈(0,1), and f(x)=xᵅ+(1−x)ᵅ for x∈[0,1]. The maximum value of f is
questions.solution: The function is strictly concave and symmetric about 1/2. Its derivative vanishes at x=1/2, so its maximum is 2(1/2)ᵅ=2^(1−α). Since 0<1−α<1, this is strictly between 1 and 2.
questions.hint: Use concavity and symmetry.

questions.stem: For a positive integer n, find ∑ from k=1 to n of k C(n,k), where C(n,k) counts choices of k out of n objects.
questions.solution: Differentiate (1+t)ⁿ=∑ₖC(n,k)tᵏ to get n(1+t)^(n−1)=∑ₖkC(n,k)t^(k−1). Evaluate at t=1 to obtain n2^(n−1).
questions.hint: Differentiate the binomial expansion.

questions.stem: An arithmetic progression begins with a and has common difference d∈(0,1). Its kth term equals the sum of an infinite geometric progression with first term a and common ratio d. If a>2 is prime, which is a possible value of d?
questions.solution: The equality is a+(k−1)d=a/(1−d), hence k−1=a/(1−d). For d=1/2 this equals 2a, an integer. For the other choices it equals 3a/2, 5a/4, or 9a/8. Since a>2 is an odd prime, none of these is an integer.
questions.hint: Solve for the integer k−1.

questions.stem: A chicken produces two chicks in period 1. In each later period, every chick born in the preceding period either produces two chicks or none; a nonproducing chicken never produces later. No chicken dies. After T periods there are 31 chickens in total. The maximum and minimum possible T are respectively
questions.answer: 15 and 4, counting the last nonempty generation.
questions.solution: Each birth event adds two chickens, so 31 total chickens require (31−1)/2=15 producing chickens. The longest possible genealogy has one producing chicken in each generation, so its depth is 15. For the shortest, all eligible chickens reproduce; through period T the maximum total is 1+2+…+2ᵀ=2^(T+1)−1. Reaching 31 requires T≥4 and full reproduction achieves T=4.
questions.hint: Represent reproduction by a full binary tree.
questions.notes: Uses the intended convention that T is the final generation containing births. If arbitrary idle periods after the final births are counted as part of T, there is no finite maximum T; this wording caveat should be shown with the solution.

questions.stem: Let a,p be positive integers and A=[[p,1,1],[0,p,a],[0,a,2]]. If det A=0, a possible value of p is
questions.solution: Expanding along the first column gives det A=p(2p−a²). Since p>0, zero determinant requires a²=2p. Among p=1,2,4, only p=2 makes 2p a square: choose a=2.
questions.hint: Expand the determinant along the first column.

questions.stem: For what value of α does (x−1)(x²−7x+α)=0 have exactly two unique roots?
questions.solution: For α=6, x²−7x+6=(x−1)(x−6), so the full polynomial is (x−1)²(x−6) and has exactly two distinct roots. The choices 10 and 12 give quadratic roots {2,5} and {3,4}, respectively, producing three distinct roots after including 1.
questions.hint: Make the quadratic share the root 1.

questions.stem: Find ∑ from k=1 to infinity of [(-1)^(k−1)/k²] logₑ(3ᵏ).
questions.solution: Because ln(3ᵏ)=k ln3, the kth summand is ln3·(-1)^(k−1)/k. The alternating harmonic series sums to ln2, giving ln2·ln3.
questions.hint: Simplify the logarithm first.
questions.notes: Visual review confirms logₑ(3ᵏ) multiplies the fraction; it is not part of the denominator.

questions.stem: Twenty persons attend a party and each shakes hands with some of the others. K is the number of persons who shook hands with an odd number of persons. Which K is possible?
questions.solution: In the handshake graph, the sum of all degrees is twice the number of edges and hence even. Thus the number of odd degrees must be even, excluding 19 and 1. K=20 is possible by pairing people into ten disjoint pairs, each of degree 1.
questions.hint: Apply the handshake lemma.

questions.stem: Independent X,Y are uniform on [0,1]. For z∈[0,1], P(max(X,Y)≤z)=P(min(X,Y)≤1−z). Find z.
questions.solution: Independence gives P(max(X,Y)≤z)=z². Also P(min(X,Y)≤1−z)=1−P(X>1−z,Y>1−z)=1−z². Thus 2z²=1 and the nonnegative solution is z=1/√2.
questions.hint: Express both probabilities using independence.

questions.stem: Let f:ℝ→ℝ satisfy f(x+y)f(x−y)=(f(x)+f(y))²−4x²f(y) for all real x,y. Which is not possible?
questions.solution: Setting x=y=0 gives f(0)²=4f(0)², so f(0)=0. Setting y=x then gives 0=4f(x)(f(x)−x²), hence f(x)∈{0,x²}. Therefore f(2) must be 0 or 4, not 2. The functions f≡0 and f(x)=x² satisfy the original identity and show the other options are possible.
questions.hint: First substitute x=y=0, then y=x.

questions.stem: Let f:ℝ→ℤ be f(x)=⌈x⌉, where the source defines ⌈x⌉ as the smallest integer larger than x. Set g(x)=|f(x)|−f(|x|). What is the range of g?
questions.answer: Under the conventional ceiling definition, (d): {−1,0}. Under the printed strict definition, {−2,−1,0}, which is not listed.
questions.solution: For conventional ceiling, x≥0 gives g=0. If x<0 is nonintegral, write t=−x>0; then |ceil(−t)|=floor(t) and ceil(t)=floor(t)+1, so g=−1. Negative integers give g=0, yielding {−1,0}. But the printed definition says strictly larger: f(x)=floor(x)+1. At x=−n for positive integer n, this instead gives g=(n−1)−(n+1)=−2. Thus the source’s wording and standard notation disagree.
questions.hint: Separate positive, negative noninteger, and negative integer arguments.
questions.notes: Confirmed visually: the source says “larger than x,” not “larger than or equal to x.” Retain the source wording and flag the ambiguity.

questions.stem: Find lim as x→−1 of (x+1)/|x+1|.
questions.answer: The two-sided limit does not exist.
questions.solution: For x>−1 the expression is 1, whereas for x<−1 it is −1. The one-sided limits differ, so the two-sided limit does not exist.
questions.hint: Compare the signs on the two sides of −1.

questions.stem: Let f:ℝ→ℝ satisfy f(x)=2 for x≤2 and f(x)=a²−3a for x>2, where a is a positive integer. Which is true?
options: f is continuous everywhere for some value of a
questions.answer: f is discontinuous at x=2 for every allowed a.
questions.solution: Continuity at 2 requires a²−3a=2, or a²−3a−2=0. Its roots are (3±√17)/2, neither a positive integer. Thus no allowed a makes the right limit equal f(2)=2, so f is not continuous at 2.
questions.hint: Check whether a²−3a=2 has an integer solution.

questions.stem: A firm is a monopolist at home with inverse demand $p=10-q$, can export at price5, and has total capacity100. Find its optimal production and sales plan when constant marginal cost is (a)4 and (b)6.
questions.answer: At MC4: domestic sales2.5, exports97.5, domestic price7.5. At MC6: domestic sales2, exports0, domestic price8.
questions.solution:
Choose domestic and foreign sales separately, subject to total capacity. Exporting at a positive margin makes unused capacity costly; when exports lose money, the domestic marginal cost becomes the production cost instead.

$$\begin{aligned}
MC=4:&\quad q_d+q_f=100,\quad MR_d=10-2q_d=5,\\
&q_d=2.5,\quad q_f=97.5,\quad p_d=7.5,\\
MC=6:&\quad q_f=0,\quad10-2q_d=6,\\
&q_d=2,\quad p_d=8.
\end{aligned}$$

The export price is the domestic opportunity cost only when an extra unit could profitably be exported. It should not replace marginal production cost in the second case, where export sales would generate a loss. This distinction explains why the same demand produces different domestic marginal conditions.

(a) Exporting earns a positive margin1, so all capacity is used. Assign a unit to the domestic market only while domestic marginal revenue exceeds the export price: $10-2q_d=5$ gives $q_d=2.5$. Export the remaining97.5.

Profit is $7.5(2.5)+5(97.5)-4(100)=106.25$. (b) Exports lose1 per unit and are zero. Set domestic MR=MC:10−2q_d=6, giving q_d=2,p_d=8 and profit4.

The capacity is slack.

At MC4: domestic sales2.5, exports97.5, domestic price7.5. At MC6: domestic sales2, exports0, domestic price8.
questions.hint: When exports have a positive margin, the domestic opportunity cost is the export price.

questions.stem: (a) A consumer has utility $-[(10-a)^2+(10-b)^2]$, nonnegative quantities, and both prices1. Find optimal quantities for income40, then10. (b) A monopolist faces $q=60-p$ (q in thousands) and total cost $C=q^2/2$. Find the deadweight loss and the price ceiling that minimizes it.
questions.answer: (a) (10,10), then(5,5). (b) Monopoly q20,p40; efficient q30,p30; DWL100 in the corresponding thousand-rupee units. Optimal ceiling30.
questions.solution:
The consumer has a bliss point rather than globally nonsatiated preferences, so first check whether the ideal bundle is affordable. In the monopoly problem, compare the private first-order condition with the social demand–marginal-cost intersection.

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{consumer: }(a,b)^*&=(10,10)\quad(M=40),\\
(a,b)^*&=(5,5)\quad(M=10),\\
MR=60-2q&=MC=q\Longrightarrow q_m=20,\\
60-q&=q\Longrightarrow q_e=30,\quad p_e=30,\\
DWL&=\int_{20}^{30}(60-2q)\,dq=100.
\end{aligned}$$

The low-income consumer minimizes squared distance from the bliss point on the budget boundary, while the high-income consumer leaves money unspent. A monopoly price ceiling at the efficient price makes demand and optimal supply meet at the efficient output, eliminating the lost-surplus triangle.

(a) The unconstrained bliss point(10,10) costs20 and is feasible with income40; the consumer need not spend the rest. With income10 the closest feasible point to(10,10) is(5,5), by symmetry or projection onto a+b=10. (b) Profit is $(60-q)q-q^2/2$, so MR=60−2q equals MC=q at q20.

The efficient demand–MC intersection is60−q=q, hence q30,p30. The welfare loss is $\int_{20}^{30}(60-2q)\,dq=100$. A ceiling30 makes the profit-maximizing supply meet demand at q30 and eliminates the loss.

(a) (10,10), then(5,5). (b) Monopoly q20,p40; efficient q30,p30; DWL100 in the corresponding thousand-rupee units. Optimal ceiling30.
questions.hint: Check satiation in(a); compare monopoly marginal revenue with marginal cost in(b).

questions.stem: (a) A cinema has150 seats. Student demand is $220-40P_s$ and non-student demand $140-20P_n$; a student-ID discount is available. Find maximum profit, and then the maximum if the two demand functions are interchanged. (b) Eleven traders each want at most one chicken, with utility $u_iD_i+m_i$. Their valuations are(10,8,7,4,3,1,3,3,5,6,8). Six indivisible chickens initially belong to traders6–11; everyone has25 units of money. Give a competitive equilibrium price and discuss uniqueness.
questions.answer: (a) Revenue/profit532.5 with student price3.25 and non-student price4. After interchange:525 if only student discounts are allowed;532.5 if unrestricted group pricing is intended. (b) Any price in[4,5], for example4.5; the six highest valuations receive chickens. Price is not unique.
questions.solution:
At a full cinema, allocate scarce seats by equating marginal revenues, not by equating group prices. For chickens, rank willingness to pay: the price must separate the six eventual owners from the remaining five.

$$\begin{aligned}
5.5-q_s/20&=7-q_n/10,\qquad q_s+q_n=150,\\
(q_s,q_n)&=(90,60),\quad(p_s,p_n)=(3.25,4),\\
R&=90(3.25)+60(4)=532.5,\\
\text{chicken values: }&10,8,8,7,6,5,4,3,3,3,1,\\
p_{\rm chicken}&\in[4,5].
\end{aligned}$$

After the demand functions are swapped, unrestricted discrimination would charge students the higher price. If the admissible instrument is a student discount, enforce its inequality; the optimum then pools prices at the capacity-clearing uniform price. In the exchange economy, ownership affects money transfers but the six highest values identify the efficient final chicken allocation.

(a) With no variable costs specified, maximize ticket revenue. Let q_s,q_n be sales. The inverse demands are5.5−q_s/40 and7−q_n/20.

The capacity binds: setting marginal revenues equal gives5.5−q_s/20=7−q_n/10 and q_s+q_n=150. Thus q_s90,q_n60; prices3.25,4; revenue292.5+240=532.5. After interchange, unrestricted discrimination swaps these prices between the groups and retains532.5, but charges students more.

If the stated instrument is a student discount, impose P_s≤P_n. This constraint binds at uniform price3.5, yielding total sales150 and revenue525. (b) Sort valuations:10,8,8,7,6,5,4,3,3,3,1.

Clearing six chickens requires the price between the sixth and seventh valuations,5 and4. At interior prices the allocation to traders1,2,3,9,10,11 is unique; endpoint indifference can be resolved to clear the market. Money allocations vary with the nonunique price.

(a) Revenue/profit532.5 with student price3.25 and non-student price4. After interchange:525 if only student discounts are allowed;532.5 if unrestricted group pricing is intended. (b) Any price in[4,5], for example4.5; the six highest valuations receive chickens. Price is not unique.
questions.hint: Use equal marginal revenues with a capacity multiplier; then check that the proposed student price really is a discount.
questions.notes: Part(a)(ii) must distinguish a student-discount constraint from unrestricted group price discrimination. Production costs are not supplied; the revenue calculation assumes zero marginal admission cost and ignores sunk costs.

questions.stem: (a) A monopolist has demand $p=20-q$, technology $q=\min\{L/2,K/3\}$, wage and capital rental1, and available capital bounded above by $\bar K$. Find q,p for capital bounds24 and18. (b) Define Samuelson’s WARP. (c) Show how WARP implies a nonpositive own-price substitution effect and the demand theorem.
questions.answer: (a) For capital bound24: q7.5,p12.5; for bound18: q6,p14. (b,c) WARP prevents mutually affordable distinct choices; compensated own-price demand cannot move in the same direction as price. With a nonnegative income effect, uncompensated own-price demand also falls.
questions.solution:
The Leontief technology requires fixed input proportions. Treat available capital as an upper bound on a variable paid-for input, as in the existing answer. For revealed preference, use income compensation making the original bundle just affordable.

$$\begin{aligned}
L=2q,\ K=3q&\Longrightarrow C(q)=5q,\quad q\le\bar K/3,\\
20-2q&=5\Longrightarrow q_u=7.5,\\
\bar K=24:&\quad q=7.5,\qquad\bar K=18:\quad q=6,\\
p\cdot(y-x)>0,\ p^\prime\cdot(y-x)\le0
&\Longrightarrow(p^\prime-p)\cdot(y-x)<0.
\end{aligned}$$

The capacity check distinguishes a slack bound from a binding one. The last inequality is the revealed-preference basis for a compensated law of demand: with only one price changed, quantity moves weakly in the opposite direction. The ordinary demand response additionally depends on the income effect, so WARP alone does not exclude Giffen goods.

(a) Cost-minimizing inputs are L=2q,K=3q, giving C=5q and q≤K̄/3. Unconstrained profit(20−q)q−5q has optimum q7.5. A bound24 allows q≤8, so it is slack; a bound18 allows q≤6 and binds.

This treats available capital as a bound on a variable paid-for input; if it is instead predetermined and fully paid for, the marginal-cost calculation differs. (b) If bundle x is chosen at prices p when distinct y was affordable, y cannot subsequently be chosen when x is affordable at its prices. In the usual unique-choice formulation, p·x≥p·y implies p′·x>p′·y when y is chosen at p′.

(c) Choose y after changing prices and compensating income so the old x is just affordable: m′=p′·x. WARP implies p·(y−x)>0 whenever y≠x, while p′·(y−x)≤0. Subtract to obtain (p′−p)·(y−x)<0.

questions.stem: Two firms choose quantities simultaneously, with costs $C_i(q_i)=q_i$ and inverse demand $p=10-q_1-q_2$. (a) Define and solve the equilibrium and reaction functions. (b) Repeat when each firm has capacity2.
questions.solution:
A Cournot–Nash quantity is a best response to the rival's quantity. Derive the unconstrained response, and then project it onto the actual feasible interval when capacity is introduced.

$$\begin{aligned}
\pi_i&=(9-q_i-q_j)q_i,\\
BR_i(q_j)&=\max\{0,(9-q_j)/2\},\\
q_1=q_2&=3\quad\text{without capacity},\\
BR_i^{\rm cap}(q_j)&=\min\{2,\max\{0,(9-q_j)/2\}\}=2
\quad(0\le q_j\le2).
\end{aligned}$$

The own-quantity second derivative is negative, so the response is a genuine profit maximum. In the capacity game the desired unconstrained quantity always exceeds two, whatever the rival does feasibly. Thus capacity output is a dominant best response and the constrained equilibrium is uniquely $(2,2)$.

A Cournot–Nash equilibrium consists of feasible quantities, each maximizing its firm’s profit holding the other fixed. Profit is $(9-q_i-q_j)q_i$, so the unconstrained reaction is $BR_i(q_j)=\max\{0,(9-q_j)/2\}$. Solving the two interior reactions gives3 each.

With capacity2, $BR_i(q_j)=\min\{2,\max\{0,(9-q_j)/2\}\}$. For every rival quantity in[0,2], the unconstrained optimum is at least3.5; thus each always chooses2 and this is the unique equilibrium.

(a) Cournot–Nash: q₁=q₂=3,p4,profit9 each. (b) q₁=q₂=2,p6,profit10 each.

questions.stem: (a) Under a rupee-for-rupee housing subsidy, the Lal family spends250 on housing and receives250 subsidy. A replacement policy offers an unrestricted lump sum250. Explain graphically which is preferred, whether indifference is possible, and how housing/other-good choices can change. (b) A patent monopolist has demand $p=100-X$ and cost $25+X^2$. Find its price/output. After the patent expires, identical firms can freely enter: find the long-run competitive price, industry output and number of firms.
questions.answer: (a) The lump sum makes the old bundle affordable, so it is weakly preferred; it can be strictly preferred or indifferent. The choice is not uniquely determined without preferences. (b) Monopoly X25,p75. Long-run competition: each firm produces5, price10, industry output90,18 firms.
questions.solution:
For the policy comparison, show the new cash-transfer budget passes through the old chosen bundle. In the patent problem, separate monopoly marginal conditions from the free-entry zero-profit condition.

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{old budget: }c+h/2&\le M,\\
\text{new budget: }c+h&\le M+250,\\
100-2X&=2X\Longrightarrow X_m=25,\quad p_m=75,\\
AC(x)&=25/x+x,\quad AC\prime(x)=-25/x^2+1,\\
x_f=5:&\quad p_c=10,\quad Q_c=90,\quad n=18.
\end{aligned}$$

Affordability of the old bundle establishes weak welfare improvement under the unrestricted transfer; the direction and strictness of quantity changes need preference assumptions. Free entry pins price to minimum average cost, not zero marginal cost or the old monopoly price. Divide industry demand by efficient firm scale to obtain the number of firms.

(a) Put housing h horizontally and other consumption c vertically. If the private income is M and the government matches out-of-pocket housing expenditure, the family’s effective budget is c+h/2≤M. Its old subsidy250 means total housing expenditure500 and its own payment250.

The replacement budget is c+h≤M+250, a steeper line passing through the old choice. Since the old bundle remains feasible, maximization makes replacement utility at least as high. Smooth strictly convex preferences at an interior old tangency give strictly higher utility and substitution away from housing at the new optimum; kinks, corners or indifference can leave the old choice optimal.

Hence an exact change in both quantities requires preferences, rather than an assertion based only on prices. (b) Monopoly MR=100−2X and MC=2X, so X25,p75,profit1225. Under free entry the minimum of AC=25/x+x is at x5, with minimum AC10.

Thus p10, industry demand90 and firm count90/5=18; each earns zero economic profit.

questions.stem: An economy has $Y_t=K_t^\alpha N_t^{1-\alpha}$ with constant employment N, $0<\alpha<1$, capital law $K_{t+1}=(1-\delta)K_t+I_t$ and $0\le\delta\le1$. (a) Express output per worker. (b) Find the effect of the saving rate on steady-state output per worker. (c) Find the saving rate maximizing steady-state consumption per worker.
questions.answer: $y=k^\alpha$; for δ>0 and s>0, $y^*=(s/\delta)^{\alpha/(1-\alpha)}$, with elasticity α/(1−α) to s. The golden-rule saving rate is α. At the allowed endpoint δ=0, no finite positive steady state exists for s>0.
questions.solution:
Divide by fixed employment and solve the positive steady-state investment-replacement condition. Raising saving increases the steady output level, but maximizing consumption requires a separate calculation.

$$\begin{aligned}
y&=k^\alpha,\qquad sk^{\alpha}=\delta k,\\
k^*&=(s/\delta)^{1/(1-\alpha)},\\
c^*&=(1-s)(s/\delta)^{\alpha/(1-\alpha)},\\
\frac{d\log c^*}{ds}&=-\frac1{1-s}+\frac\alpha{(1-\alpha)s}=0,\\
s_{GR}&=\alpha.
\end{aligned}$$

Taking logarithms simplifies the derivative of the positive consumption expression. The optimum equates the sacrifice of current consumption from saving more with the proportional increase in future productive capacity. The finite positive formulas require $\delta>0$; zero depreciation is a distinct case.

(a) Divide production by N: y=Y/N=(K/N)^α=k^α. (b) With I=sY, steady state requires sk^α=δk. For δ>0,s>0, k*=(s/δ)^{1/(1−α)} and y*=(s/δ)^{α/(1−α)}.

Therefore dy*/ds=[α/(1−α)]y*/s>0. (c) Steady consumption c*=(1−s)(s/δ)^{α/(1−α)}. Its log derivative is−1/(1−s)+[α/(1−α)]/s; setting zero yields s=α.

Equivalently the golden rule αk^{α−1}=δ combined with the steady-state equation yields s=α. If δ=0 and s>0, capital keeps accumulating and these finite steady-state formulas do not apply.

questions.stem: In IS–LM with $I=I(i,Y)$, $I_i<0$ and $I_Y>0$, compare expansionary monetary and fiscal policy effects on investment in the short run and the medium run, when aggregate demand and supply adjust. Under which policy is medium-run investment higher?
questions.answer: Short run: monetary expansion raises investment; fiscal expansion has an ambiguous net investment effect. Medium run with unchanged potential output: monetary policy is neutral, while fiscal expansion crowds out investment; investment is higher under monetary expansion.
questions.solution:
Short-run prices are fixed, so an IS–LM shift changes both output and interest. In the medium run, the standard potential-output assumption fixes output again, and price adjustment changes the real money stock.

$$\begin{aligned}
dI&=I_Y\,dY+I_i\,di,\\
\text{monetary, short run: }&dY>0,\ di<0\Longrightarrow dI>0,\\
\text{fiscal, short run: }&dY>0,\ di>0\Longrightarrow dI\text{ ambiguous},\\
\text{medium run: }dY&=0,\quad dI^{M}=0,\quad dI^{G}<0.
\end{aligned}$$

The two short-run fiscal effects oppose each other, so their magnitudes matter. Monetary expansion eventually raises prices in proportion to nominal money and is neutral in real terms. Fiscal expansion at unchanged potential output instead crowds out private investment through a higher interest rate.

At a fixed price level, monetary expansion shifts LM right/down: Y rises and i falls, so both I_Y dY and I_i di raise investment. Fiscal expansion shifts IS right: Y and i both rise, making the income effect positive and the interest effect negative; the overall sign needs parameter magnitudes. Graphically compare the new IS–LM intersections.

In the medium run, under the standard vertical long-run supply/potential-output assumption, prices adjust so Y returns to its original potential. A permanent monetary expansion is absorbed into the price level, leaving real balances, i and I at their original values. With fiscal expansion, the higher spending at unchanged Y requires a higher interest rate on the new IS curve, and I decreases.

Thus, for otherwise comparable initial conditions, medium-run investment is higher after monetary expansion than fiscal expansion. In AD–AS, each expansion initially moves AD right; wage/price adjustment shifts short-run AS until the potential-output line is reached.

Short run: monetary expansion raises investment; fiscal expansion has an ambiguous net investment effect. Medium run with unchanged potential output: monetary policy is neutral, while fiscal expansion crowds out investment; investment is higher under monetary expansion.

questions.stem: Let $C=c_0+c_1(Y-T)$ and $I=b_0+b_1Y$, with positive parameters, $c_1,b_1<1$, and constant G. (a) Solve equilibrium output with fixed T. (b) Find the multiplier and its positivity condition. (c) Find output and saving responses to a change in b₀. (d) Replace fixed taxes with $T=t_0+t_1Y$, $0<t_1<1$; compare the b₀ multiplier.
questions.answer: $Y=(c_0-c_1T+b_0+G)/(1-c_1-b_1)$. The multiplier is1/(1−c₁−b₁), positive iff c₁+b₁<1. Saving rises with b₀ under this stability condition. With proportional taxes the multiplier is1/[1−c₁(1−t₁)−b₁], which is smaller when both multipliers are positive.
questions.solution:
Collect every term proportional to income on the left of goods-market clearing. Differentiate saving as well as output, rather than assuming they have the same multiplier.

$$\begin{aligned}
(1-c_1-b_1)Y&=c_0-c_1T+b_0+G,\\
\frac{dY}{db_0}&=\frac1{1-c_1-b_1},\\
\frac{dS}{db_0}&=\frac{1-c_1}{1-c_1-b_1},\\
D_{\rm proportional\ tax}&=1-c_1-b_1+c_1t_1.
\end{aligned}$$

The induced consumption and investment coefficients together must be below one for a positive finite multiplier. Proportional taxation increases the denominator by $c_1t_1$, reducing the response. At a zero denominator, division is invalid and equilibrium may fail or be indeterminate depending on autonomous spending.

Goods-market clearing Y=C+I+G gives (1−c₁−b₁)Y=c₀−c₁T+b₀+G. For nonzero denominator this yields(a); at denominator zero there is either no equilibrium or indeterminacy depending on autonomous spending. (b) Differentiate with respect to autonomous spending; a positive finite multiplier requires c₁+b₁<1.

(c) dY/db₀=1/(1−c₁−b₁). Private saving S_p=Y−T−C has derivative (1−c₁)/(1−c₁−b₁). Public saving T−G is fixed, so national saving has the same change; it also equals dI/db₀=1+b₁/(1−c₁−b₁).

(d) The denominator becomes1−c₁(1−t₁)−b₁=(1−c₁−b₁)+c₁t₁. Under the positive-multiplier condition in(b), this is larger, so automatic tax stabilization reduces the output response.

questions.stem: An agent lives for three periods. When young she borrows e for education and obtains human capital h(e), with h′>0 and h″<0. When middle-aged she earns wh(e), repays Re, consumes c_M and saves for old age; gross borrowing/saving return R is exogenous. She consumes nothing when young and has utility $u(c_M)+\beta u(c_O)$, $0<\beta<1$. (a) Formulate the maximization and first-order conditions. (b) How does optimal education change with wage w and interest factor R?
questions.answer: Maximize utility subject to $c_M+c_O/R=wh(e)-Re$. Interior FOCs: $u′(c_M)=\beta R u′(c_O)$ and $wh′(e)=R$. Thus $de/dw=-h′/(wh″)>0$ and $de/dR=1/(wh″)<0$; human capital moves in the same direction.
questions.solution:
Education changes net lifetime wealth before the household allocates consumption between middle and old age. Combine the two period budgets so that the education decision can be separated from consumption smoothing.

$$\begin{aligned}
c_M+s+Re&=wh(e),\qquad c_O=Rs,\\
c_M+\frac{c_O}{R}&=wh(e)-Re,\\
u\prime(c_M)&=\beta R u\prime(c_O),\qquad wh\prime(e)=R,\\
\frac{de^*}{dw}&=-\frac{h\prime(e)}{wh^{\prime\prime}(e)}>0,\qquad
\frac{de^*}{dR}=\frac1{wh^{\prime\prime}(e)}<0.
\end{aligned}$$

Because utility increases with wealth, the education first-order condition maximizes the right side of the lifetime budget. Strict concavity of human capital yields the comparative-static signs. If the optimum is at zero education, replace equality by the appropriate Kuhn–Tucker inequality and interpret these effects weakly.

Let old-age saving be s, so c_M+s+Re=wh(e), c_O=Rs. Eliminating s gives the present-value lifetime budget. With increasing concave u and interior positive consumption and education, use Lagrangian u(c_M)+βu(c_O)+λ[wh(e)−Re−c_M−c_O/R].

FOCs are u′(c_M)=λ, βu′(c_O)=λ/R and λ[wh′(e)−R]=0, with the budget binding. Since λ>0, education maximizes net lifetime resources independently of consumption timing: wh′(e)=R. Implicit differentiation yields the stated signs because h′>0,h″<0.

The level of human capital h(e*) also increases with w and decreases with R. At a borrowing/education corner e=0 use wh′(0)≤R and weak rather than strict comparative statics.

Maximize utility subject to $c_M+c_O/R=wh(e)-Re$. Interior FOCs: $u'(c_M)=\beta R u'(c_O)$ and $wh'(e)=R$. Thus $de/dw=-h'/(wh'')>0$ and $de/dR=1/(wh'')<0$; human capital moves in the same direction.
questions.hint: Separate education’s maximization of lifetime wealth from allocation of wealth across consumption dates.
questions.notes: The source does not state monotonicity/concavity of u; the standard optimum and positive multiplier use increasing concave utility and R>0.

solutionSteps.title: Set up the problem
solutionSteps.body: Education changes net lifetime wealth before the household allocates consumption between middle and old age. Combine the two period budgets so that the education decision can be separated from consumption smoothing.

solutionSteps.title: Work through the equations
solutionSteps.body:
$$\begin{aligned}
c_M+s+Re&=wh(e),\qquad c_O=Rs,\\
c_M+\frac{c_O}{R}&=wh(e)-Re,\\
u\prime(c_M)&=\beta R u\prime(c_O),\qquad wh\prime(e)=R,\\
\frac{de^*}{dw}&=-\frac{h\prime(e)}{wh^{\prime\prime}(e)}>0,\qquad
\frac{de^*}{dR}=\frac1{wh^{\prime\prime}(e)}<0.
\end{aligned}$$

Because utility increases with wealth, the education first-order condition maximizes the right side of the lifetime budget. Strict concavity of human capital yields the comparative-static signs. If the optimum is at zero education, replace equality by the appropriate Kuhn–Tucker inequality and interpret these effects weakly.

solutionSteps.title: Complete the argument
solutionSteps.body:
Let old-age saving be s, so c_M+s+Re=wh(e), c_O=Rs. Eliminating s gives the present-value lifetime budget. With increasing concave u and interior positive consumption and education, use Lagrangian u(c_M)+βu(c_O)+λ[wh(e)−Re−c_M−c_O/R].

FOCs are u′(c_M)=λ, βu′(c_O)=λ/R and λ[wh′(e)−R]=0, with the budget binding. Since λ>0, education maximizes net lifetime resources independently of consumption timing: wh′(e)=R. Implicit differentiation yields the stated signs because h′>0,h″<0.

The level of human capital h(e*) also increases with w and decreases with R. At a borrowing/education corner e=0 use wh′(0)≤R and weak rather than strict comparative statics.

solutionSteps.title: Conclusion
solutionSteps.body: Maximize utility subject to $c_M+c_O/R=wh(e)-Re$. Interior FOCs: $u'(c_M)=\beta R u'(c_O)$ and $wh'(e)=R$. Thus $de/dw=-h'/(wh'')>0$ and $de/dR=1/(wh'')<0$; human capital moves in the same direction.

questions.stem: Find lim as x→0⁺ of sin({√x})/{√x}, where {x} is the decimal part of x.
questions.solution: For 0<x<1, {√x}=√x. Set t=√x; then t→0⁺ and sin t/t→1.
questions.hint: Near zero, √x lies between zero and one.

questions.stem: f:[0,1]→[0,1] is continuous. Then it is true that
options: f is differentiable only at x=1/2
f′(x) is constant for all x∈(0,1)
f(x)=x for at least one x∈[0,1]
questions.answer: There is at least one fixed point.
questions.solution: Let h(x)=f(x)−x. This function is continuous, with h(0)=f(0)≥0 and h(1)=f(1)−1≤0. By the intermediate value theorem, h vanishes somewhere in [0,1].
questions.hint: Apply the intermediate value theorem to f(x)−x.

questions.stem: f(x)=|x−2|+|x−4|. Then f is
options: Differentiable but not continuously differentiable at x=2
f has both left and right derivatives at x=2
questions.solution: For x<2, f(x)=6−2x, with slope −2. For 2<x<4, f(x)=2, with slope 0. Thus the left and right derivatives at 2 exist but are unequal, so f is not differentiable there.
questions.hint: Write the absolute values separately on either side of 2.

questions.stem: In an examination of 100 students, 70 passed Mathematics, 65 Physics and 55 Chemistry. Of these, 35 passed all three, 50 passed Mathematics and Physics, 45 Mathematics and Chemistry, and 40 Physics and Chemistry. How many passed exactly one subject?
questions.solution: The counts passing only Mathematics, Physics and Chemistry are respectively 70−50−45+35=10, 65−50−40+35=10, and 55−45−40+35=5. Their sum is 25.
questions.hint: Subtract pairwise overlaps, then restore the triple overlap for each subject.

questions.stem: The square of the matrix [[a,b],[c,0]] is a null matrix if and only if
options: a=c=0, b is any non-zero real number
a=b=0, c is any non-zero real number
a=0 and either b=0 or c=0
questions.solution: The square is [[a²+bc,ab],[ac,bc]]. If it vanishes, bc=0 and a²+bc=0 force a=0. Conversely, a=0 and bc=0 make every entry vanish.
questions.hint: Compute all four entries of the square.

questions.stem: If positive numbers x,y,z are in harmonic progression, then log(x+z)+log(x−2y+z) equals
questions.answer: Intended answer (c), with log|x−z| or an additional assumption x>z.
questions.solution: Harmonic progression gives 2/y=1/x+1/z, hence y=2xz/(x+z). Therefore (x+z)(x−2y+z)=(x−z)² and the sum of logarithms equals log((x−z)²)=2log|x−z| whenever x≠z. The printed options omit the absolute value and the question does not assume x>z. If x<z the left side is defined but all printed logarithms of x−z are not real; if x=z the left side itself is undefined.
questions.hint: Use y=2xz/(x+z), then combine the logarithms.
questions.notes: Real-domain assumptions are missing. Do not silently replace log(x−z) by log|x−z|.

questions.stem: If f(x+2y,x−2y)=xy, then f(x,y) equals
questions.solution: Put u=x+2y and v=x−2y. Then x=(u+v)/2 and y=(u−v)/4, giving xy=(u²−v²)/8. Relabel u,v as x,y.
questions.hint: Invert the linear substitution.

questions.stem: The domain of f(x)=√(x²−1)−log(√(1−x)), x≥0, is
questions.solution: For the first square root with x≥0, we need x≥1. The logarithm requires √(1−x)>0, so x<1. These conditions cannot both hold.
questions.hint: A logarithm requires a strictly positive argument.

questions.stem: The graph of y=log(1−2x+x²) intersects the x-axis at
questions.solution: At an x-intercept, log((x−1)²)=0, so (x−1)²=1. Thus x=0 or x=2, and the logarithm argument equals 1 at both points.
questions.hint: Set the logarithm equal to zero.

questions.stem: The sum of two positive integers is 100. The minimum value of the sum of their reciprocals is
questions.solution: For positive integers a+b=100, 1/a+1/b=100/(ab). The product satisfies ab≤((a+b)/2)²=2500, with equality at a=b=50. The minimum is 100/2500=1/25.
questions.hint: Maximize the product of the two integers.

questions.stem: The range of f(x)=4ˣ+2ˣ+4⁻ˣ+2⁻ˣ+3 for x∈(−∞,∞) is
questions.solution: For every x, 4ˣ+4⁻ˣ≥2 and 2ˣ+2⁻ˣ≥2, so f(x)≥7. Equality occurs at x=0. The function is continuous and tends to infinity as x→∞, so every value at least 7 is attained.
questions.hint: Pair each positive term with its reciprocal.

questions.stem: The function f:ℝ→ℝ satisfies f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y) for all real x,y, and f(1)=7. Then ∑ from r=1 to n of f(r) equals
questions.solution: Repeated addition gives f(r)=rf(1)=7r for positive integers r. Therefore the sum is 7(1+2+…+n)=7n(n+1)/2. No continuity assumption on f is needed for integer arguments.
questions.hint: Use additivity only at integer arguments.

questions.stem: Let f and g be differentiable for 0<x<1, with f(0)=g(0)=0 and f(1)=6. Suppose f′(x)=2g′(x) for all x∈(0,1). Then g(1) equals
questions.answer: Intended answer (b), 3, additionally requiring continuity at the endpoints.
questions.solution: On (0,1), h=f−2g has derivative zero and is constant. If f and g are continuous on [0,1], h(0)=0 makes that constant zero, and h(1)=0 yields g(1)=3. But differentiability only on the open interval does not constrain the endpoint values: choose f(x)=6x and g(x)=3x inside the interval and assign g(1) arbitrarily. Thus the printed assumptions do not determine g(1).
questions.hint: A zero derivative determines a constant only on the open interval. Check endpoint continuity.
questions.notes: The supplied PDF does not state continuity at 0 and 1; these are needed for the intended mean-value-theorem argument.

questions.stem: Consider f(x)=ax²+bx+c defined on [1,2]. Then it is always possible to get k∈(1,2) such that
questions.answer: (d) for the literal printed options; likely intended (c) if the left-hand side was f′(k).
questions.solution: As printed, take a=b=0. Every right-hand side in (a)–(c) equals 0, so none can equal a number k∈(1,2). Thus (d) is the literal answer. A likely intended application of the mean value theorem is f′(k)=(f(2)−f(1))/(2−1)=3a+b, which would support option (c) only if f′(k), rather than k, were printed.
questions.hint: Compute f(2)−f(1), but compare carefully with the actual options.
questions.notes: Visual review confirms all three options begin k=, not f′(k)=. The likely typo makes intended grading uncertain.

questions.stem: A sequence has first term 1/3. Each subsequent term equals the preceding term divided by one more than that preceding term. The 500th term is
questions.solution: If aₙ₊₁=aₙ/(1+aₙ), then 1/aₙ₊₁=1/aₙ+1. Since 1/a₁=3, induction gives 1/aₙ=n+2. Hence a₅₀₀=1/502.
questions.hint: Take reciprocals to obtain an arithmetic progression.

questions.stem: In how many ways can three persons, each throwing one die once, make a score of 10?
questions.solution: The number of positive integer triples with sum 10 without upper bounds is C(9,2)=36. If one die is at least 7, subtracting 6 from it gives a positive triple summing to 4, with C(3,2)=3 possibilities. There are three choices of that die and two dice cannot both exceed 6. Therefore the answer is 36−3·3=27.
questions.hint: Use stars and bars, then exclude scores above 6.

questions.stem: Let a be a positive integer greater than 2. The number of values of x for which ∫ from a to x of (x+y) dy=0 is
questions.solution: Integrating with respect to y gives x(x−a)+(x²−a²)/2=(3x²−2ax−a²)/2=(x−a)(3x+a)/2. The two distinct real roots are x=a and x=−a/3.
questions.hint: The x in the integrand is constant during integration with respect to y.

questions.stem: Let (x*,y*) solve max f(x,y) subject to g₁(x,y)≤c₁, and let (x′,y′) solve the same problem with the added constraint g₂(x,y)≤c₂. Which is always true?
questions.solution: Adding a constraint shrinks the feasible set. The new optimizer was feasible for the original maximization, so its objective value cannot exceed the original maximum. Absolute values need not preserve this inequality.
questions.hint: Compare the two feasible sets.

questions.stem: Let (x*,y*) be a real solution of max [√x+y] subject to px+y≤m, where m>0,p>0 and y*∈(0,m). Which is true?
options: x* depends on both p and m
x* is independent of both p and m
questions.solution: Because the objective is increasing in y, the budget binds: y=m−px. The objective is √x+m−px. Its derivative for x>0 is 1/(2√x)−p, which vanishes at x=1/(4p²); the second derivative is negative. The given interior condition ensures this optimum is compatible with y*∈(0,m).
questions.hint: Substitute y=m−px and differentiate.

questions.stem: Let 0<a₁<a₂<1 and f(x;a₁,a₂)=−|x−a₁|−|x−a₂|. Let X be the set of x maximizing this function. Then
questions.solution: The triangle inequality gives |x−a₁|+|x−a₂|≥a₂−a₁, with equality exactly when x lies between a₁ and a₂. Negating the sum therefore produces its maximum throughout [a₁,a₂].
questions.hint: Minimize the sum of distances to the two points.

questions.stem: Let A and B be events with positive probability on the same sample space. Find the correct answer.
questions.solution: If A and B are independent, P(A|B)=P(A), disproving both strict comparisons with P(A). Taking A=B also shows conditional probability can equal 1; alternatively choosing independent events with P(A)<P(B) disproves the third proposed universal inequality.
questions.hint: Independent events provide a simple counterexample to strict inequalities.

questions.stem: Let A and B be mutually exclusive events with positive probability on the same sample space. Find the correct answer.
options: A and B are necessarily independent
A and B are necessarily dependent
A and B are necessarily equally likely
questions.answer: They are necessarily dependent (printed option label (c)).
questions.solution: Mutual exclusivity gives P(A∩B)=0. Independence would require P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B)>0 because both probabilities are positive. The contradiction proves dependence.
questions.hint: Compare P(A∩B) with P(A)P(B).
questions.notes: The four source labels are (b),(c),(d),(e), an offset labeling error. The correct choice is the second listed option; correctIndex=1 indexes the options array, not the printed letter.

questions.stem: The salaries of 16 football-club players, in thousands of rupees, are 100,100,111,114,165,210,225,225,230,575,1200,1900,2100,2100,2650,3300. Every player receives an extra Rs. 200,000 bonus. Find the correct answer.
options: The mean increases by Rs. 200,000 but the median does not change
Both mean and median increase by Rs. 200,000
Both mean and standard deviation change
Standard deviation increases but the median is unchanged
questions.answer: Both mean and median increase by Rs. 200,000.
questions.solution: Adding the same constant to every observation translates both the arithmetic mean and every order statistic, hence the median, by that constant. Deviations from the mean remain unchanged, so standard deviation is unchanged.
questions.hint: Adding a constant shifts location but not dispersion.
questions.notes: Question begins on PDF page 5 and options continue on PDF page 6.

questions.stem: Let Pr(X=2)=1. Define μ₂ₙ=E[(X−μ)²ⁿ], μ=E(X). Then:
questions.solution: Since X=2 almost surely, μ=2 and X−μ=0 almost surely. Therefore every positive-order central moment, including μ₂ₙ, is zero.
questions.hint: A degenerate random variable has no deviations from its mean.

questions.stem: Consider a positively skewed distribution. Find the correct answer on the position of the mean and the median.
options: Mean and median are the same
questions.answer: Conventional textbook answer (a); not guaranteed by positive third-moment skewness alone.
questions.solution: A conventional right-skewed unimodal distribution is commonly summarized as mean greater than median. This is a heuristic, not a theorem for every distribution with positive standardized third central moment. For example, put masses 0.49,0.50,0.01 at −1,1,10. The mean is 0.11, the unique median is 1, yet the third central moment is positive (approximately 9.35). Thus the source needs a precise skewness convention or distributional assumptions before universal grading.
questions.hint: Check what definition of positive skewness the question intends.
questions.notes: The familiar mean–median ordering requires additional assumptions; no distribution family or skewness definition is specified.

questions.stem: Puja and Priya repeatedly play a fair game, each staking one rupee per game. Initially Puja has a rupees and Priya b rupees, where a>b. What is the probability that Puja wins all Priya’s money when play continues until one loses all her money?
questions.solution: Let u(i) be the chance of reaching capital a+b before 0 from capital i. Fairness gives u(i)=[u(i−1)+u(i+1)]/2, with u(0)=0 and u(a+b)=1. The unique solution is u(i)=i/(a+b), so u(a)=a/(a+b).
questions.hint: Use the fair gambler’s-ruin probability.

questions.stem: An urn contains w white balls and b black balls, with w,b>0. Two balls are drawn in order without replacement. Let Wᵢ mean white on draw i. Which is true?
questions.solution: Every ball is equally likely to appear in either draw position, so both marginal probabilities equal the initial white fraction w/(w+b). The fraction (w−1)/(w+b−1) is conditional on the first ball being white, not the unconditional second-draw probability.
questions.hint: Use symmetry of the two positions.
questions.notes: The unusual denominator w−b in source option (d) is preserved as printed.

questions.stem: A bag contains four papers labeled 1,2,3,4 without repeats. Draw three in order without replacement to form a three-digit number. What is the probability it is a multiple of 3?
questions.solution: A number is divisible by 3 precisely when its digit sum is. The sum of all four labels is 10, so the chosen three sum to a multiple of 3 exactly when the omitted digit is 1 or 4. Each omitted digit is equally likely, giving probability 2/4=1/2.
questions.hint: Use the digit-sum divisibility rule.

questions.stem: X takes values −2,−1,0,1,2, each with probability 1/5, and Y=|X|. Which statement is true?
options: X and Y are independent, and their Pearson correlation is 0
X and Y are dependent, and their Pearson correlation is 0
X and Y are independent, and their Pearson correlation is 1
X and Y are dependent, and their Pearson correlation is 1
questions.solution: Y is a nonconstant deterministic function of X, so they are dependent. Symmetry gives E(X)=0 and E(X|X|)=0. Consequently Cov(X,Y)=E(XY)−E(X)E(Y)=0. Both variances are positive, so the correlation is zero.
questions.hint: Dependence need not imply nonzero correlation.

questions.stem: Two friends arrive independently and uniformly at a metro station between 7:00 and 7:20. Each waits up to five minutes for the other. What is the probability that they meet?
questions.solution: Let arrival times be U,V measured in minutes after 7:00. Their joint sample space is a square of area 20²=400. They fail to meet when |U−V|>5, the union of two right triangles of total area 2·15²/2=225. Therefore the meeting probability is (400−225)/400=7/16.
questions.hint: Draw the strip |U−V|≤5 in a 20-by-20 square.
questions.notes: Independent arrivals are the standard implied interpretation of the printed uniformly random arrivals.

questions.stem: A consumer has income 20 and utility $u(x_1,x_2)=2x_1+32x_2-3x_2^2$ over nonnegative quantities. Both prices are 1. Find the optimal bundle.
questions.solution:
Utility is strictly increasing in good 1, so all income is spent. Substituting the budget leaves a one-variable concave problem; check that its stationary point satisfies both nonnegativity constraints.

$$\begin{aligned}
x_1&=20-x_2,\quad0\le x_2\le20,\\
u(x_2)&=40+30x_2-3x_2^2,\\
u\prime(x_2)&=30-6x_2=0\Longrightarrow x_2=5,\\
u^{\prime\prime}(x_2)&=-6<0,\qquad x_1=15.
\end{aligned}$$

The negative second derivative makes the feasible critical point the unique global maximum. This substitution method automatically accounts for the opportunity cost of good 2 in terms of the constant marginal utility from good 1.

Because utility rises in $x_1$, exhaust the budget: $x_1=20-x_2$. Utility is $40+30x_2-3x_2^2$, a strictly concave quadratic maximized by $30-6x_2=0$. Thus $x_2=5,x_1=15$, feasible in the nonnegative budget.

$(x_1,x_2)=(15,5)$.
questions.hint: Substitute the budget into utility.

questions.stem: A consumer has income 20 and utility $u(x_1,x_2)=2x_1+32x_2-3x_2^2$ over nonnegative quantities. Now price 2 rises to 4 and price 1 stays 1. Find the new optimal bundle.
questions.solution:
The new price changes the budget slope, so repeat the constrained optimization rather than holding the old quantities fixed. One unit of good 2 now displaces four units of good 1.

$$\begin{aligned}
x_1&=20-4x_2,\quad0\le x_2\le5,\\
u(x_2)&=40+24x_2-3x_2^2,\\
u\prime(x_2)&=24-6x_2=0\Longrightarrow x_2=4,\\
x_1&=4,\qquad u^*=88.
\end{aligned}$$

The loss of marginal utility from displaced good 1 rises from two to eight per unit of good 2. The interior condition therefore reduces demand for good 2 from five to four. Verify that the residual spending on good 1 stays nonnegative.

Use $x_1=20-4x_2$, giving utility $40+24x_2-3x_2^2$. Its derivative vanishes at $x_2=4$, so $x_1=4$. The maximum utility is $8+128-48=88$.

$(x_1,x_2)=(4,4)$.
questions.hint: The higher price reduces the linear net benefit of good 2.

questions.stem: A consumer has income 20 and utility $u(x_1,x_2)=2x_1+32x_2-3x_2^2$ over nonnegative quantities. How much extra income restores welfare after price 2 rises from 1 to 4?
questions.solution:
Compensating variation restores the original utility at the new prices. Use total compensated income as an unknown, and only subtract the old income after solving the utility-restoration equation.

$$\begin{aligned}
u_0&=2(15)+32(5)-3(5)^2=115,\\
x_2^*(m;1,4)&=4,\quad x_1^*=m-16,\\
v(m;1,4)&=2m+48,\\
2m+48=115&\Longrightarrow m=33.5,\\
CV&=33.5-20=13.5.
\end{aligned}$$

The compensated optimum is interior, so the same good-2 first-order condition remains valid. The resulting bundle has positive good 1 and exactly restores utility, providing a feasibility check on the expenditure calculation.

Initial utility at $(15,5)$ is 115. At the new prices, with income m and an interior optimum, $x_2=4$ and indirect utility is $2m+48$. Setting this to 115 gives $m=67/2=33.5$, so compensation is $33.5-20=13.5$.

The compensated bundle $(17.5,4)$ is feasible.

Compensating income $=27/2=13.5$.
questions.hint: At the compensated optimum each extra income unit raises utility by 2.

questions.stem: A public monopoly supplies internet with inverse demand $p=1-q$ and marginal cost 1/2. Official connection price is zero; tax-funded subsidy covers cost for at most 0.4 units. Bureaucrats can collect bribes but cannot supply more than 0.4. Find the equilibrium bribe per connection and social surplus.
questions.answer: Bribe $=0.6$ per connection, output $=0.4$, social surplus $=0.12$.
questions.solution:
The bureaucrats maximize bribe receipts, while society counts willingness to pay minus real production cost. Keep these objectives distinct; bribes redistribute purchasing power but do not use resources.

$$\begin{aligned}
b&=1-q,\quad0\le q\le0.4,\\
R_B(q)&=q(1-q),\qquad R_B\prime=1-2q>0,\\
q^*&=0.4,\quad b^*=0.6,\\
TS&=\int_0^{0.4}(1-q)\,dq-0.5(0.4)=0.12.
\end{aligned}$$

The unconstrained bribe-revenue maximum would require more than the permitted capacity, so the cap binds. Count the real subsidy-financed production cost once; including both taxes and costs as separate losses would double-count the same resources.

With a uniform bribe b and demand $q=1-b$, bureaucratic receipts are $bq=q(1-q)$, increasing over $0\leq q\leq0.4$. Supply is therefore at the cap 0.4, with bribe 0.6. Social surplus is gross benefit minus real production cost: $\int_0^{0.4}(1-q)dq-(1/2)(0.4)=0.32-0.20=0.12$.

Bribes and taxes are domestic transfers when all recipients enter social welfare.

Bribe $=0.6$ per connection, output $=0.4$, social surplus $=0.12$.
questions.hint: The supply cap binds before the bribe-revenue maximum.

solutionSteps.title: Set up the problem
solutionSteps.body: The bureaucrats maximize bribe receipts, while society counts willingness to pay minus real production cost. Keep these objectives distinct; bribes redistribute purchasing power but do not use resources.

solutionSteps.title: Work through the equations
solutionSteps.body:
$$\begin{aligned}
b&=1-q,\quad0\le q\le0.4,\\
R_B(q)&=q(1-q),\qquad R_B\prime=1-2q>0,\\
q^*&=0.4,\quad b^*=0.6,\\
TS&=\int_0^{0.4}(1-q)\,dq-0.5(0.4)=0.12.
\end{aligned}$$

The unconstrained bribe-revenue maximum would require more than the permitted capacity, so the cap binds. Count the real subsidy-financed production cost once; including both taxes and costs as separate losses would double-count the same resources.

solutionSteps.title: Complete the argument
solutionSteps.body:
With a uniform bribe b and demand $q=1-b$, bureaucratic receipts are $bq=q(1-q)$, increasing over $0\leq q\leq0.4$. Supply is therefore at the cap 0.4, with bribe 0.6. Social surplus is gross benefit minus real production cost: $\int_0^{0.4}(1-q)dq-(1/2)(0.4)=0.32-0.20=0.12$.

Bribes and taxes are domestic transfers when all recipients enter social welfare.

solutionSteps.title: Conclusion
solutionSteps.body: Bribe $=0.6$ per connection, output $=0.4$, social surplus $=0.12$.

questions.stem: A public monopoly supplies internet with inverse demand $p=1-q$ and marginal cost 1/2. Official connection price is zero; tax-funded subsidy covers cost for at most 0.4 units. Bureaucrats can collect bribes but cannot supply more than 0.4. The agency is privatized and deregulated but remains a monopoly because entry costs are large relative to demand. Find new price, bribe and surplus, and compare with the public regime.
questions.solution:
After privatization, the seller pays the marginal production cost directly and chooses the monopoly quantity. A higher official price can coincide with lower corruption but also lower total surplus.

$$\begin{aligned}
\pi(q)&=(1-q)q-\tfrac12q=\tfrac12q-q^2,\\
\pi\prime(q)&=\tfrac12-2q=0\Longrightarrow q^*=1/4,\\
p^*&=3/4,\qquad b^*=0,\\
TS&=\int_0^{1/4}(1-q-1/2)\,dq=3/32.
\end{aligned}$$

The quantity falls from $0.4$ to $0.25$, even though the separate bribe disappears. Compare effective consumer payments, not just the previously zero posted fee, and compare real surplus using the same accounting convention in both regimes.

The private monopolist sets $MR=1-2q=MC=1/2$, giving $q=1/4,p=3/4$. Separate bureaucratic bribery disappears. Total surplus is $\int_0^{1/4}(1-q-1/2)dq=3/32$, below the public-regime $3/25=0.12$.

The official posted price rises from zero, the effective connection payment rises from 0.6 to 0.75, and bribery falls to zero. Existing/sunk entry costs are excluded since their magnitude is not supplied.

Price $=0.75$, output $=0.25$, bribe $=0$, social surplus $=3/32=0.09375$.

questions.stem: A public monopoly supplies internet with inverse demand $p=1-q$ and marginal cost 1/2. Official connection price is zero; tax-funded subsidy covers cost for at most 0.4 units. Bureaucrats can collect bribes but cannot supply more than 0.4. After privatization, innovation lowers marginal cost to $c$, $0<c<1/2$. For which c does privatization increase consumer surplus?
questions.answer: Conventional demand-area consumer surplus rises iff $0<c<1/5$. Including the avoided public tax burden, consumers gain for every $0<c<1/2$.
questions.solution:
Derive the private monopoly output as a function of the improved marginal cost. Then compare consumer surplus triangles, while separately identifying whether taxes paid by consumers are included in the benchmark.

$$\begin{aligned}
q^*(c)&=(1-c)/2,\quad p^*(c)=(1+c)/2,\\
CS_{\rm private}&=\tfrac12[q^*(c)]^2=(1-c)^2/8,\\
CS_{\rm public}&=\tfrac12(0.4)^2=0.08,\\
CS_{\rm private}>CS_{\rm public}&\Longleftrightarrow c<1/5.
\end{aligned}$$

The threshold is a comparison of conventional demand-area consumer surplus. The existing source caveat matters: if the public tax burden also enters consumers' welfare and disappears after privatization, it changes the comparison. Present both accounting conventions instead of silently treating taxes as irrelevant to consumers while counting them elsewhere.

Private monopoly output is $(1-c)/2$ and demand-area consumer surplus is $(1-c)^2/8$. Public-regime demand-area surplus net of bribes is $(0.4)^2/2=0.08$. Comparing these gives $(1-c)^2>0.64$, hence $c<0.2$.

However, the source expressly funds public cost with taxes on consumers: public taxes total 0.2, so tax-inclusive consumer welfare is $0.08-0.2=-0.12$. If those taxes disappear on privatization, positive private demand-area surplus exceeds that benchmark for every permitted c. Both conclusions are reported because the question leaves the surplus/tax accounting convention implicit.

Conventional demand-area consumer surplus rises iff $0<c<1/5$. Including the avoided public tax burden, consumers gain for every $0<c<1/2$.

questions.stem: A circular state of radius $r>0$ has a uniformly distributed unit population. Travel costs k per distance, $k>0$, and shoppers must return home. Each resident has income/willingness to pay 10 for one good. Outside price is p and inside price is $p(1+t)<10$ due to an entry tax rate t. Imports otherwise have zero transport cost. What proportion evades the tax by shopping outside?
questions.answer: Let $z=pt$ and $a=2kr$. For $0\leq z\leq a$, evasion share $=1-(1-z/a)^2$; for $z\geq a$, it is 1.
questions.solution:
Uniform population over area implies that an evading boundary band must be measured as an annulus, not as a fraction of the radius. Use the closest point on the border and include the return trip.

$$\begin{aligned}
z&=pt,\quad a=2kr,\\
2k(r-\rho)<z&\Longleftrightarrow\rho>r-z/(2k),\\
E(z)&=\frac{\pi r^2-\pi[r-z/(2k)]^2}{\pi r^2}
=1-(1-z/a)^2\quad(0\le z\le a).
\end{aligned}$$

Once the travel-cost saving covers the trip from the centre, the whole population evades up to measure-zero ties. Clipping the annulus formula at this boundary avoids assigning a physically impossible population share when the tax is large.

A resident at radial distance rho must travel at least $r-\rho$ to cross the nearest border, costing round-trip $2k(r-\rho)$. Evasion is cheaper when $2k(r-\rho)<pt=z$. Thus evaders occupy the outer annulus of thickness $z/(2k)$, whose population share is its area divided by $\pi r^2$: $1-[1-z/(2kr)]^2$.

If the thickness reaches r, everyone evades apart from measure-zero ties.

Let $z=pt$ and $a=2kr$. For $0\leq z\leq a$, evasion share $=1-(1-z/a)^2$; for $z\geq a$, it is 1.

questions.stem: A circular state of radius $r>0$ has a uniformly distributed unit population. Travel costs k per distance, $k>0$, and shoppers must return home. Each resident has income/willingness to pay 10 for one good. Outside price is p and inside price is $p(1+t)<10$ due to an entry tax rate t. Imports otherwise have zero transport cost. Find the welfare-maximizing tax and the necessary and sufficient conditions for it to equal the revenue-maximizing tax.
questions.answer: Welfare is maximized at t=0. With positive p,k,r and the stated positive willingness-to-pay slack, every revenue-maximizing positive-feasible tax differs from zero.
questions.solution:
Domestic tax payments are transfers in total state welfare; border travel consumes resources. Revenue, however, depends on both the tax per non-evader and the remaining non-evading population.

$$\begin{aligned}
R(z)&=z(1-z/a)^2,\qquad a=2kr,\\
R\prime(z)&=(1-z/a)(1-3z/a),\\
z_R&=a/3,\qquad t_R=a/(3p),\\
t_W&=0.
\end{aligned}$$

Any positive tax induces a band of residents to incur avoidable travel costs, whereas zero tax does not. A positive revenue-maximizing tax therefore differs from the welfare optimum in the nondegenerate case. Also check the reservation-price cap; a strict upper bound can yield only a supremum rather than an attained maximizer.

Taxes are transfers inside the state, whereas evasion travel is a real resource cost. At zero tax nobody incurs that cost, so total welfare $10-p$ is maximal. For $0\leq z\leq a=2kr$, revenue is $R(z)=z(1-z/a)^2$, with derivative $(1-z/a)(1-3z/a)$.

Its unconstrained maximum is at $z=a/3$, i.e. $t=2kr/(3p)>0$. If the reservation-price restriction binds, use the largest admissible z approaching $10-p$ instead; this is still positive when p<10. Thus under the stated nondegenerate positive parameters the two optima never coincide.

Coincidence requires removing every feasible positive-revenue tax, e.g. zero willingness-to-pay slack in a weakly closed constraint; such a degeneracy lies outside $p(1+t)<10$ with positive p. Strict price inequality can mean a revenue supremum rather than an attained maximum at the cap.

Welfare is maximized at t=0. With positive p,k,r and the stated positive willingness-to-pay slack, every revenue-maximizing positive-feasible tax differs from zero.
questions.hint: A revenue transfer cannot offset the social waste of tax-evasion travel.
questions.notes: Assumes tax revenue belongs to residents’ social welfare, nonnegative tax rates and positive outside price. Strict reservation bound can prevent attainment of a constrained revenue maximum.

questions.stem: A circular state of radius $r>0$ has a uniformly distributed unit population. Travel costs k per distance, $k>0$, and shoppers must return home. Each resident has income/willingness to pay 10 for one good. Outside price is p and inside price is $p(1+t)<10$ due to an entry tax rate t. Imports otherwise have zero transport cost. Suppose the revenue-maximizing tax is initially positive. Find the elasticity of optimized tax revenue with respect to outside price p when the minister always optimizes the tax.
questions.answer: If the reservation bound is slack, elasticity is 0 because $R^*=8kr/27$. With a binding bound the elasticity is generally negative.
questions.solution:
Optimize with respect to the rupee tax wedge $z=pt$, not directly with respect to the rate. Then distinguish an interior revenue maximum from one constrained by willingness to pay.

$$\begin{aligned}
z^*&=a/3,\qquad R^*=\frac a3\left(\frac23\right)^2
=\frac{4a}{27}=\frac{8kr}{27},\\
\frac{d\log R^*}{d\log p}&=0\quad\text{if }p+a/3<10,\\
z=10-p:&\quad\frac{d\log R}{d\log p}
=\frac{p(3z-a)}{z(a-z)}.
\end{aligned}$$

At an interior optimum, the minister offsets a change in outside price by changing the tax rate so that the rupee wedge stays constant. If the reservation-price boundary binds, that adjustment is unavailable and the envelope derivative is generally negative. A merely positive tax does not identify which regime applies.

For an interior optimum $z^*=pt^*=2kr/3$, tax rate adjusts inversely with p. Maximized revenue is $(2kr/3)(2/3)^2=8kr/27$, independent of p, so elasticity is zero. This requires $p+2kr/3<10$.

If instead the willingness-to-pay bound is binding in its closed-limit interpretation, write $z=10-p<a/3$. Revenue is $z(1-z/a)^2$ and the elasticity is $p[-1/z+2/(a-z)]=p(3z-a)/[z(a-z)]<0$. Thus positivity of the optimal tax alone does not guarantee the zero-elasticity answer without the interior condition.

If the reservation bound is slack, elasticity is 0 because $R^*=8kr/27$. With a binding bound the elasticity is generally negative.
questions.hint: Optimize the tax-inclusive markup z=pt rather than t directly.
questions.notes: Literal assumption of a positive optimum does not itself ensure the reservation-price cap is slack; both cases retained.

questions.stem: Two zero-cost Cournot firms face differentiated inverse demands $p_1=a_1-b_{11}q_1-b_{12}q_2$ and $p_2=a_2-b_{21}q_1-b_{22}q_2$, all coefficients positive. Find outputs assuming both are positive.
questions.solution:
Each firm treats rival output as fixed. Own-price and cross-price slopes enter different positions in the two first-order conditions, so preserve their indices while solving the simultaneous system.

$$\begin{aligned}
2b_{11}q_1+b_{12}q_2&=a_1,\\
b_{21}q_1+2b_{22}q_2&=a_2,\\
D&=4b_{11}b_{22}-b_{12}b_{21},\\
q_1&=\frac{2a_1b_{22}-a_2b_{12}}D,\quad
q_2=\frac{2a_2b_{11}-a_1b_{21}}D.
\end{aligned}$$

Own-quantity profit curvature is negative because the own-demand coefficients are positive. These formulas therefore give mutual best responses whenever both quantities are positive and $D\ne0$. The singular case must be checked as a system of equations, not evaluated by division by zero.

Each firm’s strictly concave own-quantity profit gives FOCs $2b_{11}q_1+b_{12}q_2=a_1$ and $b_{21}q_1+2b_{22}q_2=a_2$. Solving the linear system gives the displayed expressions when its determinant is nonzero. If $D=0$, there is no unique interior formula: proportional consistent equations yield an interval of positive solutions; inconsistent equations yield none.

For $D=4b_{11}b_{22}-b_{12}b_{21}\ne0$, $q_1=(2a_1b_{22}-a_2b_{12})/D$, $q_2=(2a_2b_{11}-a_1b_{21})/D$.

questions.stem: Two zero-cost Cournot firms face differentiated inverse demands $p_1=a_1-b_{11}q_1-b_{12}q_2$ and $p_2=a_2-b_{21}q_1-b_{22}q_2$, all coefficients positive. Give necessary and sufficient parameter conditions for an equilibrium with both firms producing positive output.
questions.answer: For $D\ne0$, both displayed output numerators must have the same sign as D. A consistent $D=0$ system also has positive interior solutions.
questions.solution:
An interior Nash equilibrium requires positive quantities, but it does not by itself require stable best-response dynamics. Keep the determinant sign cases separate.

$$\begin{aligned}
N_1&=2a_1b_{22}-a_2b_{12},\qquad N_2=2a_2b_{11}-a_1b_{21},\\
D\ne0:&\quad N_1/D>0,\quad N_2/D>0,\\
D=0:&\quad a_2=\frac{b_{21}a_1}{2b_{11}}
\quad\text{for consistency}.
\end{aligned}$$

For a nonsingular system, each numerator must have the same sign as the determinant. Restricting all three to be positive would discard mathematically valid unstable interior equilibria without a stated stability assumption. A consistent singular system instead admits the positive portion of a common reaction line.

Let $N_1=2a_1b_{22}-a_2b_{12}$, $N_2=2a_2b_{11}-a_1b_{21}$. Since own profits are strictly concave, an interior solution of the FOCs is a Nash equilibrium. Thus for $D\ne0$, necessary and sufficient conditions are $N_1/D>0,N_2/D>0$: either all three are positive, or D and both numerators are negative.

For $D=0$, consistency requires $a_2=b_{21}a_1/(2b_{11})$ (equivalently both N vanish); then the positive portion of $2b_{11}q_1+b_{12}q_2=a_1$ consists of interior equilibria. The customary stable-unique interior case adds $D>0$ and both N positive. Omitting D<0 and singular cases would require an extra stability/uniqueness restriction not stated in the question.

questions.stem: Two zero-cost Cournot firms face differentiated inverse demands $p_1=a_1-b_{11}q_1-b_{12}q_2$ and $p_2=a_2-b_{21}q_1-b_{22}q_2$, all coefficients positive. Under what restrictions does this become the standard homogeneous-good Cournot model?
questions.solution:
A homogeneous product has one inverse market demand depending only on total output. Equate that expression to each differentiated inverse-demand equation coefficient by coefficient.

$$\begin{aligned}
p_1=p_2&=a-b(q_1+q_2),\\
a_1=a_2&=a,\\
b_{11}=b_{12}=b_{21}=b_{22}&=b,\\
q_1^*=q_2^*&=a/(3b).
\end{aligned}$$

questions.stem: A product monopolist and labour monopsonist has $Q=L=L_M+L_F$, inverse demand $p=A-Q/2$, and labour supplies $L_i=w_i^{\epsilon_i}$, $\epsilon_i>0$, with $\epsilon_M\epsilon_F=1$. Both groups are hired and the male wage is twice the female wage. Find the male labour-supply elasticity exactly.
questions.solution:
A monopsonist equates marginal labour expenditure, not the wage, to the common marginal revenue product. Invert each group's labour supply to differentiate its wage bill.

$$\begin{aligned}
L_i&=w_i^{\epsilon_i},\quad
ME_i=(1+1/\epsilon_i)w_i,\\
w_i&=v\frac{\epsilon_i}{1+\epsilon_i},\quad v=MR=A-Q,\\
\epsilon_F=1/\epsilon_M&\Longrightarrow w_M/w_F=\epsilon_M=2.
\end{aligned}$$

The reciprocal-elasticity restriction collapses the wage ratio to a single elasticity. It also gives the female elasticity immediately. The more elastic group receives the higher wage because the monopsony wedge between its wage and marginal expenditure is smaller.

Let common marginal revenue product be $v=MR=A-Q$. Marginal expenditure on type i is $(1+1/\epsilon_i)w_i$, so $w_i=v\epsilon_i/(1+\epsilon_i)$. Substitute $\epsilon_F=1/\epsilon_M$; the wage ratio becomes $w_M/w_F=\epsilon_M$.

The observed ratio 2 therefore gives the result.

$\epsilon_M=2$ and $\epsilon_F=1/2$.

questions.stem: A product monopolist and labour monopsonist has $Q=L=L_M+L_F$, inverse demand $p=A-Q/2$, and labour supplies $L_i=w_i^{\epsilon_i}$, $\epsilon_i>0$, with $\epsilon_M\epsilon_F=1$. questions.answer: The male labour-income share strictly increases.
questions.solution:
Insert the elasticities from part (a) into wages, employment and wage bills. To prove the share rises, it is enough to show the male-to-female wage-bill ratio rises.

\end{aligned}$$

questions.stem: A household supplies labour L to a competitive firm $Y=F(L)$ with $F\prime>0,F\prime\prime<0$, receiving wages and all firm profits. Utility is $\frac12\ln C+\frac12\ln(M/P)-d(L)$, $d\prime,d\prime\prime>0$. Budget: $PC+M=WL+\Pi+\bar M-PT$. Government budget: $M-\bar M=P(G-T)$; goods clear at $Y=C+G$. Prove $0<dY/dG<1$ and $dC/dG<0$.
questions.solution:
Combine household and firm first-order conditions to eliminate nominal variables. Goods-market clearing then leaves one real equilibrium equation in employment and government spending.

$$\begin{aligned}
M&=PC,\quad W/P=F\prime(L),\quad C=F(L)-G,\\
2[F(L)-G]d\prime(L)&=F\prime(L),\\
D\frac{dL}{dG}&=2d\prime(L),\\
D&=2F\prime d\prime+2Cd^{\prime\prime}-F^{\prime\prime},\\
\frac{dY}{dG}&=\frac{2F\prime d\prime}{D}\in(0,1).
\end{aligned}$$

The denominator exceeds the positive numerator because disutility is strictly convex and production strictly concave. Thus labour and output increase, but not enough to match the public spending increase. The residual consumption response is $dC/dG=dY/dG-1<0$.

Household FOCs give $M=PC$ and $d\prime(L)=W/(2PC)$. Firm optimality gives $W/P=F\prime(L)$, so real equilibrium satisfies $2[F(L)-G]d\prime(L)=F\prime(L)$. Differentiate in G: $[2F\prime d\prime+2C d\prime\prime-F\prime\prime]dL/dG=2d\prime$.

The bracket D is positive and exceeds $2F\prime d\prime$, because $C>0,d\prime\prime>0,F\prime\prime<0$. Multiplying by $F\prime>0$ gives $0<dY/dG<1$. Since $C=Y-G$, consumption falls.

$dY/dG=2F\prime d\prime/[2F\prime d\prime+2C d\prime\prime-F\prime\prime]\in(0,1)$; $dC/dG=dY/dG-1<0$.

questions.stem: A household supplies labour L to a competitive firm $Y=F(L)$ with $F\prime>0,F\prime\prime<0$, receiving wages and all firm profits. Utility is $\frac12\ln C+\frac12\ln(M/P)-d(L)$, $d\prime,d\prime\prime>0$. Budget: $PC+M=WL+\Pi+\bar M-PT$. Government budget: $M-\bar M=P(G-T)$; goods clear at $Y=C+G$. Everything else fixed, show increasing initial nominal money $\bar M$ raises P proportionately.
questions.answer: $P=\bar M/[Y-2G+T]$, so the price elasticity with respect to initial money is 1.
questions.solution:
The real first-order condition does not contain initial nominal balances. Once the real allocation is determined, use household money demand and the government budget to recover the price level.

$$\begin{aligned}
M&=PC,\\
M-\bar M&=P(G-T),\\
\bar M&=P(C-G+T)=P(Y-2G+T),\\
P&=\frac{\bar M}{Y-2G+T},\qquad
\frac{d\log P}{d\log\bar M}=1.
\end{aligned}$$

Holding real policies fixed holds the denominator fixed. Nominal balances therefore scale the price level proportionately rather than changing employment or consumption. The required positive denominator is an equilibrium-existence condition, not something that can be ignored when solving for $P$.

The real equilibrium equation $2[F(L)-G]d\prime=F\prime$ determines L,Y,C independently of nominal money. Household demand gives $M=PC$; government budget then yields $PC-\bar M=P(G-T)$, hence $\bar M=P(C-G+T)=P(Y-2G+T)$. Holding real policy and the resulting real allocation fixed, doubling initial money doubles P (and compatible nominal wage and final balances).

A positive-price equilibrium requires the denominator positive.

$P=\bar M/[Y-2G+T]$, so the price elasticity with respect to initial money is 1.

questions.stem: In continuous-time Solow without technological progress, the proposed intensive production function is $f(k)=k^4-6k^3+11k^2-6k=k(k-1)(k-2)(k-3)$, $k=K/L$. State the standard assumptions on extensive production F(K,L) and identify violations.
questions.answer: The polynomial violates nonnegative output, monotonicity/concavity and Inada conditions, although $F(K,L)=Lf(K/L)$ can be made constant returns.
questions.solution:
Check each neoclassical assumption separately; degree-one homogeneity of an extensive construction does not imply positive or concave intensive production.

$$\begin{aligned}
f(k)&=k(k-1)(k-2)(k-3),\\
f\prime(0)&=-6,\qquad\lim_{k\to\infty}f\prime(k)=\infty,\\
f^{\prime\prime}(k)&=12k^2-36k+22,\\
F(K,L)&=Lf(K/L)\Longrightarrow F(tK,tL)=tF(K,L).
\end{aligned}$$

The factorization identifies negative-output intervals immediately, while the derivatives reject positive diminishing marginal products and the usual Inada limits. Homogeneity survives by construction, but cannot rescue the other economic assumptions. The later dynamic analysis must therefore be described as a formal mathematical exercise.

Standard neoclassical Solow assumes nonnegative output, essential inputs, degree-one homogeneity, positive diminishing marginal products and appropriate Inada limits. Here f is negative for $0<k<1$ and $2<k<3$. Also $f\prime(0)=-6$, not positive/infinite, and $f\prime(k)\to\infty$ as k grows, not zero.

Its second derivative $12k^2-36k+22$ changes sign and is positive for sufficiently large k, violating global concavity. Defining extensive F as $Lf(K/L)$ ensures degree-one homogeneity but cannot repair those economic defects or global positive labour marginal product.

The polynomial violates nonnegative output, monotonicity/concavity and Inada conditions, although $F(K,L)=Lf(K/L)$ can be made constant returns.
