questions.stem: Robinson Crusoe lives in periods 1 and 2 on an isolated island. He harvests 100 coconuts at the beginning of each period; unconsumed coconuts spoil at 20% per period. With utility u(c₁,c₂)=min{5c₁,6c₂}, his utility-maximizing consumption choice is
questions.solution: No borrowing from the future is possible, so c₁≤100 and utility cannot exceed 5c₁≤500. Consuming each period’s harvest, (100,100), gives min(500,600)=500 and attains this bound. The spoilage constraint is c₂≤100+0.8(100−c₁).
questions.hint: Use the physical upper bound on first-period consumption.
questions.notes: There are also optimal bundles with c₁=100 and 250/3≤c₂≤100 if second-period coconuts may be discarded; C is the listed optimum.

questions.stem: Domestic supply is P=50+Q and demand P=200−2Q, with Q in thousands of kilograms and P in rupees per kilogram. The small country faces world price Rs.60. The government issues 300 permits, each allowing a foreign exporter to sell 100 kilograms domestically. What is the maximum price an exporter will pay per permit?
questions.solution: Permitted imports total 30 thousand kg. Market clearing requires (200−P)/2−(P−50)=30, giving P=80. A permit permits 100 kg with margin 80−60=20 rupees/kg, so its value is 100·20=2000.
questions.hint: Equate excess domestic demand to the permitted import quantity.

questions.stem: SeaTel has captive customers with weekly demand Q=60−P hours of calls and total cost C=20Q. It offers unlimited calls for a flat weekly access fee, with no per-hour usage charge. Which weekly fee maximizes profit?
questions.solution: With a zero marginal usage price, each customer consumes 60 hours. Their total willingness to pay is the area under inverse demand: ∫₀⁶⁰(60−Q)dQ=1800. Charging 1800 extracts it; cost is 1200 and profit 600 per subscriber.
questions.hint: Calculate total willingness to pay when the usage price is zero.
questions.notes: Uses the usual convention that an indifferent customer participates.

questions.stem: A bus stop is located at x∈[0,1]. Three people at 0.2,0.3,0.9 have utilities −|y−x|. A move is Pareto improving if at least one gains and nobody loses. Which statement about Pareto-efficient locations is true?
options: The median 0.3 is the only Pareto-efficient location
questions.answer: Every location in [0.2,0.9] is Pareto efficient
questions.solution: Any stop below 0.2 can move toward 0.2 and improve all distances; similarly a stop above 0.9 can move left. At any x between 0.2 and 0.9, moving right harms the person at 0.2 and moving left harms the person at 0.9. Thus the whole interval is efficient.
questions.hint: Use the two people at the extreme locations.

questions.stem: Match goods (a) cable television, (b) a fish in international waters, (c) a burger to descriptions: A nonrival and nonexcludable; B rival and excludable; C nonrival and excludable; D rival and nonexcludable.
questions.solution: Cable access can exclude nonpayers while one viewer does not diminish another’s viewing. An unowned fish is a rival common resource. A burger is both rival in consumption and excludable.
questions.hint: Distinguish rivalry from the ability to exclude consumers.

questions.stem: A zero-cost monopolist sells goods A,B to three unit-demand individuals with valuations (10,1),(1,10),(7,7). It can set separate prices p_A,p_B and a bundle price p_AB for one unit of each. A profit-maximizing menu is
questions.answer: None: a maximizing menu is p_A=p_B=10, p_AB=14, with revenue 34
questions.solution: At (10,10,14), the first two buy their preferred single goods for 10 each, and the third buys the bundle for 14, totaling 34. The listed menus yield respectively 33,14,33. No menu can exceed 34: if neither of the first two buys a bundle, their payments are at most 10 each and the third at most 14. If either buys a bundle, its price is at most 11 and the resulting menu cannot exceed the 33 obtainable by selling that bundle to all.
questions.hint: Compare mixed bundling with pure bundling.
questions.notes: Uses participation and favorable tie-breaking at reservation prices, as is standard in the listed menus.

questions.stem: Two Bertrand firms face demand p=10−q. Lower price wins all demand; equal prices split demand equally. Costs are 3q₁ and 2q₂. Prices must lie in {0,0.1,0.2,…}. The equilibrium is
questions.solution: Firm 1 cannot undercut 2.9 without selling below its marginal cost 3. Firm 2 earns (2.9−2)(10−2.9)=6.39, more than sharing demand at price 3 (profit 3.5). Lower prices reduce its profit on this price range, and prices above 3 lose demand.
questions.hint: Account for the discrete price grid and unequal marginal costs.

questions.stem: A monopolist faces p=20−q and operates two plants. Each plant has cost cᵢ(qᵢ)=2+4qᵢ if qᵢ>0, and 0 otherwise. Optimal monopoly profit is
questions.solution: Both plants have identical marginal cost, so use just one to avoid the second fixed charge. Profit is (20−q)q−4q−2=16q−q²−2, maximized at q=8, giving 128−64−2=62.
questions.hint: Avoid paying a second fixed cost when marginal costs are identical.

questions.stem: Labour supply L maximizes u(C,L)=C^α(1−L)^β, α,β>0, α+β<1, with consumption expenditure C=wL. Then
options: Labour supply does not depend on w
Labour supply is directly proportional to w
Labour supply is inversely proportional to w
questions.solution: Substitute C=wL. Maximizing αlnw+αlnL+βln(1−L) gives α/L−β/(1−L)=0, hence L=α/(α+β).
questions.hint: Substitute wage income into utility before differentiating.

questions.stem: In Question 9, suppose a Keynesian economy has autonomous investment I and Y=C+I. Production is Y=AL^θ with A>0 and 0<θ<1; firms equate the marginal product of labour to w. The marginal propensity to consume is
questions.solution: Competitive labour demand implies w=AθL^(θ−1). Thus consumption expenditure C=wL=θAL^θ=θY. Differentiating gives dC/dY=θ.
questions.hint: Express the wage bill as a share of output.

questions.stem: In a continuous-time Solow model, Y=F(K,AL), L̇/L=n, Ȧ/A=g, K̇=sY−δK. Let Z=K/(AL) and f(Z)=F(Z,1). Then Ż/Z equals
questions.solution: Log differentiation gives Ż/Z=K̇/K−Ȧ/A−L̇/L. Constant returns imply Y/K=f(Z)/Z, so substitution gives sf(Z)/Z−δ−g−n.
questions.hint: Log-differentiate capital per effective worker.
questions.notes: Uses the usual constant-returns production assumption of the Solow model.

questions.stem: In the Solow model of Question 11, the growth rate of aggregate output Y at steady state is
questions.solution: At steady state capital and output per effective worker are constant. Since effective labour AL grows at n+g, total output Y=ALf(Z*) grows at the same rate.
questions.hint: Distinguish aggregate output from output per effective worker.

questions.stem: An IS–LM model has IS: 0.25Y=500+G−i, and money demand M/P=2Y/eⁱ. Government spending rises and the central bank changes M to hold the short-run interest rate i constant. Which condition holds?
questions.solution: With i fixed the IS equation gives dY/dG=4. At fixed short-run P and i, M=2Pe^(−i)Y implies dM/dY=M/Y. Chain differentiation therefore gives dM/dG=4M/Y.
questions.hint: Differentiate IS at a fixed rate, then differentiate LM.

questions.stem: An agent maximizes ln c₁+βln c₂, 0<β<1, with incomes w₁,w₂ and interest rate r>0. If w₁ increases temporarily with expected w₂ unchanged, dc₁/dw₁ is
questions.solution: Present-value wealth is W=w₁+w₂/(1+r). Log utility allocates c₁=W/(1+β). With w₂ fixed, dc₁/dw₁=1/(1+β).
questions.hint: Write the present-value budget constraint.

questions.stem: In Question 14, w₁ increases permanently: expected w₂ rises by the same amount. Then dc₁/dw₁ is
questions.solution: Since c₁=[w₁+w₂/(1+r)]/(1+β), a simultaneous equal rise in both incomes changes present-value wealth by 1+1/(1+r) per unit of w₁. Divide by 1+β.
questions.hint: Differentiate along a change that raises both incomes equally.

questions.stem: For what values of a are (0,1,a),(a,1,0),(1,a,1) linearly dependent in ℝ³?
questions.answer: a=0,√2,−√2; both A and D are valid listed values
questions.solution: Their determinant is a³−2a=a(a²−2). It vanishes at 0 and ±√2. Therefore the single-choice options include two correct values, 0 and √2, and omit the negative root.
questions.hint: Set the determinant of the vector matrix to zero.
questions.notes: No unique correct option in the printed source.

questions.stem: Which set of vectors is a basis of ℝ²?
questions.solution: A basis of ℝ² has exactly two independent vectors. The last pair has determinant 1·3−2·1=1≠0. The other options have too few vectors, dependent vectors, or too many vectors.
questions.hint: Check cardinality and a 2×2 determinant.

questions.stem: A good candidate is selected in MSQE with probability 0.9, a bad candidate with probability 0.2. A candidate is equally likely good or bad. Conditional on selection, the probability the candidate is good is
questions.hint: Apply Bayes’ rule with equal prior probabilities.

questions.stem: Let S₁={2,3,4,…,9}. Draw s₁ uniformly, remove it and all its factors to get S₂, draw s₂ uniformly from S₂, remove it and all its factors to get S₃, and draw s₃ uniformly from S₃. Find P(s₁=2,s₂=3,s₃=5).
questions.solution: There are 8 initial choices. After drawing 2 only 2 is removed, since its other positive factor 1 was never in S₁. The new set has 7 elements. Drawing 3 removes only 3 from it, leaving 6. Thus the specified path has probability (1/8)(1/7)(1/6)=1/336.
questions.hint: Track the actual set after each deletion.
questions.notes: All four printed choices differ from the independently computed probability.

questions.stem: A and B independently toss coins with head probability 0.25, twice each. Given exactly two heads among all four tosses, what is the probability A got exactly one head?
questions.solution: Conditional on two heads, each of the C(4,2)=6 placements has equal probability p²(1−p)². Four placements give one head in A’s two tosses and one in B’s, so the probability is 4/6.
questions.hint: Condition on the equally likely placements of the two heads.

questions.stem: Let f:ℝ→ℝ have f(x)=x if x≤e, and f(x)=xlnx if x>e. Which is true?
options: f is not continuous at e
f is not differentiable at e
f is neither continuous nor differentiable at e
f is continuous and differentiable at e
questions.answer: Continuous but not differentiable at e
questions.solution: Both sides approach e and f(e)=e. The left derivative is 1; the right derivative of xlnx is lnx+1, tending to 2 at e. Thus differentiability fails.
questions.hint: Compare one-sided values and derivatives at e.

questions.stem: Let f:[−1,1]→ℝ be continuous and weakly increasing, with ∫₋₁¹f(x)dx=2∫₋₁¹f(−x)dx and f(−1)=0. What is the implied value of f on the interval?
questions.solution: The substitution u=−x makes the two integrals equal. Thus I=2I and I=0. Monotonicity and f(−1)=0 imply f≥0. A nonnegative continuous function with zero integral must vanish everywhere.
questions.hint: Compare the two integrals using reflection.
questions.notes: The official PDF’s line after “then” omits the requested function argument; the assumptions force f≡0, so every possible point-value target on this domain has the same answer 0.

questions.stem: A twice continuously differentiable f has f′(x*)=0. Consider (i) f″(x*)≤0 implies x* is a maximum; (ii) a local maximum at x* implies f″(x*)<0. Which is true?
questions.solution: For f=x³ at 0, f′=f″=0 but there is no maximum, disproving (i). For f=−x⁴ at 0 there is a strict local maximum with f″=0, disproving (ii).
questions.hint: Test cases where the second derivative is zero.

questions.stem: For f(x)=eˣ on ℝ, which is true?
options: f is neither quasiconvex nor quasiconcave
f is both quasiconvex and quasiconcave
questions.solution: A strictly increasing real function on an interval has convex lower and upper level sets, here half-lines. Hence the exponential is both quasiconvex and quasiconcave, and the fourth choice is the complete characterization.
questions.hint: Inspect both upper and lower level sets.
questions.notes: The fourth choice is the most complete answer; the individual properties in A and B are also true.

questions.stem: Let A=[[x,0,k],[1,x,k−3],[0,1,1]]. Its determinant is zero for two distinct real x. What is the least positive integer k?
questions.solution: The determinant is x²−(k−3)x+k. Distinct real roots require (k−3)²−4k=(k−1)(k−9)>0, so k<1 or k>9. The least positive integer allowed is 10.
questions.hint: Require a positive quadratic discriminant.

questions.stem: For positive integers, f(n)=2·4·⋯·(n−3)(n−1) if n is odd, and 1·3·⋯·(n−3)(n−1) if n is even. Find f(n+2)f(n+1).
questions.solution: The two products contain, respectively, the odd and even integers from 1 through n+1. Their product therefore contains every integer from 1 to n+1 exactly once.
questions.hint: Interleave the two double-factorial products.
questions.notes: Empty products for the smallest n are taken as 1.

questions.stem: Let x₀=1 and xₙ=Σⱼ₌₀ⁿ⁻¹xⱼ for n≥1. Find Σⱼ₌₀^∞1/xⱼ.
questions.solution: The recurrence gives x₁=1, and xₙ₊₁=xₙ+Σⱼ₌₀ⁿ⁻¹xⱼ=2xₙ for n≥1. Thus xₙ=2ⁿ⁻¹ for n≥1, so the sum is 1+Σₙ≥₁2¹⁻ⁿ=1+2=3.
questions.hint: Find the ratio between consecutive terms after x₁.

questions.stem: For what p does (p²−16)x²−(p²−4p)x+(p²−5p+4)=0 have more than two solutions in x?
questions.solution: A polynomial of degree at most two has more than two distinct roots only if all coefficients vanish. The first requires p=±4; the second excludes −4. At p=4 the constant also vanishes, so the identity 0=0 holds for all x.
questions.hint: Require all coefficients to vanish.

questions.stem: The square has vertices A,B,C,D in cyclic order. With four labeled colours, how many ways can the vertices be coloured so adjacent vertices have different colours?
questions.solution: Choose A in 4 ways and B in 3. If C matches A (1 choice), D has 3 choices. If C differs from A and B (2 choices), D has 2 choices. Total 4·3·(1·3+2·2)=84.
questions.hint: Split according to whether opposite vertices A,C match.

questions.stem: Players P₁,P₂ alternately fill unfilled entries of an even n×n real matrix, n≥2, starting with P₁. After all entries are filled, P₁ wins if the determinant is nonzero; otherwise P₂ wins. Which is true?
questions.solution: Pair rows (1,2),(3,4),…. Whenever P₁ fills an entry, P₂ fills the same column in its paired row with the same value. The counterpart is always empty, because completed entries occur in pairs after every P₂ turn. The final matrix has identical paired rows and zero determinant.
questions.hint: Use a copying strategy that forces equal rows.

questions.stem: Ms. A earns Rs. 25,000 in period 1 and Rs. 15,000 in period 2. Mr. B earns Rs. 15,000 and Rs. 30,000 respectively. Both can borrow at interest 200% and lend at interest 0%. They like consumption in both periods and choose on their budget frontiers. Write both budget constraints and draw their frontiers in the same figure, with $C_1$ and $C_2$ in thousands of rupees on the horizontal and vertical axes.
questions.solution:
Measure money in thousands, so each income pair is a point in the consumption plane. Lending moves the consumer northwest from that point at slope -1 because its gross return is 1. Borrowing moves southeast at slope -3 because the 200% interest rate means three units must be repaid per unit borrowed. Thus the budget is a kinked line, not a single line based on one average rate. To find an intercept, set the other period’s consumption to zero in the appropriate segment.

For income $(a,b)$ in thousands, saving $a-C_1\geq0$ yields $C_2=b+a-C_1$, while borrowing $C_1-a\geq0$ requires repayment $3(C_1-a)$, yielding $C_2=b-3(C_1-a)$. Feasible consumption lies on or below the piecewise frontier in the nonnegative quadrant.

Plot A through $(0,40),(25,15),(30,0)$ and B through $(0,45),(15,30),(25,0)$. Their frontiers intersect at $(17.5,22.5)$.
questions.hint: Separate the saving and borrowing segments.
questions.solutionOriginal: For income $(a,b)$ in thousands, saving $a-C_1\geq0$ yields $C_2=b+a-C_1$, while borrowing $C_1-a\geq0$ requires repayment $3(C_1-a)$, yielding $C_2=b-3(C_1-a)$. Feasible consumption lies on or below the piecewise frontier in the nonnegative quadrant. Plot A through $(0,40),(25,15),(30,0)$ and B through $(0,45),(15,30),(25,0)$. Their frontiers intersect at $(17.5,22.5)$.

solutionSteps.title: Set up the reasoning
solutionSteps.body: Measure money in thousands, so each income pair is a point in the consumption plane. Lending moves the consumer northwest from that point at slope -1 because its gross return is 1. Borrowing moves southeast at slope -3 because the 200% interest rate means three units must be repaid per unit borrowed. Thus the budget is a kinked line, not a single line based on one average rate. To find an intercept, set the other period’s consumption to zero in the appropriate segment.

solutionSteps.title: Work through the calculation
solutionSteps.body:
For income $(a,b)$ in thousands, saving $a-C_1\geq0$ yields $C_2=b+a-C_1$, while borrowing $C_1-a\geq0$ requires repayment $3(C_1-a)$, yielding $C_2=b-3(C_1-a)$. Feasible consumption lies on or below the piecewise frontier in the nonnegative quadrant.

Plot A through $(0,40),(25,15),(30,0)$ and B through $(0,45),(15,30),(25,0)$. Their frontiers intersect at $(17.5,22.5)$.

questions.stem: Ms. A earns Rs. 25,000 in period 1 and Rs. 15,000 in period 2. Mr. B earns Rs. 15,000 and Rs. 30,000 respectively. Both can borrow at interest 200% and lend at interest 0%. They like consumption in both periods and choose on their budget frontiers. B borrows Rs. 5,000 in period 1. Give an example of a consumption profile which, if chosen by A, proves their preferences differ, with explanation.
questions.answer: For example A choosing $(C_1,C_2)=(15,25)$ thousand rupees.
questions.solution:
The question asks for a choice inconsistent with common preferences, so comparing numerical incomes is insufficient. Use revealed preference: a consumer cannot select a bundle while strictly preferring another affordable one. B’s observed borrowing gives the concrete bundle (20,15). A can afford a bundle that dominates it, while some of A’s potential frontier choices are affordable to B. That creates a contradiction if those choices are attributed to the same monotone preferences.

B chooses $(20,15)$. A can afford $(20,20)$, which strictly dominates B's choice, so A's chosen bundle must be strictly preferred to $(20,15)$.

But $(15,25)$ is strictly inside B's budget (at $C_1=15$ B can consume $C_2=30$). Thus if A chose $(15,25)$ and both had the same monotonic preferences, B would have available a strictly preferable bundle to his chosen one, a contradiction.

The same revealed-preference argument applies to any A frontier choice with $C_1\leq17.5$.

questions.stem: Ms. A earns Rs. 25,000 in period 1 and Rs. 15,000 in period 2. Mr. B earns Rs. 15,000 and Rs. 30,000 respectively. Both can borrow at interest 200% and lend at interest 0%. They like consumption in both periods and choose on their budget frontiers. Now A and B have the same preferences and B borrows Rs. 5,000. (i) [6 marks] If A lends in period 1, find the maximum lending consistent with common preferences. (ii) [6 marks] Is B better off than A?
questions.answer: (i) Lending must be strictly below Rs. 7,500 (supremum Rs. 7,500). (ii) A is strictly better off than B.
questions.solution:
Both budgets intersect at the point where A’s lending segment meets B’s borrowing segment:

$$40-x=75-3x\quad\Longrightarrow\quad(x,y)=(17.5,22.5).$$

Common preferences and B’s observed choice rule out not only points strictly inside B’s budget but also this intersection, because A strictly prefers her optimum to B’s bundle. That is why the restriction on A’s lending is strict. A bound that can be approached is a supremum; it must not be reported as an attained maximum.

B chooses $b=(20,15)$ in thousands. A can afford $(20,20)$, so monotonicity implies her chosen bundle $a$ is strictly preferred to $b$.

If A lends, her choice is $(x,40-x)$ with $x\leq25$. Such a bundle is feasible for B whenever $x\leq17.5$: below 15 it lies below B's saving frontier, and from 15 onward $40-x\leq75-3x$ exactly when $x\leq17.5$.

Common preferences therefore require $x>17.5$, otherwise B could choose a bundle strictly preferred to $b$. Thus saving $25-x<7.5$ thousand.

The common frontier point at 17.5 is also ruled out, so the bound is strict; the source's word maximum should be read as supremum. The earlier comparison already proves A strictly better off.

No attained maximum under the stated monotonicity: Rs. 7,500 is a strict upper bound/supremum, not an admissible maximum.

questions.stem: An exchange economy has two agents, one unit each of goods $X,Y$, and allocations $(X_1,Y_1),(X_2,Y_2)$ summing to $(1,1)$. Utilities are $u_1=X_1Y_1$ and $u_2=2X_2+Y_2$. Describe all Pareto-efficient allocations.
questions.answer: In agent 1 coordinates: $Y_1=2X_1$, $0\leq X_1\leq1/2$, or $Y_1=1$, $1/2\leq X_1\leq1$.
questions.solution:
Use agent 1’s coordinates x,y; agent 2 then obtains utility $3-2x-y$. Holding agent 2 exactly indifferent is equivalent to holding the linear resource cost $2x+y=t$ fixed. Efficiency requires giving agent 1 the largest product xy affordable at each such cost. This converts the two-agent problem into a constrained one-agent problem. The usual tangency gives y=2x only until y reaches its upper bound 1; after that a boundary segment completes the contract curve.

Fix agent 2's utility, equivalently the resource cost $t=2X_1+Y_1\in[0,3]$. Efficiency maximizes $X_1Y_1$ subject to this cost and $0\leq X_1,Y_1\leq1$.

The unconstrained maximizer has $Y_1=2X_1$, hence $X_1=t/4,Y_1=t/2$ for $t\leq2$. For $t\geq2$, the upper bound $Y_1=1$ binds and $X_1=(t-1)/2$.

These maximizers, including both endpoints, trace the stated frontier. Any other allocation permits higher utility for agent 1 at unchanged utility for agent 2.

questions.stem: An exchange economy has two agents, one unit each of goods $X,Y$, and allocations $(X_1,Y_1),(X_2,Y_2)$ summing to $(1,1)$. Utilities are $u_1=X_1Y_1$ and $u_2=2X_2+Y_2$. An allocation is envy-free if $u_1(X_1,Y_1)\geq u_1(X_2,Y_2)$ and $u_2(X_2,Y_2)\geq u_2(X_1,Y_1)$. (i) [6 marks] Are all efficient allocations envy-free, and are all envy-free allocations efficient? Prove or give counterexamples. (ii) [6 marks] Describe all envy-free allocations.
questions.answer: Both implications are false. Envy-free set: $0\leq x,y\leq1$, $x+y\geq1$, $2x+y\leq3/2$, where $(x,y)=(X_1,Y_1)$.
questions.solution:
Envy uses each agent’s own utility to evaluate both bundles; one must not compare the two agents’ utility numbers with each other. With agent 1 receiving (x,y), her comparison is between xy and $(1-x)(1-y)$. Agent 2 compares $2(1-x)+(1-y)$ with $2x+y$. Simplify these separately before intersecting their regions. To disprove either proposed implication, one valid allocation is enough; no general converse theorem can replace checking the examples.

(i) Giving everything to agent 1 is efficient but agent 2 envies her. Equal division $(1/2,1/2)$ is envy-free but inefficient: for small $\epsilon>0$, replace agent 1's bundle by $(1/2-\epsilon,1/2+2\epsilon)$.

Agent 2's utility stays fixed while agent 1's product rises by $\epsilon/2-2\epsilon^2>0$. (ii) Agent 1's no-envy inequality is $xy\geq(1-x)(1-y)$, equivalent to $x+y\geq1$.

Agent 2's is $2(1-x)+(1-y)\geq2x+y$, equivalent to $2x+y\leq3/2$. Intersect these with the unit square; the triangle has vertices $(0,1),(1/4,1),(1/2,1/2)$.

questions.stem: An exchange economy has two agents, one unit each of goods $X,Y$, and allocations $(X_1,Y_1),(X_2,Y_2)$ summing to $(1,1)$. Utilities are $u_1=X_1Y_1$ and $u_2=2X_2+Y_2$. Each agent is endowed with half a unit of each good. Prove without direct computation that a competitive equilibrium allocation is Pareto efficient and envy-free.
questions.answer: Equal incomes imply no envy; local nonsatiation and competitive optimization imply Pareto efficiency.
questions.solution:
Equal endowments give equal wealth at every common equilibrium price vector. The agents’ tastes can differ, but the set of bundles each can afford is the same. Consequently, if one preferred the other’s chosen bundle, that agent would have failed to maximize utility. Efficiency uses a different argument: any Pareto improvement would require strictly more total expenditure than the unchanged value of aggregate resources. Keeping these two arguments separate explains both conclusions without solving demands.

At common prices both agents have the same wealth, since their endowments coincide. Each can therefore afford the other's equilibrium bundle.

Individual optimality implies neither strictly prefers the other's bundle, establishing envy-freeness. For efficiency, suppose a feasible allocation made everyone weakly better off and someone strictly better off.

Optimality and local nonsatiation require each weakly better bundle to cost at least that agent's wealth, and any strictly better bundle to cost strictly more. Summing would exceed the value of total endowments, contradicting feasibility and market clearing.

This is the first welfare theorem.

questions.stem: Two flatmates play their own music on one CD player while both are present. Let $m_i\geq0$ be music played by $i$ and $Y_i$ money holding. Utility is $u_i=8m_i-2m_i^2-\frac32m_j^2+Y_i$, $i\ne j$. How much music does each play independently? Find efficient music levels and compare, with economic intuition.
questions.solution:
The externality is the term involving the other person’s music. It is constant in an individual’s own maximization and is therefore ignored privately, but a planner counts it. Summing the two utilities counts every music benefit once and every external cost once:

$$u_1+u_2=8(m_1+m_2)-\frac72(m_1^2+m_2^2)+Y_1+Y_2.$$

Money transfers between the flatmates cancel from this sum. Comparing private and social first-order conditions isolates the source of excessive music.

Each ignores the effect on the other and sets $8-4m_i=0$, giving 2. With transfers, efficiency maximizes total utility, whose music component is $8(m_1+m_2)-(7/2)(m_1^2+m_2^2)$.

FOCs $8-7m_i=0$ give $8/7$. Independent play is excessive because its negative external effect is ignored.

questions.stem: Two flatmates play their own music on one CD player while both are present. Let $m_i\geq0$ be music played by $i$ and $Y_i$ money holding. Utility is $u_i=8m_i-2m_i^2-\frac32m_j^2+Y_i$, $i\ne j$. Individual 2 considers giving a headphone to individual 1 and gets no utility from gift-giving itself. What is the maximum price she would pay?
questions.solution:
A headphone is useful to the giver because it removes the neighbour’s noise, not because it changes the giver’s own preferred amount of music. First obtain the neighbour’s unregulated choice m=2. Its harm to the giver is $\frac32m^2$. Since utility is linear in money with coefficient one, the utility gain and maximum payment have the same numerical value. A payment above the avoided harm would make the giver worse off.

Without headphones, individual 1 plays $m_1=2$, causing individual 2 loss $(3/2)2^2=6$. A headphone removes this external harm while leaving her own optimal music unchanged. Quasilinearity makes the avoided utility loss her maximum monetary willingness to pay.

questions.stem: Two flatmates play their own music on one CD player while both are present. Let $m_i\geq0$ be music played by $i$ and $Y_i$ money holding. Utility is $u_i=8m_i-2m_i^2-\frac32m_j^2+Y_i$, $i\ne j$. A headphone costs Rs. 11. Should the flatmates jointly buy it, split the cost equally and commit to listening only via the headphone?
questions.answer: Yes; each gains Rs. 0.50 in utility-equivalent terms.
questions.solution:
The relevant comparison is each person’s utility before and after the agreement, not whether the headphone costs less than one person’s willingness to pay for the entire purchase. Joint purchase removes both external harms and splits the cost. Each person still selects m=2 because own-music preferences are unchanged. Compare the six-unit harm avoided by each person with their individual contribution 11/2; the commitment matters because it prevents one person from continuing to impose noise.

Each initially receives own-music benefit $8(2)-2(2)^2=8$ minus harm 6, giving 2 before money holdings. Headphones preserve own benefit 8, remove harm 6 and cost each $11/2=5.5$, giving 2.5. Hence each gains 0.5, so the arrangement is mutually beneficial.

questions.stem: Two flatmates play their own music on one CD player while both are present. Let $m_i\geq0$ be music played by $i$ and $Y_i$ money holding. Utility is $u_i=8m_i-2m_i^2-\frac32m_j^2+Y_i$, $i\ne j$. Now individual 1 owns the player and can prohibit individual 2 from playing. She offers a take-it-or-leave-it contract: she plays $\bar m_1$, individual 2 may play $\bar m_2$ for payment $T$. If rejected, individual 1 chooses her music unilaterally and individual 2 plays none. Find optimal $\bar m_1,\bar m_2,T$ and explain.
questions.solution:
The owner chooses both music levels and the transfer, so this is not the original noncooperative music game. First determine what person 2 receives if she rejects: person 1 plays m1=2 and person 2 cannot play. This outside option determines the largest acceptable payment. Once that binding participation constraint is substituted, the owner maximizes total surplus and extracts the other person’s gain through T. Property rights affect the division of gains, while unrestricted bargaining restores efficient music levels.

Upon rejection, individual 1 chooses 2 and individual 2's utility excluding money is $-6$. Acceptance requires $8m_2-2m_2^2-(3/2)m_1^2-T\geq-6$.

Individual 1 sets the largest acceptable transfer $T=8m_2-2m_2^2-(3/2)m_1^2+6$. Her resulting utility is total music surplus plus 6, so she chooses the efficient levels $m_1=m_2=8/7$.

Substitution gives $T=64/7-32/7+6=74/7$. She captures the gains over individual 2's outside option.

This assumes acceptance at indifference and no binding transfer/wealth constraint.

questions.stem: An employer produces $Y=F(N^A+N^B)$, where $F$ is concave and $N^i$ is employment from province $i=A,B$. Output price is $P$ and wages are $W^A,W^B$, all taken as given. Write profit as a function of both employment quantities.
questions.solution:
Output depends on total employment because the two provincial labour inputs are perfect production substitutes. Revenue is the same whichever province supplies a given unit of labour, but wage payments may differ. Write both wage bills separately rather than replacing them by one average wage:

questions.stem: An employer produces $Y=F(N^A+N^B)$, where $F$ is concave and $N^i$ is employment from province $i=A,B$. Output price is $P$ and wages are $W^A,W^B$, all taken as given. The employer maximizes $u(\pi(N^A,N^B),N^A,N^B)$, with $u_\pi>0$, direct $u_A>0$ and direct $u_B<0$. Write the first-order conditions assuming an interior solution.
questions.solution:
The employer values both money profit and the composition of employment. Therefore differentiating profit alone would omit the discrimination terms. For each province, the chain rule has two contributions:

$$\frac{dU}{dN^i}=u_\pi\frac{\partial\pi}{\partial N^i}+u_i.$$

The derivative ui is the direct taste effect while holding profit fixed. Set the total derivative to zero only under the stated interior assumption; with a zero employment corner, use the corresponding inequality instead.

By the chain rule, differentiate utility with respect to each employment quantity, including both its profit effect and its direct taste effect. Evaluate $F\prime$ at $N^A+N^B$ and all utility partials at the chosen allocation. These are necessary interior FOCs; the stated monotonicity conditions alone do not guarantee sufficiency.

questions.stem: An employer produces $Y=F(N^A+N^B)$, where $F$ is concave and $N^i$ is employment from province $i=A,B$. Output price is $P$ and wages are $W^A,W^B$, all taken as given. The employer maximizes $u(\pi(N^A,N^B),N^A,N^B)$, with $u_\pi>0$, direct $u_A>0$ and direct $u_B<0$. Do employees from both provinces receive the same wage in equilibrium? If not, who receives more and by how much?
questions.answer: With both types employed at an interior optimum, $W^A-W^B=(u_A-u_B)/u_\pi>0$.
questions.solution:
Both types have the same value marginal product $PF'$, so a wage difference cannot be attributed to production technology here. Divide the two hiring conditions by the positive marginal utility of profit, putting all direct preference effects into money units. The preferred A worker is worth an extra $u_A/u_\pi$, while the disliked B worker must be cheaper by $-u_B/u_\pi$. Subtracting cancels the common productivity term and gives the wage gap.

Rearranging the FOCs gives $W^A=PF\prime+u_A/u_\pi$ and $W^B=PF\prime+u_B/u_\pi$. Thus preferred A workers receive more despite identical marginal productivity; the wage gap is the difference in direct utility effects divided by marginal utility of profit. The claim is conditional on both labour types being hired at an interior optimum; corner hiring or market supply conditions not supplied cannot be characterized from these FOCs alone.

questions.stem: Utility $u(c,l)$ is concave, increasing in consumption $c$ and decreasing in working hours $l$. Wage is $w>0$, gross earnings $y=wl$, consumption price $p>0$, and time endowment $\bar L$. Write utility as $u(c,y/w)$. In figures use earnings $y$ horizontally and consumption $c$ vertically. Derive the slope of an indifference curve in the earnings–consumption plane.
questions.solution:
Gross income y and working time l are different variables: one extra income unit requires only 1/w additional work units. That conversion must appear in the derivative. Holding utility constant gives

$$0=u_c\,dc+u_l\,dl=u_c\,dc+\frac{u_l}{w}\,dy.$$

Since consumption is good and labour is bad, the resulting slope is positive. A downward-sloping leisure–consumption indifference curve should not be copied into this earnings–consumption diagram, whose horizontal good is costly work rather than leisure.

Along an indifference curve, $0=du=u_c\,dc+(u_l/w)\,dy$. Rearranging gives the slope. Its positivity reflects that more labour earnings require additional consumption to compensate for the disutility of working.
questions.hint: Totally differentiate utility while holding its level fixed.

Wage is $w>0$, gross earnings $y=wl$, consumption price $p>0$, and time endowment $\bar L$. Write utility as $u(c,y/w)$. In figures use earnings $y$ horizontally and consumption $c$ vertically. questions.answer: Budget $c=y/p$, $0\leq y\leq w\bar L$; an interior optimum satisfies $-u_l/(wu_c)=1/p$.
questions.solution:
Here the horizontal axis is earnings, so budget feasibility is $pc\leq y$, not the more familiar leisure budget. The feasible frontier rises from the origin and stops at the time-endowment bound $y=w\bar L$. At an interior tangency, the consumption required to compensate an additional earnings unit equals the consumption that unit can actually buy. Concavity helps verify maximization, but a tangency beyond the allowed time interval is not feasible and must be replaced by a boundary comparison.

Draw the budget segment from $(0,0)$ to $(w\bar L,w\bar L/p)$ with slope $1/p$. Indifference curves slope upward; higher utility lies above a given curve at fixed earnings.

The highest attainable curve is tangent to the segment at an interior solution, equating its slope with $1/p$. Equivalently $-u_l/u_c=w/p$.

A corner at the time bound or zero work must be checked when the tangency is not feasible; positive consumption is not otherwise guaranteed by the stated general utility.

questions.stem: Utility $u(c,l)$ is concave, increasing in consumption $c$ and decreasing in working hours $l$. Wage is $w>0$, gross earnings $y=wl$, consumption price $p>0$, and time endowment $\bar L$. Write utility as $u(c,y/w)$. In figures use earnings $y$ horizontally and consumption $c$ vertically. Experiment 1: increase $w$. In the same figure show which budget or indifference curves change and compare the old and new earnings and consumption, with explanation.
questions.answer: The budget ray’s slope stays $1/p$ and its endpoint extends. Preferences in the earnings–consumption coordinates change; welfare weakly rises, but earnings/hours need not move unambiguously under the stated general assumptions.
questions.solution:
Increasing the wage does not rotate the budget ray c=y/p in these particular axes. Instead it changes how much work is represented by each horizontal coordinate y and extends the maximum feasible earnings. Thus the preference map changes even though preferences over actual consumption and work have not changed. For a fixed displayed earnings bundle, the worker now needs fewer hours. This coordinate effect is essential to drawing the comparative-static diagram correctly.

At the same $(y,c)$, a larger wage requires less labour $l=y/w$, so utility rises. The budget segment remains on $c=y/p$, extending to $y=w_{new}\bar L$.

Draw the new indifference map using $u(c,y/w_{new})$, with the new optimum where its relevant curve touches the budget. The old labour–consumption choice can be replicated with less labour or can finance more consumption, so welfare weakly improves.

In labour–leisure coordinates the wage increase has opposing substitution and income effects on labour. Neither normality nor restrictions on the cross partial are stated, so a universal movement of earnings or consumption should not be asserted; along the budget earnings and consumption move together.

Under customary additional normality assumptions their standard directions can be shown in the diagram.

questions.stem: Utility $u(c,l)$ is concave, increasing in consumption $c$ and decreasing in working hours $l$. Wage is $w>0$, gross earnings $y=wl$, consumption price $p>0$, and time endowment $\bar L$. Write utility as $u(c,y/w)$. In figures use earnings $y$ horizontally and consumption $c$ vertically. Experiment 2: instead impose a proportional income tax $\tau$, so disposable income is $(1-\tau)y$. Draw old and new optima and show the budget and preference changes, comparing outcomes.
questions.answer: For $0<\tau<1$, budget rotates down to $c=(1-\tau)y/p$; the preference map is unchanged and welfare weakly falls. Labour/earnings response is generally ambiguous.
questions.solution:
A proportional earnings tax leaves the number of hours needed to earn gross y unchanged, so it leaves the indifference map unchanged. It reduces how much consumption that gross income purchases:

$$c=\frac{(1-\tau)y}{p}.$$

That is a clockwise budget rotation at the origin, unlike the wage experiment’s change in the preference map. Welfare falls because every newly feasible bundle was already feasible before. An assertion about the direction of labour must separately resolve income and substitution effects.

In the same earnings–consumption axes, retain the original indifference curves because $w$ is unchanged. Rotate the budget segment clockwise through the origin from slope $1/p$ to $(1-\tau)/p$, keeping horizontal endpoint $w\bar L$.

An interior new optimum satisfies $-u_l/(wu_c)=(1-\tau)/p$. The feasible consumption set contracts, so utility cannot rise.

The lower net wage produces opposing substitution and income effects on labour; without further preference restrictions its sign, and thus gross earnings, is ambiguous. Consumption also has no universal sign under the fully general preferences stated.

questions.stem: An agent lives three periods and consumes only in periods 2 and 3, with utility $\log c_2+\beta\log c_3$, $0<\beta<1$. She borrows education expenditure $e\geq0$ in period 1 at interest $r>0$. Period-2 earnings are $wh(e)$, with fixed $w>0$ and increasing concave $h$. She repays $(1+r)e$, saves $s$, and in period 3 consumes saving plus interest, with no other income. Write separate period-2 and period-3 budget constraints.
questions.solution:
Education debt is incurred in period 1 but repaid in period 2. It therefore reduces the resources available for period-2 consumption and saving by the full gross repayment, not merely the interest. There is no period-3 wage and no bequest, so all accumulated saving is consumed then. These timing facts lead to two separate equations; combining them too early can hide the education repayment or count saving twice.

Period-2 resources are labour earnings minus repayment of the education loan. They finance consumption and saving. In period 3, gross saving returns are the sole resources and are consumed.

questions.stem: An agent lives three periods and consumes only in periods 2 and 3, with utility $\log c_2+\beta\log c_3$, $0<\beta<1$. She borrows education expenditure $e\geq0$ in period 1 at interest $r>0$. Period-2 earnings are $wh(e)$, with fixed $w>0$ and increasing concave $h$. She repays $(1+r)e$, saves $s$, and in period 3 consumes saving plus interest, with no other income. Write the first-order conditions for utility maximization.
questions.solution:
Saving shifts resources between consumption dates, whereas education changes the total resources available at those dates. Differentiate the reduced objective with respect to these two choices separately. The education condition compares marginal earnings $wh'(e)$ with the gross repayment on one more borrowed education unit, 1+r. The saving condition compares marginal utilities across periods. An education equality is only an interior condition; a person who optimally buys no education satisfies the boundary inequality.

Differentiate the reduced objective. Its derivative with respect to $e$ is $[wh\prime(e)-(1+r)]/c_2$, giving the education condition.

With respect to $s$ it is $-1/c_2+\beta/s=0$, equivalent to the Euler condition since $c_3=(1+r)s$. At $e=0$, replace equality by $wh\prime(0)\leq1+r$ when the derivative exists.

Strict concavity of $h$ gives uniqueness of an interior education optimum; mere concavity allows multiple maximizers.

questions.stem: An agent lives three periods and consumes only in periods 2 and 3, with utility $\log c_2+\beta\log c_3$, $0<\beta<1$. She borrows education expenditure $e\geq0$ in period 1 at interest $r>0$. Period-2 earnings are $wh(e)$, with fixed $w>0$ and increasing concave $h$. She repays $(1+r)e$, saves $s$, and in period 3 consumes saving plus interest, with no other income. Derive the ratio $c_2/c_3$ in terms of the parameters.
questions.solution:
A saved unit costs one consumption unit in period 2 and delivers 1+r consumption units in period 3. The saving Euler equation must include both that gross return and the preference discount beta:

$$\frac1{c_2}=\beta(1+r)\frac1{c_3}.$$

Solving for the ratio gives $c_2/c_3=1/[\beta(1+r)]$. If beta(1+r)=1 the path is flat; otherwise the ratio shows the direction of the optimal tilt. Education affects the consumption level through earnings but cancels from this intertemporal ratio.

The saving FOC gives $s=\beta c_2$. Period-3 consumption is $(1+r)s=\beta(1+r)c_2$. Divide to obtain the stated ratio.

She borrows education expenditure $e\geq0$ in period 1 at interest $r>0$. Period-2 earnings are $wh(e)$, with fixed $w>0$ and increasing concave $h$. She repays $(1+r)e$, saves $s$, and in period 3 consumes saving plus interest, with no other income. Explain how optimal investment in education depends on $\beta$.
questions.answer: The education optimum is independent of $\beta$ under the stated unconstrained borrowing setup.
questions.solution:
The absence of beta from the interior education condition is a useful clue, but a complete argument should cover all feasible education choices, including a boundary. Optimize saving conditional on education and substitute it back into utility. Education then appears only through a positive multiple of the logarithm of net resources. Since multiplying an objective by a positive constant does not change its maximizers, patience changes the consumption split but not the set of optimal education investments.

Let net period-2 resources be $M(e)=wh(e)-(1+r)e$. Conditional optimal saving is $s=\beta M(e)/(1+\beta)$ and $c_2=M(e)/(1+\beta)$.

Substitution into utility gives $(1+\beta)\log M(e)$ plus terms independent of $e$. Thus every $\beta>0$ gives the same education argmax, maximizing net resources.

At an interior optimum $wh\prime(e)=1+r$, which has no $\beta$ term. Greater patience changes saving and the consumption split rather than education.

questions.stem: A street is $[0,1]$. Three agents live at $x_1\leq x_2\leq x_3$ and a hospital is located at $p\in[0,1]$. Find the square-optimal $p$ minimizing $\sum_{i=1}^3(x_i-p)^2$.
questions.solution:
Squared distance is smooth in the hospital location, so differentiate the sum rather than considering three separate nearest-agent cases. Each resident contributes 2(p-xi) to the derivative:

$$\frac{d}{dp}\sum_i(p-x_i)^2=2\left(3p-\sum_i x_i\right).$$

The positive second derivative proves global uniqueness. Finally check feasibility: the arithmetic mean lies between the smallest and largest residence, so it belongs to the allowed street interval without needing a constrained boundary correction.

questions.stem: A street is $[0,1]$. Three agents live at $x_1\leq x_2\leq x_3$ and a hospital is located at $p\in[0,1]$. An absolute-optimal $p$ minimizes $\sum_{i=1}^3|x_i-p|$. (i) Show an optimum lies in $[x_1,x_3]$. (ii) Derive an absolute-optimal location.
questions.solution:
Absolute distance has corners, so a geometric cancellation is more convenient than differentiating through them. A location outside the extreme residences can move toward all residents at once, reducing every distance. Inside their interval, the distances to the two extreme residents add to their fixed separation. Only distance to the middle resident remains variable. This explains why the median minimizes absolute distances, whereas the preceding squared-distance problem selected the mean.

questions.stem: On street $[0,1]$, $n$ agents have ordered locations $x_1\leq\cdots\leq x_n$, where $n$ is odd. Derive $p$ minimizing $\sum_{i=1}^n|x_i-p|$.
questions.solution:
Let n=2m+1 and pair the outermost residents, then the next outermost, leaving the central resident unpaired. For any pair a≤b,

$$|p-a|+|p-b|\geq b-a,$$

with equality exactly when p lies between a and b. The median belongs to every paired interval simultaneously, achieving every pair’s lower bound and making the unpaired distance zero. Any other p leaves the central distance positive without reducing any pair below its lower bound.

Pair the extreme locations: $(x_1,x_n),(x_2,x_{n-1}),\ldots$. Each pair contributes at least its separation, with equality whenever $p$ lies between that pair.

All these intervals contain the median $m=x_{(n+1)/2}$. The unpaired median contributes $|p-m|$, which is zero only at $m$.

Thus the median uniquely minimizes total distance.

questions.stem: Two random variables $x_1,x_2$ are uniformly drawn from $[0,1]$. For $p\in[0,1]$, define $G(p)=p\,\mathbb P[p\geq\max(x_1,x_2)]$. Derive $G(p)$ with clear explanation.
questions.solution:
The event that the maximum is at most p means that both draws are at most p. This is an intersection of events, not a union. For independent uniform draws its probability is the area of the square [0,p]² inside the unit square, namely p². The extra prefactor p in the definition of G then gives p³. If independence is not part of the draw mechanism, a joint distribution is needed; marginal uniformity alone does not justify multiplying probabilities.

The event is $x_1\leq p$ and $x_2\leq p$. Each has probability $p$; independence makes the joint probability $p^2$.

Multiplication by $p$ gives $p^3$. If only uniform marginals are intended, the answer is instead $pH(p,p)$ for the joint CDF $H$, and is not determined: perfectly comoving uniforms give $p^2$, for example.

A correct plot needs both the endpoints and the curvature, not just a line joining (0,0) and (1,1). Under independent draws, $G'(p)=3p^2$ is nonnegative and $G''(p)=6p$ is positive away from zero. questions.stem: Two random variables $x_1,x_2$ are uniformly drawn from $[0,1]$. For $p\in[0,1]$, define $G(p)=p\,\mathbb P[p\geq\max(x_1,x_2)]$. Is $G$ convex or concave in $p$? Explain.
questions.answer: Under independent draws, strictly convex and not concave on $[0,1]$.
questions.solution:
Convexity concerns the slope’s direction of change; it does not mean the function must be decreasing or have an interior minimum on the domain. Here $G(p)=p^3$ is increasing and its slope $3p^2$ is itself increasing. questions.stem: Let $X\subset\mathbb R$ and $f:X\to X$. For continuous $f$ and $X=[0,1]$, use the intermediate value theorem to show there exists $x^*\in X$ with $f(x^*)=x^*$.
questions.solution:
The desired fixed point is a zero of the difference between the graph of f and the 45-degree line. Define h(x)=f(x)-x. Because f is a self-map of the closed interval, its value at the left endpoint cannot lie below that endpoint and its value at the right endpoint cannot lie above it. These opposite weak signs, together with continuity, are exactly the conditions the intermediate value theorem needs; handle a zero endpoint directly.

Define $h(x)=f(x)-x$, continuous on $[0,1]$. Since $f$ maps the interval into itself, $h(0)=f(0)\geq0$ and $h(1)=f(1)-1\leq0$. If either is zero it is a fixed point; otherwise the intermediate value theorem supplies an interior zero.

questions.stem: Let $X\subset\mathbb R$ and $f:X\to X$. Determine whether fixed-point existence is guaranteed in each case, giving proof or counterexample: (i) $X=(0,1)$ and $f$ continuous; (ii) $X=[0,1]\cup[2,3]$ and $f$ continuous; (iii) $X=[0,1]$ but $f$ not continuous.
questions.answer: No guarantee in any of the three cases.
questions.solution:
A single counterexample suffices to show that existence is not guaranteed. Each example must still satisfy all the conditions that remain: the open-interval example must map into the open interval, the disconnected-domain example must be continuous relative to that domain, and the discontinuous example must still map into [0,1]. Checking these requirements is as important as observing that no algebraic fixed point belongs to the permitted set.

(i) $f(x)=(1+x)/2$ is a continuous self-map of $(0,1)$ whose only algebraic fixed point is 1, excluded from the domain. (ii) Set $f(x)=x+2$ on $[0,1]$ and $f(x)=x-2$ on $[2,3]$.

This is continuous on the disconnected domain, maps it into itself and has no fixed point. (iii) Set $f(0)=1$ and $f(x)=0$ for $x>0$.

It maps $[0,1]$ into itself, is discontinuous and never equals $x$.

questions.stem: Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be independent and identically distributed random variables with a uniform distribution on $(0,\theta]$, where $\theta>0$. Write down their joint probability density function.
questions.solution:
For one observation, a uniform density is constant 1/theta only inside its theta-dependent support. Independence lets us multiply densities, but it does not remove those support restrictions. The joint density is therefore theta to the power -n on the n-dimensional box where every observation lies in (0,theta], and zero everywhere else. Writing the indicator explicitly is crucial for the likelihood maximization in the next part.

Each marginal density is $\theta^{-1}$ on $(0,\theta]$ and zero otherwise. Independence makes the joint density the product of the marginal densities.

questions.stem: Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be independent and identically distributed random variables with a uniform distribution on $(0,\theta]$, where $\theta>0$. Given observations $x_1,\ldots,x_n$, find the value of the unknown $\theta$ that maximizes the joint density (the maximum likelihood estimate).
questions.solution:
The observed largest value is a lower bound on theta: a proposed uniform distribution whose upper endpoint lies below an observed point cannot have generated the sample. Above that bound the likelihood decreases as theta increases. Therefore first restrict the parameter to its feasible range, then choose its smallest value. Differentiating theta to the power -n and looking for a zero derivative would miss the optimum because the maximum lies at the support boundary.

For valid positive observations let $m=\max_i x_i$. The likelihood is zero for $\theta<m$ and equals $\theta^{-n}$ for $\theta\geq m$. The latter is strictly decreasing, so its maximum occurs at the smallest admissible value, $m$.

questions.stem: Consider $f(x,y)=x^2+y^2-2x$. (i) Find its maximum over $2x^2+3y^2-2x\leq100$. (ii) Find its minimum over $2x^2+3y^2-2x\geq100$.
questions.solution:
Both questions are global optimization problems, so a stationary point alone would not prove the answer. Introduce $h=2x^2+3y^2-2x$ and use identities that give valid bounds throughout the entire feasible set:

$$f=\frac h2-x-\frac{y^2}{2},\qquad h=3f+4-(x-2)^2.$$

For the first region the constraint also bounds x through a quadratic inequality. For the second region a nonnegative square gives a lower bound on f. In each case an explicit feasible equality point proves the bound is attained.

Put $h=2x^2+3y^2-2x$. If $h\leq100$, then $2x^2-2x\leq100$, hence $x\geq a=(1-\sqrt{201})/2$.

Therefore $f=h/2-x-y^2/2\leq50-a$, with equality at $(a,0)$. For (ii), the identity $h=3f+4-(x-2)^2$ gives $3f=h-4+(x-2)^2\geq96$.

Equality requires $h=100,x=2$, giving $y^2=32$.
questions.hint: Express one quadratic as a multiple of the other plus squares.

questions.stem: A tournament has $n$ players, one match between every pair and no ties. A player's score is her number of wins. Order the scores $s_1\geq\cdots\geq s_n$. For $2\leq k\leq n$, show that $s_1+\cdots+s_k\geq k(k-1)/2$.
questions.solution:
Every tournament match creates exactly one win and no draw. Focus on the matches played entirely within the chosen k players. There are k(k-1)/2 such unordered pairs, and whichever player wins, that win is counted in the same sum of k scores. Matches against players outside the group add a nonnegative number of further wins. In fact this counting bound holds for any k players, even before ordering scores.

The matches among these $k$ players contribute exactly $\binom{k}{2}$ wins to their combined score. Wins against the remaining players can only add to this total.
questions.hint: Count the matches within the chosen set.

questions.stem: A tournament has $n$ players, one match between every pair and no ties. A player's score is her number of wins. Order the scores $s_1\geq\cdots\geq s_n$. Suppose $n>3$ and players 1, 2 and 3 beat every player in $\{4,\ldots,n\}$. Find $s_4+\cdots+s_n$.
questions.solution:
Separate the bottom group’s matches into two types. Against the top three, the assumption forces every bottom player to lose, so these matches contribute zero. Against each other, every bottom-group match contributes exactly one win to the group total. There are n-3 players in this smaller tournament, so its internal pair count gives the entire requested sum; no individual pattern of winners needs to be specified.

The bottom $n-3$ players obtain no wins against the top three. Every match among the bottom players contributes exactly one win to their total, so their total score equals the number of those matches.

questions.stem: A tournament has $n$ players, one match between every pair and no ties. A player's score is her number of wins. Order the scores $s_1\geq\cdots\geq s_n$. Suppose $s_n=s_0$, $s_{n-1}=s_0+1$, $s_{n-2}=s_0+2$, where $s_0$ is a positive integer and $n\geq3$. Show $s_0\leq(n-2)(n-3)/(2n)$.
questions.solution:
All tournament scores sum to the number of matches, n(n-1)/2. Ordering gives a lower bound on each of the top n-2 scores: each is at least the third-smallest score s0+2. Keep the two lowest scores separately rather than assigning them the same lower bound:

$$\sum_{j=1}^n s_j\geq(n-2)(s_0+2)+(s_0+1)+s_0.$$

Comparing this lower bound with the fixed total and solving for s0 yields the inequality.

The top $n-2$ scores are each at least $s_0+2$. Thus $\binom n2=\sum s_j\geq(n-2)(s_0+2)+(s_0+1)+s_0=ns_0+2n-3$. Rearranging gives the result.

questions.stem: A tournament has $n$ players, one match between every pair and no ties. A player's score is her number of wins. Order the scores $s_1\geq\cdots\geq s_n$. Suppose $s_j-s_{j+1}=1$ for $j=1,\ldots,n-1$. Find the score vector and identify whom each player $j$ beats.
questions.solution:
Consecutive differences of one force the score list to be an arithmetic progression, but its starting value must still be found. The total-win identity determines the lowest score to be zero. The score pattern then also determines all match outcomes: the top player has to beat everyone, the next has already lost that one match and must beat all remaining players, and so on. This inductive argument establishes the orientation, not merely the numerical scores.

Writing $s_j=s_n+n-j$ and summing gives $ns_n+n(n-1)/2=n(n-1)/2$, hence $s_n=0$. Player 1 has $n-1$ wins and beats everyone.

Player 2 has already lost to player 1 and must beat all remaining players to attain $n-2$ wins. Induction gives the stated orientation for every pair.

A quadratic with a positive leading coefficient is bounded below; it need not take every real value just because x itself can be any real number. Complete the square to identify its exact range:

$$P_2(x)=(x-1)(x-2)=\left(x-\frac32\right)^2-\frac14.$$

Any k below -1/4 is therefore a counterexample. The question asks whether a universal assertion is true, so one excluded value of k already disproves it.

An odd-degree polynomial with positive leading coefficient has opposite signs of divergence at the two ends of the real line. For any target k, choose one sufficiently negative and one sufficiently positive x so that the polynomial lies below and above k respectively. Continuity on the finite interval between them guarantees a crossing. The argument uses the degree’s parity and does not require finding the cubic’s roots explicitly.

The monic cubic is continuous, tends to $-\infty$ as $x\to-\infty$ and to $+\infty$ as $x\to+\infty$. The intermediate value theorem gives every real value $k$.

questions.stem: Let $P_n(x)=(x-1)(x-2)\cdots(x-n)$, where $n>1$ is an integer. Determine whether the statement is true or false, with proof or counterexample: For every $k<0$ and every odd integer $n>1$, $P_n(x)=k$ has a real solution.
questions.solution:
The claim fixes an odd n but permits any negative target. A monic odd-degree product tends to minus infinity on the left and plus infinity on the right, so its image is all real numbers. Choose endpoints that bracket the particular negative target and use continuity. This proof also shows the stronger statement for all real k; it is the odd-degree condition that matters, not whether the displayed individual linear factors are negative at a specific point.

For odd $n$, the continuous monic polynomial tends to opposite infinite limits at the two ends of the real line. It therefore attains every real value, including every negative $k$.

questions.stem: Let $P_n(x)=(x-1)(x-2)\cdots(x-n)$, where $n>1$ is an integer. Determine whether the statement is true or false, with proof or counterexample: For every $k<0$, there exists an even positive integer $n$ such that $P_n(x)=k$ has a real solution.
questions.solution:
Unlike the previous part, n may now be chosen to suit k, but must be even. Evaluate every product at the same point x=3/2. For even n there are an odd number of negative factors, so the product is negative, and adding later factor pairs makes its magnitude grow without bound. Once it lies below the desired k, use the nearby fixed root x=1 to bracket k by continuity. This avoids the false claim that any particular even-degree polynomial covers all negative numbers.

For even $n$, $P_n(3/2)=-\frac14\prod_{j=3}^n(j-3/2)$. Its magnitude is at least $\frac14(3/2)^{n-2}$, which tends to infinity along even $n$.

Choose even $n$ with $P_n(3/2)\leq k<0=P_n(1)$. Continuity between 1 and $3/2$ provides a solution.

questions.stem: An economy has mass 1 of identical agents with $u(c,l)=c^\alpha(24-l)^{1-\alpha}$, $0<\alpha<1$, and technology $c=Al$, $A>0$. Both markets are perfectly competitive, with wage $w>0$ and commodity price $p>0$. (i) [13 marks] Set up household utility maximization, its first-order conditions, and derive $l^S,c^D$. (ii) [7 marks] Set up firm profit maximization and derive $l^D,c^S$. (iii) [5 marks] Determine the competitive equilibrium allocation and $w/p$.
questions.solution:
Three separate pieces are needed for a competitive equilibrium: household optimization, firm optimization, and market clearing. The household chooses a split between labour and leisure, using wages to finance consumption. The firm has linear technology, so its profit is linear in hired labour and may be unbounded away from the equilibrium price ratio. Do not force an interior firm first-order condition at arbitrary prices. Market clearing selects the zero-profit relative price and the particular employment level that households supply.

(i) Maximize $\alpha\ln c+(1-\alpha)\ln(24-l)$ subject to $pc\leq wl$, $0\leq l\leq24$. FOCs give $\alpha/c=\lambda p$ and $(1-\alpha)/(24-l)=\lambda w$, with $pc=wl$.

Hence $l^S=24\alpha$ and $c^D=24\alpha w/p$. (ii) The firm maximizes $(pA-w)l$ over $l\geq0$.

If $w/p>A$, choose $l^D=c^S=0$; if $w/p=A$, any $l\geq0$ with $c^S=Al$ maximizes profit; if $w/p<A$, profit is unbounded and no finite maximizing demand exists. (iii) Positive finite clearing requires $w/p=A$.

Taking $l^D=l^S=24\alpha$ then clears both markets and yields the stated consumption.

questions.stem: An economy has mass 1 of identical agents with $u(c,l)=c^\alpha(24-l)^{1-\alpha}$, $0<\alpha<1$, and technology $c=Al$, $A>0$. Both markets are perfectly competitive, with wage $w>0$ and commodity price $p>0$. Define Pareto efficiency for this economy and find a Pareto efficient allocation of consumption and labour, with explanation.
questions.solution:
An efficient allocation uses the production frontier because extra feasible consumption is desirable. Substitute c=Al into the household’s utility and maximize directly over labour. This asks which technologically feasible choice gives the highest utility, independently of whether a market decentralizes it. The log transformation preserves the positive utility ranking and makes the labour–leisure tradeoff transparent. Verify that the maximizer is strictly between zero and the 24-hour time endowment.

An allocation is Pareto efficient if no feasible allocation makes some agent better off without making another worse off. In the representative identical-agent allocation, maximize utility subject to $c\leq Al$.

Monotonicity makes $c=Al$. The log objective is $\alpha\ln(Al)+(1-\alpha)\ln(24-l)$; its derivative vanishes at $\alpha/l=(1-\alpha)/(24-l)$, so $l=24\alpha$.

Strict concavity establishes the maximum and efficiency. The competitive allocation attains it.

questions.stem: Ms. A receives an annual pension of Rs. 100,000 and harvests 2,000 kg of rice. She spends income on rice $x$ and other expenses $y$, whose price is 1. Last year rice cost Rs. 20/kg and she consumed exactly 2,000 kg. This year rice costs Rs. 30/kg. She has standard convex preferences. Without utility functions or indifference curves: (i) [7 marks] does rice consumption increase, decrease or remain unchanged? (ii) [5 marks] is she better or worse off?
questions.answer: Rice consumption weakly decreases; she is weakly better off.
questions.solution:
Rice is both a consumption good and an endowment. The price increase therefore changes the value of wealth as well as the price paid; treating pension alone as her fixed income would give the wrong budget. Both budget lines pass through her old no-trade choice. Above 2000 kg, the new budget offers less other consumption than the old one; below it, the new budget offers more. Revealed preference excludes a move to the dominated, net-buying side while guaranteeing the old utility is still attainable.

The old budget is $y\leq100000+20(2000-x)$; the new one is $y\leq100000+30(2000-x)$. The old choice $(2000,100000)$ remains available.

Every new feasible bundle with $x>2000$ lies strictly inside the old budget, and hence cannot outperform the old optimum under standard monotonic preferences. Thus the new optimum cannot have $x>2000$.

Because the old optimum is still feasible, the new optimum is weakly preferred to it. A strict fall and strict welfare gain require additional smoothness/strictness conditions; convexity alone allows the same choice.

questions.stem: Mr. B has standard convex preferences, endowment $(e_x,e_y)>0$, no other income, and price of $y$ equal to 1. At price $p_x$ for $x$, he neither buys nor sells $x$. Now selling $x$ earns $p_L<p_x$ and buying $x$ costs $p_H>p_x$. (i) [8 marks] Write and draw the new budget constraint, labelling important points. (ii) [10 marks] Will he buy or sell $x$, and how much? Explain without utility functions or indifference curves.
questions.answer: Piecewise budget through $(e_x,e_y)$ with slopes $-p_L,-p_H$; no trade.
questions.solution:
The consumer’s no-trade endowment remains feasible after the buying–selling spread is introduced. Any sale now earns less than before, and any purchase now costs more. Thus the new budget frontier lies strictly inside the old one at every trade quantity and touches it only at the endowment. No utility formula or indifference-curve drawing is needed: since the endowment was optimal in the larger old set, shrinking the set around it cannot make a formerly available trade preferable.

The frontier is $y=e_y+p_L(e_x-x)$ for $0\leq x\leq e_x$, and $y=e_y-p_H(x-e_x)$ for $x\geq e_x$ with $y\geq0$. Draw a kink at $(e_x,e_y)$, vertical intercept $e_y+p_Le_x$ and horizontal intercept $e_x+e_y/p_H$.

The left segment has slope $-p_L$ and the right has slope $-p_H$. Every new feasible trade bundle was strictly inside the old budget $y\leq e_y+p_x(e_x-x)$.

The old optimum, the endowment itself, remains available; no trade bundle can improve on it. Thus purchases and sales are both zero.

questions.stem: A moneylender has funds for one loan $L$ and faces two applicants, one safe and one risky, whose types he cannot identify. The safe project returns $R>L$ for sure; the risky project returns $R\prime>R$ with probability $p$ and zero otherwise. Borrowers repay only when returns cover repayment; each knows his type. If both apply, the lender selects one by a fair coin. He lends his own resources and has zero opportunity cost. Find the highest interest rates $i_s$ and $i_r$ at which safe and risky borrowers respectively want a loan. Who is willing to pay more?
questions.solution:
The borrower compares the loan repayment with project receipts, not with the lender’s expected repayment. With limited liability the risky borrower repays only after success. Her surplus conditional on success falls to zero when repayment reaches the high project return. Multiplication by the success probability changes the expected surplus magnitude but does not change the zero-surplus cutoff, provided that probability is positive. This explains why the risky type can accept a higher interest rate.

The safe borrower receives nonnegative project surplus if $(1+i)L\leq R$; the risky borrower receives nonnegative expected surplus $p[R\prime-(1+i)L]$ when success permits repayment. These yield the cutoff rates.

Since $R\prime>R$, the risky type accepts the higher rate. This uses the usual convention that a zero-surplus borrower applies at the cutoff.

These yield the cutoff rates. Since $R\prime>R$, the risky type accepts the higher rate. This uses the usual convention that a zero-surplus borrower applies at the cutoff.

questions.stem: A moneylender has funds for one loan $L$ and faces two applicants, one safe and one risky, whose types he cannot identify. The safe project returns $R>L$ for sure; the risky project returns $R\prime>R$ with probability $p$ and zero otherwise. Borrowers repay only when returns cover repayment; each knows his type. If both apply, the lender selects one by a fair coin. He lends his own resources and has zero opportunity cost. The lender maximizes expected profit. Argue that his effective choice is between $i_s$ and $i_r$, excluding rates below both, above both or strictly between them.
questions.answer: Conditional on making a loan, only $i_s$ and $i_r$ need consideration; no lending must also be considered.
questions.solution:
Within a range of interest rates that leaves the applicant pool unchanged, a higher rate increases expected receipts. This pushes candidate lending optima to the two participation cutoffs. But that argument only compares rates at which lending occurs. A profit-maximizing lender can also keep the principal and earn zero; it is essential to retain that option because the next part subtracts the original loan amount as a real cost.

Below $i_s$, both types apply, and raising the rate to $i_s$ raises repayment without changing the pool. For $i_s<i<i_r$, only the risky type applies; raising the rate to $i_r$ raises expected repayment.

Above $i_r$, neither applies, so the lender makes no loan and earns zero. Thus among positive lending outcomes only the two cutoffs are candidates.

However, if both cutoff profits are negative, a rate above $i_r$ and no lending is optimal. The unqualified source assertion therefore omits a necessary outside option.

Source claim omits no-lending outside option despite subtracting principal L in part (c). Cutoff applications require an indifference convention.

The safe project returns $R>L$ for sure; the risky project returns $R\prime>R$ with probability $p$ and zero otherwise. Borrowers repay only when returns cover repayment; each knows his type. If both apply, the lender selects one by a fair coin. He lends his own resources and has zero opportunity cost. Show that expected profit at $i_r$ is $p(1+i_r)L-L$, and derive expected profit at $i_s$.
questions.solution:
Construct expected receipts in the order events occur. First the rate determines who applies. If both apply, the fair coin selects the borrower type. Conditional on selecting a risky borrower, the project succeeds only with probability p. The principal L is paid out in every actual lending event, irrespective of type or success, so subtract it once after averaging receipts. This separates selection risk from default risk and prevents double-counting the loan cost.

At $i_r$, only the risky borrower applies and repayment $R\prime$ occurs with probability $p$, so expected net profit is $pR\prime-L=p(1+i_r)L-L$. At $i_s$, both apply.

With probability $1/2$ the loan goes to the safe type, repaying $R$ for sure; with probability $1/2$ it goes to the risky type, repaying $R$ with probability $p$. Expected repayment is $(1+p)R/2$; subtract principal $L$.

If both apply, the lender selects one by a fair coin. He lends his own resources and has zero opportunity cost. Credit rationing means some willing borrowers cannot obtain loans and lenders do not raise rates to eliminate excess demand. Explain the assertion that a credit-rationing equilibrium occurs when $p<R/(2R\prime-R)$.
questions.answer: The inequality makes $i_s$ preferable to $i_r$. For actual lending also require $(1+p)R/2\geq L$.
questions.solution:
The printed inequality compares the profit from lending to the mixed pool with lending only to the risky applicant. To call the resulting choice an equilibrium with rationing, it must also be optimal to lend at all. A numerical counterexample is an appropriate way to expose a missing participation condition: if both candidate loan profits are negative, their ranking is irrelevant because the lender selects zero lending and nobody receives a loan.

Comparing cutoff profits gives $\Pi_s>\Pi_r$ iff $(1+p)R/2>pR\prime$, equivalently $p<R/(2R\prime-R)$. At $i_s$, both applicants want the loan but only one is funded; raising the rate selects only the risky type and reduces expected profit.

This is rationing provided lending is preferred to keeping funds, requiring $\Pi_s\geq0$. The source inequality alone is insufficient: $L=100,R=110,R\prime=200,p=0.1$ satisfies it but gives $\Pi_s=-39.5$ and $\Pi_r=-80$, so no lending is optimal.

Strictly positive $\Pi_s$ avoids indifference with no lending.

questions.stem: Identical agents of mass 1 live for youth and old age. Utility is $\log c_{1,t}+\beta\log c_{2,t+1}$, $0<\beta<1$. questions.stem: Identical agents of mass 1 live for youth and old age. Utility is $\log c_{1,t}+\beta\log c_{2,t+1}$, $0<\beta<1$. Each supplies one unit of labour when young, earning $w_t$, and faces $c_{1,t}+s_t=w_t$, $c_{2,t+1}=(1+r_{t+1})s_t$. Write the first-order conditions, derive saving, and explain its dependence on the interest rate.
questions.answer: $s_t=\beta w_t/(1+\beta)$, independent of $r_{t+1}$ holding wages fixed.
questions.solution:
The second-period utility term decomposes as $\beta\ln[(1+r)s]=\beta\ln(1+r)+\beta\ln s$. Holding the wage fixed, a change in the return adds a constant to utility, leaving the saving argmax unchanged. The first-order condition formalizes this exact cancellation of income and substitution effects for logarithmic utility. It is not a general claim that saving never responds to interest, nor that consumption in old age is return-independent.

The derivative is $-1/(w_t-s_t)+\beta/s_t=0$. Thus $\beta(w_t-s_t)=s_t$, giving the answer.

The second derivative is $-1/(w_t-s_t)^2-\beta/s_t^2<0$, so the solution is the unique maximum. Since the interest rate appears only in the additive term $\beta\log(1+r_{t+1})$, it does not affect the optimal saving amount for positive gross return.

questions.stem: Identical agents of mass 1 live for youth and old age. Utility is $\log c_{1,t}+\beta\log c_{2,t+1}$, $0<\beta<1$. Each supplies one unit of labour when young, earning $w_t$, and faces $c_{1,t}+s_t=w_t$, $c_{2,t+1}=(1+r_{t+1})s_t$. Production is $Y_t=AK_t^\alpha L_t^{1-\alpha}$, $0<\alpha<1$, competitive factor prices and full capital depreciation. Derive the equilibrium wage $w_t$ in terms of $K_t$, remembering $L_t=1$.
questions.solution:
The competitive wage is the marginal product of an additional unit of labour, holding capital fixed. Differentiate the aggregate production function before substituting the equilibrium labour supply:

$$\frac{\partial Y}{\partial L}=(1-\alpha)AK^\alpha L^{-\alpha}.$$

Because population has mass one and everyone supplies one labour unit, aggregate L equals one. This is why the result can be expressed solely in K without an additional population denominator.

The competitive wage equals $\partial Y_t/\partial L_t=(1-\alpha)AK_t^\alpha L_t^{-\alpha}$. Unit labour supply makes $L_t=1$, giving the result.

A fraction $0<\theta<1$ of aggregate savings is lost during financial intermediation. Derive $K_{t+1}$ as a function of $K_t$.
questions.solution:
Capital depreciates fully, so next period does not inherit a surviving fraction of today’s installed capital. Its whole capital stock must come from current saving that reaches production. First derive the saving share of wages, then the wage share of output, then apply the fraction 1-theta that survives intermediation. With a unit population individual and aggregate saving coincide, avoiding any extra population multiplier.

With full depreciation, next period capital equals newly intermediated saving: $K_{t+1}=(1-\theta)s_t$. Using $s_t=\beta w_t/(1+\beta)$ and $w_t=(1-\alpha)AK_t^\alpha$ yields the stated law of motion.

Production is $Y_t=AK_t^\alpha L_t^{1-\alpha}$, $0<\alpha<1$, competitive factor prices and full capital depreciation. A fraction $0<\theta<1$ of aggregate savings is lost during financial intermediation. Derive steady-state capital.
questions.solution:
A steady state is a fixed point of the capital transition, not a point where the current saving amount is zero. For positive K, dividing $K=BK^\alpha$ by $K^\alpha$ gives $K^{1-\alpha}=B$. The exponent is positive because 0<alpha<1, so there is a unique positive solution. The zero fixed point is a separate boundary: it is mathematically stationary but cannot support the positive consumptions required by logarithmic utility.

Write the law of motion as $K_{t+1}=BK_t^\alpha$. A positive fixed point satisfies $(K^*)^{1-\alpha}=B$, hence the formula. Zero is also a mathematical fixed point if the zero-capital boundary is admitted, but does not permit positive log consumption.

Production is $Y_t=AK_t^\alpha L_t^{1-\alpha}$, $0<\alpha<1$, competitive factor prices and full capital depreciation. A fraction $0<\theta<1$ of aggregate savings is lost during financial intermediation. How does steady-state capital depend on financial-sector inefficiency $\theta$?
questions.solution:
The parameter theta is a loss rate, so the effective-investment coefficient is proportional to 1-theta. Raising theta must therefore lower the positive capital fixed point. Logarithmic differentiation is convenient because it turns the steady-state power into a constant multiplier. The elasticity of K with respect to surviving efficiency 1-theta is $1/(1-\alpha)$, showing that the long-run capital response magnifies the direct investment loss.

Take logs of the positive steady state: $\log K^*=[\log(1-\theta)+\log(\beta(1-\alpha)A/(1+\beta))]/(1-\alpha)$. Differentiating gives the stated derivative. More intermediation losses reduce effective investment and steady-state capital.

questions.stem: Consider $Y=K^\alpha(AL)^{1-\alpha}$, $\alpha\in[0,1]$, $\dot K=sY-\delta K$, $s,\delta\in[0,1]$, population growth $n>0$, $Z=K/(AL)$, and output per worker $Q=AZ^\alpha$. Initially technology grows at the constant rate $g>0$. Derive $\dot Z/Z$.
questions.solution:
Z divides capital by effective labour AL, so its proportional growth is capital growth minus both population and technology growth. Capital growth itself is saving times the output–capital ratio, less depreciation. Express that ratio in Z before combining the terms. Forgetting the technology term would treat Z as capital per person rather than capital per effective worker and would give the wrong steady-state dilution rate.

Log differentiation gives $\dot Z/Z=\dot K/K-\dot A/A-\dot L/L$. Since $Y/K=Z^{\alpha-1}$, substitute $\dot K/K=sZ^{\alpha-1}-\delta$, technology growth $g$ and population growth $n$. The ratio formula is for $Z>0$.

questions.stem: Consider $Y=K^\alpha(AL)^{1-\alpha}$, $\alpha\in[0,1]$, $\dot K=sY-\delta K$, $s,\delta\in[0,1]$, population growth $n>0$, $Z=K/(AL)$, and output per worker $Q=AZ^\alpha$. Instead assume learning by doing, $\dot A=\gamma Q$. Show $\dot Z=(s-\gamma Z)Z^\alpha-(\delta+n)Z$.
questions.solution:
The new assumption specifies a change in the technology level, not a constant technology growth rate. Divide $\dot A=\gamma Q$ by A and use $Q=AZ^\alpha$ to obtain the endogenous rate $\dot A/A=\gamma Z^\alpha$. Only then substitute it into the growth accounting identity for Z. Multiplying by Z explains the additional power in the technology-dilution term $-\gamma Z^{1+\alpha}$.

Learning implies $\dot A/A=\gamma Q/A=\gamma Z^\alpha$. Replace $g$ by this endogenous technology growth rate in $\dot Z/Z=sZ^{\alpha-1}-\delta-n-g$ and multiply by $Z$ to obtain the required law.
