questions.stem: Consider $Y=K^\alpha(AL)^{1-\alpha}$, $\alpha\in[0,1]$, $\dot K=sY-\delta K$, $s,\delta\in[0,1]$, population growth $n>0$, $Z=K/(AL)$, and output per worker $Q=AZ^\alpha$. With $\dot A=\gamma Q$, draw a diagram describing growth dynamics, with $Z$ on the horizontal axis and suitable functions on the vertical axis.
questions.answer: For $0<\alpha<1$, $s>0$, $\gamma>0$, the unique positive steady state solves $s=\gamma Z^*+(\delta+n)(Z^*)^{1-\alpha}$ and is stable.
questions.solution:
For a phase diagram it is useful to divide the capital law by positive Z. Plot the investment-to-capital term on one side and effective dilution on the other:

$$\frac{\dot Z}{Z}=sZ^{\alpha-1}-[\delta+n+\gamma Z^\alpha].$$

In the interior parameter case the first curve decreases while the second increases, giving exactly one positive intersection. Read stability from the sign of their vertical gap. Endpoint exponents change these curve shapes, so they must be handled separately rather than copied into the same strict-monotonicity proof.

Let $d=\delta+n>0$. For $Z>0$, plot $sZ^{\alpha-1}$ (strictly decreasing from infinity to zero) and $d+\gamma Z^\alpha$ (strictly increasing from $d$).

Their unique intersection is $Z^*$. The vertical gap equals $\dot Z/Z$: arrows point right below $Z^*$ and left above it.

Equivalently plot $(s-\gamma Z)Z^\alpha$ and $dZ$. Endpoints require separate treatment: for $\alpha=0$, $\dot Z=s-(\gamma+d)Z$ with $Z^*=s/(\gamma+d)$; for $\alpha=1$, $\dot Z=(s-d)Z-\gamma Z^2$, so a positive steady state exists only if $s>d$, at $(s-d)/\gamma$.

If $s=0$, no positive steady state exists.

questions.stem: Consider $Y=K^\alpha(AL)^{1-\alpha}$, $\alpha\in[0,1]$, $\dot K=sY-\delta K$, $s,\delta\in[0,1]$, population growth $n>0$, $Z=K/(AL)$, and output per worker $Q=AZ^\alpha$. With learning by doing, does a higher investment rate raise the balanced-growth rate, unlike the model without learning? Use the diagram to distinguish level effects and growth effects.
questions.answer: For $0<\alpha<1$, $s>0$, $\gamma>0$, higher $s$ raises $Z^*$ and per-worker growth $g^*=\gamma(Z^*)^\alpha$.
questions.solution:
Learning makes the technology growth rate depend on the steady-state capital intensity. Thus a permanent change in saving can change a growth rate even after the adjustment of Z is complete. With exogenous technology, the same saving change shifts only the level of capital per effective worker. In either model the level may grow during transition, so distinguish a temporary acceleration from a changed balanced-growth rate. The alpha=0 endpoint removes the channel because technology growth then equals gamma whatever Z is.

In the phase diagram, raising $s$ shifts the declining curve $sZ^{\alpha-1}$ up, moving its intersection with $d+\gamma Z^\alpha$ right. Since $s=\gamma Z^*+d(Z^*)^{1-\alpha}$ has a strictly increasing right-hand side, $Z^*$ rises.

On the balanced-growth path, $Z$ is constant, so $Q=AZ^\alpha$ grows at $g^*=\gamma(Z^*)^\alpha$, which therefore rises. Aggregate output grows at $n+g^*$.

In the standard interior Solow model with exogenous $g$, changing $s$ changes the level but not long-run per-worker growth $g$. Endpoint qualifications: at $\alpha=0$, $g^*=\gamma$ is independent of $s$; at $\alpha=1$, a positive steady state requires $s>d$ and then $g^*=s-d$.

The usual exogenous-growth Solow comparison also presumes $0<\alpha<1$.

questions.stem: A household lives from $t$ through $T$, maximizes $\sum_{n=t}^T\beta^{n-t}\ln c_n$ with $0<\beta<1$, earns income $y_n$, saves $s_n$, and faces constant gross return $R=1+r>0$. Its only activities are consuming and saving. Write all period budget constraints and combine them into a lifetime budget constraint with consumption on the left and income on the right.
questions.solution:
Savings links consecutive period budgets. To add those budgets without counting the same transferred resources twice, discount period n by $R^{n-t}$. The discounted saving carried out of one period then cancels the discounted saving returned next period. Initial wealth and terminal assets are boundary terms, so specify them explicitly; zero initial wealth and no bequest are what make the final constraint contain only income and consumption.

Set initial wealth $s_{t-1}=0$ and terminal saving $s_T=0$ (no bequest). For each $n=t,\ldots,T$, the budget is $c_n+s_n=y_n+Rs_{n-1}$.

Divide by $R^{n-t}$ and sum. Intermediate saving terms cancel telescopically, and the endpoint terms vanish, giving the present-value budget in the answer.

Its only activities are consuming and saving. Find the condition relating $\beta$ and $r$ under which optimal consumption is constant, $\widetilde C$, in every period.
questions.solution:
The optimum equates marginal utility per unit of present-value cost across dates. A future consumption unit costs 1/R of a current unit but is weighted by beta in utility. With logarithms this yields a constant growth factor beta R between adjacent consumption levels. Flat consumption is therefore a special balance of patience and market return, not an automatic consequence of concavity or a constant interest rate.

The first-order conditions for the lifetime present-value budget are $\beta^{n-t}/c_n=\lambda R^{-(n-t)}$. Taking consecutive ratios gives $c_{n+1}=\beta R c_n$. Hence a positive constant consumption path requires and, for the unconstrained optimum, is implied by $\beta R=1$.
questions.hint: Use the Euler equation.

questions.stem: A household lives from $t$ through $T$, maximizes $\sum_{n=t}^T\beta^{n-t}\ln c_n$ with $0<\beta<1$, earns income $y_n$, saves $s_n$, and faces constant gross return $R=1+r>0$. Its only activities are consuming and saving. Assume $\beta R=1$. (i) [3 marks] Calculate the change in constant consumption from a transitory income change in period $t$. (ii) [3 marks] Calculate the change from a transitory income change in period $t+k$ only.
questions.answer: Let $H=\sum_{j=0}^{T-t}R^{-j}$. For income increase $\Delta$, (i) $\Delta\widetilde C=\Delta/H$; (ii) $\Delta\widetilde C=R^{-k}\Delta/H$.
questions.solution:
When consumption is flat, one extra unit of that constant level costs the annuity factor $H=\sum_{j=0}^{T-t}R^{-j}$ in present value. Convert an income shock to the same units before dividing by H. A current shock adds its full amount to wealth; an equally sized later shock adds only its discounted value. This distinguishes the size of an income change from the smaller consumption response financed over all remaining periods.

Under constant consumption, the lifetime budget becomes $H\widetilde C=\sum_{j=0}^{T-t}R^{-j}y_{t+j}$. A one-period income change at $t$ raises its right side by $\Delta$, while one at $t+k$ raises it by $R^{-k}\Delta$. Divide each change by the unchanged annuity factor $H$.
questions.hint: Convert the income shock to present value.
questions.notes: Source introductory sentence calls c_n income although the objective and subsequent questions use it as consumption. Solutions use c_n as consumption, zero initial wealth, no bequest and unrestricted intertemporal borrowing/lending.

questions.stem: A household lives from $t$ through $T$, maximizes $\sum_{n=t}^T\beta^{n-t}\ln c_n$ with $0<\beta<1$, earns income $y_n$, saves $s_n$, and faces constant gross return $R=1+r>0$. Its only activities are consuming and saving. Assume $\beta R=1$. For the same permanent income change in every remaining period, calculate the change in $\widetilde C$ and compare it with a transitory change in period $t$ only.
questions.answer: A permanent increase $\Delta$ raises constant consumption by $\Delta$, versus $\Delta/H$ for a current transitory increase.
questions.solution:
A permanent income increase is an annuity itself, so its present value contains exactly the same H factor as a permanent consumption increase. Those factors cancel. For a one-period shock the income present value contains only one term, so spreading it over the rest of life gives a smaller response. The distinction vanishes only in the last period, when there is no future over which to spread resources.

The permanent change raises lifetime present-value resources by $\Delta\sum_{j=0}^{T-t}R^{-j}=\Delta H$. Dividing by the annuity factor raises consumption by exactly $\Delta$. For more than one remaining period, $H>1$, so this exceeds the consumption response $\Delta/H$ to the same-sized one-period increase; with only one remaining period they coincide.
questions.hint: The permanent shock affects every term of the annuity.

questions.stem: If the nth partial sum of Σₙ₌₁^∞aₙ is sₙ=(2n²+2)/(3n²+1), then the infinite series is
questions.solution: A series sums to the limit of its partial sums. Dividing numerator and denominator by n² gives sₙ→2/3.
questions.hint: Take the limit of the partial sums.

questions.stem: From a sample of size n, OLS regression of y on x gives intercept a and slope b. Which statement is false?
questions.answer: Both C and D are generally false as printed; D is the intended contrast
questions.solution: OLS satisfies the normal equations in A and B. It minimizes squared residuals, but the minimum need not equal zero, contrary to the trailing “=0” in C. OLS also need not minimize absolute residuals, making D false. For data (−1,1),(0,0),(1,1), OLS fits the constant 2/3 with positive residual sum of squares 2/3.
questions.hint: Distinguish the OLS normal equations from the objective’s minimized value.
questions.notes: Both optimization choices literally end in =0. Without those endings, C describes OLS and D describes least absolute deviations, so intended D would be unique.

questions.stem: Production is z=2x+3y. For what input price ratio pₓ/pᵧ can a cost-minimizing solution for positive output z₀ have x=0?
questions.solution: The cost per output unit is pₓ/2 from x and pᵧ/3 from y. Using only y can minimize cost exactly when pᵧ/3≤pₓ/2, or pₓ/pᵧ≥2/3. At equality every input mix is cost-minimizing.
questions.hint: Compare input cost per unit of output.
questions.notes: The second choice gives the full condition; equality in A is one special case. Positive input prices are implicit.

questions.stem: A number is chosen uniformly from the first billion natural numbers. The probability that its product with its two immediate successors is divisible by 24 is closest to
questions.solution: Three consecutive integers always contain a factor of 3. Modulo 8, n(n+1)(n+2) is divisible by 8 for n≡0,2,4,6,7, five of the eight residues. Since 10⁹ is divisible by 8, the fraction is exactly 5/8.
questions.hint: Check divisibility by 8; divisibility by 3 is automatic.

questions.stem: Each entry of a 2×2 matrix is independently 1 or −1 with equal probability. What is the probability the matrix is singular?
questions.solution: For matrix [[a,b],[c,d]], singularity means ad=bc. The independent products ad and bc are each equally likely ±1, so they agree with probability 1/2.
questions.hint: Compare the two products in the determinant.

questions.stem: How many 3×3 matrices with entries 0 or 1 have exactly one zero in each row and exactly one zero in each column?
questions.solution: The zero positions form a permutation matrix: choose the zero column in the first row in 3 ways, the second in 2, and the last in 1. Total 3!=6.
questions.hint: Match each row to a distinct zero column.

questions.stem: Let f:[0,1]→ℝ be convex with f(0)=0. Which is always true?
options: f may fail differentiability but is continuous
f(x)≥xf′(x) for all x∈[0,1] if differentiable
questions.solution: Convexity need not give continuity at a closed-domain endpoint: f(x)=0 for 0≤x<1 and f(1)=1 is convex and discontinuous at 1. Differentiability is not guaranteed either. For differentiable convex f, the supporting line at x evaluated at 0 gives 0≥f(x)−xf′(x), so the correct inequality is f(x)≤xf′(x), opposite to C. For f=x², C fails.
questions.hint: Check the endpoints and the direction of the supporting-line inequality.

questions.stem: If f:ℝ→ℝ is strictly quasiconcave, which follows?
options: If f is quadratic, its x² coefficient is ≤0
questions.answer: A quadratic f must have a nonpositive quadratic coefficient
questions.solution: A positive quadratic coefficient would give a strict interior minimum; taking two equidistant points around it violates quasiconcavity. A negative coefficient is possible, as with −x², and a nonconstant affine function is also strictly quasiconcave. The exponential is strictly convex and strictly quasiconcave, while −x² is not monotonic.
questions.hint: Test the other claims with monotone functions and a concave quadratic.

questions.solution: Its determinant is 2(2·1−(−1)·1)−1(1·1−(−1)(−1))=6. A nonzero determinant gives full rank 3.
questions.hint: Compute the determinant.

questions.stem: Let V be the real polynomials of degree at most 2. Which definition gives a linear transformation T:V→V?
questions.solution: Differentiation preserves sums and scalar multiplication and lowers degree to at most 1, remaining in V. A does not send zero to zero. B and D can produce degree 3 from a quadratic, so they do not map all V into V.
questions.hint: Check both linearity and the stated codomain.

questions.stem: X takes values only in [0,10], with P(X>5)≤2/5 and P(X<1)≤1/2. Then
questions.solution: At least half the mass lies at X≥1, giving E(X)≥0.5. Also E(X)≤5P(X≤5)+10P(X>5)≤5+5·0.4=7, which is stronger than the listed upper bound 8.5. A fails for equal mass at 0 and 1; B fails for masses 0.6 at 5 and 0.4 at 10.
questions.hint: Bound the expectation separately on the specified events.

questions.stem: For data (−1,1),(0,0),(1,1), the standard deviations of x,y and their correlation are
questions.solution: The means are x̄=0 and ȳ=2/3. Dividing central sums by 3 gives variances 2/3 and 2/9. The cross-product sum is −1/3+0+1/3=0, so covariance and correlation are zero.
questions.hint: Compute the means and central second moments.
questions.notes: Uses the descriptive-data standard deviations with denominator n, as in the printed choices.

questions.stem: Two vaccine firms incur fixed R&D costs f₁,f₂. After R&D, each has a unit manufacturing cost uniformly drawn from [0,1]. Both invest, and the firm with the lowest unit cost supplies the entire one-unit demand. The total expected cost is
questions.answer: f₁+f₂+1/3 if the two cost draws are independent
questions.solution: With independent U[0,1] draws, P(min(c₁,c₂)>t)=(1−t)², so E[min]=∫₀¹(1−t)²dt=1/3 and intended B follows. Independence is not stated. If both costs share the same uniform draw, the minimum instead has mean 1/2, giving A. Marginal uniformity alone cannot identify a unique expected minimum.
questions.hint: The distribution of a minimum depends on the joint distribution.
questions.notes: The source omits independence of cost draws; keep the intended independent-draw answer conditional.

questions.stem: India and China produce shirts and phones using high-skilled and low-skilled labour. Shirts are high-skill intensive; phones low-skill intensive. Technologies are identical. Both have equal low-skilled labour, but India has more high-skilled labour. Which good will India import?
questions.answer: Phones in the standard Heckscher–Ohlin setting
questions.solution: India is relatively abundant in high-skilled labour. Comparative advantage therefore favors its high-skill-intensive shirts; it exports shirts and imports the low-skill-intensive phones.
questions.hint: Match relative factor abundance to factor intensity.
questions.notes: Uses the standard Heckscher–Ohlin assumptions underlying this question.

questions.stem: A duopoly has demand p=10−q and costs 7q₁ and 2q₂. In equilibrium firm 2 charges which price?
questions.solution: Firm 2’s unconstrained monopoly profit is (p−2)(10−p), maximized at p=6. Since 6 is below firm 1’s marginal cost 7, firm 1 cannot profitably undercut it. Thus firm 2 can charge 6 and serve the market. In the standard Cournot model the same price results, with q₁=0,q₂=4.
questions.hint: Check whether the low-cost firm’s monopoly price deters the high-cost firm.
questions.notes: The source does not explicitly name the competition model; Bertrand and standard Cournot both yield the listed answer.

questions.stem: Virat and Mithali initially consume the same rice and milk quantities. Rice’s price falls. Virat then buys less rice and more milk; Mithali buys more of both. Both exhaust their budgets on these goods. Under standard well-behaved preferences, rice for Virat must be a
questions.answer: Giffen good, and therefore also inferior
questions.solution: Virat’s rice demand falls when its own price falls, the defining Giffen response. The substitution effect alone would increase rice consumption, so a sufficiently strong opposing income effect must dominate, implying inferiority. B gives the more specific classification.
questions.hint: Identify the direction of the own-price demand response.
questions.notes: Inferiority in A is also necessary; B is the most specific classification of the described behavior.

questions.stem: If short-run IS–LM equilibrium income is above natural output, output returns to its natural level in the long run via
options: An increase in the price level
A decrease in the interest rate
A downward shift of the consumption function
questions.answer: An increase in the price level
questions.solution: Above-natural output creates upward pressure on wages and prices. With nominal money fixed, a higher price level reduces real balances, shifts LM left, raises interest rates and reduces demand toward natural output.
questions.hint: Track how price adjustment changes real money balances.

questions.stem: If the short-run aggregate supply curve is steep, the Phillips curve will be
questions.solution: A steep SRAS means a given output-gap change causes a large price/inflation response. Through the inverse output–unemployment relation, this corresponds to a large inflation response per unemployment-gap change, hence a steep Phillips curve.
questions.hint: Relate the output gap to the unemployment gap.

questions.stem: There are no capital controls between the US and UK. If the US interest rate exceeds the UK interest rate, which is the standard implication?
options: The dollar is expected to appreciate against the pound
The pound is expected to appreciate against the dollar
The US interest rate is expected to increase
The US interest rate is expected to decrease
questions.answer: The pound is expected to appreciate under uncovered interest parity
questions.solution: Under uncovered interest parity with comparable assets and no risk premium, a higher dollar interest return is offset by expected dollar depreciation. Equivalently the pound is expected to appreciate relative to the dollar.
questions.hint: Compare expected returns in a common currency.
questions.notes: The implication uses the textbook uncovered-interest-parity assumptions; absence of capital controls alone does not establish risk neutrality or zero risk premia.

questions.stem: Countries B,C trade and transact financially only with each other. B imports goods worth 10 million bollars (its currency) from C and has no exports. Which must be true?
options: C is buying assets from B
questions.answer: C acquires claims on B in the standard trade-financing accounting
questions.solution: B’s trade deficit is matched by a financial inflow: C’s export receipts finance its acquisition of B’s assets or claims, including currency claims. C has the corresponding external surplus, and nothing fixes the numerical exchange rate.
questions.hint: Use the balance-of-payments counterpart to a trade deficit.
questions.notes: Uses the usual simplified accounting with no offsetting net transfers or investment-income flows, which the question does not model.

questions.stem: Other things equal, inventory investment is expected to
options: Rise when the real interest rate rises
Be independent of the real interest rate
Fall when the real interest rate rises
Depend only on the change in real GDP
questions.answer: Fall when the real interest rate rises
questions.solution: Holding inventories ties up funds. A higher real interest rate raises their financing and opportunity cost, reducing desired stocks and inventory investment, other things equal.
questions.hint: Treat the interest rate as a cost of holding inventories.

questions.stem: A unit cake is divided between two people, with shares x₁,x₂≥0. Utilities are u₁=x₁ and u₂=x₂+|x₁−x₂|. Which listed division is Pareto optimal?
questions.solution: At (1,0), person 1 already obtains the entire cake; maintaining her utility requires x₁=1 and hence x₂=0, leaving no strict improvement. At the other listed divisions utilities are respectively (1/2,1/2) and (3/4,3/4), both strictly dominated by the utility pair (1,1) at (1,0).
questions.hint: Compare both people’s utility at each listed allocation.

questions.stem: Rohit exhausts his weekly budget on dosas and coffee. In Delhi their prices are equal and he buys (15,35). In Chennai equal prices let him just afford (40,10). In Bangalore one dosa costs twice one coffee and he can just afford (10,20). Where does he prefer to stay?
questions.solution: In Delhi and Chennai the normalized budget set is d+c≤50, so his attainable choices and maximum utility are identical. Bangalore’s budget is 2d+c≤40, a strict subset of d+c≤50 for nonnegative goods. With usual monotone preferences, it cannot improve on Delhi/Chennai.
questions.hint: Write each city’s budget set in comparable quantity units.
questions.notes: Assumes preferences and the relevance of the two consumption goods are unchanged across cities.

questions.stem: In an IS–LM diagram with real interest rate R vertical and output Y horizontal, the central bank fixes R=R̄. The LM curve will
questions.solution: An interest-rate-targeting central bank adjusts money supply to accommodate money demand at its selected interest rate. Consequently every output level is associated with the same targeted rate.
questions.hint: Let money supply adjust to defend the rate target.

questions.stem: Labour supply slopes upward and demand slopes downward. A rigid wage w̄ lies above the market-clearing wage. A reduction in labour demand causes
options: A larger employment reduction than with flexible wages
A smaller employment reduction than with flexible wages
The same employment reduction as with flexible wages
questions.answer: A larger employment reduction in the standard demand-shift comparison
questions.solution: At the rigid wage firms reduce employment along the shift of their demand curve. With flexible wages the demand reduction also lowers the wage, partially cushioning the employment loss through additional demand at the lower wage. Thus wage rigidity amplifies the employment reduction.
questions.hint: Compare fixed-wage adjustment with a fall in the clearing wage.
questions.notes: Uses the standard inward demand shift while the wage remains binding above equilibrium.

questions.stem: Let $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be continuously differentiable with at least three distinct zeros, and let $g(x)=e^{x/2}f(x)$. Prove that $g$ has at least three distinct zeros. [10 marks]
questions.answer: Every zero of $f$ is a zero of $g$; in fact the zero sets coincide.
questions.solution:
Multiplication can remove or introduce zeros only if the multiplying factor can itself vanish or become undefined. Here $e^{x/2}$ is defined and strictly positive at every real x. Therefore

$$g(x)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f(x)=0.$$

The functions have exactly the same zero set, not merely at least the same number of zeros. Choose any three distinct zeros of f and apply this equivalence to each.

Since $e^{x/2}>0$ for every real $x$, $g(x)=e^{x/2}f(x)=0$ iff $f(x)=0$. Thus the three distinct zeros of $f$ remain three distinct zeros of $g$.
questions.hint: The exponential factor never vanishes.

questions.stem: Let $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be continuously differentiable with at least three distinct zeros, and let $g(x)=e^{x/2}f(x)$. Prove that $f+2f'$ has at least two distinct zeros. [20 marks]
questions.answer: Apply Rolle's theorem to $g$ between consecutive zeros.
questions.solution:
The coefficient 2 in f+2f′ suggests differentiating an exponential multiple of f. Indeed,

$$g'(x)=\frac12e^{x/2}[f(x)+2f'(x)].$$

Choose three ordered distinct zeros of g. Rolle’s theorem applies once on the interval between the first two and again between the next two. The two resulting derivative zeros are distinct because the open intervals do not overlap. Since the exponential factor never vanishes, each derivative zero gives a zero of f+2f′.

Choose three distinct zeros $a<b<c$ of $f$, and hence of $g$. Since $g$ is continuously differentiable, Rolle's theorem gives $u\in(a,b)$ and $v\in(b,c)$ such that $g'(u)=g'(v)=0$.

These points are distinct. Differentiating gives $g'(x)=\frac12e^{x/2}[f(x)+2f'(x)]$.

The prefactor is nonzero, so $f(u)+2f'(u)=f(v)+2f'(v)=0$.
questions.hint: Differentiate $e^{x/2}f(x)$ and use Rolle's theorem on two disjoint intervals.

Since $g$ is continuously differentiable, Rolle's theorem gives $u\in(a,b)$ and $v\in(b,c)$ such that $g'(u)=g'(v)=0$. These points are distinct. Differentiating gives $g'(x)=\frac12e^{x/2}[f(x)+2f'(x)]$. The prefactor is nonzero, so $f(u)+2f'(u)=f(v)+2f'(v)=0$.

questions.stem: Find all solutions of $\max(x^2+y^2)$ subject to $x+y\leq1$ and $x,y\geq0$. [12 marks]
questions.answer: Maximum value1, attained only at $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$.
questions.solution:
The feasible region is the closed triangle with vertices (0,0), (1,0) and (0,1). A global inequality is more efficient here than solving unconstrained first-order conditions: nonnegativity makes the cross term 2xy nonnegative, so the sum of squares is no larger than the square of the sum. To identify every optimizer, record when both inequalities become equalities. A maximum value without its equality conditions would not answer the instruction to find all solutions.

For nonnegative $x,y$, $x^2+y^2=(x+y)^2-2xy\leq(x+y)^2\leq1$. Equality requires both $x+y=1$ and $xy=0$, yielding exactly $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$. No other feasible point attains1.
questions.hint: Compare $x^2+y^2$ with $(x+y)^2$ and track equality conditions.

questions.stem: In the fictional puzzle, 1000 senators each bring one bottle of wine to a king. Exactly one bottle is poisoned, indistinguishable in advance. There are10 prisoner taste testers. The poison's binary outcome appears exactly24hours later, and there is time for only one round of tests. How can the poisoned bottle be identified with certainty? [18 marks]
questions.answer: Encode bottle labels in10 binary digits; the10 test outcomes identify the label, since $2^{10}=1024\geq1000$.
questions.solution:
Treat the fictional test results as binary symbols in a one-round information problem. With m independent binary observations there are at most 2^m distinct outcome patterns; identifying one item among 1000 requires at least ten bits because $2^9<1000\leq2^{10}$. Assigning each bottle a unique ten-bit label turns this lower bound into an achievable encoding. The all-zero word is a legitimate code because the puzzle guarantees exactly one marked item.

As an abstract coding problem, label the bottles0 through999 and write each label as a10-bit binary word. Associate one tester with each bit position.

The test for bit position $j$ combines samples from exactly those bottle labels whose $j$th bit is1. In the puzzle's assumptions, after24hours the positive/negative outcome of each test states whether the unique poisoned label has that bit equal to1 or0.

Read the ten outcomes as a binary integer to recover the unique bottle. The all-zero label corresponds to all-negative outcomes, which is still informative because exactly one poisoned bottle is assumed.

Ten bits distinguish1024 possibilities; nine bits distinguish only512, so ten binary tests are also the minimum needed in one round.
questions.hint: Use binary information rather than assigning one tester to one bottle.
questions.notes: Presented strictly as the source fictional binary-coding puzzle; no real-world poison preparation or exposure information is involved.

With m independent binary observations there are at most 2^m distinct outcome patterns; identifying one item among 1000 requires at least ten bits because $2^9<1000\leq2^{10}$. Assigning each bottle a unique ten-bit label turns this lower bound into an achievable encoding. The all-zero word is a legitimate code because the puzzle guarantees exactly one marked item.

solutionSteps.title: Complete the argument
solutionSteps.body:
As an abstract coding problem, label the bottles0 through999 and write each label as a10-bit binary word. Associate one tester with each bit position.

The test for bit position $j$ combines samples from exactly those bottle labels whose $j$th bit is1. In the puzzle's assumptions, after24hours the positive/negative outcome of each test states whether the unique poisoned label has that bit equal to1 or0.

Read the ten outcomes as a binary integer to recover the unique bottle. The all-zero label corresponds to all-negative outcomes, which is still informative because exactly one poisoned bottle is assumed.

Ten bits distinguish1024 possibilities; nine bits distinguish only512, so ten binary tests are also the minimum needed in one round.

questions.stem: Let matrices $A,B$ have a defined product $AB$. Prove that if the columns of $B$ are linearly dependent, then the columns of $AB$ are linearly dependent. [15 marks]
questions.answer: A nonzero vector $z$ satisfying $Bz=0$ also satisfies $(AB)z=0$.
questions.solution:
Linear dependence means that some combination of columns with not-all-zero coefficients vanishes. Collect those coefficients into one vector z; the statement becomes Bz=0 with z nonzero. A linear transformation sends the zero vector to zero, so applying A preserves that relation. The coefficients themselves do not change, which is why the transformed columns remain dependent even if A has a large kernel or is not square.

Column dependence of $B$ means there exists a nonzero coefficient vector $z$ such that $Bz=0$. Multiplying by $A$ gives $(AB)z=A(Bz)=0$.

The same nonzero coefficients form a vanishing linear combination of columns of $AB$, proving their dependence. No invertibility assumption on $A$ is needed.

questions.stem: Let $e_i$ be the standard basis vectors of $\mathbb R^3$. A linear map $L:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ satisfies $L(e_1)=e_1$, $L(e_2)=e_1+e_2$ and $L(e_3)=e_2+e_3$. Is $L$ onto? Prove your answer. [15 marks]
questions.answer: Yes. Its matrix is upper triangular with determinant1.
questions.solution:
A linear map is completely determined by what it does to a basis. Place the three given image vectors as columns of its matrix, not as rows. Surjectivity in a map from R³ to R³ is equivalent to rank three. The triangular matrix has nonzero diagonal entries, so its determinant is nonzero; alternatively solve backwards for an input producing an arbitrary target, which directly proves every target is reached.

The columns of the matrix of $L$ are its values on the standard basis: $M=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&0\\0&1&1\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}$. It is upper triangular with determinant1, hence invertible and onto. Explicitly, for a desired image $(a,b,c)$ choose input $(a-b+c,b-c,c)$; multiplication by $M$ gives $(a,b,c)$.

questions.stem: A consumer may buy up to a ration quota $q$ of rice at subsidised price $p_s$, and additional rice at open-market price $p>p_s$. Rice has uniform quality. Preferences have downward-sloping, smooth, convex indifference curves. Assume initially that the consumer exhausts the quota and also buys from the open market. Graphically depict the consumer's equilibrium. [10 marks]
questions.answer: The optimum is a tangency on the steeper post-quota budget segment, with marginal rate of substitution equal to the market price.
questions.solution:
This is an incremental two-price purchase scheme: the first q units stay cheap even when extra units are bought. Therefore the budget is continuous at the quota, unlike a tariff that reprices all earlier units. On the second segment, the quota acts like a fixed income benefit $(p-p_s)q$ while the marginal price of an extra rice unit is p. The given initial open-market purchase assumption tells us to place the optimum beyond the kink, not at it.

Let income be $m$ and let the other consumption good have price1. With total rice $x$ on the horizontal axis and other consumption $y$ on the vertical axis, the budget frontier is $y=m-p_sx$ for $0\leq x\leq q$, then $y=m+(p-p_s)q-px$ for $x\geq q$.

It is continuous at the kink $(q,m-p_sq)$ and becomes steeper there, changing slope from $-p_s$ to $-p$. By the given assumption, the optimum lies strictly to the right of the kink on the second segment, at a tangency with the highest attainable indifference curve.

The absolute slope of that curve, $MRS_{x,y}$, equals $p$, and open-market purchases are $x-q>0$.

questions.stem: A consumer may buy up to a ration quota $q$ of rice at subsidised price $p_s$, and additional rice at open-market price $p>p_s$. Rice has uniform quality. Preferences have downward-sloping, smooth, convex indifference curves. Assume initially that the consumer exhausts the quota and also buys from the open market. Suppose rice is normal. What happens to the amount purchased from the open market if the ration quota is cut? Explain. [10 marks]
questions.answer: Total rice consumption falls, but the change in open-market purchases is not determined by normality of rice alone. With both goods normal, open-market purchases rise.
questions.solution:
A quota cut has two effects on the number bought outside the ration system. It reduces the cheap rice automatically available, but it also makes the consumer poorer and can reduce total rice demand. Define open-market purchases z=x-q before differentiating. Normality signs the change in x, not automatically the change in z. These are different quantities, so subtracting the moving quota is necessary to avoid an unjustified conclusion about market purchases.

While the consumer remains beyond the kink, the relevant budget is equivalent to income $M=m+(p-p_s)q$ at marginal rice price $p$. Let total Marshallian rice demand be $x(p,M)$ and open-market purchases $z=x-q$.

A quota cut lowers $M$, so normality implies total rice $x$ falls. But $dz/dq=(p-p_s)x_M-1$: the quota itself is also falling, so the sign of the change in $z$ is ambiguous unless the strength of the income effect is bounded.

If $0<x_M<1/(p-p_s)$, a cut in $q$ raises open-market purchases; if $x_M>1/(p-p_s)$, it lowers them. Under the additional usual assumption that both rice and the other good are normal, budget differentiation gives $px_M<1$, implying the first case and higher open-market purchases.

Normality of rice alone does not impose that bound when the other good may be inferior.

questions.notes: The source assumes only rice normal, not the other good. An unconditional increase in open-market purchases would require an additional bound on the rice income effect. The answer states both the general ambiguity and the standard both-normal-goods case.

questions.stem: A consumer may buy up to a ration quota $q$ of rice at subsidised price $p_s$, and additional rice at open-market price $p>p_s$. Rice has uniform quality. Preferences have downward-sloping, smooth, convex indifference curves. Assume initially that the consumer exhausts the quota and also buys from the open market. If rice is normal, what happens to open-market purchases when the subsidised price rises but remains below the market price? Does the conclusion change if rice is inferior? Explain. [10 marks]
questions.answer: Normal rice: open-market purchases fall. Inferior rice: they rise, as long as the consumer continues to use the open-market segment.
questions.solution:
With a fixed quota and positive extra purchases, the household still pays p for its last rice unit. Raising only the subsidized price therefore changes effective income but not the relevant marginal price. This is a pure income effect locally. Normal and inferior rice respond in opposite directions to that income loss. The calculation applies while the consumer stays on the second segment; reaching the quota introduces a boundary that must be checked separately.

With the quota unchanged, increasing $p_s$ lowers the effective income $M=m+(p-p_s)q$ while leaving the marginal price $p$ unchanged. Thus $dx/dp_s=-q x_M$.

For normal rice $x_M>0$, total rice falls and so do open-market purchases $z=x-q$; purchases may reach zero at the quota kink. If rice is inferior, $x_M<0$, the income loss instead raises total rice demand and open-market purchases.

There is no substitution effect at the margin on the post-quota segment because the open-market marginal price is unchanged.

questions.stem: Total monthly fish-sale revenue from $x$ boats on Dull Lake is $R(x)=10{,}000(4x-x^2/2)$ rupees. Hiring a boat costs20,000rupees per month. Derive marginal and average revenue per boat. [5 marks]
questions.solution:
Average revenue answers what each boat receives when lake revenue is shared over all active boats; marginal revenue answers what one more boat adds to total lake receipts. These are different because extra entry changes the productivity of boats already fishing. For positive x,

$$AR(x)=\frac{R(x)}x,\qquad MR(x)=\frac{dR(x)}{dx}.$$

Keep the rupee factor 10000 in both expressions; dropping it would make comparison with the 20000 boat cost dimensionally inconsistent.

Differentiate total revenue to get $MR=R'(x)=10{,}000(4-x)$. Divide revenue by the number of boats to get $AR=R(x)/x=10{,}000(4-x/2)$ for $x>0$.
questions.hint: Differentiate total revenue for MR, and divide by boat numbers for AR.

questions.stem: Total monthly fish-sale revenue from $x$ boats on Dull Lake is $R(x)=10{,}000(4x-x^2/2)$ rupees. Hiring a boat costs20,000rupees per month. If fishing permits are allocated freely, how many boats fish each month? [10 marks]
questions.solution:
With freely available permits, an entrant compares the revenue it expects to receive, average revenue per boat, with its own boat-hiring cost. Entry continues until that private return is exhausted. It does not compare the change in everyone’s combined receipts with its cost, because the losses imposed on existing boats are external to the entrant. This distinction explains why free entry and total-profit maximization select different boat counts.

With unrestricted free entry, each boat receives average revenue. Entry continues while $AR$ exceeds the hiring cost20,000.

Zero net return requires $40{,}000-5{,}000x=20{,}000$, hence $x=4$. Total revenue80,000 then exactly covers the four boats' total real cost80,000.

questions.stem: Total monthly fish-sale revenue from $x$ boats on Dull Lake is $R(x)=10{,}000(4x-x^2/2)$ rupees. Hiring a boat costs20,000rupees per month. How many boats maximize total profit? [5 marks]
questions.answer: Two boats; maximum pre-permit resource profit is20,000rupees.
questions.solution:
A sole owner or planner internalizes the revenue effects on all boats. Total profit is R(x) minus 20000x, and its derivative is marginal revenue minus that cost. The strict negative second derivative of the quadratic revenue function verifies the optimum. Compare the result with open access to see the common-resource overentry: some entrants earn private revenue at others’ expense without adding enough total revenue to justify their hiring cost.

Joint profit is $R(x)-20{,}000x=20{,}000x-5{,}000x^2$. It is a concave quadratic maximized at $x=2$, where marginal revenue equals the real boat cost20,000. Total revenue is60,000 and total hiring cost is40,000, leaving20,000.

questions.stem: Total monthly fish-sale revenue from $x$ boats on Dull Lake is $R(x)=10{,}000(4x-x^2/2)$ rupees. Hiring a boat costs20,000rupees per month. What per-boat permit charge induces the total-profit-maximizing number of boats? [10 marks]
questions.solution:
A permit price changes the entrant’s private cost but does not change the lake’s physical revenue function. To implement the efficient boat count, set the combined boat-plus-permit cost equal to average revenue at that count. The permit is the difference between the average private receipt and the true marginal contribution. Revenue collected by the permit authority is a transfer, not an additional social resource cost; it changes entry incentives while preserving the planner’s allocation.

At the desired $x=2$, average revenue per boat is $AR(2)=30{,}000$. Free entry with a permit charge $t$ equates this to $20{,}000+t$, giving $t=10{,}000$.

The permit absorbs the congestion rent and implements two boats rather than four. The two permits raise20,000 for the municipality, equal to the maximized resource rent; permit payments are transfers, so private net boat profits are zero under free entry even though total pre-transfer resource surplus is maximized.

questions.stem: A monopoly campus theatre has faculty demand $Q_F=500-4P_F$ and student demand $Q_S=100-2P_S$, with each demand truncated at zero. Capacity is sufficient for everyone. The total cost of servicing demand is500. If both groups must face the same price, find the profit-maximizing ticket price. [15 marks]
questions.answer: Uniform price62.5, serving250faculty tickets and no student tickets; profit15,125.
questions.solution:
At a common ticket price the two demand curves must be added only where each is positive. Students stop buying above 50, while faculty remain willing to pay up to 125. The combined demand therefore changes formula at price 50. Optimize ticket revenue on both price intervals, check their boundaries, and compare the maxima with the cost of opening. Treating aggregate demand as one untruncated line can report a price at which the supposedly active student demand is actually negative.

At a common price $p\leq50$, aggregate demand is $600-6p$ and revenue is $600p-6p^2$, maximized over this interval at $p=50$ with revenue15,000. At $50\leq p\leq125$, students buy zero and faculty demand is $500-4p$.

Revenue $500p-4p^2$ is maximized at $p=62.5$, giving quantity250 and revenue15,625. This exceeds the best revenue from the lower-price segment.

Subtracting the fixed cost500 gives profit15,125. Ignoring the student choke price would incorrectly select50 as the global optimum.

questions.stem: A monopoly campus theatre has faculty demand $Q_F=500-4P_F$ and student demand $Q_S=100-2P_S$, with each demand truncated at zero. Capacity is sufficient for everyone. The total cost of servicing demand is500. If different prices can be charged to faculty and students, find the profit-maximizing prices. [15 marks]
questions.answer: Faculty price62.5, student price25; total profit16,375.
questions.solution:
With group-specific prices and no binding capacity constraint, the theatre can choose student and faculty prices separately. The stated cost is fixed rather than per additional attendee, so it affects the decision to open but does not enter each group’s marginal revenue calculation. Optimize both revenue quadratics independently, then add their receipts and subtract the fixed cost once. Charging every group the same price would unnecessarily retain the restriction removed in this part.

With zero marginal servicing cost and a fixed total cost, maximize the two group revenues separately. Faculty revenue $p_F(500-4p_F)$ has first-order condition $500-8p_F=0$, giving $p_F=62.5$ and $Q_F=250$.

Student revenue $p_S(100-2p_S)$ gives $100-4p_S=0$, so $p_S=25$ and $Q_S=50$. Revenues are15,625 and1,250, respectively.

questions.stem: In a Solow economy, $Y(t)=K(t)^\alpha L(t)^{1-\alpha}$, $0<\alpha<1$, with both factors fully employed. Labour grows at rate $\eta>0$. A fraction $s\in(0,1)$ of output is saved and invested, so $\dot K=sY$; there is no depreciation. Let $k=K/L$ and $k^*$ be its positive steady state. If initially $k(0)<k^*$, compare initial aggregate-output growth $g_Y(0)$ with steady-state output growth. Prove the comparison. [20 marks]
questions.solution:
Being below the steady state refers to capital per worker, not necessarily a small aggregate capital stock. Convert the production identity to growth rates:

$$g_Y=\alpha g_K+(1-\alpha)g_L,\qquad g_K=s\frac YK=s k^{\alpha-1}.$$

The exponent alpha-1 is negative, so low k means a high output–capital ratio and fast proportional capital accumulation. At steady state capital and labour grow together, making aggregate output growth equal labour-force growth.

Capital per worker obeys $\dot k=sk^\alpha-\eta k$, so $k^*=(s/\eta)^{1/(1-\alpha)}$. Log differentiation of production gives $g_Y=\alpha g_K+(1-\alpha)\eta=\alpha s k^{\alpha-1}+(1-\alpha)\eta$.

At $k^*$, $s(k^*)^{\alpha-1}=\eta$, giving $g_Y^*=\eta$. Since $\alpha-1<0$, $k(0)<k^*$ implies $sk(0)^{\alpha-1}>\eta$.

Substitution yields $g_Y(0)>\eta$.

A fraction $s\in(0,1)$ of output is saved and invested, so $\dot K=sY$; there is no depreciation. Let $k=K/L$ and $k^*$ be its positive steady state. Compare the initial output-growth rates in two scenarios $k(0)<k'(0)<k^*$ for the same economy. [5 marks]
questions.solution:
Use the aggregate-output growth formula as a function of the initial per-worker capital stock. Although both scenarios lie below the same fixed point, their distances from it matter because diminishing returns make the output–capital ratio decrease with k. Differentiate the growth formula to establish the ordering rigorously. It ranks proportional growth rates, not the levels of output, which can be lower in the faster-growing scenario.

The formula from part(i) is $g_Y(k)=\alpha s k^{\alpha-1}+(1-\alpha)\eta$. Its derivative with respect to $k$ is $\alpha s(\alpha-1)k^{\alpha-2}<0$. Thus output growth is strictly higher at the lower initial capital per worker; both rates exceed their common steady-state rate because both initial stocks are below $k^*$.

questions.stem: In a Solow economy, $Y(t)=K(t)^\alpha L(t)^{1-\alpha}$, $0<\alpha<1$, with both factors fully employed. Labour grows at rate $\eta>0$. A fraction $s\in(0,1)$ of output is saved and invested, so $\dot K=sY$; there is no depreciation. Let $k=K/L$ and $k^*$ be its positive steady state. Two otherwise similarly described economies A and B have $s_A>s_B$. Their initial capital per worker is below their respective steady states. The printed condition is on aggregate capital: $K^A(0)<K^B(0)$. Can their initial output-growth rates be ranked? If the information is insufficient, say so. [5 marks]
questions.answer: Insufficient information as printed: aggregate capital does not determine capital per worker without initial labour-force sizes.
questions.solution:
The larger saving rate and the smaller aggregate K point in suggestive directions, but the growth formula uses K/L. Different labour populations can reverse the order of these per-worker stocks. To show that the stated information is insufficient, keep the given aggregate-K and saving-rate comparisons but vary labour sizes to obtain opposite growth rankings. A single ranking under an unstated equal-population assumption would not establish the claim for the original data.

The ranking depends on $s_A[k_A(0)]^{\alpha-1}$ versus $s_B[k_B(0)]^{\alpha-1}$. Although $s_A>s_B$, the inequality $K_A(0)<K_B(0)$ does not order $k_A=K_A/L_A$ and $k_B=K_B/L_B$ without initial labour sizes.

For example, take $\alpha=1/2$, $\eta=0.1$, $s_A=0.4$, $s_B=0.2$, $K_A=1<K_B=2$. The steady per-worker stocks are16 and4.

If both initial per-worker stocks are1, A grows faster. But if $k_A=9$ and $k_B=1/4$ (achieved with different labour-force levels), both remain below their own steady states and B grows faster.

Thus either ranking is possible. If the intended condition had instead been $k_A(0)<k_B(0)$, A would unambiguously grow faster, but that is not the printed aggregate-capital condition.

questions.stem: What is the money multiplier, what determines it, and how is it related to monetary base and money supply? Which variables can the central bank change, and in which direction, to change money supply? [15 marks]
questions.answer: In the textbook currency-deposit model, $M=mH$ with $m=(1+c)/(c+\rho)$, where $c=C/D$ and $\rho=Res/D$.
questions.solution:
Derive the multiplier from two accounting definitions rather than memorizing a formula. Deposits D support both currency demand and bank reserves. Broad money counts currency plus deposits, while the monetary base counts currency plus reserves. Dividing these definitions eliminates D and shows exactly which behavioural ratios enter the multiplier. The central bank controls some policy instruments, but the public’s currency preference and banks’ desired excess reserves can change independently, so a fixed multiplier is an additional simplification.

Let currency be $C=cD$ and bank reserves $Res=\rho D$. Broad transaction money is $M=C+D=(1+c)D$ and monetary base is $H=C+Res=(c+\rho)D$.

Thus $M=mH$, where $m=(1+c)/(c+\rho)$. More currency leakage or a higher reserve ratio reduces deposit creation; specifically $m_\rho<0$ and $m_c<0$ when $\rho<1$.

The central bank can raise the monetary base through asset purchases or lending to banks, increasing money supply at a given multiplier; base contraction has the reverse effect. Lowering a binding reserve requirement can raise the multiplier and money supply, while raising it can reduce them.

Currency preferences and excess reserves are behavioural rather than mechanically controlled, so the multiplier need not be constant or directly settable by the central bank. If using the question's reserve-to-assets terminology, the simple no-bank-equity balance-sheet model equates bank assets with deposits; otherwise the ratio must be converted to reserves per deposit before using this formula.

questions.stem: Why might the cash/deposit ratio and reserve/asset ratio fall when interest rises? How does an interest-sensitive money supply affect the LM curve compared with the standard LM? Explain the resulting effectiveness of counter-cyclical fiscal policy in a closed economy, using a diagram. [15 marks]
questions.answer: Higher interest makes currency and excess reserves more costly to hold. The money multiplier rises with interest, making LM flatter and fiscal policy more effective.
questions.solution:
An interest increase can reduce idle cash and reserve holdings by raising their opportunity cost. If that raises the money multiplier, the money supply expands endogenously as the interest rate increases. Differentiate the entire money-equilibrium equation, including this supply response. A fiscal expansion then needs a smaller rate increase to clear the money market than under fixed broad money, which reduces investment crowding out. Draw both LM curves through the same initial equilibrium so their slope comparison is meaningful.

Holding cash forgoes interest on deposits or other assets, so a higher return can reduce the currency-deposit ratio. Likewise, higher lending or bond returns increase the opportunity cost of excess reserves, reducing the reserve ratio above any legal minimum.

If both ratios decline, the multiplier $m(r)$ rises. With a fixed base $H$ and price level $P$, money equilibrium becomes $Hm(r)/P=L(Y,r)$, with $L_Y>0,L_r<0,m'(r)>0$.

Its slope is $dr/dY=L_Y/[Hm'(r)/P-L_r]$, smaller than the fixed-money-supply slope $L_Y/(-L_r)$. Draw the standard upward-sloping LM and a flatter interest-sensitive LM through the same initial $(Y,r)$ point.

A fiscal expansion shifts IS right; induced money expansion limits the interest rise and investment crowding-out, producing a larger output increase. The reverse applies to contraction.

Required reserves and other balance-sheet restrictions limit the size of the response.

questions.stem: Explain the difference between nominal and real exchange rates, with an example. Is a rise in the real cost of imports an improvement or deterioration in the terms of trade? [10 marks]
questions.answer: A nominal rate exchanges currencies; a real rate compares goods prices. A higher real import cost is a deterioration in the terms of trade.
questions.solution:
A nominal exchange rate converts currency units; a real exchange rate compares goods prices after conversion. State the exchange-rate quotation convention first, since its reciprocal reverses every numerical appreciation/depreciation direction. Terms of trade compare what exports buy in imports. If imports become dearer relative to exports, the country must give up more exports per imported unit, which is a deterioration regardless of how the exchange rate variable is named.

Define $e$ as Home-currency units per Foreign-currency unit. It is a nominal exchange rate.

The real exchange rate $q=eP^*/P$ compares the Home-currency price of a Foreign goods basket with the price of a Home basket. For a purely hypothetical example, if $e=80$, a Foreign basket costs10 Foreign units and a Home basket costs400 Home units, then $q=80\cdot10/400=2$: the imported basket costs two Home baskets.

Terms of trade measure export prices relative to import prices. If imports become more expensive in real terms, more exports are needed to obtain a given quantity of imports, so the terms of trade deteriorate.

Authors defining the exchange rate reciprocally reverse the numerical direction, but not this economic interpretation.

questions.stem: A small open economy has a government budget surplus and a trade deficit. Identify the private sector's financial balance. Using the short-run Mundell-Fleming model with perfect capital mobility, explain how a sudden fall in private consumption affects output, the trade balance and the government budget under fixed and flexible exchange rates, including adjustment mechanisms. [20 marks]
questions.answer: The private sector is in deficit. With a peg, output falls and the trade balance improves. With a float and fixed monetary base, depreciation offsets the demand fall, leaving output unchanged and improving the trade balance. Budget effects depend on tax rules.
questions.solution:
Begin with the sectoral-balance identity to identify the private deficit; it follows from the simultaneous public surplus and external deficit without an IS–LM graph. For the shock, keep the consumption decline fixed and compare the policy rule across exchange regimes. Under a peg the central bank adjusts money to maintain the exchange rate; under a float the currency adjusts instead. Those different accommodating variables explain why the same private-demand shock has different output effects.

The sectoral identity is $(S-I)+(T-G)=NX$. Since $T-G>0$ and $NX<0$, private net saving $S-I=NX-(T-G)<0$, so the private sector is in financial deficit.

Under fixed exchange rates, lower consumption shifts IS left and creates downward pressure on the domestic interest rate relative to the world rate. Capital outflow puts depreciation pressure on the currency. To defend the peg the central bank sells foreign reserves and contracts domestic money, shifting LM left. The new equilibrium has the world interest rate, lower output, and lower imports; net exports improve at the unchanged exchange rate. With income-dependent tax receipts the budget surplus shrinks as output falls; with fixed lump-sum taxes and fixed spending, the budget balance is unchanged.

Under flexible exchange rates with an unchanged monetary base and price level, the lower-consumption shock also creates capital outflow and depreciation pressure, but the central bank does not defend a peg. Depreciation raises net exports and shifts IS back until goods and money markets clear at the world interest rate. LM at that interest rate fixes output at its initial level, so the trade balance improves enough to offset the consumption loss while output is unchanged. The government budget is then unchanged under either fixed taxes or a tax rule depending only on unchanged income. These are the standard short-run model assumptions; an epidemic's additional supply effects are outside this specified consumption shock.

questions.notes: The source does not state a tax-revenue rule. Fixed-rate budget deterioration requires income-sensitive taxes; under the basic fixed-T,G version it is unchanged. Both cases are stated rather than imposing an unstated unique budget response.

questions.stem: Find all maxima and minima of $f(x,y)=xy$, subject to $x+4y=120$ and $x,y\geq0$. [10 marks]
questions.solution:
Use the linear constraint to remove one variable: x=120-4y and 0≤y≤30. The product becomes a concave quadratic in y. Its stationary point supplies the maximum, while the two endpoints must be checked for minima. Because all feasible quantities are nonnegative, zero is already a lower bound; identifying where one factor becomes zero locates every minimizer without relying on a misleading unconstrained saddle-point calculation.

The feasible set has $x=120-4y$ with $0\leq y\leq30$. Hence $f(y)=120y-4y^2=900-4(y-15)^2$.

The unique maximum is900 at $y=15,x=60$. Since both coordinates are nonnegative, $xy\geq0$; equality occurs only at the two endpoints $(120,0)$ and $(0,30)$, which are the minima.

questions.stem: Find the points on the circle $x^2+y^2=50$ that are closest to and farthest from $(1,1)$. [15 marks]
questions.answer: Closest $(5,5)$, at distance $4\sqrt2$; farthest $(-5,-5)$, at distance $6\sqrt2$.
questions.solution:
The squared distance to (1,1) is $x^2+y^2-2(x+y)+2$. On the circle x²+y²=50, only the linear term x+y varies. Thus nearest and farthest points are obtained by maximizing and minimizing x+y respectively. The Cauchy–Schwarz bound makes these extreme values easy to find, and its equality condition tells us the point lies along the radial direction (1,1). This also gives a geometric explanation independent of Lagrange multipliers.

On the circle the squared distance is $(x-1)^2+(y-1)^2=52-2(x+y)$. Cauchy-Schwarz gives $|x+y|\leq\sqrt{2(x^2+y^2)}=10$, with equality when $x=y$.

Thus distance is minimized at $x=y=5$ and maximized at $x=y=-5$. The respective squared distances are32 and72, giving $4\sqrt2$ and $6\sqrt2$.

questions.stem: For which real $\alpha$ are $(0,1,\alpha)$, $(\alpha,1,0)$ and $(1,\alpha,1)$ in $\mathbb R^3$ linearly independent? [5 marks]
questions.solution:
Three vectors in R³ are independent exactly when the matrix with those vectors as columns has nonzero determinant. Independence fails only at roots of that determinant polynomial. Record whether the vectors were inserted as rows or columns, although transposing does not change the zero/nonzero test. After factoring the polynomial, exclude every real root, including zero; checking only the two nonzero square-root values would miss a degenerate case.

Use the vectors as rows of a matrix. Its determinant is $\det\begin{pmatrix}0&1&\alpha\\\alpha&1&0\\1&\alpha&1\end{pmatrix}=\alpha^3-2\alpha=\alpha(\alpha^2-2)$. Three vectors in $\mathbb R^3$ are linearly independent precisely when this determinant is nonzero, giving the result.
questions.hint: Compute the determinant of the matrix with the three vectors as rows.

Three vectors in $\mathbb R^3$ are linearly independent precisely when this determinant is nonzero, giving the result.

questions.stem: Let $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be continuous and let $\mathbb Q$ be the rational numbers. Prove that if $f(\mathbb Q)\subseteq\{1,2,3,\ldots\}$, then $f$ is constant. [20 marks]
questions.answer: $f(x)=k$ for every real $x$, for some positive integer $k$.
questions.solution:
Two properties of the real line work together. Density of the rationals lets continuity transfer the restriction from rational arguments to every real argument. Then the intermediate value theorem prevents a continuous function from jumping between distinct integer outputs. Neither idea alone is enough: knowing integer values on a dense set needs continuity, and merely knowing integer values everywhere needs connectedness of the domain to force constancy.

For any real $x$, choose rational $q_m\to x$. Continuity gives $f(q_m)\to f(x)$.

A convergent sequence of positive integers is eventually constant, so its limit is a positive integer. Thus $f$ takes positive-integer values everywhere, not merely on rationals.

If it were nonconstant, two values would be distinct integers. The intermediate value theorem would then force a noninteger value strictly between them, a contradiction.

Therefore $f$ is constant, and its value is a positive integer.

Therefore $f$ is constant, and its value is a positive integer.

questions.stem: Let $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. Calculate $f'(0)$ when $f$ is differentiable and $|f(x)|\leq x^2$ for all real $x$. [10 marks]
questions.solution:
First substitute x=0 into the bound; this determines f(0), which must be subtracted in the derivative definition. Next divide the bound at h by |h|, not by h without tracking its sign. The bound becomes

$$\left|\frac{f(h)-f(0)}h\right|\leq|h|.$$

Since the right side tends to zero from either direction, the derivative follows by squeezing. In fact no global differentiability assumption is needed: this local bound itself proves differentiability at zero.

Putting $x=0$ gives $f(0)=0$. For $h\neq0$, $|(f(h)-f(0))/h|\leq h^2/|h|=|h|$.

The right side tends to zero as $h\to0$, so the difference quotient tends to zero by squeezing. Thus $f'(0)=0$.

In fact the stated bound alone guarantees differentiability at zero.

questions.stem: There are $n\geq2$ political parties and $V$ voters, each voting for exactly one party. Party $i$ receives $V_i$ votes, with $V=\sum_iV_i$. Let $P_1$ be the probability that two randomly drawn voters voted for different parties when sampling with replacement, and $P_2$ the corresponding probability without replacement. Derive $P_2/P_1$ as a function of $V$ alone. [25 marks]
questions.answer: $P_2/P_1=V/(V-1)$ whenever $V\geq2$ and at least two parties receive votes.
questions.solution:
Sampling with replacement allows the same voter to be drawn twice, while sampling without replacement excludes that possibility. It is easiest to count the complementary event that the two votes belong to the same party. In the without-replacement count, the second choice from party i has Vi-1 rather than Vi available voters. Simplifying both complements reveals a common numerator; cancel it only when it is nonzero, because unanimous voting makes the requested ratio undefined.

With replacement, the probability of matching parties is $\sum_i(V_i/V)^2$, so $P_1=(V^2-\sum_iV_i^2)/V^2$. Without replacement it is $\sum_iV_i(V_i-1)/[V(V-1)]$, so $P_2=(V^2-\sum_iV_i^2)/[V(V-1)]$.

Cancelling the common positive numerator gives $P_2/P_1=V/(V-1)$. If all votes go to one party, both probabilities are zero and the ratio is undefined; the identity $P_2=VP_1/(V-1)$ remains valid.

Sampling without replacement itself requires $V\geq2$.
questions.hint: Compute the complement probability that both voters support the same party in each sampling scheme.
questions.notes: The ratio needs P1>0. The printed n>=2 by itself does not exclude all voters supporting one party, so the zero-over-zero exception is stated explicitly.

If all votes go to one party, both probabilities are zero and the ratio is undefined; the identity $P_2=VP_1/(V-1)$ remains valid. Sampling without replacement itself requires $V\geq2$.

Let $P_1$ be the probability that two randomly drawn voters voted for different parties when sampling with replacement, and $P_2$ the corresponding probability without replacement. Suppose $V_i=V/n$ for every party. Find $P_1$ and $P_2$. [5 marks]
questions.solution:
Equal party vote counts imply equal population shares, so the with-replacement probability of matching a party is the sum of n identical squares. The without-replacement probability is slightly less likely to match, because removing the first voter reduces that party’s remaining representation. Apply the ratio derived above only after checking V≥2 and that V/n is an integer; otherwise the stipulated equal-count electorate cannot exist.

questions.stem: A two-period agent maximizes $U(C_1)+U(C_2)/(1+\rho)$, where $\rho>0$, with $C_1+s=w$ and $C_2=(1+r)s$. Period1 labour is supplied inelastically; period2 has no wage income. Per-period utility is represented, up to a positive affine transformation, by $U(C)=(C^{1-\theta}-1)/(1-\theta)$, $0<\theta<1$. Derive the response of optimal saving to the interest rate $r$. [20 marks]
questions.answer: Holding $\rho$ fixed, saving increases with $r$. With $z=(1+r)^{(1-\theta)/\theta}(1+\rho)^{-1/\theta}$, $s=wz/(1+z)$ and $ds/dr>0$.
questions.solution:
Saving one more first-period unit sacrifices current marginal utility and buys 1+r second-period consumption units, discounted by 1/(1+rho). Insert the power marginal utility C to the power -theta and solve for the saving-to-consumption ratio before differentiating. This isolates interest inside a single positive quantity z. Keep rho fixed in this experiment; allowing it to move with r changes both preferences and returns and produces a different sign in the next part.

The interior Euler equation is $(w-s)^{-\theta}=[(1+r)/(1+\rho)]((1+r)s)^{-\theta}$. Therefore $s/(w-s)=z$, where $z=(1+r)^{(1-\theta)/\theta}(1+\rho)^{-1/\theta}$.

Solving gives $s=wz/(1+z)$. At fixed $\rho$, $z_r=z(1-\theta)/[\theta(1+r)]>0$.

Thus $ds/dr=wz(1-\theta)/[\theta(1+r)(1+z)^2]>0$. The parameter restriction $\theta<1$ makes the substitution incentive dominate the income effect of the interest increase.

What happens to saving if $r$ and $\rho$ rise by the same amount, preserving $r=\rho$? [10 marks]
questions.solution:
The condition r=rho is maintained during the change, so the financial incentive to postpone consumption is exactly offset by the subjective discount wedge at every compared optimum. Equal marginal utilities and strict concavity then imply equal consumption levels. Saving must finance the same consumption as that retained in period 1; as the gross return rises, less principal is needed to do so. This is why saving can fall here even though it rose in the fixed-preference experiment.

When $r=\rho$, the discount factor times the gross interest factor equals1. The Euler equation then gives $U'(C_1)=U'(C_2)$, hence $C_1=C_2$ by strict concavity.

From $w-s=(1+r)s$, $s=w/(2+r)$. Along the specified joint change, $ds/dr=-w/(2+r)^2<0$.

This is not the same experiment as part(a), which held the time-preference parameter fixed.
questions.hint: Along this change the Euler equation continues to imply equal consumption in both periods.

questions.stem: A monopolist has cost $C(x)=cx$, $c>0$, and sells all output $x\geq0$ to one consumer. The consumer can buy $0\leq y\leq x$ and has utility $\theta\sqrt y-T(y)$, $\theta>0$. For positive purchases $T(y)=py+t$, with $p,t\geq0$, while $T(0)=0$. Find monopoly profit when any nonnegative two-part tariff $(p,t)$ can be chosen. [10 marks]
questions.answer: Maximum profit is $\theta^2/(4c)$, attained by $p=c$, $t=\theta^2/(4c)$ and $x=y=\theta^2/(4c^2)$ under participation at indifference.
questions.solution:
With one known consumer, a fixed fee can extract utility without changing the marginal purchase incentive. Total profit can never exceed gross consumption benefit minus production cost, since the buyer must be at least as well off as buying nothing. Maximizing that surplus gives an upper bound on profit. A per-unit price equal to marginal cost implements the efficient quantity, and a fixed fee equal to the resulting surplus attains the bound under acceptance at indifference.

A fixed fee cannot exceed the consumer's surplus before the fee. Hence profit at any sold quantity is bounded by total surplus $\theta\sqrt y-cy$.

Maximizing this expression gives $\theta/(2\sqrt y)=c$, so $y^*=\theta^2/(4c^2)$ and total surplus $\theta^2/(4c)$. Set the per-unit price to marginal cost, $p=c$, to induce this quantity, and extract its remaining gross consumer surplus through $t=\theta\sqrt{y^*}-cy^*=\theta^2/(4c)$.

The consumer obtains zero net utility and profit equals all total surplus. If the consumer refuses purchases when exactly indifferent, use a fee arbitrarily below this level; the displayed amount is then the profit supremum.

Other equivalent tariffs can implement the same quantity when the available-output cap binds, so the displayed tariff need not be unique.
questions.hint: The fixed fee can extract consumer surplus; choose quantity to maximize total surplus.
questions.notes: Usual participation-at-indifference convention is made explicit. The source allows a supply cap y<=x, so no uniqueness of the implementing two-part tariff is asserted.

questions.stem: A monopolist has cost $C(x)=cx$, $c>0$, and sells all output $x\geq0$ to one consumer. The consumer can buy $0\leq y\leq x$ and has utility $\theta\sqrt y-T(y)$, $\theta>0$. For positive purchases $T(y)=py+t$, with $p,t\geq0$, while $T(0)=0$. Now impose $t=0$ but allow any nonnegative $p$. Find profit and compare it with part(a). [10 marks]
questions.solution:
Removing the entry fee forces the monopolist to recover surplus through the per-unit markup alone. Derive the buyer’s demand from marginal benefit equal to p, then invert it so revenue and cost can be expressed in the actual sold quantity. The firm’s marginal revenue is less than the consumer’s marginal willingness to pay, which explains why uniform linear pricing chooses less than the efficient quantity and yields lower profit than the two-part tariff.

For a positive per-unit price, the consumer's first-order condition gives $y=\theta^2/(4p^2)$. Equivalently inverse demand is $p=\theta/(2\sqrt y)$.

Revenue is $\theta\sqrt y/2$, so monopoly profit is $\theta\sqrt y/2-cy$. Maximization gives $\sqrt y=\theta/(4c)$, hence $y=\theta^2/(16c^2)$ and $p=2c$.

Profit is $\theta^2/(16c)$, exactly one quarter of the unrestricted two-part-tariff profit. Without a fixed fee, extracting surplus through a price markup distorts quantity downward.

For positive purchases $T(y)=py+t$, with $p,t\geq0$, while $T(0)=0$. Calculate which tariff regime has higher social surplus and explain. [5 marks]
questions.answer: Two-part pricing has surplus $\theta^2/(4c)$, versus $3\theta^2/(16c)$ under linear pricing.
questions.solution:
A fee is a transfer between buyer and seller; it does not destroy social resources. To compare social surplus, use the quantity each tariff induces and subtract only production cost from gross benefit. The efficient two-part tariff maximizes that expression. Linear monopoly leaves mutually beneficial marginal trades unrealized, so its welfare shortfall is a quantity distortion rather than the existence of a high payment by itself.

Social surplus is gross utility minus real production cost, $\theta\sqrt y-cy$. At the efficient two-part-tariff quantity it equals $\theta^2/(4c)$.

At the linear monopoly quantity it equals $\theta^2/(4c)-\theta^2/(16c)=3\theta^2/(16c)$. Thus two-part pricing raises total surplus by $\theta^2/(16c)$ by removing the quantity distortion.

questions.stem: A monopolist has cost $C(x)=cx$, $c>0$, and sells all output $x\geq0$ to one consumer. The consumer can buy $0\leq y\leq x$ and has utility $\theta\sqrt y-T(y)$, $\theta>0$. For positive purchases $T(y)=py+t$, with $p,t\geq0$, while $T(0)=0$. Calculate which tariff regime has higher consumer surplus and explain. [5 marks]
questions.answer: Consumer surplus is zero under surplus-extracting two-part pricing and $\theta^2/(8c)$ under linear pricing.
questions.solution:
Consumer surplus is the buyer’s residual utility after all payments, not total social surplus. With the optimal two-part tariff, the fixed fee deliberately exhausts that residual, even though output is efficient. With no fixed fee, the seller cannot fully appropriate the buyer’s gain, so the consumer keeps a positive amount. Thus the tariff preferred by society need not be the tariff preferred by the consumer; distribution and efficiency are separate comparisons.

The optimal two-part fee extracts all surplus, leaving the buyer with zero net utility. Under linear pricing, gross utility at $y=\theta^2/(16c^2)$ is $\theta^2/(4c)$ and payment is $2c\cdot\theta^2/(16c^2)=\theta^2/(8c)$.

Their difference is $\theta^2/(8c)>0$. Thus the buyer prefers linear pricing even though it generates lower total surplus, because the monopolist cannot extract all surplus without a fixed charge.

questions.stem: At unit output, conditional input demands are $x_1=1+3w_1^{-1/2}w_2^a$ and $x_2=1+bw_1^{1/2}w_2^c$, where $w_1,w_2>0$ are input prices. Find $a,b,c$ for a profit-maximizing competitive firm. [10 marks]
questions.solution:
Conditional factor demands come from derivatives of a cost function. Such a function is homogeneous of degree one in input prices, so its derivatives are homogeneous of degree zero; demand depends on relative prices, not the scale of all prices. If the cost function is smooth, its two cross derivatives must also agree. Use these two restrictions to identify the exponents and the remaining coefficient, rather than treating the two demand formulas as unrelated equations.

Conditional factor demands are homogeneous of degree zero in all prices. Applying this to $x_1$ gives $a-1/2=0$, so $a=1/2$.

Integrability requires symmetric cross-price derivatives: $\partial x_1/\partial w_2=(3/2)w_1^{-1/2}w_2^{-1/2}$ must equal $\partial x_2/\partial w_1=(b/2)w_1^{-1/2}w_2^c$. Equality for every positive price pair implies $c=-1/2$ and $b=3$.

These demands are indeed generated by the homogeneous concave unit cost $w_1+w_2+6\sqrt{w_1w_2}$, so the restrictions are consistent.

questions.stem: A competitive firm's observed choices are: observation1 $(p,w,q,x)=(50,20,20,25)$; observation2 $(45,15,24,36)$; observation3 $(40,20,16,16)$. Here $p,w$ are output/input prices and $q,x$ output/input quantities. Are these choices consistent with profit maximization? [10 marks]
questions.answer: Yes. Each observed choice yields at least as much profit as the other observed feasible choices at its own prices.
questions.solution:
Revealed profit maximization compares the chosen production plan with every other observed plan at the prices of the current observation. Build a matrix whose row i evaluates all available observed plans at row i prices. Each diagonal value must be at least every other entry in that row. Do not compare profits across rows, because a higher price or a different wage can change profit even when every choice is optimal.

At prices from observation1, profits from choices1,2,3 are respectively $(500,480,480)$. At prices from observation2 they are $(525,540,480)$.

At prices from observation3 they are $(300,240,320)$. Every diagonal entry is the largest in its row.

Therefore no observed alternative would have made higher profit at any observation's own prices. A technology containing these observed production plans (or their convex free-disposal hull) rationalizes all three choices.

Thus the data pass the revealed-profit-maximization restrictions.

questions.stem: A competitive firm has cost $c(q;w)=w_1^\alpha w_2^{1-\alpha}q$, with $0<\alpha<1$. Derive conditional factor demands and a production function consistent with this cost. [5+5=10 marks]
questions.solution:
Use Shephard’s lemma to differentiate the cost function with respect to each input price. These are quantities needed to produce q at minimum cost. To recover a technology consistent with the result, remember that a Cobb–Douglas production function generally carries a normalization constant. Choosing that constant correctly makes the minimized unit cost exactly $w_1^\alpha w_2^{1-\alpha}$, rather than that expression multiplied by an extra parameter-dependent factor.

By Shephard's lemma, differentiating cost with respect to each input price yields $x_1=\alpha q w_1^{\alpha-1}w_2^{1-\alpha}$ and $x_2=(1-\alpha)q w_1^\alpha w_2^{-\alpha}$. Substitute these demands into $(x_1/\alpha)^\alpha(x_2/(1-\alpha))^{1-\alpha}$: powers of both prices cancel and the result is $q$.

This normalized Cobb-Douglas technology has minimized unit cost exactly $w_1^\alpha w_2^{1-\alpha}$, hence is consistent with the given cost. Under the usual closed convex free-disposal production-set assumptions, cost duality recovers this efficient frontier.

questions.stem: Home and Foreign each produce one good at fixed full-employment outputs $Y$ and $Y^*$. Foreign's good is the numeraire and $p$ is the relative price of Home's good. Home expenditure $E$ is measured in Home goods and treated as a parameter; Foreign expenditure $E^*$ is measured in Foreign goods and is endogenous. Cobb-Douglas import shares are $\alpha$ at Home and $\alpha^*$ abroad, with $1-\alpha>\alpha^*$. World income equals world expenditure and both goods markets clear. Suppose $E$ falls. What happens to $p$? Prove it. [20 marks]
questions.answer: The relative price of Home's good falls.
questions.solution:
A reduction in Home absorption is not just a fall in one country’s demand holding everyone else’s expenditure fixed: world expenditure must still equal world income. First eliminate Foreign expenditure using that accounting restriction. Then impose market clearing for the Home good, expressing both countries’ spending in the same numeraire. The home-bias condition makes a Home spending reduction disproportionately reduce demand for its own good, explaining the sign of the resulting relative-price change.

World expenditure balance gives $E^*=p(Y-E)+Y^*$. Home-good market clearing in Foreign-good value units gives $pY=(1-\alpha)pE+\alpha^*E^*$.

Substituting yields $p[(1-\alpha^*)Y-(1-\alpha-\alpha^*)E]=\alpha^*Y^*$. Let $d=1-\alpha-\alpha^*>0$ and $D=(1-\alpha^*)Y-dE$.

At an interior positive-price equilibrium $D>0$, and $p=\alpha^*Y^*/D$. Therefore $dp/dE=\alpha^*Y^*d/D^2>0$.

A fall in Home expenditure lowers $p$: with home bias, it disproportionately reduces world demand for the Home good.

questions.notes: Uses positive outputs and positive interior Cobb-Douglas expenditure shares, as usual for the stated model.

Cobb-Douglas import shares are $\alpha$ at Home and $\alpha^*$ abroad, with $1-\alpha>\alpha^*$. World income equals world expenditure and both goods markets clear. Suppose $E$ falls. What happens to Home's trade balance in Foreign-good units, $p(Y-E)$? Prove it. [10 marks]
questions.solution:
The trade balance is a value, so both the physical surplus Y-E and the relative price p change when expenditure moves. Differentiate their product, or substitute the solved price and use the quotient rule. Looking only at the decrease in imports would miss the terms-of-trade response. The algebra shows that the direct absorption effect dominates the adverse Home-price movement in this specified Cobb–Douglas model.

Using $p=\alpha^*Y^*/D$ from part(a), $TB=\alpha^*Y^*(Y-E)/D$, where $D=(1-\alpha^*)Y-(1-\alpha-\alpha^*)E$. Differentiating and simplifying gives $dTB/dE=-\alpha\alpha^*YY^*/D^2<0$.

Consequently a fall in $E$ raises the Home trade balance. Although the relative price of the Home good falls, the direct fall in Home absorption dominates in this model.
