Using $p=\alpha^*Y^*/D$ from part(a), $TB=\alpha^*Y^*(Y-E)/D$, where $D=(1-\alpha^*)Y-(1-\alpha-\alpha^*)E$. Differentiating and simplifying gives $dTB/dE=-\alpha\alpha^*YY^*/D^2<0$.

Consequently a fall in $E$ raises the Home trade balance. Although the relative price of the Home good falls, the direct fall in Home absorption dominates in this model.

questions.stem: Consider the standard Solow model with constant saving propensity $s$, labour-force growth rate $n$, no technological progress and zero depreciation. Let $v=K/Y$ be the capital-output ratio. Prove that $s/v=n$ at the steady state. [8 marks]
questions.answer: At a steady capital-labour ratio, $sY/K=n$, hence $s/v=n$.
questions.solution:
At a Solow steady state, per-worker quantities are constant, while aggregate capital and output can keep growing with population. Since investment equals saving and there is no depreciation, aggregate capital growth is sY/K=s/v. Constant capital per worker requires that rate to equal labour growth n. The statement is therefore a balanced-growth condition, not the assertion that aggregate capital stops changing.

Capital accumulation is $\dot K=sY$. Thus the growth rate of capital is $g_K=\dot K/K=sY/K=s/v$.

At the steady state capital per worker is constant, so capital and labour grow at the same rate: $g_K=g_L=n$. Therefore $s/v=n$.

The equivalent discrete-time steady-state accumulation equation is $sY=nK$.

questions.stem: Consider the standard Solow model with constant saving propensity $s$, labour-force growth rate $n$, no technological progress and zero depreciation. Let $v=K/Y$ be the capital-output ratio. Initially $s/v>n$. Explain how the economy restores equality over time. [16 marks]
questions.answer: Capital per worker rises; diminishing returns increase $v$ and lower $s/v$ until it equals $n$.
questions.solution:
When s/v exceeds n, capital grows faster than the labour force. The adjustment variable is therefore k=K/L. Diminishing marginal productivity means output rises less than proportionately with capital per worker, raising the capital–output ratio v=k/f(k). That reduces s/v toward n. This is the Solow adjustment mechanism that restores a balanced growth relation without requiring households to change their exogenous saving propensity.

Write output per worker as $f(k)$, where $k=K/L$, under the usual neoclassical Solow assumptions. Then $\dot k=sf(k)-nk=k(s/v-n)$.

The assumed inequality makes $k$ rise. The capital-output ratio is $v=k/f(k)$, whose derivative is $[f(k)-kf'(k)]/f(k)^2>0$ when the marginal product of labour is positive.

Thus accumulating capital relative to labour raises $v$, reducing $s/v$. Diminishing returns progressively reduce excess capital growth until $sf(k^*)=nk^*$, equivalently $s/v^*=n$.

Factor prices adapt as relative factor scarcity changes; continued saving need not make output grow as fast as capital because capital has diminishing marginal productivity.
questions.hint: Use the law of motion of capital per worker and how $k/f(k)$ changes with $k$.
questions.notes: The standard neoclassical Solow assumptions (constant returns, positive marginal products and diminishing returns to capital per worker) underlie this adjustment; the question invokes the model by name rather than specifying a production function.

questions.stem: Consider the standard Solow model with constant saving propensity $s$, labour-force growth rate $n$, no technological progress and zero depreciation. Let $v=K/Y$ be the capital-output ratio. During the adjustment in part(b), how do the real wage and real rental on capital change? Explain. [6 marks]
questions.answer: The real wage rises and the real rental on capital falls.
questions.solution:
Factor rewards are marginal products, not fixed factor shares in physical units. Increasing capital relative to labour makes an extra capital unit less productive, lowering the rental. It makes each worker more productive, raising the wage. The wage formula $w=f(k)-kf'(k)$ allows its derivative to be evaluated directly, with the cancellation of the two first-derivative terms leaving $-kf''(k)>0$.

Competitive factor rewards are $r_K=f'(k)$ and $w=f(k)-kf'(k)$. As capital per worker rises and $f''(k)<0$, the rental falls: $dr_K/dk=f''(k)<0$.

The real wage rises because $dw/dk=-kf''(k)>0$. Capital becomes less scarce relative to labour, increasing labour productivity and reducing capital's marginal product.

questions.stem: Using a simple Keynesian income-determination model, derive and explain conditions under which an increase in the marginal propensity to save reduces aggregate saving. [15 marks]
questions.answer: With positively income-induced investment, higher thrift lowers income and equilibrium investment/saving. With purely autonomous investment, aggregate saving stays constant rather than falling.
questions.solution:
The ordinary paradox of thrift with autonomous investment lowers income but leaves actual saving fixed at investment. To prove a strict fall in aggregate saving, add a channel by which investment itself falls when income contracts. A positive induced-investment coefficient provides that channel. State the stability condition before differentiating equilibrium income; otherwise a formal algebraic response can have the opposite sign in an unstable model.

Consider a closed underemployment economy with $C=C_0+(1-\sigma)Y$ and $I=I_0+bY$, where $\sigma$ is the marginal propensity to save, $b\geq0$, $C_0+I_0>0$, and stability requires $\sigma>b$. Goods-market clearing gives $Y=(C_0+I_0)/(\sigma-b)$, so increasing $\sigma$ lowers income.

Aggregate saving is $S=Y-C=\sigma Y-C_0=(\sigma I_0+bC_0)/(\sigma-b)$. Its derivative is $dS/d\sigma=-b(C_0+I_0)/(\sigma-b)^2$.

Thus saving falls strictly if $b>0$: the income contraction reduces induced investment, which equals saving in equilibrium. If $b=0$, the conventional autonomous-investment model gives $S=I_0$ and the derivative is zero, not negative.

More generally, a positive response of investment to income supplies the extra condition for a strict paradox of thrift in this simple framework.
questions.hint: Distinguish the desire to save at fixed income from equilibrium saving; examine whether investment itself falls when income falls.

questions.stem: Using an aggregate-demand and aggregate-supply model, explain how an increase in fuel prices affects aggregate output, employment and the price level. [15 marks]
questions.answer: A fuel-cost supply shock lowers output and employment and raises the price level, other things equal.
questions.solution:
Fuel costs affect the price firms need to cover production at a given output. They therefore move short-run aggregate supply, rather than initially shifting aggregate demand. Draw the old and new AS curves against one unchanged AD curve. The new intersection combines a higher price level with lower output, unlike a demand expansion that raises both. Employment follows output under a fixed increasing labour–output relation; policy or further demand effects would be separate shocks.

Fuel is a production input, so a higher fuel price raises firms' marginal cost at any given output. Holding aggregate demand and other conditions fixed, short-run aggregate supply shifts upward/left.

In a graph with output on the horizontal axis and the price level on the vertical axis, the unchanged downward-sloping AD curve meets the new SRAS at a point with lower $Y$ and higher $P$ than initially. Lower output requires less employment when production increases with labour input.

The simultaneous inflation and output contraction is stagflation. A temporary input-cost shock need not shift long-run potential output; a persistent change affecting productive capacity can have longer-run effects.

The stated short-run signs are the standard isolated supply-shock comparison, not a claim that AD can never respond too.
questions.hint: Treat higher fuel prices as a rise in marginal production costs and shift SRAS, leaving AD fixed for the comparison.

questions.stem: A consumer has demand $x(p_x,p_y,m)=2m/(5p_x)$. Income is Rs.1000 and $p_y=20$. When $p_x$ falls from 5 to 4, which change is the substitution effect?
questions.solution: Under Slutsky compensation, the initial bundle is $x_0=80$, $y_0=30$. Its cost at new prices is $m^S=4(80)+20(30)=920$. New compensated demand is $2(920)/(5\cdot4)=92$, giving option C. If “substitution effect” means Hicks compensation, Cobb–Douglas preferences implied by these demands give $x^H=80(5/4)^{3/5}\approx91.46$, which is not listed.
questions.hint: Price the original bundle at the new prices before evaluating compensated demand.
questions.notes: The finite-change compensation convention is not stated. Option C is the Slutsky answer; a Hicks answer differs.

questions.stem: At year-1 prices $(100,100)$, a consumer chooses quantities $(100,100)$. At year-2 prices $(100,80)$, quantities are $(120,x)$. Which range guarantees a violation of WARP?
questions.solution: Year 2’s bundle is affordable in year 1 if $12000+100x\le20000$, or $x\le80$. Year 1’s bundle is affordable in year 2 if $18000\le12000+80x$, or $x\ge75$. Therefore the entire listed open interval $75<x<80$ violates WARP, with strict budget comparisons.
questions.hint: Test each bundle at the other year’s prices.
questions.notes: The listed interval guarantees the violation; depending on the weak/strict WARP convention, the boundary values can also violate it.

questions.stem: Demand is $p=100-Q$. There are 23 Cournot firms, each with cost $c_i(q_i)=q_i^2/2$. The Nash equilibrium involves each firm producing:
questions.solution: The first-order condition is $100-Q_{-i}-2q_i=q_i$. At a symmetric equilibrium this becomes $100-(23+2)q_i=0$, so $q_i=4$. The objective is strictly concave in own quantity.
questions.hint: Equate marginal revenue to the marginal cost $q_i$.

questions.stem: Demand is $p=100-Q$. Ten firms compete in quantities, each with cost $c_i(q_i)=q_i$. Find total deadweight loss.
questions.solution: With ten identical Cournot firms and marginal cost 1, each produces $(100-1)/(10+1)=9$. Hence $Q=90$ and $p=10$. Competitive output is 99. The welfare-loss triangle is $(99-90)(10-1)/2=81/2$.
questions.hint: Compare Cournot output with the competitive benchmark.

questions.stem: Demand is $p=100-Q$. Many identical firms have $c_i(q_i)=10+2q_i$ if $q_i>0$ and zero cost at zero output. Which statement is correct?
options: Competitive equilibrium price is not well defined
questions.answer: Competitive equilibrium price is not well defined
questions.solution: At $p\le2$ every firm prefers zero output because positive output incurs the setup cost. Demand is positive at such prices. At $p>2$, profit $(p-2)q_i-10$ increases without bound, so no finite profit-maximizing supply exists. Thus no finite competitive equilibrium clears this market.
questions.hint: Examine profit maximization both at and above marginal cost.

questions.stem: Two firms have cost zero for $q_i\le10$ and infinite cost above 10. They set prices simultaneously. The lower-price firm faces demand $100-p_i$, equal prices split that demand equally, and the higher-price firm receives zero demand. Which listed pair is a Bertrand–Nash equilibrium?
questions.answer: The stated demand/capacity model does not uniquely identify one listed equilibrium.
questions.solution: The answer depends on how unserved demand is handled. If a firm must serve its full allocated demand, both (80,80) and (90,90) are Nash equilibria: a price cut below either rival price gives demand greater than capacity and infinite cost, while a price increase loses all demand. If instead sales are capped at 10 and the higher-price firm receives no residual demand, all equal-price pairs from 0 through 80 are Nash equilibria, so multiple listed answers again qualify. A rationing or equilibrium-selection convention is needed to select a unique option.
questions.hint: At price 80, equal splitting exactly exhausts both firms’ capacities.
questions.notes: No official answer key is being asserted. The cost and demand equations omit the rationing convention needed for a unique multiple-choice answer.

questions.stem: Five hundred consumers are uniform on [0,1]. The government may open two hospitals, or none. Treatment is free; each patient incurs travel cost equal to distance. Each hospital costs 300 to establish and 2 per patient, and treatment is worth 4 per patient. Which listed decision maximizes welfare?
questions.solution: All consumers find treatment worthwhile. With two hospitals, treatment benefits and costs and the setup cost are location-independent. Minimize total distance: each hospital should lie at the median of its half of the population, giving 1/4 and 3/4. Mean travel distance is 1/8. Welfare is $500(4-2)-600-500/8=337.5>0$.
questions.hint: Minimize travel distance within each hospital’s catchment.
questions.notes: This answer compares the stated two-hospital and zero-hospital choices. If opening only one hospital were an allowed choice, its separate fixed-cost comparison would be necessary.

questions.stem: A unit mass of consumers buys one unit or none. Valuations have CDF $F(\theta)$ on an interval. Let $p(q)$ be inverse demand. What is its slope where the CDF is differentiable with positive density?
questions.solution: Demand is $q=1-F(p)$. Differentiating $q=1-F(p(q))$ gives $1=-F\prime(p(q))p\prime(q)$, yielding the first expression.
questions.hint: Invert the demand relation $q=1-F(p)$.
questions.notes: The derivative formula applies where a differentiable inverse exists and the density is positive.

questions.stem: In a demand-determined economy, workers receive income share $\lambda\in(0,1)$ and capitalists the rest. Saving propensities are $s_w>s_c$, both in $(0,1)$. Investment I is autonomous. If both saving propensities rise, what happens in the new equilibrium?
questions.solution: The aggregate saving propensity is $\bar s=\lambda s_w+(1-\lambda)s_c$. Equilibrium requires $\bar sY=I$, so $Y=I/\bar s$. A rise in both propensities raises $\bar s$ and lowers Y, while total saving remains I.
questions.hint: Use the equilibrium identity between saving and autonomous investment.

questions.stem: In a demand-determined economy, workers receive income share $\lambda\in(0,1)$ and capitalists the rest. Saving propensities are $s_w>s_c$, both in $(0,1)$. Investment I is autonomous. If saving propensities are fixed but the workers’ income share rises, what happens?
questions.solution: $d\bar s/d\lambda=s_w-s_c>0$. Since $Y=I/\bar s$, equilibrium income falls. Saving remains equal to the unchanged autonomous investment I.
questions.hint: The question states that workers have the higher saving propensity.

questions.stem: Aggregate production is $Y=\bar K^\alpha L^{1-\alpha}$, $0<\alpha<1$, with capital fixed in the short run. Competitive firms maximize profit; nominal wage is W and price level is P. Find labour demand as a function of the real wage.
questions.solution: Competitive hiring sets $(1-\alpha)\bar K^\alpha L^{-\alpha}=W/P$. Rearranging yields $L_d=\bar K[(1-\alpha)/(W/P)]^{1/\alpha}$.
questions.hint: Set the marginal product of labour equal to the real wage.

questions.stem: Aggregate production is $Y=\bar K^\alpha L^{1-\alpha}$, $0<\alpha<1$, with capital fixed in the short run. Competitive firms maximize profit; nominal wage is W and price level is P. A household has time endowment $\bar L$, labour supply $L_s$, and utility $C^\beta+(\bar L-L_s)^\beta$, $0<\beta<1$. Its only income is wages, all spent on consumption. Find labour supply.
questions.solution: Let $w=W/P$ and substitute $C=wL_s$. The FOC is $w^\beta L_s^{\beta-1}=(\bar L-L_s)^{\beta-1}$. Therefore $L_s/(\bar L-L_s)=w^{\beta/(1-\beta)}$, which rearranges to option A. Strict concavity gives the optimum.
questions.hint: Substitute the wage-income budget into utility before differentiating.

questions.stem: Aggregate production is $Y=\bar K^\alpha L^{1-\alpha}$, $0<\alpha<1$, with capital fixed in the short run. Competitive firms maximize profit; nominal wage is W and price level is P. Use the labour supply in the preceding question. With flexible wages and labour-market clearing, what is the aggregate supply curve with Y horizontal and P vertical?
questions.solution: Labour demand and supply depend only on the real wage W/P and real parameters. Their intersection fixes the equilibrium real wage, employment, and output independently of P; nominal W adjusts proportionately. Output is therefore fixed as P varies.
questions.hint: Ask whether a change in the price level changes the equilibrium real wage.

questions.stem: Goods-market clearing is $S(Y,r)=I(r)$, with $0<S_Y<1$, $S_r>0$, $I_r<0$. Money-market clearing is $M/P=L(Y,r)$, with $L_Y>0$, $L_r<0$. Holding M fixed, find the AD slope $dP/dY$.
questions.solution: Differentiate IS: $S_YdY+(S_r-I_r)dr=0$. Substitute $dr=-S_YdY/(S_r-I_r)$ into $-(M/P^2)dP=L_YdY+L_rdr$. Solving gives option B, which is negative under the stated signs.
questions.hint: Eliminate dr between the total differentials of IS and LM.

questions.stem: To test Solow growth, regress country growth $g_i$ on initial log income, log population growth, log saving, and other controls: $g_i=\alpha+\beta_0\log y_{i,0}+\beta_1\log n_i+\beta_2\log s_i+\gamma X_i+\epsilon_i$. What sign does Solow predict for $\beta_0$?
questions.solution: Conditional convergence predicts that, holding steady-state determinants fixed, a country further below its steady-state income grows faster. Thus a higher initial income predicts slower subsequent growth and $\beta_0<0$.
questions.hint: Use conditional convergence, holding the other regressors fixed.

questions.stem: Find the rank of $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&1\\0&1&1\\1&1&0\end{pmatrix}$.
questions.solution: Expanding along the first row gives $\det A=-1-1=-2\ne0$. Hence the matrix has full rank 3.
questions.hint: A nonzero determinant implies full rank.

questions.stem: Bowl A has two red coins, B has two white coins, and C has one white and one red coin. A bowl is chosen uniformly, then one of its coins uniformly. Given the coin is white, what is the probability that the other coin is red?
questions.solution: The event requires choosing C and then its white coin, with probability $1/6$. White overall has probability $0+1/3+1/6=1/2$. The conditional probability is $(1/6)/(1/2)=1/3$.
questions.hint: The other coin is red exactly when the selected bowl is C.

questions.stem: A girl chooses n uniformly from $\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}$, then chooses a number uniformly from $\{1,\ldots,n\}$. What is the probability that the second number is 5?
questions.solution: Only n=5 or n=6 can produce 5. Total probability is $(1/6)(1/5)+(1/6)(1/6)=11/180$.
questions.hint: Condition on the first choice n.

questions.stem: Bearing diameters are normal with unknown mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$. Eight percent fall below 1.8cm and 5.5% exceed 2.4cm. Standard-normal values include $F(1.4)=0.92$, $F(-1.6)=0.055$, $F(0.14)=0.555$, $F(-0.2)=0.42$. Find the mean.
questions.solution: Symmetry gives $(1.8-\mu)/\sigma=-1.4$ and $(2.4-\mu)/\sigma=1.6$. Subtraction gives $0.6=3\sigma$, so $\sigma=0.2$ and $\mu=1.8+1.4(0.2)=2.08$.
questions.hint: Convert the lower and upper rejection rates to z-scores.

questions.stem: A differentiable function has strictly increasing derivative, $f(1/2)=1/2$, and $f(1)=1$. Which statement is true?
questions.solution: The secant slope on [1/2,1] is 1. The mean value theorem gives an interior point with derivative 1. Strict increase of the derivative places the endpoint derivatives strictly below and above this value.
questions.hint: Apply the mean value theorem.

questions.stem: Let $f(x)=\lfloor x\rfloor$ for $x\ge0$. Evaluate $\int_0^{\sqrt5}f(x^2)\,dx$.
questions.solution: Split at $1,\sqrt2,\sqrt3,2,\sqrt5$. The integral is $(\sqrt2-1)+2(\sqrt3-\sqrt2)+3(2-\sqrt3)+4(\sqrt5-2)=4\sqrt5-\sqrt3-\sqrt2-3$. Values at the endpoints do not affect the integral.
questions.hint: Find the intervals on which the floor is constant.

questions.stem: Find the constant term in $(x+1/x^2)^{19}$.
questions.solution: A general term has exponent $19-3k$, for integer $0\le k\le19$. This exponent cannot be zero because 19 is not divisible by 3. There is no constant term, so its coefficient is 0.
questions.hint: Track the power of x in the general binomial term.

questions.stem: Arjun and Gukesh each toss three independent fair coins. Arjun wins if he gets strictly more heads than Gukesh. What is his win probability?
questions.solution: The tie probability is $[1^2+3^2+3^2+1^2]/64=20/64=5/16$. Symmetry divides the remaining probability equally, giving $(1-5/16)/2=11/32$.
questions.hint: Compute the tie probability, then use symmetry.

questions.stem: How many real solutions satisfy $x|x|+1=3|x|$?
questions.solution: For $x\ge0$, solve $x^2-3x+1=0$, giving two positive roots. For $x<0$, solve $x^2-3x-1=0$, which has exactly one negative root. Total: three.
questions.hint: Split into the positive and negative half-lines.

questions.stem: Positive integers $k_1,\ldots,k_n$ satisfy $\sum k_i=5n-4$ and $\sum1/k_i=1$. What is the largest possible n?
questions.solution: Cauchy–Schwarz gives $(\sum k_i)(\sum1/k_i)\ge n^2$, so $5n-4\ge n^2$ or $(n-1)(n-4)\le0$. Hence n≤4. Equality is attainable with four integers all equal to 4.
questions.hint: Bound n using the arithmetic–harmonic mean inequality.

questions.stem: A monkey starts at the origin and jumps exactly 5 units to a point with integer coordinates. How many locations are possible after one jump?
questions.solution: Integer solutions to $x^2+y^2=25$ are $(\pm5,0),(0,\pm5)$, and the eight sign/order variants of (3,4). Thus there are 12 locations.
questions.hint: List the integer lattice points on the radius-five circle.

questions.stem: A strip contains n white squares between two black end squares, where n≥1. A girl picks a white square uniformly and then one of its adjacent squares uniformly. What is the probability that the adjacent square is white?
questions.solution: There are 2n equally likely directed neighbour choices. Exactly two point to a black endpoint, including when n=1. Thus the white probability is $(2n-2)/(2n)=1-1/n$.
questions.hint: Count directed moves from white squares into black squares.

questions.stem: Let $f(x)=\max(|x|,x^2)$ on $\mathbb R$. Which statement is true?
questions.solution: The maximum of continuous functions is continuous. Near zero, $f(x)=|x|$, whose one-sided derivatives are −1 and 1. Thus f is not differentiable on all of R. It is neither globally increasing nor globally decreasing.
questions.hint: Identify which branch dominates near zero.

questions.stem: For $f(x)=\max(|x|,x^2)$ define $D=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:y\ge f(x)\}$. Which statement is true?
questions.solution: Both constituent functions are convex, hence f and its epigraph D are convex, ruling out A. Points (2,3) and (4,15) lie in the complement, including within the positive quadrant, but their midpoint (3,9) lies on D because f(3)=9. Therefore neither complement in B or C is convex.
questions.hint: Use the epigraph test for D and a two-point counterexample for its complement.

questions.stem: $f:[-1,1]\to\mathbb R$ satisfies $f(x)=\frac{2-x^2}{2}f\left(\frac{x^2}{2-x^2}\right)$ for every x. Find $f(-1)$.
questions.solution: Set x=1 to obtain $f(1)=f(1)/2$, hence f(1)=0. Setting x=−1 gives $f(-1)=f(1)/2=0$.
questions.hint: Substitute the two endpoints into the functional equation.

questions.stem: A used-car market has 600 buyers, each willing to buy at most one car, and 500 sellers, each owning one car. There are 400 good cars (peaches) and 100 bad cars (lemons). Buyers value a peach at Rs.100 and a lemon at Rs.10. Sellers value their own peach at Rs.50 or their own lemon at Rs.10. Sellers know their car's quality; buyers know only the aggregate numbers and all valuations. What outcome maximizes aggregate surplus? Explain. [4 marks]
questions.answer: Trade all 400 peaches; lemon trade is optional. Maximum gains from trade are Rs.20,000.
questions.solution:
Efficiency concerns which cars are traded when their qualities are known, not the price paid for them. A good car creates surplus equal to the buyer’s valuation minus the current owner’s value. A lemon creates no gain from trade at the specified equal values. Transfers cancel from total welfare, so identify all positive-gain trades and count them, while treating zero-gain trades as optional in the efficient set.

Trading a peach generates a gain of $100-50=50$, while trading a lemon generates $10-10=0$. There are enough buyers to buy all 500 cars, so no beneficial peach transaction needs to be crowded out by another trade.

Thus every peach should move from its seller to a buyer, generating $400\cdot50=20{,}000$. Any number of lemons may also trade without changing aggregate gains from trade.

This is the gains-from-trade surplus, relative to sellers retaining their cars.
questions.hint: Compare buyer value with seller opportunity cost for each quality.

questions.stem: A used-car market has 600 buyers, each willing to buy at most one car, and 500 sellers, each owning one car. There are 400 good cars (peaches) and 100 bad cars (lemons). Buyers value a peach at Rs.100 and a lemon at Rs.10. Sellers value their own peach at Rs.50 or their own lemon at Rs.10. Sellers know their car's quality; buyers know only the aggregate numbers and all valuations. (i) Derive the supply of used cars as a function of price, and draw it with quantity on the horizontal axis and price on the vertical axis. (ii) Derive and draw demand in the same figure. Label all important points. (iii) Find all competitive equilibria and identify the qualities traded. [20 marks]
questions.answer: With weak participation at reservation prices: price 10 with any quantity from 0 to 100 lemons; price 50 with 100 lemons and 80 peaches; or price 82 with all 500 cars.
questions.solution:
With full information, good cars and lemons are separate markets. Buyers can condition their bids on quality, so no pooled expected valuation is needed. Compare demand and supply for each type and retain participation at indifference: when valuation and price coincide, an agent can be willing to trade without strictly preferring it. This is especially relevant for the lemon market, where all possible trades have zero surplus.

Supply is a correspondence: $S(p)=0$ for $p<10$; $S(10)=[0,100]$; $S(p)=100$ for $10<p<50$; $S(50)=[100,500]$; and $S(p)=500$ for $p>50$. Plot horizontal supply segments at prices 10 and 50, with vertical segments at quantities 0, 100 and 500 as appropriate.

Demand must use the quality mix of cars actually offered. A lemon-only pool is worth 10 per car. If all 100 lemons and $k$ peaches are offered, the expected buyer value is $v(k)=(1000+100k)/(100+k)$. For a given pool, demand is 600 below its expected value, zero above it, and any amount in $[0,600]$ at equality. Equivalently, for offered quantity $q>100$, the zero-surplus buyer valuation curve is $p=100-9000/q$, rising from $(q,p)=(100,10)$ to $(500,82)$; for a lemon-only pool it is $p=10$.

At $p=10$, sellers and buyers of lemons are indifferent, so any quantity $q\in[0,100]$ of lemons can clear; if indifference is resolved in favour of full participation, $q=100$. At $p=50$, all lemons are supplied and peach sellers are indifferent. Setting $v(k)=50$ gives $k=80$, so $q=180$ clears. At $p>50$, every car is supplied and expected quality value is $(400\cdot100+100\cdot10)/500=82$. Thus $p=82$, with 500 buyers trading and 100 abstaining, is the full-pooling equilibrium. No other prices clear: on $(10,50)$ only overpriced lemons are offered, and outside these boundary cases demand and supply disagree.
questions.hint: At price 50, peach sellers are indifferent; do not automatically assume all 400 peaches must be offered. Match buyers' expected value to the actual offered pool.
questions.notes: Reservation-price indifference is handled as a correspondence. A convention forcing all indifferent sellers to trade removes the partial-peach equilibrium at p=50 and fixes lemon-only trade at 100. The source does not specify such a tie-breaking convention. Demand is conditional on offered quality, so an unconditional single-valued demand curve is not well-defined without a selection convention.

questions.stem: A used-car market has 600 buyers, each willing to buy at most one car, and 500 sellers, each owning one car. There are 400 good cars (peaches) and 100 bad cars (lemons). Buyers value a peach at Rs.100 and a lemon at Rs.10. Sellers value their own peach at Rs.50 or their own lemon at Rs.10. Sellers know their car's quality; buyers know only the aggregate numbers and all valuations. Now buyers also know each individual car's quality. Use demand and supply analysis to find all competitive equilibria. [6 marks]
questions.answer: All 400 peaches trade at price 100. Lemons have price 10 and any traded quantity in $[0,100]$, under weak participation.
questions.solution:
Under hidden quality, buyers pay for expected quality among cars actually offered, while each seller knows her own type. Thus the seller pool itself depends on price. Solve by price regimes: lemons alone, possible partial entry of good cars at their reservation price, and full entry. At a reservation-price tie, a subset of indifferent sellers may enter, changing expected quality. Ignoring this partial-entry regime can wrongly remove an equilibrium.

With quality observable, buyers can choose peach and lemon markets separately. At a peach price below 100, each of the 600 buyers strictly prefers a peach to abstaining or a fairly priced lemon.

Since there are only 400 peaches, a lower price cannot clear. At price 100 buyers are indifferent and 400 of them can be assigned peaches; all peach sellers strictly prefer selling because 100 exceeds 50.

Thus $p_P=100$, $q_P=400$. In the lemon market both buyer value and seller opportunity cost are 10, so $p_L=10$, with any quantity $q_L\in[0,100]$ under indifference; at most 100 of the remaining 200 buyers are needed.

Full participation gives $q_L=100$. These allocations achieve the efficient Rs.20,000 gains from peach trade.

questions.stem: A private firm $r$ and a public firm $u$ choose nonnegative quantities $q_r,q_u$ of a homogeneous good. Inverse demand is $p=a-bQ$, where $Q=q_r+q_u$, $a,b>0$. Both firms initially have total cost $cq_i$, with $0<c<a$. Derive (i) each firm's profit, (ii) consumer surplus, and (iii) welfare, defined as consumer plus producer surplus. [5 marks]
questions.solution:
Profits include revenue minus each firm’s resource cost; consumer surplus is the area under inverse demand above the market price. When they are added, market payments cancel because what consumers pay is received by firms. This cancellation is why welfare can be written as gross benefit minus total production cost and depends only on total Q when both firms have the same marginal cost.

Revenue minus cost gives $\pi_r=(a-b(q_r+q_u)-c)q_r$ and $\pi_u=(a-b(q_r+q_u)-c)q_u$. The area below inverse demand and above market price is $CS=\int_0^Q(a-bz)\,dz-pQ=bQ^2/2$. Adding profits cancels transfers through the price and gives $W=\int_0^Q(a-bz)\,dz-cQ=(a-c)Q-bQ^2/2$.
questions.hint: Consumer surplus is a triangle; total welfare equals gross willingness to pay minus production cost.

questions.stem: A private firm $r$ and a public firm $u$ choose nonnegative quantities $q_r,q_u$ of a homogeneous good. Inverse demand is $p=a-bQ$, where $Q=q_r+q_u$, $a,b>0$. Both firms initially have total cost $cq_i$, with $0<c<a$. For given $q_u$, set up the private firm's profit maximization problem and derive its reaction function. [3 marks]
questions.solution:
A best response optimizes only the private firm’s output while taking public output as fixed. Its extra output earns revenue on that unit but also lowers the price on its existing units. This gives the factor two on its own quantity in the first-order condition. Because a negative output is infeasible, truncate the interior response at zero; the reaction curve is a line segment plus a corner segment, not a whole unbounded line.

The private firm solves $\max_{q_r\geq0}(a-c-bq_u-bq_r)q_r$. The interior first-order condition is $a-c-bq_u-2bq_r=0$, and the second derivative is $-2b<0$. Enforcing nonnegativity yields $BR_r(q_u)=\max\{(a-c-bq_u)/(2b),0\}$.
questions.hint: Differentiate private profit with respect to $q_r$, holding $q_u$ fixed.

questions.stem: A private firm $r$ and a public firm $u$ choose nonnegative quantities $q_r,q_u$ of a homogeneous good. Inverse demand is $p=a-bQ$, where $Q=q_r+q_u$, $a,b>0$. Both firms initially have total cost $cq_i$, with $0<c<a$. For given $q_r$, set up the public firm's welfare maximization problem and derive its reaction function. [3 marks]
questions.solution:
The public firm maximizes total welfare, so its price effect on the other firm is not an external loss in the same way as in private profit maximization: price transfers cancel. Its extra output is valuable until demand price equals the common marginal resource cost. Therefore it supplies the gap between the efficient total output and the private firm’s chosen amount, unless that gap is negative, in which case its best response is zero.

The public firm solves $\max_{q_u\geq0}(a-c)(q_r+q_u)-\frac b2(q_r+q_u)^2$. Its interior first-order condition is $a-c-b(q_r+q_u)=0$; the second derivative is $-b<0$. Therefore $BR_u(q_r)=\max\{(a-c)/b-q_r,0\}$.
questions.hint: The public firm chooses total output to equate inverse demand with marginal production cost.
questions.solutionOriginal: The public firm solves $\max_{q_u\geq0}(a-c)(q_r+q_u)-\frac b2(q_r+q_u)^2$. Its interior first-order condition is $a-c-b(q_r+q_u)=0$; the second derivative is $-b<0$. Therefore $BR_u(q_r)=\max\{(a-c)/b-q_r,0\}$.

questions.stem: A private firm $r$ and a public firm $u$ choose nonnegative quantities $q_r,q_u$ of a homogeneous good. Inverse demand is $p=a-bQ$, where $Q=q_r+q_u$, $a,b>0$. Both firms initially have total cost $cq_i$, with $0<c<a$. Define equilibrium under quantity competition, find equilibrium outputs, price, profits, consumer surplus and welfare, and illustrate it using reaction functions with $q_u$ on the horizontal axis and $q_r$ on the vertical axis. [11 marks]
questions.solution:
An equilibrium is an intersection of the complete reaction correspondences, including zero-output corners. Solving just two interior equalities may yield a boundary and does not by itself rule out another corner. Check the public-output-zero case separately. The public firm’s welfare objective ultimately eliminates the private markup, driving total output to the efficient quantity; at that price the private firm’s best response can be zero even though the market is active.

A Nash equilibrium is a pair of quantities at which neither firm can improve its objective by changing its own quantity while holding the other's fixed. Put $A=(a-c)/b>0$.

The reactions are $q_r=\max\{(A-q_u)/2,0\}$ and $q_u=\max\{A-q_r,0\}$. If the public output is positive, substituting $q_u=A-q_r$ into the private reaction gives $q_r=q_r/2$, hence $q_r=0$ and $q_u=A$.

A corner with $q_u=0$ cannot be an equilibrium because the private best response is $A/2$, at which the public firm wants $A/2>0$. Thus the stated equilibrium is unique.

Total output is $A$, price is $a-bA=c$, and each firm's margin and profit are zero. Consumer surplus and welfare are $bA^2/2=(a-c)^2/(2b)$.

In the requested graph the private reaction joins $(0,A/2)$ to $(A,0)$ before lying along the horizontal axis; the positive public reaction is the line from $(0,A)$ to $(A,0)$. Their equilibrium intersection is $(q_u,q_r)=(A,0)$.
questions.hint: Intersect the two reaction functions, including nonnegative-output corners.

questions.stem: A private firm $r$ and a public firm $u$ choose nonnegative quantities $q_r,q_u$ of a homogeneous good. Inverse demand is $p=a-bQ$, where $Q=q_r+q_u$, $a,b>0$. Both firms initially have total cost $cq_i$, with $0<c<a$. The private firm's marginal cost falls to $c_r<c$, while public marginal cost remains $c$. Draw the new reaction functions and explain how $q_r,q_u,Q$, price, both profits, consumer surplus and welfare change. Exact expressions are not required. [8 marks]
questions.answer: Private output and profit rise; public output falls (possibly to zero). Total output and consumer surplus weakly rise, price weakly falls, public profit remains zero, and welfare rises.
questions.solution:
The public reaction depends on its own marginal cost, which stays c, while the private reaction moves as its cost falls. Initially the public firm can substitute away from its own production one for one, keeping the efficient total and price unchanged. That adjustment cannot continue below zero public output. A large enough cost reduction crosses this corner and leaves a private monopoly, so the comparative statics must distinguish small and large cost changes rather than extrapolate one interior regime.

The public reaction remains $q_u=\max\{(a-c)/b-q_r,0\}$, because the effect of its own output on welfare is still $p-c$. The private reaction shifts upward to $q_r=\max\{(a-c_r-bq_u)/(2b),0\}$. Let $\delta=c-c_r>0$ and $A=(a-c)/b$. If $\delta\leq a-c$, the intersection is $q_r=\delta/b$ and $q_u=A-\delta/b$. Thus output shifts from the public firm to the cheaper private firm while $Q=A$, $p=c$ and consumer surplus remain unchanged. Private profit becomes $\delta^2/b>0$, public profit remains zero, and welfare rises by the production-cost saving $\delta^2/b$.

questions.stem: A unit mass of consumers each buys at most one unit. Consumer valuation $v$ is uniform on $[0,1]$. A monopoly has total cost $q^3$ and initially cannot identify consumers, so must set one uniform price. Derive demand as a function of price. [6 marks]
questions.solution:
Each consumer chooses at most one unit, so market demand is the mass of consumers whose valuation reaches the posted price. For a uniform distribution this mass is the length of the valuation interval above p. The total population is normalized to one, making the mass and interval length numerically equal. Truncate at the endpoints because a quantity above one or below zero cannot be demanded.

A consumer buys when $v\geq p$. For $0<p<1$, the uniform distribution puts mass $1-p$ above $p$, so demand is $1-p$.

At a nonpositive price all consumers buy, while a price at least 1 generates zero demand except for a measure-zero indifferent endpoint. Economically relevant nonnegative prices therefore give inverse demand $p=1-q$ for $0\leq q\leq1$.

questions.stem: A unit mass of consumers each buys at most one unit. Consumer valuation $v$ is uniform on $[0,1]$. A monopoly has total cost $q^3$ and initially cannot identify consumers, so must set one uniform price. Derive the monopoly price and profit. [4 marks]
questions.solution:
Use inverse demand to express both revenue and cost in q. The cost is total cost q³, so its marginal cost is 3q²; using q³ directly as marginal cost would produce a different answer. The profit derivative has a feasible positive root and an infeasible negative root. Check the second derivative over the full feasible interval, not just at the candidate, to establish that the positive root is the unique global maximum.

Using inverse demand, profit is $\pi(q)=(1-q)q-q^3$. The first derivative is $1-2q-3q^2$, which vanishes at $q=1/3$ (the other root is -1).

The second derivative $-2-6q$ is strictly negative on $[0,1]$, so this is the unique maximum. Consequently $p=1-q=2/3$ and $\pi=2/9-1/27=5/27$.

questions.stem: A unit mass of consumers each buys at most one unit. Consumer valuation $v$ is uniform on $[0,1]$. A monopoly has total cost $q^3$ and initially cannot identify consumers, so must set one uniform price. For a cost the firm can learn whether a consumer's valuation is in $[0,4/5]$ or in $(4/5,1]$. What is the maximum amount it is willing to pay for this information? Explain. [20 marks]
questions.solution:
Information permits two group-specific prices, but not individualized perfect discrimination within each group. Group quantities are actual population masses, so the high group has a strict capacity of one fifth. Build inverse demands for those masses and subtract the shared cost of total output once. If unconstrained first-order conditions ask for more high buyers than exist, the optimum lies on a group-demand boundary. The value of information is the increase in optimized profit, not the entire informed profit.

With information the firm can price separately to the two groups. Let $l\in[0,4/5]$ and $h\in[0,1/5]$ be quantities sold to the low- and high-valuation groups. Inverse group demands are $p_L=4/5-l$ and $p_H=1-h$. The profit objective is $(4/5-l)l+(1-h)h-(l+h)^3$, a strictly concave function over the rectangle of feasible quantities.

An unrestricted interior solution would require $4/5-2l=1-2h=3(l+h)^2$. It gives $h>1/5$, which is infeasible. The optimum therefore serves the entire high group: $h=1/5$, at $p_H=4/5$. If $Q=l+1/5$, the remaining first-order condition is $4/5-2l=3Q^2$, or $3Q^2+2Q-6/5=0$. Thus $Q=(\sqrt{115}-5)/15$ and $l=(\sqrt{115}-8)/15$. Low-group price is $p_L=1-Q=(20-\sqrt{115})/15$. The high-group marginal revenue at its upper quantity is $3/5$, exceeding marginal cost $3Q^2$, as required for this boundary optimum. Substitution yields informed profit $(46\sqrt{115}-347)/675\approx0.2167334$. Subtracting the uninformed profit $5/27$ gives the willingness to pay $(46\sqrt{115}-472)/675\approx0.0315482$.

questions.stem: In a short-run AD-AS model capital is fixed at $\bar K$. Production is $Y=AL+\bar K$, $A>0$. The union fixes a minimum nominal wage $\bar W$. Each of the $\bar L$ workers supplies one unit if $W>\bar W$, supplies none if $W<\bar W$, and is indifferent at equality. Aggregate demand is a standard downward-sloping curve. Derive aggregate labour supply as a function of nominal wage $W$. [4 marks]
questions.answer: $L^S(W)=0$ below $\bar W$, $[0,\bar L]$ at $\bar W$, and $\bar L$ above $\bar W$.
questions.solution:
Every worker has the same reservation nominal wage. Below it nobody supplies labour; above it everyone supplies their endowed unit. At the reservation wage, indifference permits any quantity between those extremes, so labour supply is a correspondence there. This distinction is important because equilibrium at that wage can have partial employment. Replacing the indifferent segment by an arbitrary single quantity would remove legitimate equilibria.

All workers have the same reservation nominal wage. Below it none supplies labour.

Above it every worker supplies the endowed unit. At exactly $\bar W$, any number from zero to the available workforce may supply because workers are indifferent.

With employment on the horizontal axis and nominal wage on the vertical axis, supply has a horizontal segment at $\bar W$ between 0 and $\bar L$, and a vertical segment at $L=\bar L$ above it.

questions.stem: In a short-run AD-AS model capital is fixed at $\bar K$. Production is $Y=AL+\bar K$, $A>0$. The union fixes a minimum nominal wage $\bar W$. Each of the $\bar L$ workers supplies one unit if $W>\bar W$, supplies none if $W<\bar W$, and is indifferent at equality. Aggregate demand is a standard downward-sloping curve. (i) Derive aggregate labour demand as a function of the real wage $W/P$. (ii) Derive it as a function of nominal wage $W$ for given $P$. [6 marks]
questions.answer: Desired labour is zero if $W/P>A$, arbitrary nonnegative if $W/P=A$, and unbounded if $W/P<A$; in nominal terms compare $W$ with $PA$.
questions.solution:
The production function is linear in labour, so the marginal product A does not diminish. Consequently competitive profit is linear in the amount hired. Away from the zero-margin wage there is no interior labour first-order condition selecting a finite desired quantity: the firm either hires none or wants unbounded labour in an unconstrained problem. The workforce limit constrains equilibrium supply, not the firm’s technological desire for workers at a profitable wage.

The labour-dependent part of competitive profit is $(PA-W)L$. If $W/P>A$, every extra worker loses money, so desired employment is zero.

If $W/P=A$, every nonnegative employment level yields the same labour profit. If $W/P<A$, the linear technology gives a positive constant profit per extra worker and hence no finite unconstrained maximizer: desired labour is unbounded.

The finite workforce constrains realized equilibrium employment, not unconstrained desired labour. For a fixed price level, replace the comparison $W/P$ versus $A$ with $W$ versus $PA$.

The inverse labour-demand curve is horizontal at $W=PA$.

questions.stem: In a short-run AD-AS model capital is fixed at $\bar K$. Production is $Y=AL+\bar K$, $A>0$. The union fixes a minimum nominal wage $\bar W$. Each of the $\bar L$ workers supplies one unit if $W>\bar W$, supplies none if $W<\bar W$, and is indifferent at equality. Aggregate demand is a standard downward-sloping curve. Draw labour supply and demand for an arbitrary $P$, using $L$ on the horizontal axis and $W$ on the vertical axis. Derive equilibrium employment as a function of $P$. [10 marks]
questions.answer: $L^*=0$ if $P<\bar W/A$, $L^*\in[0,\bar L]$ at equality, and $L^*=\bar L$ if $P>\bar W/A$.
questions.solution:
In the nominal-wage diagram, labour demand is horizontal at the value marginal product PA. Compare that height with the workers’ reservation wage. Below it, no positive employment can satisfy both sides; above it, the full workforce clears at the value marginal product. At exact equality, both the firm and workers are indifferent over a range, which creates the continuum of employment levels. Keep this equality case when deriving the price-dependent supply relation.

For fixed $P$, inverse demand is the horizontal line $W=PA$. Supply is horizontal at $\bar W$ over $0\leq L\leq\bar L$ and vertical at the full workforce above that wage.

If $PA<\bar W$, no mutually acceptable wage supports positive labour: firms will not pay the reservation wage, and workers will not accept their marginal revenue product. Equilibrium employment is zero.

If $PA>\bar W$, labour-market clearing requires $W=PA$ and all $\bar L$ workers are employed. If $PA=\bar W$, both sides are indifferent, so any employment between 0 and $\bar L$ clears at that wage.

These are the stated cases after dividing by $A>0$.

Translate the labour equilibrium through the production function rather than drawing a conventional smooth AS curve by habit. Zero labour still produces Kbar in this unusual additive technology, so the low-output vertical part is not at Y=0. The critical price P0=Wbar/A supports every employment level and hence a horizontal output segment. Once all labour is employed, further price increases cannot raise output in the fixed-capacity short run.

questions.stem: In a short-run AD-AS model capital is fixed at $\bar K$. Production is $Y=AL+\bar K$, $A>0$. The union fixes a minimum nominal wage $\bar W$. Each of the $\bar L$ workers supplies one unit if $W>\bar W$, supplies none if $W<\bar W$, and is indifferent at equality. Aggregate demand is a standard downward-sloping curve. Explain the effectiveness of standard monetary and fiscal policies. [5 marks]
questions.answer: Demand expansion raises output on the horizontal AS segment, but raises only prices on either vertical segment until a regime boundary is reached.
questions.solution:
Demand policy shifts AD but the amount of resulting output adjustment depends on which AS segment it meets. On a horizontal AS segment, the price is pinned and output adjusts. On a vertical segment, capacity or the wage threshold fixes output and price adjusts. Describe all three regimes because a low-output state below the reservation-price threshold is different from the familiar intermediate Keynesian segment with spare labour at the threshold.

Expansionary monetary or fiscal policy shifts aggregate demand to the right. If equilibrium lies on the horizontal AS segment at $P_0=\bar W/A$ with spare labour, this raises employment and output without changing the price level, until full employment is reached.

If equilibrium is already on the full-employment vertical segment, further expansion raises only the price level. If it lies on the lower-output vertical segment at $Y=\bar K$ with $P<P_0$, a small expansion initially raises only $P$; output begins to increase only when demand is strong enough to bring the price to $P_0$.

Contraction has the reverse regime-dependent effects. Thus it is not correct to state that demand policy always changes output in this model.

questions.stem: In a discrete-time Solow model $Y_t=K_t^\alpha L_t^{1-\alpha}$, $0<\alpha<1$. Competitive factors receive marginal products. Households save a fraction $0<s<1$ of disposable income, and all private savings are invested. There is no depreciation. Labour grows at rate $n>0$. Let $k_t=K_t/L_t$. The government taxes interest earnings at rate $0<\tau<1$, does not tax wages, and spends all tax revenue on consumption. (i) Derive aggregate wage earnings, interest earnings and savings in terms of $Y_t$. (ii) Derive the law of motion for $k_t$. (iii) Find its steady state and its response to $\tau$. [14 marks]
questions.answer: Wages $(1-\alpha)Y_t$, gross interest $\alpha Y_t$, savings $s(1-\tau\alpha)Y_t$; $k_{t+1}=[k_t+s(1-\tau\alpha)k_t^\alpha]/(1+n)$; positive $k^*=[s(1-\tau\alpha)/n]^{1/(1-\alpha)}$, decreasing in $\tau$.
questions.solution:
Competitive factor shares identify the tax base: capital income is alpha times aggregate output, while wages are the remaining share. Taxing only capital returns therefore reduces disposable income by tau alpha Y, not by tau times all output. Because revenue is consumed by the government, none of that amount is added to capital. Derive investment first, then divide next period’s aggregate capital by next period’s labour to obtain the per-worker transition.

The marginal products are $w_t=(1-\alpha)(K_t/L_t)^\alpha$ and $r_t=\alpha(K_t/L_t)^{\alpha-1}$. Thus total wage earnings are $(1-\alpha)Y_t$ and total gross interest earnings are $\alpha Y_t$.

Disposable household income is $(1-\alpha)Y_t+(1-\tau)\alpha Y_t=(1-\tau\alpha)Y_t$, so $S_t=s(1-\tau\alpha)Y_t$. Since tax revenue is consumed rather than invested, $K_{t+1}=K_t+S_t$.

Dividing by $L_{t+1}=(1+n)L_t$ gives $k_{t+1}=[k_t+s(1-\tau\alpha)k_t^\alpha]/(1+n)$. At a positive steady state, $nk^*=s(1-\tau\alpha)(k^*)^\alpha$, yielding the expression above.

Its logarithmic derivative is $\partial\log k^*/\partial\tau=-\alpha/[(1-\alpha)(1-\tau\alpha)]<0$. A higher tax reduces private saving and hence positive steady-state capital.

Zero capital is also an absorbing steady state if admitted; the displayed solution is the economically relevant positive one.

questions.stem: In a discrete-time Solow model $Y_t=K_t^\alpha L_t^{1-\alpha}$, $0<\alpha<1$. Competitive factors receive marginal products. Households save a fraction $0<s<1$ of disposable income, and all private savings are invested. There is no depreciation. Labour grows at rate $n>0$. Let $k_t=K_t/L_t$. Interest is still taxed at rate $\tau$ and wages are untaxed, but all tax revenue is now invested by the government. (i) Find total investment. (ii) Derive the new law of motion. (iii) Find the new positive steady state $k^{**}$ and compare it with $k^*$. (iv) Determine how $k^{**}$ changes with $\tau$, and explain the difference from part(a). [16 marks]
questions.solution:
The private saving response to taxation is unchanged from the previous policy, but the government now reinvests the tax receipts. A unit of capital-income tax reduces private saving by only s units while creating one unit of public investment, giving a net addition 1-s. This is why the same tax can raise capital under this spending rule while lowering it when revenue was consumed. Keep separate the comparison with the old regime at a fixed tax and the derivative within the new regime.

Private saving remains $s(1-\tau\alpha)Y_t$, but government investment adds $\tau\alpha Y_t$. Therefore aggregate investment is $I_t=[s+(1-s)\tau\alpha]Y_t$.

The new accumulation equation is $k_{t+1}=\{k_t+[s+(1-s)\tau\alpha]k_t^\alpha\}/(1+n)$. The positive steady state is $k^{**}=\{[s+(1-s)\tau\alpha]/n\}^{1/(1-\alpha)}$.

It exceeds $k^*$ because their effective investment coefficients differ by $\tau\alpha>0$: revenue that was previously consumed is now invested. Moreover $\partial\log k^{**}/\partial\tau=(1-s)\alpha/\{(1-\alpha)[s+(1-s)\tau\alpha]\}>0$.

Although taxation reduces private saving by $s\alpha$ per unit increase in the tax rate, government investment rises by $\alpha$, leaving a positive net effect $(1-s)\alpha$. This reverses the response in part(a).

questions.stem: An individual lives for two periods. First-period wage income is $W$, personal savings are $s$, and the gross interest factor is $R>1$. The government takes a first-period lump-sum tax $T$ and returns exactly $T$ in period2. Lifetime utility is $u(c_1)+\beta u(c_2)$, with $0<\beta<1$ and $u$ strictly increasing and strictly concave. Specify the utility maximization problem and budget constraint. Derive the first-order condition and interpret it economically. [9 marks]
questions.answer: Maximize $u(W-T-s)+\beta u(Rs+T)$ over feasible saving; an interior optimum satisfies $u'(c_1)=\beta R u'(c_2)$.
questions.solution:
The government scheme shifts T rupees forward without paying interest. Its present value is therefore less than the first-period tax, so the policy is not a pure timing change at an unchanged lifetime wealth. Write both period budgets before differentiating. One additional privately saved rupee lowers present consumption by one and raises future consumption by R, producing the Euler condition. Borrowing or consumption constraints require inequalities if they bind.

The two period budgets are $c_1=W-T-s$ and $c_2=Rs+T$. Equivalently $c_1+c_2/R=W-T+T/R$.

Choose $s$ to maximize $u(W-T-s)+\beta u(Rs+T)$ subject to nonnegative consumption (and $s\geq0$ if borrowing is disallowed). Differentiating at an interior optimum gives $-u'(W-T-s)+\beta R u'(Rs+T)=0$.

Strict concavity makes an interior solution unique. The condition equates the marginal utility lost by saving one additional first-period rupee to the discounted utility gained from its $R$ rupees of second-period consumption.

At a binding constraint a one-sided/KKT inequality replaces the equality.
questions.hint: Write both consumption levels as functions of personal saving before differentiating.
questions.notes: The derivative conclusions use a differentiable interior optimum with positive consumption. The source does not impose Inada conditions or explicitly rule out binding saving/consumption constraints.

questions.stem: An individual lives for two periods. First-period wage income is $W$, personal savings are $s$, and the gross interest factor is $R>1$. The government takes a first-period lump-sum tax $T$ and returns exactly $T$ in period2. Lifetime utility is $u(c_1)+\beta u(c_2)$, with $0<\beta<1$ and $u$ strictly increasing and strictly concave. Would a more myopic individual save more or less? Verify by determining the sign of $ds/d\beta$. [5 marks]
questions.answer: At an interior optimum $ds/d\beta>0$; a more myopic (smaller $\beta$) individual saves less.
questions.solution:
To determine whether saving rises with patience, differentiate the Euler equation implicitly. The positive denominator comes from the strict concavity of utility in both periods. The numerator is the extra weight on future marginal utility and is positive. More myopia corresponds to a smaller beta, so make that translation explicit; otherwise a correct derivative sign could be interpreted backwards.

Set $F(s,T,\beta)=u'(W-T-s)-\beta R u'(Rs+T)=0$. Write $A=-u''(c_1)>0$ and $B=-u''(c_2)>0$.

Then $F_s=A+\beta R^2B>0$ and $F_\beta=-Ru'(c_2)<0$. Hence $ds/d\beta=Ru'(c_2)/(A+\beta R^2B)>0$.

A larger discount factor increases the value attached to future consumption, inducing higher personal saving; a more myopic individual has a smaller discount factor and saves less.

questions.stem: An individual lives for two periods. First-period wage income is $W$, personal savings are $s$, and the gross interest factor is $R>1$. The government takes a first-period lump-sum tax $T$ and returns exactly $T$ in period2. Lifetime utility is $u(c_1)+\beta u(c_2)$, with $0<\beta<1$ and $u$ strictly increasing and strictly concave. Does government-mandated saving $T$ increase or decrease personal saving? Verify by finding the sign of $ds/dT$. [6 marks]
questions.solution:
A larger compulsory transfer simultaneously removes current resources and adds future resources. At the old saving level both changes make private saving less attractive: current marginal utility rises and future marginal utility falls. The implicit derivative combines these two effects, so personal saving falls. Because the government return is lower than the private gross return R, the response is not the one-for-one neutrality of a present-value-preserving transfer scheme.

Using the Euler-equation function from part(a), its partial derivative in $T$ is $F_T=-u''(c_1)-\beta Ru''(c_2)=A+\beta RB>0$. Since $F_s=A+\beta R^2B>0$, implicit differentiation gives $ds/dT=-F_T/F_s=-(A+\beta RB)/(A+\beta R^2B)<0$.

The compulsory transfer toward period2 crowds out personal saving. It also reduces lifetime wealth because the government returns no interest, so the crowding-out is not a simple one-for-one adjustment.

The government takes a first-period lump-sum tax $T$ and returns exactly $T$ in period2. Lifetime utility is $u(c_1)+\beta u(c_2)$, with $0<\beta<1$ and $u$ strictly increasing and strictly concave. One rupee of period2 benefit could be financed privately by saving $1/R$ in period1. Does mandated saving cause personal saving to fall at a rate greater or smaller than $1/R$? Verify. [4 marks]
questions.answer: The magnitude exceeds $1/R$ but is below1: $1/R<-ds/dT<1$.
questions.solution:
The previous derivative is a ratio of positive curvature terms. Bound that ratio directly rather than assuming one of the periods dominates. Comparing its numerator with its denominator gives an upper bound of one; multiplying the numerator by R before comparing gives a lower bound of 1/R. These inequalities mean the household partly offsets the compulsory transfer but cannot neutralize its lifetime resource loss.

The crowding-out magnitude from part(c) is $(A+\beta RB)/(A+\beta R^2B)$. It is smaller than1 because the denominator exceeds the numerator by $\beta R(R-1)B>0$.

It is greater than $1/R$ because $R(A+\beta RB)-(A+\beta R^2B)=(R-1)A>0$. Therefore $-1<ds/dT<-1/R$.

A transfer of one rupee in period2 by itself would replace $1/R$ rupees of private saving, but the associated first-period tax is larger than that present value and reduces lifetime wealth. The combined response cuts saving by more than $1/R$ but by less than one rupee.

questions.stem: An individual lives for two periods. First-period wage income is $W$, personal savings are $s$, and the gross interest factor is $R>1$. The government takes a first-period lump-sum tax $T$ and returns exactly $T$ in period2. Lifetime utility is $u(c_1)+\beta u(c_2)$, with $0<\beta<1$ and $u$ strictly increasing and strictly concave. Prove that more myopic individuals reduce their personal savings at a higher rate in response to a rise in $T$. [6 marks]
questions.answer: The claim does not follow from the stated assumptions and is false in general. Log utility gives the opposite ranking.
questions.solution:
The request is a universal claim under general concave utility. Before differentiating a complicated expression, test it using a simple admissible utility such as log consumption. If the direction reverses in one feasible interior example, no proof of the printed universal statement is possible. The key danger in a general derivative is that curvature terms are evaluated at optimal consumption, which itself changes with beta; they cannot be treated as fixed constants when comparing different individuals.

Take the permitted utility $u(c)=\log c$ and an interior solution. The Euler equation gives $s=\beta W/(1+\beta)-(\beta R+1)T/[R(1+\beta)]$.

Therefore $ds/dT=-(\beta R+1)/[R(1+\beta)]$. The derivative of its absolute magnitude with respect to $\beta$ is $(R-1)/[R(1+\beta)^2]>0$.

Thus a larger discount factor (less myopia), not a smaller one, produces the larger absolute cut in saving in this example. For example $R=2,W=10,T=1$ yields interior savings at both $\beta=1/4$ and $\beta=1/2$; the crowding-out magnitudes are $3/5$ and $2/3$, respectively.

More myopia therefore yields a smaller cut. In general, the curvatures $u''(c_1)$ and $u''(c_2)$ in part(c) are evaluated at consumption levels that also change with $\beta$, so one cannot hold them fixed to infer the comparative static requested here.

Additional restrictions, or a corrected claim, are necessary.

The printed claim is mathematically false for the stated general class of utility functions. It must not be presented as proved. A log-utility counterexample is given, with strictly positive interior saving and consumption.

questions.stem: Let $C=\{(x,y):0\leq x\leq1,\ 0\leq y\leq1,\ y\leq x\}$ and maximize $ax+by$ over $C$. For $a\neq0$ and $b\neq0$, show that an optimal solution can be chosen from $(0,0),(1,0),(1,1)$. Describe all coefficient values for which each vertex is optimal. [20 marks]
questions.answer: $(0,0)$ is optimal iff $a\leq0$ and $a+b\leq0$; $(1,0)$ iff $a\geq0$ and $b\leq0$; $(1,1)$ iff $b\geq0$ and $a+b\geq0$, subject to the stated nonzero coefficients.
questions.solution:
A linear objective over a triangle attains a maximum at some vertex, but may have other optimal points on an edge. Express every feasible point as a convex combination of the three vertices to prove the vertex assertion without assuming a general linear-programming theorem. Then compare the three vertex objective values 0,a,a+b. Use weak inequalities for a vertex to be an optimizer and strict inequalities when claiming it is the unique optimizer.

The feasible set is the triangle with vertices $(0,0),(1,0),(1,1)$. Every feasible point can be expressed as $(x,y)=(1-x)(0,0)+(x-y)(1,0)+y(1,1)$, with nonnegative coefficients summing to1.

Its objective is therefore a convex combination of the vertex values $0,a,a+b$, so at least one vertex maximizes the objective. Comparing these values gives the stated conditions.

Because $a,b\neq0$, the middle vertex is uniquely optimal exactly when $a>0,b<0$. For the origin, strict uniqueness requires $a<0,a+b<0$; for $(1,1)$ it requires $b>0,a+b>0$.

questions.stem: Let $C=\{(x,y):0\leq x\leq1,\ 0\leq y\leq1,\ y\leq x\}$ and maximize $ax+by$ over $C$. Suppose $a$ and $b$ are independently drawn from $[-1,1]$ with common cumulative distribution function $F$. What is the probability that the unique optimum is $(1,0)$? [10 marks]
questions.answer: $P=(1-F(0))F(0^-)$; for a continuous cdf this is $F(0)[1-F(0)]$.
questions.solution:
The desired vertex must beat both other vertices strictly: a>0 beats the origin, and b<0 makes a exceed a+b. Because these are strict events, a mass at zero must be excluded on each side. A general cumulative distribution F gives P(a>0)=1-F(0) but P(b<0)=F(0−), not F(0). Independence then permits multiplication. The probability one quarter follows only from the extra uniform-draw assumption.

The vertex $(1,0)$ is uniquely optimal iff $a>0$ and $b<0$. By independence the probability is $P(a>0)P(b<0)=[1-F(0)]F(0^-)$, where $F(0^-)=\lim_{t\uparrow0}F(t)$.

If $F$ is continuous at zero, this reduces to $F(0)[1-F(0)]$. For a uniform distribution on $[-1,1]$ it is $1/4$, but uniformity is not assumed in the question.

An atom at zero must be excluded from the strict negative event.

questions.stem: Real coefficients satisfy $A\neq0$, $a\neq0$ and $|ax^2+bx+c|\leq|Ax^2+Bx+C|$ for every real $x$. Also $B^2-4AC>0$. Argue that $|A|\geq|a|$. [5 marks]
questions.solution:
An inequality between two quadratics that holds for every real x must also hold at arbitrarily large x. Far from zero, lower-order terms vanish relative to x², leaving a comparison of leading coefficients. Divide by x² before taking the limit so that the absolute-value expressions have finite limits. Continuity of absolute value justifies passing to their coefficient magnitudes.

For $x\neq0$, divide the inequality by $x^2>0$. This gives $|a+b/x+c/x^2|\leq|A+B/x+C/x^2|$. Taking $x\to\infty$ and using continuity of absolute value yields $|a|\leq|A|$.

questions.stem: Real coefficients satisfy $A\neq0$, $a\neq0$ and $|ax^2+bx+c|\leq|Ax^2+Bx+C|$ for every real $x$. Also $B^2-4AC>0$. Show that $b^2-4ac>0$. [10 marks]
questions.answer: The smaller quadratic has the same two distinct real roots as the larger one, hence positive discriminant.
questions.solution:
The larger quadratic’s positive discriminant supplies two distinct real roots. At either root its absolute value is zero, so the absolute-value bound forces the smaller quadratic to be zero at the same point. Since its leading coefficient is nonzero, it is a genuine quadratic and cannot avoid the conclusion that it has these two distinct roots. This argument is stronger and simpler than trying to bound its coefficients separately.

Since $B^2-4AC>0$, $G(x)=Ax^2+Bx+C$ has two distinct real roots $r_1,r_2$. At either root the assumed inequality forces $|ar_i^2+br_i+c|\leq0$, so the quadratic $g(x)=ax^2+bx+c$ also vanishes at both.

Because $a\neq0$, it is a genuine quadratic with two distinct real roots. Therefore its discriminant $b^2-4ac$ is strictly positive.

questions.stem: Real coefficients satisfy $A\neq0$, $a\neq0$ and $|ax^2+bx+c|\leq|Ax^2+Bx+C|$ for every real $x$. Also $B^2-4AC>0$. Show that $B^2-4AC\geq b^2-4ac$. [15 marks]
questions.solution:
Two genuine quadratics sharing the same two distinct roots differ only by a nonzero constant multiplier. Compare their factorizations to obtain that proportionality for all coefficients, not merely the leading one. A discriminant is quadratic in the coefficients, so it scales by the square of that multiplier. The leading-coefficient bound from part (a) then limits the scale factor and transfers the discriminant inequality directly.

By part(b), both quadratics have the same two distinct roots. Hence $ax^2+bx+c=\lambda(Ax^2+Bx+C)$, where $\lambda=a/A\neq0$.

Thus $b=\lambda B$ and $c=\lambda C$. Part(a) implies $|\lambda|\leq1$.

Consequently $b^2-4ac=\lambda^2(B^2-4AC)\leq B^2-4AC$, since the latter discriminant is positive.

questions.stem: Let $\mathcal F$ be a class of functions from $[0,\infty)$ to $[0,\infty)$. It contains $f_1(x)=e^x-1$ and $f_2(x)=\ln(x+1)$. It is closed under addition and composition. It is also closed under $f-g$ whenever $f,g\in\mathcal F$ and $f(x)\geq g(x)$ for every $x\geq0$. For every positive integer $n$, show that $h(x)=nx$ belongs to $\mathcal F$. [5 marks]
questions.answer: Compose $f_1$ with $f_2$ to obtain $x$, then add $n$ copies.
questions.solution:
The class is not initially stated to contain x itself, so first construct the identity from the two given generators. Their exponential and logarithmic forms cancel under composition. Once x is available, repeated addition gives every positive integer multiple nx. Do not assume arbitrary scalar multiplication is a permitted closure rule: only the stated addition operation is needed for integer multiples.

Closure under composition implies $f_1(f_2(x))=\exp(\ln(1+x))-1=x$ is in $\mathcal F$. Repeated closure under addition then shows that the sum of $n$ copies of this identity function, namely $nx$, is in $\mathcal F$ for every positive integer $n$.
questions.hint: First construct the identity function using the two given functions.

questions.answer: These are the compositions $f_2\circ f$ and $f_2\circ g$.
questions.solution:
Closure under composition can be used only if the inner function’s values lie in the outer function’s domain. Every class function is nonnegative and the logarithmic generator is defined on [0,infinity), so this condition holds for both f and g. Composing with the generator produces the requested logarithms directly, and their outputs remain nonnegative, as required for membership in the same class.

Because $f$ and $g$ are nonnegative, both compositions with $f_2(t)=\ln(1+t)$ are defined on the required domain and remain nonnegative. Closure under composition gives $f_2(f(x))=\ln(1+f(x))$ and $f_2(g(x))=\ln(1+g(x))$ in $\mathcal F$.

It is also closed under $f-g$ whenever $f,g\in\mathcal F$ and $f(x)\geq g(x)$ for every $x\geq0$. If $f,g\in\mathcal F$, prove that $f(x)g(x)+f(x)+g(x)$ belongs to $\mathcal F$. [15 marks]
questions.solution:
The class is not known to be closed under multiplication, so writing fg as a product does not prove membership. Instead use the identity that a sum of logarithms becomes a product after exponentiation:

$$e^{\ln(1+f)+\ln(1+g)}-1=(1+f)(1+g)-1=fg+f+g.$$

Every construction on the left uses only an allowed composition or addition. This synthesizes multiplication from the given generators without assuming it as a rule.

Part(b) and addition show $H(x)=\ln(1+f(x))+\ln(1+g(x))$ is in $\mathcal F$. Closure under composition with $f_1$ then gives $e^{H(x)}-1\in\mathcal F$. Algebraically, $e^{H(x)}-1=(1+f(x))(1+g(x))-1=f(x)g(x)+f(x)+g(x)$.

questions.answer: Subtract $f+g$ from the nonnegative dominating function $fg+f+g$.
questions.solution:
Subtraction is allowed only when the result is pointwise nonnegative. Therefore construct fg+f+g and f+g as class members first, then check their order at every nonnegative input. Since f and g are nonnegative, the difference fg is nonnegative as well. This verification is what licenses the final subtraction; merely subtracting expressions algebraically without checking order would use a stronger closure property than the question grants.

By part(c), $fg+f+g$ is in $\mathcal F$, and by addition $f+g$ is in $\mathcal F$. Since $f,g\geq0$, their product is nonnegative and therefore $fg+f+g\geq f+g$ pointwise. The permitted subtraction rule applies, yielding $(fg+f+g)-(f+g)=fg\in\mathcal F$.
